The New Testament

-- 824 --

-- 825 --

Matthew

'Tis evident by John 11:50–52 that occurrences in the history of the New Testament as well as Old have a mystery in them, and that they are ordered on purpose to represent and shadow forth spiritual things.

Matthew 1.] Concerning the birth of Christ, see no. 204.Works, 15, 127–28.

Concerning the difficulties in Matthew's and Luke's genealogies, see Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2nd, pp. 108–68.This paragraph is a later addition. Kidder devotes chs. 6–15 in Pt. 2 to a detailed examination of the objections against the New Testament accounts of the genealogy of Jesus and his efforts to reduce the force of those considerations. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 108–68.

That Jesus was indeed of the posterity of David. "Res inter Judaeos fuit notissima certissimaque, Mariam ex eadem cum Josepho familia fuisse; ut quam primum probatum fuerit Jesum per Josephum patrem suum putatitium ex Abrahamo et Davide oriundum esse, etiam probatum sit, non minus per Mariam illum prosapiam suam inde ducere. Apostolus enim Paulus ad hoc, ceu nemini non notum, provocat, dicens; Perspicuum est enim, à Juda esse [exortum] Dominum nostrum. Hebrews 7:14. Neque si hoc falsum fuisset, Evangelistae etiam hoc ceu Messiae characterem adducere fuissent ausi, dum si contrarium ipsis demonstrari potuisset, jamjam de Messia suo actum fuisset, neque amplius à quoquam Judaeorum fides ipsis fuisset habita. Neque denique Judaei tacuissent, quando Apostoli, et ipse etiam Jesus Christus, tam publice in concilio, quam privatim, uno ore ipsum Davidis filium dixerunt, hac enim ratione Apostoli optime falsi potuissent convinci." Stapferus, Theolog. Polem, Tome III, p. 149.Stapfer, Institutiones Theologiae Polemicae Universae, Tome III (3rd ed. Tiguri, 1757), 149–50. Stapfer (1708–75), a Swiss theologian, writes, "The matter was extremely well known and certain among the Jews, that Mary had been from the same family as Joseph, so that, as soon as it will have been proven that Jesus was to descend through Joseph, his supposed father, from Abraham and David, it has also been proven that he no less traced his own family through Mary. For the Apostle Paul refers to this, as everyone knows, saying, 'for it is clear that our Lord [descended] from Judah' (Hebrews 7:14). Nor, if this had been false, would the evangelists even have dared to introduce it as a mark of the Messiah, while if something contradicting these things could have been shown, it would already have been all over with their Messiah, and no more would any of the Jews have put faith in these things. Nor, finally, would the Jews have kept quiet when the Apostles and even Jesus Christ himself said with one mouth (as often publicly, in gatherings, as privately) that he himself was the son of David. For on this ground the apostles would have been able most opportunely to be convicted of a lie." For more on Stapfer, see Works, 23, 17–18. See Matthew 1; and Matthew 2:1, Matthew 2:5–6, Matthew 2:8, Matthew 2:16; Matthew 9:27; and Matthew 14:22; and Matthew 20:30–31; Matthew 12:23; Matthew 21:9, Matthew 21:15; Matthew 22:45; Mark 10:47–48; and Mark 11:10; Mark 12:35–37; Luke 3:23

-- 826 --

Luke 3:23 ff.; Luke 20:41–44; John 7:42; Luke 1:27, Luke 1:32, Luke 1:69; Luke 2:4, Luke 2:11; Luke 18:38–39; Acts 2:30; Acts 13:22–23; Acts 15:16; Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8; Revelation 5:5; and Revelation 22:16.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 1:3.] See no. 11.Works, 15, 51.

Matthew 1:8. "And Joram begat Ozias."] Here three generations are omitted that descended from Athaliah, the daughter of Jezebel, viz. Ahaziah, and Joash, and Amaziah. Thus God has been pleased to animadvert on that wicked woman and the sin of Jehoram in marrying her, to the fourth generation, they being blotted out of the records of Christ's family, and omitted as if they never had been. Thus "the name of the wicked rots" [Proverbs 10:7], and God visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children unto the third and fourth generation. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 44–45.

Matthew 1:16.] See no. 124.Works, 15, 85.

Matthew 1:19.] This is a remarkable and eminent instance of a Christian spirit. And this verse is an evidence that that meekness, gentleness, forgiveness, and kindness to enemies that the gospel prescribes were duties under the law, and before Christ came.

Matthew 1:25. "And knew her not," etc.] A wonderful instance of self-denial, and a subjecting of the inferior appetite and inclination to superior principles, to respect and reverence to divinity. Though he entirely loved this virgin, and she was his wife, and he took her to him, and she dwelt with him, and he had never yet known her, yet he abstained from her out of reverence to that divine conception that she went with.

Matthew 2:10. "When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy."] The wise men that sought Christ traveled through a vast howling wilderness,

-- 827 --

full of pits, and drought, and serpents, hideous rocks and mountains, even the desert of Arabia, before they had this joy of seeing that star. And soon after they inquired of the priests, the star arose, which well represents what commonly is before persons have that joy which arises from the discovery of the person represented by this star, even Christ, the bright and morning star.

Matthew 2:11. "Gold, and frankincense, and myrrh."] Gifts proper to be offered to a king and a god. Gold, such as was wont to be given to kings; frankincense and myrrh, the chief ingredients of the incense that was offered to God in the temple. This was a specimen or earnest of the fulfillment of that prophecy, Isaiah 60:6. "The multitude of camels shall cover thee, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from Sheba shall come. They shall bring gold and incense; and they shall show forth the praises of the Lord."

"Presented unto him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh." Thus the charge of their journey into Egypt was provided for.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 2:15.] The words in the place referred to in the Old Testament are spoken of Israel, who therein was a type, and are spoken of as what happened to Israel when a child. Hosea 11:1, "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt," which makes 'em the more applicable to Christ's being called out of Egypt in his childhood. See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 76–70.Kidder employs a typological argument to answer Jews who accused the Evangelist of misapplying the scriptural text, allowing both a literal sense first with Israel of old, and "then a spiritual meaning and reference to the Messias." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 76–79.

Matthew 2:16.] Concerning Herod's destroying all the young children in Bethlehem. This was a just punishment of the people of Bethlehem for their treatment of the blessed virgin and her young child, by inhumanly refusing to entertain her in their houses when her travail came upon her, thereby greatly exposing the life of her child, and not only refusing to entertain the virgin in travail, but suffering her afterwards to remain in the stable with her child. For this treatment of this divine infant and his mother, God by a terrible judgment destroys their infants, and dreadfully afflicts their mothers. They were inhuman and cruel to the blessed virgin and her young child, and they are justly punished with the effects of dreadful inhumanity and cruelty executed on their young children.

-- 828 --

Matthew 2:17–18.] Herod commanded that the infants, not only in Bethlehem, but "in all the coasts thereof" Matthew 2:16] [be slain]. Wells, in his Sacred Geography, says Bethlehem, lying southwest from Jerusalem about six miles distant, that Ramah, though it lay in the tribe of Benjamin, was neighboring to it. Benjamin, in whose tribe it lay, was a child of Rachel; and that Ramah, or very near it, was the place where Rachel died, being in travail with this her son, and was there buried. Upon which account, upon the murdering the innocents in Ramah as well as Bethlehem, the lamentation of their mothers in general is properly and elegantly represented by the mourning of Rachel, forasmuch as from her not only the Benjamites of Ramah sprang, but also because she lay buried in those parts.Historical Geography of the New Testament (2nd ed. London, 1712), pp. 30–31. See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 79–82.This reference is a later addition. Kidder addresses the objection of Jewish critics who accuse the Evangelist of misapplying the prophecy of Jeremiah, for literally the children of Bethlehem were the children of Leah, not Rachel. Kidder's defense of Matthew rests not on a literal sense, but rather on a notion of accommodation in language whereby an allusion is used to express meaning. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 79–82.

Matthew 2:20. "They are dead which sought the young child's life."] "It is a very ingenious conjecture of Mr. M. […]"JE marked this unfinished entry with a large "X."

Matthew 2:23. "And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene."] "The deity, careful to obviate and rouse the inattention of mankind, ordinarily connected some analogous external circumstance, with the spiritual completion of the types and prophecies, in the person of the Messiah. For this reason, all the miracles he wrought, were only indexes unto the spiritual circumstances of mankind, and how divine power was to be exerted for extricating and delivering them. The external glory which some of the disciples were favored with a view of, was only a shadow of that which they behold, to whom he gives 'power to become the sons of God' [John 1:12]. His bodily thirst upon the cross coincided with the thirsting of his soul for the living God, 'as the hart panteth after the water brooks' [Psalms 42:1]; as that part of his sufferings is predicted in one of the psalms, when he cried out, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' [Matthew 27:46]. When he was spiritually under the power of darkness, then was it darkness all over the land. When, through the veil of his flesh, access was opened through the holiest of

-- 829 --

all, then was 'the veil of the temple rent in twain' [Matthew 27:51]. So here, when he was to enter on fulfilling his vow as the true Nazarite, the divine precaution provided a circumstance relating to him, which gave occasion to his being called by that name, that the people's attention might the more effectually be fixed upon him, while fulfilling that character." Creation the Ground-Work of Revelation, pp. 63–64.Wilson, Creation the Ground-Work of Revelation. See also Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 64–68.This reference is a later addition. Kidder acknowledges the difficulties this passage presents, for there is no location in the Old Testament which prophesies thus. Kidder uses two approaches in his defense of the Evangelist. He suggests that a tradition of such a prophecy may have existed at Jesus' time. He also points out the diverse meanings of the term "Nazarene," suggesting its use for "Nazarite." In several ways, he asserts, Jesus was a "separate" person. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 64–68.

Matthew 3:2. "The kingdom of heaven is at hand."] See the places of the Old Testament whence the Jews mainly took their notion of the kingdom of heaven, no. 332.Works, 15, 316.

Matthew 3:4. "His raiment of camel's hair," etc.] This was a sort of sackcloth. See Revelation 6:12. So that John prophesied "in sackcloth," as the witnesses (Revelation 11:3). Thus John's way of appearing and living, in all respects, was agreeable to his particular office or special business, which was to promote conviction and repentance of sin, to prepare the way for the consolation of Israel to be introduced by Christ.

Matthew 3:7.] See no. 9.Ibid., 51.

"You Pharisees, who are so conceited of your own righteousness, that you think you are in no danger of hell; and you Sadducees, that think there is none." Dr. Annesley, in the Casuistical Morning Exercises, vol. 4, p. 2.This paragraph is a later addition. Sermon 1, based on Matthew 11:9, addresses the question, "How may we give Christ a satisfying Account, why we attend upon the Ministry of the Word?" in Samuel Annesley, Casuistical Morning-Exercises. The Fourth Volume. By Several Ministers in and about London, Preached in October, 1689 (London, 1690), p. 2. Annesley (1620–96) was an eminent English Puritan.

Matthew 3:7–8 ff.] It seems that "upon this many of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who expected to be treated with greater respect, were so provoked, that they turned their backs, and refused to be baptized (Compare Luke

-- 830 --

Matthew 7:29–30; Matthew 21:25.)." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 96.

Matthew 3:12.] By this 'tis very manifest that when the Scripture speaks ofJE deleted "the fire that never shall be quenched, or 'unquenchable fire.'" everlasting fire, as it often does, thereby is not meant a fire whose effect shall be everlasting, in that sense that it would put an everlasting end to their being, and so in that sense the destruction occasioned by the fire should be perpetual. For,

1. If this was all that was intended, it would not be at all natural to express it by such a term as "unquenchable fire," or the fire that never shall be quenched, which is such an expression as strongly implies in it that the misery of those that are cast into it will arise from the continuance of the fire itself, and not merely the continuance of an effect that the fire did produce, that was a great while ago, and would necessarily remain of itself without any cause to continue it, as though the cause should have ceased immediately as soon as the effect. The expression naturally leads us to suppose that the wicked will want to have the fire extinguished, but will be able to find no means for it.

2. Especially would it be unnatural to use such an expression concerning such light substances as chaff or tow, whose nature it is when cast into the fire immediately to be burnt up, and for the fire that they are fuel to, to go out. If it had been spoken of some substance that will naturally endure the fire a great while, and be long a-burning, the terribleness of the fire might be more naturally set forth by its being unquenchable, because in such a case there might be opportunity to try to quench the fire before the fuel was destroyed; and the terribleness of the fire does more naturally consist in the length of the burning. The fire that is here called "unquenchable" with respect to chaff, is so with respect to tow (Isaiah 1:31).

3. The words themselves speak of the chaff's being burnt up. Now if thereby was meant that the wicked should suddenly have their beings abolished, as light chaff is at once consumed and utterly ceases, how unnatural would it be in the very same sentence to observe that the fire never shall be quenched, as a thing that renders it more terrible to that chaff.

Isaiah 4:4.This reference is a separate entry.

-- 831 --

Matthew 4:6. "For it is written, He shall give his angels," etc.] See Bp. Sherlock's Use and Intent of Prophecy, pp. 305 ff.On pp. 304–5, Thomas Sherlock cites Moses' prophecy in Deuteronomy 33:12 which speaks of the tribe of Benjamin dwelling "in safety," for "the Lord shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders." The protective care of God is the common theme with Matthew 4:6 (The Use and Intent of Prophecy, in the Several Ages of the World. In Six Discourses, Delivered at the Temple-Church, in April and May, 1724 (3rd ed. London, 1732).

Matthew 4:21–22. "Mending their nets."] Being broken by a vast number of fish they had caught just before (See Doddridge.),Family Expositor, 1, 201. which makes their being willing to forsake their fishing the more remarkable, that it should be at that time when they had just had extraordinary success in it, and be willing also to forsake all that multitude of fish they had just taken, and the "hired servants," without receiving the benefit of the expense they had been at in hiring them. See Mark 1:20. Note the evangelist Luke gives a more particular account of the occasion of their net's breaking (Luke 5:6).

Matthew 5:1–11.] By these verses it is evident that the religion, and virtues, and duties that Christ taught were the same that was taught in the Old Testament; and the spirit of the gospel, and temper of the Christian church, is the same with the spirit that God's church was of under the old testament, for most of these beatitudes are taken from the Old Testament.

In these beatitudes Christ seems to have a special design to correct those corrupt notions the Jews entertained of the "kingdom of heaven," or the kingdom that the Messiah was about to correct. As in Matthew 5:3, he has respect to the expectation they had in the Messiah's days of enjoying great outward wealth, and being made much of by the Messiah, as more excellent, and honorable, and worthy than other nations, and so vaunting themselves in those things that should greatly gratify their pride and covetousness. In Matthew 5:4, he has respect to their expectations of great worldly mirth, and pleasure, and festivity. In Matthew 5:5, he has respect to an imagination that military courage, and martial exploits, and fierce revenge on the Romans and other Gentile nations that had injured 'em, were to introduce their glory under the reign of the Messiah. In Matthew 5:5, he has respect to their carnal desires of worldly possessions and sensitive appetites, which they hoped would be abundantly gratified in the Messiah's days. Matthew 5:6, he has respect to their expectation of scenes of slaughter and desolation in the Gentile world, which they expected and hoped to see and

-- 832 --

have a hand in in the Messiah's days. Matthew 5:8, he has respect to those impure and luxurious delights which usually attend worldly victories, and princes' courts, and great and flourishing earthly kingdoms, which things they supposed the Messiah would introduce. In Matthew 5:9, he has respect to those desolating wars and bloody battles with which they supposed the Messiah would set up and propagate his kingdom. Matthew 5:10, he has still respect to their expectation of nothing but pomps, pleasures, wealth, and triumphs in the kingdom of heaven or of the Messiah. Matthew 5:11, he has respect to their expectation of being advanced to great honor as a kind of priests and princes under the Messiah their king, having the Gentiles their slaves, and even their kings and great men bowing down and licking up the dust of their feet. That Christ has a design in these beatitudes to give 'em right notions of the kingdom of heaven is manifest, for he several times in them makes express mention of the kingdom of heaven, as Matthew 5:3 and Matthew 5:10. And Matthew 5:5 speaks of inheriting the earth, which his hearers doubtless understood of that inheritance of the earth, and reigning over the world, that is promised to God's people in the days of the Messiah. And that being "comforted," which he promises, Matthew 5:4, they doubtless understood him of that, that [in] ancient prophecies, such as Isaiah 40 at the beginning, and others, was commonly called among them the "consolation of Israel," viz. the comfort that should be introduced by the Messiah. And in the promise, Matthew 5:6, of being "filled," Christ probably has respect to such promises made in the Old Testament concerning what God would do for his people in the Messiah's days, that "they should be filled as bowls, and as the corners of the altar" (Zechariah 9:15); that they should be abundantly filled or "satisfied with the goodness" of God's house, and that he would make 'em to drink of the river of his pleasures (Psalms 36:8 and Psalms 65:4); that they should eat "that which is good," and delight themselves "in fatness" (Isaiah 55:2); that they should eat when others were hungry, and drink when others were thirsty (Isaiah 65:13); that they should be satisfied with God's goodness, and their soul satiated "with fatness" (Jeremiah 31:14); and that he would replenish "every sorrowful soul" (Jeremiah 31:25), that bread should be given 'em (Isaiah 33:16), that their poor should be satisfied "with bread" (Psalms 132:15); and many other parallel prophecies. And in the promise of obtaining mercy (Matthew 5:7), Christ probably has respect to such promises made to God's people in the Messiah's times, as those, Isaiah 49:10, and Isaiah 54:10, and Isaiah 60:10, and in other parallel places. And in the promise of seeing God, in the Matthew 5:8, Christ probably has respect to such prophecies concerning the glory of the Messiah's times, as that then God's glory should be revealed [Isaiah 40:5]; their

-- 833 --

eye should "see the king in his beauty" [Isaiah 33:17]; they should "see eye to eye" [Isaiah 52:8]; that they should "walk in the light of the Lord" [Isaiah 2:5], and walk in the light of God's countenance [Psalms 89:15], and the like, and God's being their light instead of the sun [Isaiah 60:19]. And in the promise of being "the children of God" (Matthew 5:9), there is great reason to think Christ has respect to the many prophecies of the Messiah's kingdom that speak of God's people's being then especially owned and treated as his children, his sons and daughters. See "Fulfillment of Prophecies of Messiah," §111, p. 86.This paragraph is a separate entry. JE writes, "The prophecies do represent the people of God in the days of the Messiah as being distinguishingly privileged in being admitted to an extraordinary nearness to God, a more intimate union, and more free and friendly access and converse. God treats them not so much as servants, but more as friends, and children, and his dear spouse." JE then cites numerous passages from the Old Testament that strike this note ("Miscellanies," no. 1068).

Matthew 5:4.] True mourning is generally presently followed with comfort in first conversion, and commonly grace is infused before the first comfort, or at least before that joy which is commonly called the first comfort. Commonly there goes a holy mourning upon the infusion of grace, after a legal sorrow, before joy arises.

Matthew 5:5.] See "Miscellanies," no. 871.Works, 20, 110–11. See Romans 4:13.This reference is a later addition.

That this is by the generation of the righteous inheriting the earth in the latter days is confirmed by that, Psalms 25:13, where a like promise is expressed thus, "His seed shall inherit the earth."This paragraph is a later addition.

Matthew 5:8–9.] Christians should be "first pure, then peaceable" (James 3:17, Mark 9:50).

Matthew 5:9. "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God."] Because they are therein like Jesus Christ, the child of God, the Prince of Peace, and the great peacemaker, and are of a peaceable spirit, as becomes those that are brethren in God's family.

Matthew 5:13. "Ye are the salt of the earth."] See sermon on the words.JE's MS sermon on Matthew 5:13, n. d. (no. 151, winter—summer 1730), with the doctrine, "That the church of God in this depraved and corrupt world is as the salt that preserves it from utter ruin" (p. 3).

-- 834 --

"If the salt have lost its savor, wherewith shall it be salted?" I.e. wherewith shall it have its saltness restored to it again? Salt is made use to season other things that in themselves are insipid. But if the salt itself is become insipid, what will you find to season that, that it may not remain unsavory? It is past cure. "It is thenceforth good for nothing," and fit for nothing, but to be thrown away and "trodden underfoot."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 5:18. "Verily I say unto you."] The manner and style in which Christ taught, as well as the way in which he wrought miracles, was different from that of other prophets. Other prophets were wont to say, "Thus saith the Lord." But Christ used to express himself thus, "Verily I say unto you," as became the Lord himself, the Lord that sent and inspired the prophets, and in whose name they spake, and whose word they delivered.

Matthew 5:20. "For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees."] The particle "for"γάρ. connects this with the foregoing verse, intimating that the Pharisees broke some of the commandments, and taught men so. And Christ shows how, in the following part of the chapter, viz. in that they taught men that they must not kill, but tolerated rash anger, etc.

Matthew 5:22.] See Turretin, vol. 1, p. 660.The fourth question in Francis Turretin's ninth topic, De Peccato, in Genere et Specie, asks "Whether all sins are of themselves and in their own nature mortal. Or whether any venial sin can be granted?" Turretin's answer in § XVII asserts that Christ's reference in Matthew 5:22 to some sinners seemingly experiencing only hell fire does not establish the category of venial sins. Rather Christ's design was "to show that there is an inequality of punishments from the inequality of sins" and that sin also "consists in internal passion and irritating insults." Even the smallest degree of passion is worthy of death in God's sight (Institutio Theologiae Elencticae, in qua Status Controversiae Perspicue exponitur, Praecipua Orthodoxorum Argumenta proponuntur & vindicantur, & Fontes Solutionurn aperiuntur [3 vols., Editio Nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum, 1696]. See James T. Dennison, Jr., ed., and George Musgrave Giger, trans., Institutes of Elenctic Theology [3 vols. Phillipsburg, N.J., 1992–97], I, 596, 599). Turretin (1623–87) was a professor of theology in Geneva.

Matthew 5:22. "Shall be in danger of hell fire."] Hell in the Syriac language takes its name from the valley of the son of Hinnom. This valley, that was also called Topheth, had been the scene of those detestable sacrifices in which children were burnt alive to Molech (Compare 2 Kings 23:10, 2 Chronicles 28:3, Jeremiah 19:2–5, and Jeremiah 32:35.), and was afterwards defiled by

-- 835 --

Josiah (2 Kings 23:10), and made a receptacle for the filth of the city, where fires were kept continually burning to consume it. And it is probable that if any criminals were executed on the statute (Leviticus 20:14 or Leviticus 21:9), this accursed and horrible place might be the spot of ground on which they were consumed. However that were, it seemed, both with regard to its former and latter state, a fit emblem of hell itself See Isaiah 30:33 and Jeremiah 19:11–13).

Matthew 5:25. "The way with him."] Psalms 2:12.

Matthew 5:26. "The uttermost farthing."] See Psalms 10:15.

Matthew 5:29–30.] The metaphor is taken from surgeons whose manner it is, when the whole is in danger by any part, to cut it off, lest all perish.

Matthew 5:32. "Saving for the cause of fornication."] This can't be understood that a man or woman can never be free from a wife or husband while living in no other case, but that it is not lawful for either to be active in putting the other away in any other. Not but that, if either of the married parties shall unlawfully desert and leave the other, or as the Apostle calls it, "depart," the other is free. The Apostle is express as to that matter. 1 Corinthians 7:15, "But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or sister is not under bondage in such cases." Or if the husband puts away the wife, which is equivalent, and is what the Apostle evidently includes in the word "depart." For when the unbelieving husband departs from his Christian wife, 'tis not to be supposed that he goes and leaves his house, and leaves his wife in possession, but he turns her away. When an husband does so, either by declaredly prohibiting her living with him as his wife, or by doing it in effect by making it utterly intolerable for her to live with him, as when she cannot live with him without apparent hazard of life, etc., she is at liberty. Her husband departs from her.

Matthew 5:34. "Swear not at all."] See Owen on Hebrews 6:16, pp. 149d ff.John Owen used Hebrews 6:16 to develop the conditions for a lawful, solemn oath. He maintained that it is proper for Christians to swear in the name of God so long as the principles of truth, judgment, and righteousness prevail. The primary purpose of such oaths is to put an end to strife by appeal to a higher tribunal (Hebrews 6–10).

Matthew 5:37. "Cometh of evil, ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἐστιν. The word πονηρός, signifies wicked, malicious, envious, cruel, and with an article is commonly used

-- 836 --

for the devil. So it is, according to our translation, Ephesians 6:16 and 1 John 2:13; and so it probably signifies in the Lord's Prayer, and in Christ's prayer (John 17:15). And as Dr. Doddridge observes, "some copies in this place read διαβόλου, 'cometh from the devil.'" If it be so, how evident is [it] hence, that when Christ says, Matthew 5:34, "Swear not at all," it must be understood only in common conversation, or with some such limitation, for it is certain that swearing in some cases is not from the devil, but from God, being not only allowed, but required by him in the Mosaic law (See Exodus 22:11; Leviticus 5:1; Numbers 5:19, Numbers 5:21; Deuteronomy 29:12, Deuteronomy 29:14.). And if we understand the word here, not the devil, but malignant, wicked, it will prove that the swearing meant is properly an immorality. But it is absurd to suppose that any divine law establishes an immorality. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 236, n. k.

Matthew 5:39.] See Turretin, vol. 2, p. 26.The third question in Turretin's eleventh topic, De Lege Dei, asks "Is the moral law so perfect a rule of life and morals that nothing can be added to it or ought to be corrected in it for the true worship of God? Or did Christ fulfill it not only as imperfect, but also correct it as contrary to his doctrines?" Turretin's partial answer in § XVII suggests that Christ's words about "turning the other cheek" are to be understood "figuratively and hyperbolically" in the sense that one should endure another injury rather than attempting to avenge a first injury. So it is "the sense and scope" of his command concerning patience rather than the literal words that are intended. "Therefore culpable resistance, arising from revenge, is forbidden here, but not that of lawful defense and unblamable protection" (Institutio Theologiae Elencticae [Trajecti ad Rhenum, 1696]. See Dennison, ed., Institutes of Elenctic Theology, II, 18, 24).

Matthew 5:44.] This duty of loving our enemies, etc., is plainly implied in that precept of the law of Moses, Leviticus 19:18. For he that we are there required to love as ourselves, is the same that we are forbidden to avenge ourselves upon, or bear a grudge against, which doubtless is he that does us hurt. See "Miscellanies," no. 600.Works, 18, 141–42. See note on Matthew 1:19.

Matthew 6:5. "For they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets."] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, p. 551.Prideaux links this practice of the hypocrites with their desire "more to be seen of Men, than to be accepted of by God" (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 551).

Matthew 6:10–11. "Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread."] The order of these petitions is agreeable to the direction given in Matthew 6:33. "Seek first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added to you."

-- 837 --

So here Christ directs first to pray for the kingdom of God, and then to pray for other things.

Matthew 6:13.] See no. 36.Works, 15, 57. The remainder of this entry is a later addition. "But deliver us from evil." The same is doubtless signified here by "evil" as in the John 17:15, when Christ in his prayer says, "I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from the evil." The same word is used here as there, and with an article, as 'tis there. 'Tis τοῦ πονηροῦ in both places.

Matthew 6:22.] A man has a single eye when he looks on things of religion, inquires what he should believe, and what he should practice with a single heart, an heart wholly devoted to God, when he has not two masters to serve in his inquiry, which will infinitely perplex and confound his judgment, and darken his mind. For in all his inquiries he is under the power of prejudice; he is like a man that has an eye or that looks through a glass that multiples the objects of vision, and so confounds them, that nothing is seen in its distinct true form. But he that has the stream of his affections wholly towards God, and so has but one inclination to serve, he looks on objects through a single clear eye that represents objects single, and distinct, and each one in his true state, agreeable to what Christ elsewhere says, "If any man will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself" [John 7:17]. And therefore it follows, in the Matthew 6:24, "No man can serve two masters."

Matthew 6:23.] See Job 10:22. There the exceeding darkness of the place of the dead is set forth by that, that there "the light is as darkness."

Matthew 6:25. "Is not your life more than meat, and the body more than raiment?"] Therefore he that made the body, and gave life, can without your care provide meat to support that life that he has given, and can clothe the body, which he has so fearfully and wonderfully made and curiously wrought. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 253–54.

Matthew 6:27.] ThisJE joined this paragraph to a Pierpont entry which reads, "27: 'one cubit'] viz. either in a natural or civil way." JE deleted "seems to be a proverbial expression, or at least." is a metaphorical expression, and thereby is only signified that you can't better yourself "by taking thought." Men never better their case by an excessive thoughtfulness and care about the world. It seems

-- 838 --

to [have been] a common phrase amongst the Jews. When they would signify that persons could not better themselves by anything, they were wont to say, You cannot "add one cubit" to your stature by it.

Matthew 6:29. "Was not arrayed like one of these."] I.e. "in garments of so pure a white, as the Eastern princes were often clothed in white robes, and they were generally counted a magnificent apparel. Compare Esther 8:15 and Daniel 7:9." See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 255.

Matthew 6:30. "And tomorrow is cast into the oven."] The word κλίβανον does as properly signify furnace or still, as "oven." 'Tis most likely that Christ here means a still, into [which] the flower was thrown to extract its virtue. See Doddridge.Ibid., 256, n. 1.

Matthew 6:33. "Seek ye first the kingdom of God."] "Miscellanies," no. 857.Works, 20, 84.

Matthew 7:1–2. "Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged."] The hearts of men are naturally all full of the same corruption. As in water, face answers to face, so the heart of man to man. And those persons that censure and condemn others, if they would strictly examine themselves might [find] many things of a like nature in themselves; and not only so, but 'tis very observable that these persons that are most addicted to censoriousness are commonly the persons that are in a special and peculiar manner guilty of those things that they censure and condemn in others. As if a man be very much in censuring others for pride, it commonly may be observed that he is a very proud man. He that is most in censuring others for malice is a very malicious man. That professor of godliness, that is most in censuring other professors as pharisaical and self-righteous, is commonly in a peculiar manner a self-righteous and pharisaical man, which seems to be one reason of our omniscient and all-wise Savior's expressing himself as he does in the Matthew 7:1–5 of this chapter, and also as he does by his Spirit in the Apostle in the beginning of the Romans 2.

Matthew 7:13–14.] Such sayings as these, "Few there be that find it," etc., not intended of the glorious times of the latter day. See "Miscellanies," no. 1339.Ibid., 23, 356–59.

-- 839 --

Matthew 7:23. "I never knew you."] Exodus 2:25, "And God had respect unto them." In the originalאֳלהִים וַיַּדַע it is, "God knew them." See note on Romans 8:29.

Matthew 7:25.] The similitudes here seem to be taken from Ezekiel 13:11–14.

Matthew 8:4. "See thou tell no man."] See sermon on Matthew 16:21–23, the second instance under the first reason of the doctrine.JE's MS sermon on Matthew 16:21–23, n. d. (no. 234, Aug. 1731–Dec. 1732), with the doctrine, "It was a thing exceeding offensive to Christ to hear said anything against enduring those great sufferings which he came into the world to undergo" (p. 4). The "second instance" points to proof that Christ chose to suffer for sinners because he instructed his disciples "to conceal what they knew of him" till after the resurrection, a pattern he repeated after the Transfiguration and also when he worked miracles.

"For a testimony unto them." That they may see and acknowledge (and by offering your gifts) confirm your real cure, that when they afterwards come to understand that it was I that healed you, it may be matter of conviction to them of the truth of my mission, which they are so prejudiced against. Christ directs the man to say nothing about it till this is done probably because, if the priests should hear that he wrought the cure before they had pronounced him clean, they through prejudice against him might deny the reality of the cure. He therefore dispatched the man away with speed to Jerusalem to the priests (Mark 1:43). This was also a testimony to the priests, not only of Christ's miraculous and divine power (for the law of Moses seems to suppose it to be a peculiar work of God to cleanse the leper), but also a testimony of his strict regard even to the ceremonial law. Doddridge.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 1, 272–73.

Matthew 8:9.] By reason of my being "a man under authority," I am an officer under the Romans that are heathen, and have so much to do with men that are heathen, or a profane sort of men as the publicans and soldiers, and having so many such in mine house that attend upon me, and do the business of my house, therefore my house is not fit for thee to enter into.JE deleted this opening sentence with a large "X" and marked it with a vertical line near the left margin. The centurion's meaning is that diseases were Christ's servants, to go at his bidding, and obey his word, as his soldiers were his servants, which interpretation Luke's manner of giving the accountJE deleted "seems to favor." confirms, for he adds the conjunctionκαί. "also"; "for I also am a man under authority" [Luke 7:8].

-- 840 --

Matthew 8:18–19 ff.] Jesus was then going to leave that shore, and to cross the sea, when these persons manifested a forwardness to follow him. In order to be true followers of Christ we must as it were leave all that we have, and venture ourselves with him across a tempestuous ocean, seeking another country.

Matthew 8:19.] See note on Luke 9:57–62.

Matthew 8:21. "Bury my father."] I.e. let me stay till my aged father is dead. He was not willing to follow him yet, and pleads this as an excuse, that his father was old, and needed his care, or he was dear to him, and he was loath to leave him while he was alive. But after he should be dead, he would be willing to follow him.

Matthew 8:24. "The ship was covered with the waves."] Note on Mark 4:37–38.

Matthew 8:25.] See no. 12.Works, 15, 51.

Matthew 8:28. "Gergesenes."] They seem to be the same that are called Girgashites in the Old Testament,See, for example, Nehemiah 9:8. or at least are so called, because they dwelt in that which was formerly the country of the Girgashites.

Matthew 8:32.] The owners of these swine, if they were the posterity of the old Girgashites, yet ought to have conformed to the law of Moses with respect to swine's flesh, their ancestors probably having been not only subdued, but proselyted of old by the Israelites. But it seems these their posterity were apostates that despised the law. More fitly therefore did Christ suffer the devils to destroy their swine. If they were Jews (As Josephus speaks of the inhabitants of GadaraA city of the Decapolis in the eastern part of the Jordan valley. as Jews; see Doddridge.), who kept swine "to sell to the Roman soldiers and other Gentiles," Christ might justly punish them thus for their covetousness, in having so much to do with such unclean animals for the sake of gain.Family Expositor, 1, 427–31.

Matthew 8:34. "They besought him to depart out of their coasts."] Thus wicked men prefer their swine to Jesus Christ; they set up their vile lusts above him. The devil was aware of this, and what he principally aimed at when

-- 841 --

he besought Christ that he might enter into the swine was not so much the destruction of the swine, and the temporal loss of their owners, as the raising a prejudice in the people against Christ, and so to prevent their conversion.

Matthew 9:5. "For whether is easier," etc.] Healing diseases and forgiving iniquities are mentioned, in the Psalms 103:3, as being alike divine works.

Matthew 9:10.] See no. 10.Works, 15, 51.

Matthew 9:24.] See no. 61.Ibid., 67.

Matthew 10:4. "Iscariot."] I.e. īsh Carioth,᾽Ισκαριώτης. "a man of Carioth," or Kerioth,Possibly a city in Moab. a city mentioned, Joshua 15:25.

Matthew 10:17. "But beware of men."] To understand how this comes in, and how the particleδέ. "But" connects it with what went before, it must be observed that Christ here explains himself in what he said in the preceding verse. There he told that he sent them forth "as sheep in the midst of wolves." "But," says he, "beware of men"; these are the wolves that I mean. 'Tis men and not wolves I bid you beware of.

Matthew 10:18.] Or rather, "for a testimony unto them." See Hervey's Dialogues, vol. 2, [p.] 276, margin.Providence permitted preachers "to be brought before Rulers and Kings," according to Hervey, in order that "even the Potentates of the Earth, prejudiced and supercilious as they were, might hereby have an Opportunity, of hearing the Christian Doctrine, and seeing its Efficacy on the Spirits of Men" (Dialogues, 2, 276, note).

Matthew 10:23. "Till the Son of man be come."] That is, to your rescue. The thing they were to preach was that the kingdom of heaven was at hand. Here he gives them to understand that they "shall not have gone over the cities of Israel," before the kingdom of heaven be actually come, till the Son of man, spoken of in Daniel 7:13–14, be come in his kingdom; and then they should be delivered from them that persecute them. Christ tells 'em,

-- 842 --

in the foregoing verse, that they should "be hated of all men" for his sake, "but" (says he), "he that endures to the end shall be saved." That is, he that endures persecution, and don't faint, till Christ comes in his kingdom, he shall be saved; him whom the Son of man, when he comes, finds to have done so, him he will acknowledge and will grant deliverance to. And here in this verse, Christ encourages them, that this end or coming of the Son of man was near, that they might be upheld under their persecutions with this hope. He directs 'em how they may keep from perishing till he comes. When they were persecuted in one city, they should flee to another. And he tells 'em they should not have gone through all; they should not be beat out of their last refuge. Before they were reduced to such extremity that they should have nowhere else to flee, and so be under a necessity of perishing, Christ would appear for their salvation.

The thing principally aimed at by Christ in this seems to be this, that his church never should be reduced to such an extremity as to have no means left to keep itself alive before Christ would appear for its deliverance. Christ will not suffer his church to be swallowed up by its enemies. It is Christ's manner, when his church is almost swallowed up, then to appear.

Matthew 10:26. "Fear them not therefore: for there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; nor hid, that shall not be known."] Let this encourage you when they shall judge you wrongfully, for the time is coming that your innocency, and righteousness, and [the] gloriousness of your cause will appear. They have called me Beelzebub. And if they in like manner reproach you, this may comfort you, that the time is coming when it will appear what you are.

Matthew 10:38. "Taketh not up his cross, and followeth after me."] This alludes to the custom of persons' carrying the cross, to which they were to be fastened. So that the precepts of taking up the cross, and following Christ, so often given by our Savior, imply not only that we should be willing to deny ourselves, and suffer, and bear aJE deleted "heavy cr burden to the." very heavy and grievous [burden] to the flesh while we live, but be willing to suffer on the cross for Christ's sake at last, and so follow Christ in bearing the cross, bear it as he carried his cross, and at last suffered upon it.

Matthew 11:3. "Art thou he that should come?"] This title taken from Genesis 49:10, and Psalms 118:25, and several other passages of the Old Testament. See John 6:14 and John 11:27.

-- 843 --

Matthew 11:5. "The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached unto them."] τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέπουσιν καὶ χωλοὶ περιπατοῦσιν, λεπροὶ καθαρίζονται καὶ κωφοὶ ἀκούουσιν, καὶ νεκροὶ ἐγείπονται καὶ πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται. By the "poor" here seems pretty evidently to be meant the poor in spirit. In the last effect here mentioned, viz. "the poor are evangelized," the manner of speaking and connection of the words leads us to suppose there is the like relation and opposition between the benefit and character of the subject of that benefit, as in the foregoing effects mentioned, such as between receiving sight and blindness, and being raised up and death.

The word εὐαγγελίζονται, "are evangelized," implies not only being the subject of the preaching of the gospel, or the telling the good news, but a being encouraged, refreshed, and revived, and made joyful and happy by it. And between such a benefit, and a being poor in spirit, of a broken heart, or heart mourning, humbled, being wretched, miserable, and undone in his own eyes, and despairing in the world and in himself: I say, a being evangelized in the sense mentioned has a like relation to such a qualification of the subject, as sight has to blindness, light to darkness, walking to lameness, life to death. The poor's being evangelized is the last effect mentioned, it being that which crowns all, representing the main thing which Jesus came into the world for, the blessed effect that he had respect to in all that he said and did, and the great thing of which the other things here mentioned were but types and representations. In these last words Christ has a plain reference to Isaiah 61:1. "The Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings to the meek. He hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted." In Luke 4:18, Christ cites these words thus, "He hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." See SSS.Synopsis Criticorum, IV (London, 1674), Pt. 1, cols. 303–4.

Matthew 11:11. "Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist. But he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he."JE deleted with horizontal lines and a large "X" the following: "These last words are true in several senses, each of which it is probable Christ had respect [to]. 1. It is true of the ministers or true members of the Christian church here on earth, which is often called the 'kingdom of heaven.'" John was the greatest, not as he was the holiest man, but he was the greatest prophet, as it is expressed in Luke 7:28. And he was the greatest prophet these two ways. First, as he had a greater and clearer revelation of gospel mysteries than any of the preceding prophets. A prophet was great as a prophet, according as

-- 844 --

he was great in revelation of gospel, for that was the business of all the prophets, to declare the things pertaining to the Messiah; and that was the great end for which they were raised up, gradually to promulgate the gospel, and bring gospel light into the world. And secondly, his place and peculiar work was the most honorable. He had the honor to be the immediate forerunner of Christ. The end of all the prophets was to introduce the Messiah, gradually to bring in gospel light, and prepare the way for Christ's coming, and to make way for the bringing in the kingdom of heaven. But John the Baptist had the highest place of 'em all, for he was Christ's herald, to go before him, and proclaim his coming. He was the prophet that actually brought him in, and did the finishing stroke for making way for the kingdom of heaven. The greatest and most honorable part of the work of John, the most dignifying act that he was called to, and that upon the account of which principally he is called the greatest, was the baptizing Christ. It was an honorable office that God called Samuel to, when he sent him to anoint king David [1 Samuel 16]. But how much more honorable an office was John's, who was called to baptize and inaugurate the great antitype of David.

John, the immediate forerunner of Christ, was the greatest of all the old testament prophets, as the daystar, the immediate forerunner of the day, is the brightest of all the stars or lights of the night. Elias was one of the greatest of the prophets, but he was not greater than John the Baptist, for John the Baptist, when prophesied of, is called Elias. But 'tis not the manner of prophets to represent gospel things by things in their times that were greater than the things prophesied of.

These last words, "he that is least in the kingdom of heaven," etc., are true in several senses, each of which it is probable that Christ had respect to.

1. It is true of the ministers and true members of the Christian church, which is often called the "kingdom of heaven." These are greater than John the Baptist, inasmuch as the least of them has a clearer knowledge of gospel mysteries, of the office, the righteousness and satisfaction of the Mediator, and a future world, and eternal judgment, and the like, than any of them. And then they have greater honor in this respect, as they are actually in that kingdom of heaven, which John only prepared the way for. They are the people that Christ brings with him when he comes. They stand in that relation to Christ of disciples, members, and to God as children, which is now much more visible than under the old testament. The least subject, and disciple, and child of God in the kingdom of the Messiah was greater than the greatest of those servants that

-- 845 --

were sent before to make preparation for the kingdom of the Messiah. The least of God's people in that glorious dispensation introduced by the Messiah had greater dignity and honor than the greatest under the former low and carnal administration, that was a ministration of the letter and of death, which administration was so much inferior to that of the new that it had no glory in comparison of it. The meaning is that the privileges and honor that the least saint shall be admitted to in the kingdom of the Messiah shall be greater than the greatest privilege appertaining to the ancient dispensation that properly was a privilege appertaining to that administration, and which was under that dispensation, was most visible, exclusive of those invisible privileges of the kingdom of the Messiah which the old testament saints anticipated. Thus the least saint in the kingdom of the Messiah is said [to] be greater than the greatest prophet of the old testament, in the same sense as it may be said that the least Christian is admitted to greater privileges than the Jewish high priest. His highest honor and privilege was that he was admitted once a year into the holy of holies, to see God's glory over the mercy seat. Herein the high priest had a privilege above all the rest of Israel. But the Christian has greater honor than this. He has free access at all times to the mercy seat, and as every Christian may be said to be admitted to higher honor than Moses. Moses' highest honor was to be admitted to see God's glory, when he saw his backparts in Mt. Sinai, which was but once, and that when God only passed by, and hid his eyes with his hand till he was gone by. But 'tis foretold in the Psalms 36 and Psalms 89, and Isaiah 2 and Isaiah 60, as the privilege of all God's people in the kingdom of the Messiah, that they should see the glory of God's face, or light of his countenance, and should live and walk in it from day to day, as men do in the light of the sun. And the Apostle, in 2 Corinthians 3, comparing the privileges of Christians with that of Moses, in this respect says, "We all, with open face, behold as in a glass the glory of the Lord, and are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" 2 Corinthians 3:18]. The Apostle teaches us that the new testament has a better priesthood, better sacrifices, a better tabernacle, a better holy of holies, and better promises than the old. Therefore it may, in a similar way of representing things, be said that the least of God's people under the new testament has greater privileges than [he that] had the best inheritance in the land of Canaan, the land promised under the first, or than he that [had] the highest dignity in ancient Jerusalem, or in the ancient external temple. In like manner it is said that he that is least in the kingdom of the Messiah is greater than the greatest in the old testament church.

-- 846 --

2. As Christ himself is greater than John the Baptist, who is "the least in the kingdom of heaven," in the sense of Luke 9:48, "He that is least among you, the same shall be great," i.e. least in humility, as that is evidently meant in that place. He was least, as he descended lowest in his humiliation; none in the kingdom of heaven ever descended so low. He did as it were descend into the depths of hell. He suffered most; he suffered shame. He was made a curse. He went lower in those things than ever any of his people did; and this he did as a servant, not only to God, but to men, for he "came not to be ministered to, but to minister" [Matthew 20:28]. He was among the disciples as he that doth serve (Luke 22:27). His thus abasing himself to minister to his people is typified by that action of his in washing his disciples' feet, which he did for that end. Christ, who humbled himself lowest, is made the highest, agreeable to Matthew 23:11–12. Christ says he is "a worm, and no man" (Psalms 22:6).This and the preceding sentence are later interlineations. That the second sense here given was meant by Christ is much confirmed from Matthew 20:26–28 and Mark 10:42–45, where he tells his disciples that he amongst them that was the chief, should be "servant of all," according to the pattern which he himself had set them, who (though he was the chief, yet was the servant or least of all, in that he) "came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many," and therein became as the least of those many.

3. And lastly, as by the "kingdom of heaven" is meant the kingdom of the resurrection, as it isJE deleted "sometimes meant." often meant. So Luke 14:15. So where we read of Christ's coming in his kingdom, meaning his coming to judgment. And in the kingdom of the resurrection, the least shall be greater than John the Baptist was when here on earth.This entry, which was not written at one time, has been rearranged following JE's directions.

"Hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist." We can't conclude from hence that John was the greatest in all respects as in holiness, favor with God, wisdom, etc., or in every respect more honored of God. As we can't conclude that Melchizedek was in all respects greater or more honored of God than Abraham, from what the Apostle says, Hebrews 7:4, Hebrews 7:7.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 11:12.] See note on Luke 16:16.

Matthew 11:18–19. "John came neither eating nor drinking.… But the Son of man came eating and drinking."] This diverse manner of living of John

-- 847 --

the Baptist and Christ with respect to their diet was agreeable to the diverse errand they came upon. John's errand was to call men to repentance, to awaken them to a sense of their sin and misery, and to bring ['em] to mourn for their sins, and to humble themselves deeply before God for them, as preparatory to the comforts and blessings of the gospel or kingdom of heaven that were to be brought in by Christ. A life of abstinence and meanness of diet and apparel was agreeable to such awakening, mourning, and humiliation, as it was especially John's business to preach and set an example of. He came with tokens of sorrow and mourning, as the children in the marketplace mourned to their fellows Matthew 11:16]. But Christ's errand was to administer comfort to those that were thus prepared for it, as Isaiah 61:1–3. "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings to the meek, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord;… to comfort those that mourn, to appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, and to give them beauty for ashes, and the oil of joy for mourning, and the garments of praise for the spirit of heaviness." And therefore when Christ first begins his public ministry which succeeded John's, he declares this to be his business from this Scripture (Luke 4:16 ff.) Thus Christ came with tokens of spiritual mirth, as the children piped to their fellows.

"John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said, He hath a devil." I.e. he is mad, or overrun with melancholy, so as to bereave him of his reason, for such as these they called "possessed with devils." The same reflection is still wont to be cast by carnal men on persons that are the subjects of those convictions of sin preparatory to the comforts of the gospel, that John was a minister of. The world calls 'em melancholy, brainsick people, and enthusiasts, and under the influence of false spirits and diabolical delusions.

Matthew 11:19. "Wisdom is justified of her children."] See note on Proverbs 8:9.

Matthew 11:25. "Thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth."] No. 356.Works, 15, 341–42.

Matthew 11:27. "Neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son."] "Miscellanies," no. 777.Ibid., 2, 427–34.

-- 848 --

Matthew 11:30 "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."] These words have a relation to the words of the invitation, Matthew 11:28. The invitation is to them "that labor" and are burdened. A yoke is what is put on the necks of the cattle in order to their laboring. And when Christ says, "my burden is light," the word burthenτό φορτίον. is the noun of the verb or participleφορτίζω, or πεφορτισμένος. translated "heavy laden."

Matthew 12:5. "Priests… profane the sabbath."] In kindling "fires, killing, flaying, and dressing" beasts offered in sacrifice, and other servile works that appertain to their office. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 306.

Matthew 12:25–26. "Every kingdom divided against itself," etc.,… "and if Satan cast out Satan, how shall his kingdom stand?"] The argument is good against them, for what they said was not, The devils had agreed together to go out of men as Christ commandsMS: "Command." that so men might be deceived to believe Christ's doctrine, but that Christ had a devil that was stronger and mightier than other devils, and by his mastery over them dispossessed them of those men that were possessed by them. And besides, there is no need that we should understand it that Christ builds his argument upon the opposition that there is simply in this miracle of casting out devils out of men's bodies. But as the objection that they made respected all his works and acts that he performed in the course of his public ministry, they meant that the spirit that they were all done under the conduct and by the influence of was Satan. So the unreasonableness of their objection appears in that, that all were against Satan; all had that tendency, viz. to cast him out, to cast him out of men's souls as well as bodies. And as Dr. Tillotson observes, p. 522, third volume of his Works, "The force of his argument is this, that it cannot be imagined, that he who preacheth a doctrine so contrary to the design which the devil carried on in the world, and so destructive to his kingdom, as our Savior did, should be assisted by him to confirm the doctrine by any miraculous effects, especially such as did so directly tend to the overthrow of his own kingdom, and to dispossess him of the advantage of tyrannizing over men, which he was so desirous to get and hold."John Tillotson, The Works of the Most Reverend Dr. John Tillotson, Lord Archbishop of Canterbury (3 vols. 4th ed., London, 1728), 2, 522. Sermon 183 is part of a series entitled "The Evidences of the Truth of the Christian Religion." JE cites other sermons from this same volume by Tillotson in "Miscellanies," no. 716 (Works, 18, 34–48).

-- 849 --

Matthew 12:30. "He that is not with me is against me."] The true reason of Christ's observing this in this place, where he is reproving the Pharisees' saying that he cast out devils by Beelzebub Matthew 12:24], is this, that these Pharisees had till now appeared to exercise that kind of prudence, falsely so called, which is commonly to be seen among them that count themselves wise and great men, who think it becomes 'em to let matters of religion much alone, and not to appear forward and zealous, or apt to show their minds. When Christ appeared working great miracles, with which the multitude appeared much affected, and some appeared zealous to commence his disciples and followers, they thought it their prudence to hold their tongues, till Christ proceeded so far in his wonderful works and the esteem that he gained among the people, that they apprehended themselves in apparent danger of having their glory eclipsed, and of losing the esteem and honor of the people. And then they could bear it no longer. They openly showed what was in their hearts before, viz. a bitter enmity against Christ, and that truly they never had been indifferent, as they appeared.

Matthew 12:32.] See no. 22.Works, 15, 54. "It is observed, both by Lightfoot and Grotius, that through a fond imagination of the final happiness of all the seed of Abraham, the Jews supposed, there were some sins that had not been forgiven here, that would be expiated by death, and be forgiven after it; and that our Lord designed by this expression to assure them that there was no forgiveness to be had for those that should be guilty of this sin, neither before, nor after death.… And some think that it refers to the Messiah's kingdom, which was often called 'the age to come.'" Doddridge.This Doddridge citation is a later addition. Family Expositor, 1, 377. See Pfaffius, Theol., p. 233.This reference is a later addition. Concerning the notion of the gravest sins being forgiven after death, Christoph Matthew Pfaff (1686–1760), a professor of theology at Tubingen, writes, "At vero haec verba nemo intellexerit, nisi qui novit Judaeorum de gradibus & remissione peccatorum sententiam. Statuerunt autem ii, esse peccata, quae abstergat poenitentia, esse alia, ad quorum remissionem opus fit sacrificiis, alia rursus, tam gravia esse, ut non remitti possint, nisi in die expiationis, iterum esse alia his adhuc graviora, quae mors deleat, denique esse & peccata gravissima, quae nonnisi in seculo futuro, id est, post mortem remittantur" (Institutiones theologiae dogmaticae et moralis, p. 233).

Matthew 12:34–35.] See note on Proverbs 10:20. See also Proverbs 15:7 and Psalms 37:30–31.

-- 850 --

Matthew 12:39. "An adulterous generation."] I.e. a generation or race from adultery, not trueborn children of Abraham and of God, bastards and not sons, "a spurious race degenerated from the piety of their ancestors." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 384.

Matthew 12:40. "In the whale's belly."] "It is nowhere said in the Old Testament, that Jonah was swallowed by a whale; and it is the less probable, as whales are seldom found in the Mediterranean, and as the gullet of the whale is said to be so small, as not to be capable of receiving even the head of a man. It is therefore much more probable it was a shark. And the word κήτος, in Greek (as well as תַּנִּים in Hebrew) may signify any large fish, as some of the Greek lexicographers have observed." Doddridge.This paragraph was written later than the following paragraph. Family Expositor, 1, 384.

"Three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." I.e. three natural days, or part of three. The natural day was a day and night. According to the Hebrew dialect,בֹּקֶר עֶרֶב an evening morning, as Daniel 8:14; νυχθήμερον, according to the Greeks. Christ did not lie three whole natural days in the grave, because the time was shortened for this elect person's sake, in whom God's soul delighteth. God was as it were in haste to deliver his son from the grave.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"It is of great importance to observe, as many good writers have done, that the Easterns reckoned any part of a day of twenty-four hours for a whole day, and say a thing was done after three or seven days, etc., if it was done on the third or seventh day from that last mentioned. (Compare 1 Kings 20:29, 2 Chronicles 10:5, 2 Chronicles 10:12, and Luke 2:21.) And as the Hebrews had no word exactly answering to the Greek νυχθήμερον, to signify a natural day of twenty-four hours, they use night and day, or day and night for it. So that to say a thing happened after three days and three nights was the same as to say it happened after three days, or on the third day. Compare Esther 4:16, and Esther 5:1; Genesis 7:4, Genesis 7:12; Exodus 24:18, and Exodus 34:28."This paragraph is a separate entry. Doddridge, Family Expositor, 1, 384–85.

See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 1, pp. 104d–e and 105a, and Pt. 2, pp. 61–64.This reference is a later addition. In both of these locations Kidder reconciles conflicting time references in the Bible by asserting that "'tis a received maxim among the Jews, that any part of a precise time is to be reckoned for the whole." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 104–5; Pt. 2, 61–64.

-- 851 --

Matthew 12:41.] Note on Jonah 3:5.

Matthew 12:44. "He findeth it empty."] Not filled or inhabited by the spirit of God, or any good, to possess his former room there, and keep him out. For though the unclean spirit was turned out for a time, yet the house is still reserved empty for him. There has been only an external reformation. Wicked practices have been forsaken for a while, but the heart is still reserved empty. It is never possessed by God and his grace to prevent the return of sin and Satan. "Swept and garnished." That cleansing and garnishing that there seemed to be in those false professors, that afterwards are guilty of backsliding, is far from doing those apostates any good. It is but the occasion of Satan's having the greater advantage. Such reformations, and religious professions, and performances, if they backslide, do but prepare the heart for Satan's more full possession, like a house that is "swept and garnished" for an inhabitant.

Matthew 12:49–50.] The figure of speech Christ here uses will appear the more natural and beautiful, if it be considered that there were probably then sitting by, not only his male disciples, but also Mary Magdalene, and "Joanna, the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna," and many other women that were his disciples, who at that time attended him, ministering to him of their substance, as seems by Luke 8:1–3, with Luke 8:21.

Matthew 13:5–6.] See Job 8:17.

Matthew 13:11–12.] See Proverbs 1:5 and Proverbs 2:7.

Matthew 13:32. "Which indeed is the least of all seeds."] The least of the seeds that they used, or that they were wont to sow in their land.

Matthew 13:33.] See no. 2.Works, 15, 49.

Matthew 14:16–21.] One thing probably intended to be taught by that which we have here an account [of] was boldness in liberality to them that need, and that we ought not to excuse ourselves because we have but little, and need not be afraid of bringing ourselves to want by deeds of charity.

Matthew 14:24–25.] This which we are told of Christ shows what he was, viz. a divine person, for it is spoken of in the Job 9:8, as a property

-- 852 --

or act of God that he "treadeth on the waves of the sea." Christ here not only walks on the waters of the sea, but that when it is tossed with high waves, he treadeth on its boisterous waves, for it is said here that "the ship was tossed with waves." And it is said in the John 6:18, that "the sea arose by reason of a great wind that blew."

Matthew 14:24–27.] What we have here an account of seems livelily to representJE deleted "the manner of God's." what very frequently comes to pass to persons in the affair of their conversion. Christ did not appear unto them till they had been long tossed with a great tempest. The wind arose in the beginning of the night, and it was against them. And they had been rowing all night, and striving to get to the desired haven, and all to no purpose, so that by this time probably they were almost discouraged, and just ready to yield the case, and see that it was utterly in vain for them to strive any more to reach their port. Then Christ, in the latter part of the night, appears to them, and comes to their help, and appears as one above their difficulties, walking on the boisterous waves that distressed and threatened to destroy them, treading them under his feet. So it commonly is with sinners under conviction before Christ appears for their help. They are first made sensible of their danger, and brought into great exercise and distress, and reduced to the last extremity, and to see that they can never reach the haven they seek of themselves. They are brought to yield the case as to their own strength. And then Christ appears as one that is above their guilt, and above all those evils that threaten to swallow them up, as it were treading under his feet those mighty waters that encompass them on every side, that they are ready to sink in, and upon those raging waves that toss them, and are ready to overwhelm them. These difficulties the disciples met with were in the night, a time of darkness, as Jacob's wrestling was in the night [Genesis 32:24], signifying the darkness that persons meet with while under those convictions that are preparatory to conversion. And 'tis remarkable that the time when Christ appeared was near the breaking of the day, for it was in the fourth watch, which [is] the last part of the night. Though "weeping may continue for a night, yet joy comes in the morning" [Psalms 30:5]. It seems to be an emblem of the light that arises to the soul after darkness, when Christ appears. This was the time when Christ arose from the dead, and this was the time when Jacob obtained the blessing after long wrestling. See further in note on Mark 4:37–38.This sentence is a later addition. It is also worthy of notice that when Christ first appeared,

-- 853 --

they did not know what it was. They were troubled at the sight, and said, "It is a spirit, and cried out for fear." So very often at the first spiritual discoveries that persons have after great awakenings and distresses of conscience, they don't know what it is. They fear it is only a delusion, and are terribly afraid to receive it, as has been often seen in the time of the late extraordinary pouring out of the Spirit here in Northampton.

Matthew 14:30–31.] Here is a lively image of what afterwards came to pass with respect to Peter, when he denied his Lord. That was as it were a time of storm, wherein the wind was boisterous. And when Peter saw it, his faith began to fail; and he began to sink. And had not his Lord stood by him at that time, and as it were stretched forth his hand and caught him, he would have utterly sunk and perished.

Matthew 15:21–22.] See no. 39.Works, 15, 58.

Matthew 16:20.] Christ had never before so expressly owned himself to be the Messiah before his disciples. And as he chose still to be on the reserve with respect to that thing before the people, he charges them not to tell that he had so expressly owned it.

"He charged his disciples that they should tell no man that he was Jesus the Christ." "The reason was, that the Jews had such notions of the temporal kingdom of the Messiah, that they would have construed an open declaration of himself, under that character, as a claim to the throne of David; in consequence of which, many would have taken up arms in the cause (John 6:15), and others would have accused him to the Roman governor, as a rebel against Caesar (Luke 20:20), as they afterwards did (Luke 23:2). This Mr. Locke has stated at large, in his Reasonableness of Christianity, pp. 59–77." Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 1, 177, n. q.

Matthew 16:23. "Get thee behind me, Satan."] We are not to understand it that Christ here calls Peter "Satan." No. Christ speaks to Satan, that he saw had a hand in this matter, and that influenced Peter thus to think and speak. He speaks to Peter's indwelling sin, which was as it were the devil in Peter. It was not an instance of Christ's severity towards Peter that he thus speaks, but his love and grace that he would not impute what Peter says to himself, but to Satan. He graciously makes a distinction between his disciple Peter and his indwelling corruption. As Paul says, Romans 7:20, "'Tis no more I, but sin that dwelleth in me."

-- 854 --

Matthew 16:26. "For what is a man profited if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?"] The preciousness or value of anything above other things will appear by comparing it with other things, considering of it either as to be sold for them, or to be bought with them. If it be considered as to be sold for them, then the preciousness of it above them appears in the unprofitableness of the bargain. If it be considered as to be bought with other things, then its superior value appears by their insufficiency to buy it. The preciousness of the soul is set forth in this verse both these ways as being more precious than the whole world. It is first set forth by the unprofitableness of the bargain in case that it should be sold for the whole world. And nextly, it is set forth by the insufficiency of anything in the world, or of the whole world, to buy it or redeem it, in that last expression, "What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?" In the former part is set forth the insufficiency of the whole world to be received in case the soul be exchanged for other things. In the latter part is set forth the insufficiency of the whole world to be given in case other things are to be exchanged for the soul.

Matthew 16:28.] See nos. 197,Works, 15, 115–19. and 414;This reference and all the following are later additions. Works, 15, 421–22. "Scripture," no. 484;Works, 15, 581–82. "Miscellanies," no. 1199.Ibid., 23, 119–23. Nos. 1199 and 1198 were both entitled "Christ's Coming being spoken of as nigh at hand." See note on Matthew 21:43. See "Miscellanies," nos. 842, 1198.Works, 20, 57–64; 2, 119.

'Tis evident that Christ did expect that all that were then alive would be in their graves before his last coming at the end of the world, by what he says, John 6:39–40, John 6:44, John 6:54, where he repeats the promise again and again concerning all that believed on him, that he would raise 'em "up at the last day."

Matthew 16:28-17:2 ff.] The seeing of Christ thus transfigured was given as an earnest of that which Christ had foretold to his disciples immediately before the transfiguration. [It] immediately followed that prediction, according to the accounts of all the evangelists, Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It is mentioned as an evidence of the truth of that prediction by Peter, Matthew 16:17.

-- 855 --

Matthew 17:1–5.] What we have an account of in these verses is a remarkable specimen on earth of the glorified state of the church in heaven. See note on the Exodus 34. And 'tis a signification of the sweet harmony of the Old and New Testament, and of the union of both old and new testament church in Christ as their common head, and that they shall be but one society in heaven. Here is Christ, the glorious head, and Moses and Elias, the two principal old testament prophets, and the three chief disciples of the new testament, together on the mount.

See note on 2 Peter 1:16–18. See note on Exodus 34, and particularly note on Exodus 33:18–23.This paragraph is a later addition.

Matthew 17:2. "And his raiment was white as the light."] This denoted who he was, viz. he that was spoken of, Daniel 7:9 and Psalms 104:2. [See 2 Peter 1:16–18, [in] no. 265.Works, 15, 213–17. JE added this fragmentary reference later. See entry on Matthew 17:1–5.

Matthew 17:5. "Behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them."] This cloud was not bright merely as clouds are oftentimes very bright by the reflection of the light of the sun. But there was a more excellent and glorious brightness in it, which rendered it a suitable symbol of the divine presence, such as perhaps was in the Shekinah, or cloud above the mercy seat, in the tabernacle and temple. Peter, speaking of the glory of this cloud, calls it "the excellent glory" (2 Peter 1:17). Luke says, "They feared as they entered into the cloud" [Luke 9:34]. It was because of that appearance of divine majesty and glory that was in the cloud.

Matthew 17:9. "Until the Son of man be risen again from the dead."] Luke 9:21–22.

Matthew 17:10. "Why then say the scribes that Elias must first come?"] The disciples did not distinctly understand Christ when he spake of the Son of man's "rising from the dead," as appears by Mark 9:10. They did not understand him particularly of his own resurrection, for they had not yet learnt that he was to die and rise. They thought therefore that he had respect to the resurrection of men, which was a received doctrine among the scribes and Pharisees, which they supposed would be at the beginning of the kingdom of heaven, or kingdom of the Messiah. Now it was

-- 856 --

what the scribes taught, that Elias was to come before this; and this was what the disciples meant.

Matthew 17:11. "Elias truly shall first come, and restore all things."] Elijah was called the "Tishbite" [1 Kings 17:1], which "wordהַתִּשְׁבִּי signifies a restorer, or converter." See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, p. 182e.Kidder declares that John the Baptist was the "perfect anti-type of the Tishbite." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 182.

It was from these words of Christ a prevalent opinion among the ancient fathers of the Christian church, that another Elias was yet to come. See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 186–87.Kidder comments on the opinion among some ancient writers that another Elias is still to come. He suggests the possibility that the ancients were mistaken.
