He also notes that only some Christians, not all, especially Roman Catholics, held this view. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 186–87.

Matthew 17:15.] The devil sometimes cast the possessed man into the fire, and sometimes into the water, which represents the manner of Satan's dealing with souls in his possession. He sometimes leads 'em into one extreme, and sometimes into another. Sometimes he flatters 'em, and leads 'em to presumption, and sometimes discourages 'em, and drives 'em to despair, and so leads 'em to extremes in other respects.

Matthew 17:21.] See no. 75.Works, 15, 71–72. Therefore fasting is a part of Christian worship.

Matthew 17:25–26. "Of their own children, or of strangers," etc.] The kings of the earth don't require tribute of their heirs. Christ was the heir of the empire of the world; the kingdom by inheritance belonged to him. His right it was to rule and reign, and that because he was the child of him who was the head and fountain of all the authority and power. The kings of the earth reign only by a derived dependent authority; they rule only as invested with some of God's authority, as his vicegerents or ministers of his authority. Christ is not properly the child of kings; but yet the argument is the same, for he is the child and heir of him who is the head of all kingly authority, and whose vicegerents and ministers they are in reigning.

Matthew 17:27. "And when thou hast opened his mouth."] No. 326.Ibid., 310.

-- 857 --

Matthew 18:3.] The disciples were concerned who of them should be greatest. But Christ intimates to them that they were too big already, and that unless they were turned and become less than they were, even "as little children," instead of being the greatest in the kingdom of heaven, they should have no part in it.

Matthew 18:6.] Mark 9:42.

Matthew 18:10. "Angels do always behold the face," etc.] This denotes the honor and dignity of the angels in heaven, as being as it were the barons and nobles of the court of heaven, which is confirmed by Esther 1:14, 2 Samuel 16:19, 1 Kings 10:8 and 1 Kings 12:6. And it may signify that the highest of the angels are ministering spirits to the "little ones" Christ speaks of, as it is the chief ministers in the king's court that are nearest to him, and most continually in his presence. So the dignity of the angel Gabriel, as one of the highest of the angels, seems to be denoted by that, that he was he that stood "in the presence of God" (Luke 1:19). So Satan's being the highest angel in heaven (under the type of the prince of Tyrus), is represented by comparing him to one of the cherubs in the holy of holies that were always by the throne, covering the mercy seat with their wings (Ezekiel 28:14).

Matthew 18:16.] See no. 45.Ibid., 59–60.

Matthew 18:34. "Delivered him to the tormentors."] Referring to the sufferings he should undergo in prison. "Imprisonment is a much greater punishment in the Eastern parts of the world than here. State criminals especially, when condemned to it, are not only forced to submit to a very mean and scanty allowance, but are frequently loaded with clogs, or yokes of heavy wood, in which they cannot either lie or sit at ease, and by frequent scourgings, and sometimes by racking, are quickly brought to an untimely end." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 33.

Matthew 19:8.] See Turretin, vol. 2, p. 27.The third question in Turretin's eleventh topic, De Lege Dei, asks "Is the moral law so perfect a rule of life and morals that nothing can be added to it or ought to be corrected in it for the true worship of God? Or did Christ fulfill it not only as imperfect, but also correct it as contrary to his doctrines?" Turretin's partial answer in § XIX involves Christ's command about not divorcing a wife except for fornication. The conflict is between the Pharisees' interpretation of Moses' law which construed the words of Moses as approval of divorce without limitations and Christ's instruction. Turretin declares that Christ's command "agrees with the law of Moses" (Institutio Theologiae Elencticae). See Dennison, ed., Institutes of Elenctic Theology, II, 18, 24. The remainder of this entry is a later addition. See note on Exodus 21:8, and on Deut.

-- 858 --

Matthew 17:14–15. We have an instance of God's tolerating under the old testament, what yet we can't suppose he approved, in the laws about the avenger of blood, his slaying him that accidentally slew another if he overtook him before he got to the city of refuge [Numbers 35:27]. See SSS on Deuteronomy 21:15. See also SSS on Deuteronomy 24:1.These two references are a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 828, 843–44.

Matthew 19:9. "Committeth adultery."] A clear evidence of the unlawfulness of polygamy, or that a man's marrying another wife while his first wife is living is not a lawful marriage, but is adultery.

Matthew 19:11–12. "All men cannot receive this saying."] I.e. this saying following, that which I am now about to say. The saying that respect is had to is that which follows in the next verse. There is the like manner of expression and connection of sentences in Luke 9:44.

Matthew 19:17. "Why callest thou me good?" etc.] Probably Christ, who knew what was in men, saw that this young man, though he had no notion of Christ's being a divine person, and thought him but a mere man, yet thinking him a prophet, came to him trusting in him for eternal life, in a manner that no mere man is to be trusted in. Which is the reason why he says that to him, "Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God," i.e. there is none else who has a goodness that is to be depended upon but God. For Christ don't find fault simply with any man's being called "good," for he, using the same word, calls some men good himself, as Matthew 12:35, "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart," etc. So Luke 19:17, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant."

Matthew 19:17 ff.] Watts, Orthodoxy and Charity, pp. 110–11.Isaac Watts, in his sermon on Matthew 19:17, "The True Use of the Moral Law under the Gospel," asserted that though works are not sufficient atonement for sin, "yet there is a rewardable Condecency in the Works of Holiness." Only perfect obedience, however, would suffice for eternal life. Nevertheless, "a sincere Endeavour after universal Obedience… is one necessary Requisite" of approval by Christ. The "great and necessary Duty of Christianity," he declared, "is Faith which works by Love" (Orthodoxy and Charity united: In several Reconciling Essays on the Law and Gospel, Faith and Works (2nd ed., Boston, 1749).

-- 859 --

Matthew 19:17–18. "If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments.… Thou shalt do [no] murther. Thou shalt not commit adultery," etc.] This answer of Christ might be profitable to the young [man] in what sense soever the words could be taken, if they were to mean a sincere and universal obedience to these commands. There is matter of direction in them, for by such an obedience he would be entitled to eternal life, according to the tenor of the covenant of grace. An universal, persevering conformity to the duties of the Second Table alone, the duties of love to our neighbor, are often in the New Testament mentioned as signs of faith and true godliness. See Luke 10:28, Luke 10:37. And the commandments were given in the law of Moses partly for this end, to be of real direction to them how to obtain eternal life. See Matthew 5:19.

Or 2. If they were understood of perfect obedience, they would tend to his conviction. The law is proposed to us in our fallen state, for our conviction of the impossibility of our being justified by our own righteousness, that we might be shut up, and see our own helplessness and our necessity of a mediator. And it seems chiefly to be for his trial that Christ proposes this to him.JE deleted "But then here is a question arises, viz." For it was true that if the young man should attend that direction, and keep the commandments perfectly, he should have eternal life; and therefore Christ promises life upon these terms (Luke 10:28). And so doth God still in theJE deleted "Old Testament." law of Moses promise life upon condition of perfect obedience, that men, by trial and experience of themselves, might be convinced of the impossibility of their being justified by the law. God promises life for future obedience, for though if a man should perfectly obey for the future, he could not be justified according to the tenor of the law, because he is guilty of Adam's sin and of original sin. Yet it may be proper to make such a promise, because if a man should perfectly obey the law in his life, it would be an evidence that he was free from original sin, and free of the guilt of Adam's sin, for the guilt of Adam's sin and original corruption are connected one with the other. Christ proposes the duties of the Second Table, because 'tis most easily known whether we keep these commands, or no. Our obedience or disobedience to them is most sensible; and an obedience to them will be an evidence of our obedience to the laws of the First Table.

And also because the duties of the Second Table make the most essential part of religion, as it appears in its fruits in practice and conversation. And besides, the duties of the First Table would not have been so

-- 860 --

fit for the conviction of a Pharisee, as this young man probably was, for they were exceeding strict in the externals of the First Table, though they devoured widows' houses, and greatly failed in their obedience to the commands of the Second Table, as taken in their true meaning, and interpreted by Christ in his sermon in the mount, though not as the Pharisees, and among them this young man, corruptly understood them.This paragraph is a later addition.

Matthew 19:25. "They were exceedingly amazed."] See note on Mark 10:24 and Mark 10:26.

Matthew 19:28–29.] How this argues that the saints in heaven share in the glory of the glorious things done for the church on earth, see "Miscellanies," no. 811.Works, 18, 520–22.

Matthew 19:29. "Receive an hundredfold."] See no. 148.Ibid., 2, 92–93.

Matthew 20:16.] See "Tractate," in "Apocalypse," ch. 16, v. 12.JE deleted this reference to the "Tractate" (Works, 5, 298–305).

Matthew 20:22. "Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of?"] What Christ says in this verse seems to imply that God has connected the greatest glory and advancement in his kingdom and the greatest sufferings together, that that is the way that God has appointed to the highest seats in glory. And therefore Christ tells them that they know not what they ask, when they ask that one of them may sit on his right hand, and the other on his left, in his kingdom. They did not know what great sufferings this gift is connected [with]. If they did, it would be a damp to them. They would not appear so forward and earnest to ask it. These sufferings seem therefore to be called here a "baptism," because they are as it were the ordained, appointed consecration and rite of introduction to so glorious a state, as persons were of old fitted to enter into the house of the Lord, and as officers were fitted to enter into their places of honor and dignity in Israel by legal washings or baptisms. "Of the cup that I shall drink of." See note on Psalms 16:5.

Matthew 20:23. "Is not mine to give, but it shall be given unto them for whom it is prepared of my Father."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, p. 58.Kidder denies that this statement by Jesus implies that he is not one with the Father (a Jewish and Socinian judgment). Rather Kidder interprets its meaning as a declaration that the request was not fit for Jesus to grant. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 58.

-- 861 --

Matthew 20:28.] See notes on Matthew 11:11.

Matthew 20:29. "And as they departed from Jericho."] Concerning the seeming inconsistence with Luke's account, see no. 233.Works, 15, 182–84.

Matthew 21:1–11.] See notes on Luke 19:37, Luke 19:40. See no. 324.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 307–10.

Matthew 21:8. "Spread their garments in the way."] This represents men's spreading the garments of their own righteousness and excellency on the earth under Christ's feet. "Others cut down branches from the trees, and strewed them in the way." These seem to have been "branches of palm trees" (John 12:13), which were used as ensigns of glory at festivities and triumphs. (See Wilson's Christian Dictionary.)Thomas Wilson writes in an entry entitled "Palm tree," "The branches hereof were anciently taken as ensignes of victory" (Complete Christian Dictionary [6th ed.], p. 462). They in their joy and praises wherein they triumphed cast down their glory at the feet of Christ, and ascribed the glory and the victory wholly to him. They triumphed in him in the commencement of the glorious state of the church, wherein the saints shall obtain such a glorious victory over all their enemies. They shall glory only in the Lord. They shall cast down their crowns of victory at his feet, and wipe his feet with their hair, which is their glory.

Matthew 21:12–13.] See note on Mark 11:17.

Matthew 21:12–16.] See no. 330.Works, 15, 313–14.

Matthew 21:13.] "Bishop Smalbroke, in his Answer to Woolston,MS: "Smallbroke." Richard Smalbroke (1672–1749), Lord Bishop of St. David's, wrote A Vindication of the Miracles of Our Blessed Saviour; in which Mr. Woolston's Discourses on them are Particularly Examin'd (2 vols. London, 1729–31). well observes that our Lord in this expression seems to allude to the custom which robbers in those parts had, of sheltering themselves in dens and caves of the wilderness, where great multitudes of 'em often joined in sharing their plunder." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 300. See note on Jeremiah 7:11.This reference is a later addition.

-- 862 --

Matthew 21:15–16.] This here mentioned of the children crying, "Hosanna," did both prefigure the approaching glory of Christ at his ascension, and the songs of the saints in heaven on that occasion, and also was a prelude, and specimen, and earnest of that wonderful and glorious success of his gospel that there should be, upon his ascension, on earth. Their being children, as it were "babes and sucklings," was a figure of the quality of the persons in whom the gospel should be successful on his ascension, who were as children in several respects. They were chiefly the poorer sort, not many wise, not many mighty, etc. And then they all, when they were converted, became as little children spiritually. Thus Christ, before his sufferings, was encouraged with an earnest of the joy that was set before him, both in his own glory in heaven, and the success of his gospel on earth.

Matthew 21:21. "Unto this mountain."] I.e. this Mount Olivet, for Bethany, from whence they were coming to Jerusalem, was built on part of Mount Olivet. Wells, Sacred Geography.Historical Geography of the New Testament (2nd ed.), pp. 114–15.

Matthew 21:32. "And ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him."] By this it appears that faith and repentance are implied in the nature, the one of the other. The soul, in repenting, believes, and in believing, repents. Faith is necessary in order to repentance, and repentance is necessary in order to faith. And therefore 'tis said, "Ye repented not, that ye might believe."

Matthew 21:40–41.] See no. 4.Works, 15, 49–50.

Matthew 21:43. "The kingdom of heaven shall be taken from you, and given to a nation," etc.] By this it is evident that when Christ speaks of the kingdom of heaven as at hand, and of there being some there that shall not taste of death till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom, and the like, there is no need to understand him of that coming of his that shall be at the end of the world, which is spoken of in the Matthew 24-25. For here he speaks of the kingdom of heaven, or kingdom of God, as subsisting while the world standsMS: "stand." inhabited by various nations, as it was when he spoke.

-- 863 --

Matthew 22:14. "For many are called, but few are chosen."] This has reference not to what was last said of the man that came in not having a wedding garment, as though the bigger part of those that came in would be rejected as found without wedding garments. But it has reference to the whole parable, and to all that had been invited to the wedding, them that were called, spoken of in the Matthew 22:3–8, of whom it is said, "They that were bidden were not worthy," as well as to him that came in without a wedding garment, and was not counted worthy on that account. Many that are called never come into the house; and of those that do come in, not all are chosen. And so from the whole, Christ infers this inference, that "many are called, but few chosen."

Matthew 22:16. "Neither carest thou for any man, for thou regardest not the person of men."] This they say to influence him to speak the more boldly, even in an affair wherein Caesar himself was concerned. They hoped that by their commending of him for his not caring "for any man," they should prompt him to show that he did not regard the person of Caesar himself, by saying that it was not lawful to give tribute to Caesar. And then they intended to accuse him of treason against Caesar.

Matthew 22:21. "Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's."] Christ, by giving this answer, not only evaded their malicious design against him, but gave them that counsel that they very much needed. For there were some of two opposite sects that came to him with this question to ensnare him, viz. the Pharisees and Herodians. And he cautions each against those opposite iniquities which by their principles they were inclined to. "He cautions the Pharisees against using religion as a pretense to justify sedition, and warns the Herodians, that they should not, as they were too inclinable to do, make a complimentJE writes "complement" although Doddridge wrote "compliment." of their religion to the Romans, by complying with those things which were forbidden by the divine law, that they might ingratiate themselves with Caesar's party. See Prideaux, Connection, vol. 2, pp. 366–68." See Doddridge.The quotation is from Family Expositor, 2, 343, n. d. Doddridge's citation of Prideaux, Old and New Testament Connected (London, 1718), vol. II, Pt. 1, is from the first edition, a different edition than JE was using in the "Blank Bible."

Matthew 22:32.] How Christ's argument here proves that Abraham, etc., do see and enjoy the fulfillment of the promises God made of glorious things

-- 864 --

to be accomplished to their seed on earth, and that the departed souls of saints do share in the glory of the church on earth. "Miscellanies," no. 811.Works, 18, 520–22. See "Scripture," no. 379.This and the following reference are later additions. Works, 15, 363–65. See also note on Psalms 144:3–4.

Matthew 23:24. "Which strain," etc.] It should have been rendered, "which strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel." They were wont in those countries in their feasts and banquets to use a strainer through which they strained their wine as they drank it, by reason of a certain "sort of gnat that loved mightily to sip wine," as Mr. Chishull observes. Present State of the Republic of Letters, vol. 1, p. 440.The review of the volume by the Anglican divine, Edmund Chishull (1671–1733), Antiquitates Asiaticæ. Christianum Æram antecedentes, appeared in the June, 1728, issue of the Present State of the Republic of Letters.

Matthew 23:29 ff.] See notes on Luke 11:48.

Matthew 23:33. "How can ye escape the damnation of hell?"] "RapheliusGeorg Raphel (1673–1740), Prussian philologist and annotator, author of Annotationes in Sacram Scripturam, Historicae in Vetus, Philologicae in Novum Testamentum, ex Xenophonte, Polybio, Arriano et Herodoto: Collectae (1715–21, reissued 1747). has abundantly proved, that ἀποφύγειν κρῖμα properly signifies to 'evade conviction' in a court of judicature, which is often done by the artifice of the criminal." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 365–66.

Matthew 23:35. "Zacharias, the son of Barachias," etc.] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 73–75.Kidder answers the charge made by the Jews that there is a "manifest error" in the text because the Zacharias who was slain was the son of Jehojadah, not Barachias. But he points out that it was common for Jews to be called by two names. Furthermore, both names are translated into English with the same "praise God." Thus the objection has no merit, in his judgment. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 73–75.

Matthew 24.] See no. 197, notes on Matthew 16:28.Works, 15, 115–19. In this chapter respect is had especially to two events, one the destruction of Jerusalem and the works of God that accompanied it, the other the end of the world. And some things are most applicable to one, and others to another, as is common in those parts of Scripture that have respect to various events, and is particularlyMS: "particular." evident in the Psalms 8, which has respect both to the

-- 865 --

creation of man and incarnation of Christ, where what is much the most applicable to the former is applied by the Apostle to the latter. Compare Psalms 8:5, Hebrews 2:7.

See how the prophecy in this chapter concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, with its preceding events and attending circumstances, was exactly and remarkably accomplished in every particular, in Tillotson's Works, vol. 3, Sermons 184–186, beginning at p. 525.This paragraph is a separate entry. These three sermons, pp. 525–35, are part of a series entitled "The Evidences of the Truth of the Christian Religion," pp. 503–50. JE quotes at length from it in "Miscellanies," no. 972 (Works, 10, 254–73).

What Christ says in this chapter is "in answer to the apostles' inquiry concerning his 'coming, and the end of the world' (Matthew 24:3). For so we translate τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αιῶνος; we must understand the disciples here to put their question, according to the notion and way of speaking of the Jews. For they had two 'worlds,' as we translate it, ὁ νῦν ἀιὼν καὶ ὁ μέλλῶν ἀιὼν, 'the present world' and 'the world to come.' The kingdom of God, as they called it, or the time of the Messiah, they called ὁ μέλλῶν ἀιὼν, 'the world to come,' which they believed was to put an end to this world. And that then the just should be raised from the dead, to enjoy, in that new world, a happy eternity, with those of the Jewish nation who should be then living. These two things, viz. the visible and powerful appearance of his kingdom, and the end of the world, being confounded in the apostles' question, our Savior does not separate them, nor distinctly reply to them apart; but leaving the inquirers in the common opinion, answers at once concerning his coming to take vengeance of the Jewish nation, and put an end to their church, worship, and commonwealth; which was their ὁ νῦν ἀιὼν, 'present world,' which they counted should last till their Messiah came. And so it did, and then had an end put to it. And to this he joins his last coming to judgment, in the glory of his Father, to put a final end to this world, and all the dispensation belonging to the posterity of Adam upon earth." Locke's Reasonableness of Christianity as Delivered in the Scriptures, vol. 2 of his Works, p. 510.This paragraph is a separate entry. John Locke, The Works of John Locke, Esq; in Three Volumes (3 vols. London, 1714).

The destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish state is often in the Old Testament represented as a dissolution of the world (Isaiah 2:10–17; Isaiah 24:1–6, and Isaiah 24:16–23; Jeremiah 22:29; Micah 1:1–5). As the erecting the New Jerusalem is spoken of as the creating "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17–18), so the destruction of the old Jerusalem is compared to the dissolution of the old heavens and earth. And as, in this prophecy in

-- 866 --

the twenty-fourth of Matthew, Christ is represented as coming down from heaven at the destruction of Jerusalem and the land, church, and state of the Jews, so in the Old Testament God is represented as coming down from heaven in the destruction of that people (Micah 1:3).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 24:3. "End of the world."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 3, pp. 162–65.Kidder argues that the Old Testament writers used the term "the last days" to speak of the times of the Messiah, a practice followed by the New Testament. When the phrase, "the end of the world," is used in connection with the coming of the Messiah, it refers to an end to the Jewish polity and the Mosaic economy. Jesus did appear, he asserts, in the last days. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 162–65.

Matthew 24:8.] No. 292, §11.Works, 15, 259–60.

Matthew 24:15. "The abomination of desolation."] See note on Daniel 9:27, no. 413;Ibid., 419–21. and Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 11–13.This reference is a later addition. Kidder pens an extended footnote arguing that the "abomination of desolation" refers to the siege and destruction of Jerusalem by the emperor and general Titus Flavius Vespasianus and the Roman army. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 11–13.

Matthew 24:17–18. "Let him which is on the house top not come down to take anything out of his house. Neither let him which is in the field turn back to take his clothes."] Flying out of Jerusalem is a type of flying out of a state of sin, as flying out of Sodom was to which it is compared by Christ in the words subjoined to those in Luke 17:32, "Remember Lot's wife."See JE's sermon, "The Folly of Looking Back in Fleeing Out of Sodom," which has as its text Luke 17:32, "Remember Lot's wife" (Works, 19, 321–35). Flying out of that unbelieving city that had the wrath of God impending over it typified our flying from a state of unbelief and danger of wrath. They were directed to fly out of Jerusalem, in these words, without staying to take anything out of their houses, etc., to signify with what haste and greatness of concern we should fly out of a natural condition, that no respect to any worldly enjoyment should prevent or delay us one moment, and that we should so fly to Jesus Christ, the refuge of souls, our strong rock, and the mountain of our defense, as in flying to him in our hearts to leave and forsake all worldly things. As Lot was directed to flee out of Sodom, to haste and escape for his life, not to tarry in all the plain, nor to look behind him, but to escape to the mountain [Genesis 19:17].

-- 867 --

And as we readJE deleted "from time to time." of one and another, when called by Christ, how they immediately arose, and left all, and followed him. Thus of Peter and Andrew. Matthew 4:19–20, "And they straightway left their nets, and followed him." And so of James and John. Matthew 4:22, "And immediately they left the ship and their father, and followed him." Luke 5:27–28, Christ saw Levi the publican "sitting at the receipt of custom; and he said unto him, Follow me. And he left all, rose up, and followed him." So Christ said to the scribe that said he would follow Christ wherever he went, Matthew 8:19–20, "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." And to the other that desired first to go and bury his father, Matthew 8:21–22, "Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead." So when Elisha, when Elijah cast his mantle, and though at first he desired to go first and kiss his father and his mother, yet he was soon of another mind, and forsook all, and went and took the oxen that he was plowing with, "and slew them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave unto the people," and arose and followed Elijah, as in 1 Kings 19:19–21. So the spouse, in Psalms 45:10–11, is directed to "hearken, and consider, and incline" her ear to forget her own people and father's house; and so the king should greatly delight in her beauty. See note on Psalms 45:10. Ruth also was a type of a true Christian, who forsook her own country and kindred with a firm resolution of mind to cleave to Naomi's people, and to her God (Ruth 1:16). She left her father, and her mother, and the land of her nativity, and came to trust under the wings of the Lord God of Israel (Ruth 2:11–12).

"Let him which is in the house top not come down," etc. It so came to pass that if any neglected to flee out of Jerusalem in season or till the last siege of Jerusalem, there could be no opportunity afterwards, for then their enemies kept them in on every side, as Christ foretold. And not only so: it was not suffered to any to flee out of the city to the enemy, but as many as were suspected of any endeavor to escape were cruelly murdered by the soldiers within. And those that did find means to escape (choosing rather to fall into the hands of the Romans than endure the calamities of extreme famine and cruelty of the factious inhabitants within), they were commonly treated with great cruelty by the Romans. Some thousands of 'em were crucified, and they once ripped open the bowels of 2000 of those that fled out in one night on a report that they had swallowed gold. See a particular account of these things, "Miscellanies," no. 972.This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 20, 254–74.

-- 868 --

Matthew 24:21 ff.] See no. 292.Works, 15, 251–64.

Matthew 24:21–22.] See no. 55.Ibid., 66.

The days that "should be shortened," that are here more directly and immediately intended, are the days of the siege of Jerusalem. While the days of that siege lasted, the inhabitants exceedingly wasted away, died by famine and the sword, one of another, so that unless those days had been shortened, no flesh in Jerusalem had been saved, but all had died. Therefore "for the elect's sake," those days were shortened. It was for the elect's sake two ways. 1. Because thereMS: "they." were some Christians then left in Jerusalem that could not flee. Some were with child, and some gave suck, and some might be sick. The days were shortened out of respect to these few. 2. They were shortened for the sake of the elect that should hereafter be born, that were to come out of the loins of many of those Jews that were then in Jerusalem. (Compare Genesis 44:7.)This insertion is a later addition. And it may be also for the sake of some of the unbelieving Jews then living, that were afterwards to be brought in. But perhaps that time of great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world, etc., is not meant only [of] the days of Jerusalem's siege, but also the days of tribulation that precede or accompany other comings of Christ, viz. at the overthrow of the heathen empire, at the destruction of Antichrist, and the end of the world, all which comings of Christ respect seems to be had to in this chapter. And therefore it is said, vv, Matthew 24:29–30, "Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened," etc., "and then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven. Then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory," where 'tis evident Christ's last coming at the end of the world is especially aimed at. And if this be "immediately after the tribulation of those days," "the tribulation of those days" must be meant not only of the tribulation before Christ's coming at the destruction of Jerusalem, but also some other tribulation before another coming of Christ. See no. 292.This paragraph is a later addition. This reference is an even later addition. Works, 15, 251–64.

Matthew 24:22.] No. 292, §11.Works, 15, 259–60.

-- 869 --

Matthew 24:24.] No. 292, Corol. 1.Ibid., 263–64.

Matthew 24:24–25.] See the following note.

Matthew 24:24–28.] These "false Christs" here spoken [of] are not persons that set up for messiahs in opposition to Jesus and all that have appeared before, but are impostors that should pretend to be the same Jesus that was crucified, returned a second time, according to his promise. Christ warns his disciples not to be deceived by these impostors; and particularly, if any should tell them that Christ [is] "in the desert," or in any secret obscure place, they should determine upon it that he was an impostor. "For," says he, "as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even to the west, so shall the coming of the Son of man be." This distinguishes his coming from the coming of these false Christs, in two respects. 1. These false Christs would come in a private manner, in the deserts, and "in the secret chambers." But Christ, when he comes, he will come openly, and in a very public manner, as Matthew 24:30, in the sight of all the world, with clear manifestation, with a most evident and conspicuous glory, like lightning that can't be hid but glares in everyone's eyes, and shines from east to west, from one side of heaven to another, and is seen all over the face of the earth. This is eminently applicable to Christ's coming at the end of the world. 2. As it relates to Christ's coming at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, it not only denotes the publicness and openness of his coming, but particularly this circumstance of his coming, viz. that the light of his glory, i.e. the light of his glorious gospel, should shine from the east to the west, from the Jews to the Romans, that the Jews should be forsaken, and the Romans should be "the people of the prince that should come," according to Daniel's prophecy (Daniel 9:26). And then again, his coming is further distinguished from the coming of those impostors, in the next verse, "For wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together," for this determines the very time and place of his coming, concerning which, see notes on Luke 17:37.

Matthew 24:28.] No. 292, §4.Ibid., 253.

Matthew 24:29. "Immediately after the tribulation of those days."] See notes on Matthew 24:22.

-- 870 --

Matthew 24:29–30.] No. 292, §§12–16.Ibid., 260–64.

Matthew 24:30. "Then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven."] "The sign," i.e. the wonder. Christ had been telling, in the foregoing verse, of signs and wonders that should appear in heaven, as the sun's being darkened, the moon's not giving her light, the stars falling from heaven, and the powers of heaven being shaken. And after them shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, the greatest wonder of them all. Extraordinary appearances in the heavens are called "signs" (Luke 21:11), and those very things mentioned in the foregoing verse are called signs in Luke's account of this discourse (Luke 21:25).

'Tis evident beyond all dispute that by the coming of Christ, spoken of [in] this chapter, respect is not only had to his coming at the destruction of Jerusalem, by its description in this verse, and also by its more particular description in the next chapter, which is a continuation of the same discourse, and where Christ's respect [is] to the same coming.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Matthew 24:31.] See Isaiah 27:13.

Matthew 25:5. "While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept."] Hence we may observe that in a time of general declension, the godly themselves are wont greatly to decline, and to be as it were asleep. Thus it will be before the last coming of Christ, the bridegroom; and thus it commonly is before any remarkable coming of Christ to work any great change and revolution in the world for the advancement of his kingdom.

Matthew 25:12. "I know you not."] To determine the force of this expression, see Deuteronomy 33:9 and Job 9:21; Psalms 31:7.

Matthew 25:21. "Enter thou into the joy of thy lord."] The happiness that the saints enjoy in heaven, they enjoy in fellowship with Christ, as partaking with him of that joy that he has in the enjoyment of his Father's love, being members of him, and as such partaking of the joy of the head.

Matthew 25:24–27. "Then he which had received the one talent came and said," etc.] His excuse was the excuse that wicked men commonly make, viz. that his master was hard to his servants, and required more of ['em] than he had given them ability to do, that he required more gain and increase

-- 871 --

of his servants than he had given them wherewithal to make, than the talents that he had given them would produce. But this could be no excuse for his not doing what was in his power, and which he had ability and advantage, or his not improving the talent that he had, and making that gain and increase that his master had given wherewithal to make. As his master tells him, he is condemned out of his own mouth, seeing he owns that he was sensible that his master would exact gain of him, and, as he pretends, even with rigor, so that he ought to have done what he could. He ought to have made what gain he could of the talent that he had. If his master was such "an hard man," as to reap where he had not sown, doubtless he would expect to reap where he had sown.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. By saying this master was "a hard man," he has respect to his master's giving him so little; he had given him but one talent. This he despises, and makes nothing of, and excuses himself by it in a total negligence, as though it were unreasonable to expect anything at all from one that had received no more.

Matthew 25:29. "For unto everyone that hath, shall be given."] See note on James 4:6.

Matthew 25:34. "Prepared for you," etc.] That this has a special respect to the decree of election may be argued from Mark 10:40 and Matthew 20:23. See Exodus 23:20.

Matthew 25:35. "For I was an hungred."] The particleγάρ. "For" here don't necessarily show that this kingdom is bestowed for those good works as the reward that purchased it, anymore than it shows that forgiveness of sin is in such a manner bestowed for love to Christ, in Luke 7:47, "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven her, for she loved much," where it is evident by the context and particularly the words immediately following, that this love of Christ is spoken of as the consequent of the forgiveness of sin.

Matthew 26.] See no. 21.Works, 15, 54.

Matthew 26:6. "Now when Jesus was in Bethany."] See note on Mark 14:3.

Matthew 26:8–9.] A pretense of regard to the poor is often made a cloak of covetousness in Christ's professing disciples, and particularly in objecting against expense to put honor upon Christ in things that concern

-- 872 --

out [ward] decency, as in building decent houses for his worship, in honorably maintaining his ministers, as here what this woman did in anointing Christ was not for necessity, or any real external profit, but for decent respect.

Matthew 26:12. "She hath done it for my burial."] She was moved at this time to put this extraordinary respect on Christ by beholding the extraordinary contempt and rage of others, for it was now a time wherein the mortal enmity of his enemies did especially prevail. She anointed him with perfumed ointment in his suffering and low state, wherein he was treated as an outcast and one not fit to live, from like principles and like respect with that whence persons are wont to embalm the dead bodies of their dear departed friends, that are deeply affected, and their love greatly excited by their suffering of death. And so it was now, as Christ knew, that not only did a mortal enmity against him greatly rage, but prevailed in such a manner that it was likely soon to be effectual in his death; and perhaps this woman apprehended it from what she saw. This tended to justify the woman to the objectors, for it was looked upon by 'em all a warrantable and proper thing to be at considerable cost to put respect on dear departed friends, those that were very honorable especially, by embalming their dead bodies.

Matthew 26:15.] "Thirty pieces of silver" was the price of a servant, according to the law (Exodus 21:32).

Matthew 26:26. "This is my body."] See Galatians 4:24–25.

Matthew 26:29. "Till I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."] Not that new wine was more excellent than old, but it refers to the joy of the vintage, which was a time of great rejoicing, wherein they drank new wine. And wine was drank freely and plentifully; and it was liberally given to rich and poor, young and old (Isaiah 16:10).

Matthew 26:31. "All ye shall be offended because of me this night."] This expression imports that when they came to see their master apprehended and bound as a malefactor, they should be stumbled by it, and their faith shocked; and they should begin to think they had been mistaken in thinking that he was the Messiah. The expression is commonly so used in Scripture. So it implies, Matthew 13:55–57, "Is not this the carpenter's son," etc.… "And they were offended in him." And in many other

-- 873 --

places. So were the disciples stumbled and offended by the ignominy and sufferings Christ underwent. And therefore some of them said that day he rose, "We verily thought it had been he that should have redeemed Israel" [Luke 24:21].

Matthew 26:37–38. "Began to be sorrowful," etc.] "The words which our translators use here are very flat, and fall vastly short of the emphasis of those terms in which the evangelists describe this awful scene. For λυπεῖσθαι signifies to be penetrated with the most lively and piercing sorrow, and ἀδημονεῖν to be quite depressed and almost overwhelmed with the load. And Mark expresses it, if possible, in a more forceable and stronger manner; ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι [Mark 14:33] imports the most shocking amazement mingled with grief. And περίλυπός, in the next verse, intimates that he was surrounded with it on every side, so that it broke in upon him with such violence that, humanly speaking, there was no way of escape." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 498.

Matthew 26:39. "This cup."] See note on Psalms 16:5.

"O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me." See note on John 12:27–28.This reference is a separate entry.

Matthew 26:51. "And smote off his ear."] Note on Luke 22:50–51.

Matthew 26:54. "The scriptures be fulfilled."] See Psalms 40:70.

Matthew 26:64.] Christ's answer to the high priest is remarkable. The high priest asks him whether he be "the Son of god." He consents, but says he, "Nevertheless, ye shall hereafter see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven." He did not deny himself to be the Son of man, though he professed himself to be the Son of God. He teaches the union of the human and divine nature. It was wonderful, and what the high priest could not believe, that the Son of God should be arraigned as a criminal before his judgment seat. And Christ tells him he should see another thing equally wonderful, and that is "the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven," sitting the judge of the world, and be brought before his judgment seat. Nevertheless, though I be the Son of God, yet "ye shall see the Son of man at the right hand of power," etc.

-- 874 --

Matthew 26:65. "The high priest rent his clothes."] Contrary to that law, Leviticus 21:10. This probably foreboded that the Levitical priesthood was soon to be abolished, their priestly garments to be rent, and they to be divested of the honors and prerogatives of their office.

Matthew 26:74–75.] See "Shadows of Divine Things," no. 110.Works, 11, 92–93.

Matthew 27:1. "When the morning was come."] The Jews had anciently a tradition that on this day, viz. the fifteenth day of the month Nisan, the Messiah should redeem Israel. See SSS on Exodus 12:14.Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 365.

Matthew 27:4. "What is that to us? See thou to that."] From his bringing to them the money with which they had hired him, theyJE deleted "understood." supposed that he meant to have him released again, and that makes them make such a reply. As much as to say, We ben't bound to release him to ease your conscience. If you repent that you have betrayed him, we don't repent that we have apprehended him.

Matthew 27:7. "And bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in."] The mystery of it is this. The price of Christ's blood was paid to procure a place, a resting place for the souls of strangers and aliens when they die. It was the potter's field, because men are like earthen vessels. God is the potter, and we are the clay. Therefore hereby is signified our weakness and frailty, and God's sovereignty with respect to the disposition of us. We are the clay, so that Christ's redemption of us by his blood is here signified by a double type, viz. 1. the buying the potter's field. In the potter's field's being bought, the vessels are bought, or at least the clay, which we are. 2. It was a field bought to bury strangers in, which we just now explained. The types are two and distinct. See note on Matthew 26:15.

Matthew 27:9.] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, p. 76a–c.Kidder discusses the evidence that Jeremiah probably wrote the Zechariah 9-14, including the fact that the circumstances described there agree well with Jeremiah's time, but not with that of Zechariah. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 76.

Matthew 27:14.] See no. 105.Works, 15, 80.

-- 875 --

Matthew 27:22. "Let him be crucified."] "To have inflicted such a crimeHenry reads "punishment." as this on any free Jew would probably have been sufficient to have thrown the whole city and nation into an uproar; but now they were deaf to everything but the clamor of passion, and in their madness forgot with how dangerous a precedent they might furnish the Roman governor. And indeed it turned dreadfully on themselves, when such vast numbers of 'em were crucified for their opposition to the Romans, during the time of their last war." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 542, n. f.

Matthew 27:26. "Then released he," etc.] There seems to be a mystery in this. Barabbas, who in the Matthew 27:16 is said to be "a notable prisoner," and that was so notorous an offender, seems here to typify sinners in general, in whose room Christ suffered. Here the case was such that it must be so, that either Jesus or Barabbas must suffer, and one or the other must be released, which is the case with Christ and elect sinners. If they perish, there will be no need of Christ's suffering; if Christ suffers, they must be released; and if they are released, Christ must suffer. By Christ's suffering, Barabbas, though so great a sinner, was released, which shows the virtue of the blood of Christ for the redemption of the greatest sinners. And if it had not been for Christ's suffering, Barabbas must have been executed. So that he escaped by his death; he died as it were in his room.

Matthew 27:28. "Put on him a scarlet robe."] See note on John 19:2.

Matthew 27:29–30.] Here is represented what all do that bow the knee to Christ, and have no love nor honor to him in their hearts, and act in their practice as his enemies and despisers. They mock him, and smite him with the scepter they put into his hands, or make their pretended honor to him a means of his disgrace and wounding.

Matthew 27:33. "A place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull."] Christ, it seems, suffered in the common burying place of the city. He suffered among the dead; thus "was he numbered with the transgressors" [Isaiah 53:12]. He suffered over the dead, as dying for those that were dead. If Christ died for all, then were all dead. He conquered death in his own territories, that the dead might be released from the bonds of death. Accordingly, when he arose, many bodies of saints arose with him from that burying place.

-- 876 --

Matthew 27:35.] The manner of Christ's suffering, which was by wounding his hands and feet, is typical of the way in which he suffers in his cause and interest in the world from his enemies. He suffers as it were in his hands with which he works, and his feet which he goes upon. His works and his ways are found fault with, and reproached, and maligned. The works of his hands in his saints and in his church are hated and persecuted; his works are hindered and opposed.

Matthew 27:36. "And sitting down, they watched him there."] I.e. to guard him and the other two, that none might come there to rescue them till they were quite dead.

Matthew 27:45. "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness."] No. 339.Works, 15, 324.

Matthew 27:51. "The veil of the temple was rent."] This was at the ninth hour of the day, and therefore at "the time of the evening sacrifice," and so the time for "the priest to be ministering at the golden altar" before the veil. "And this being a high day, it is probable that Caiaphas himself might now be performing the solemn act of burning incense just before the veil." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 574.

"Rocks rent." See additional note 89, in the Appendix at the end of volume 3, of Doddridge, Family Expositor, p. 21.This paragraph is a later addition. Doddridge cites multiple sources, including accounts from travelers, testifying to the existence of "the extraordinary Cleft which still appears in a Rock at Mount Calvary."

"And behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain." No. 340.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 324–25.

Matthew 27:54. "This was the Son of God."] "Eisner,Jakob Eisner (1692–1750), author of Observationes sacrae in Novi Foederis libros, quibus plura illorum librorum loca ex auctoribus potissimum graecis & antiquitate exponuntur & illustrantur (2 vols. Trajecti ad Rhenum, 1720, 1728). in a very learned note on this place, has shown that some of the heathens had some notion among them that prodigies, especially storms and earthquakes, sometimes attended the death of extraordinary persons peculiarly dear to the gods." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 576.

Matthew 27:60.] See no. 98.Works, 15, 79.

-- 877 --

Matthew 28:1.] How to reconcile the seeming differences in the accounts of the evangelists about the time when the women come to the sepulcher, see Mr. Prince's Essay on the resurrection of Christ, p. 17.Nathan Prince (1698–1748), a tutor at Harvard College, reconciles the "seeming differences" in time by ascribing to the Greek verb the full sense of progression from daybreak to sunrise, thus allowing for the beginning, continuance, and end of their journey, or from the terminus a quo to the terminus ad quem. Prince affirms "perfect agreement" in the texts. An Essay to Solve the Difficulties that attend the Several Accounts given by the Evangelists of Our Saviour's Resurrection and His Appearances to his Followers on the day He rose. Wherein the Opinion of the most celebrated Harmonists and Commentators whether Protestants or Papists, of our own Nation or Foreigners are impartially represented and examined (Boston, 1734). On Prince, see Works, 15, 155, n. 3. See also no. 220.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 154–56.

Matthew 28:2–4.] Christ arose as the head of believers, to deliver them from a state of death, spiritual, temporal, and eternal. He as their head and captain of salvation broke the prison, set the doors wide open, broke the seal, rolled away the stone, laid the keepers dead, and left the sepulcher open, that all the dead that he has redeemed may come forth.

Matthew 28:9.] It may be pleasant and profitable to consider the various passions that these women felt in their hearts on this occasion. Christ was a person exceeding dear to them, and they lately had had their hearts filled and overwhelmed with sorrow upon occasion of the cruel and ignominious death that they with their own eyes had seen Christ put to. See Matthew 27:55–56. And they never expected to see him alive any more. And they had with great cost prepared precious ointments to anoint his body, and doubtless were much exercised that they could not have opportunity to do it, by the reason of the sabbath's coming on, till the third day after his death. And now they came very early the first day of the week, greatly engaged in their minds to do it. But when they came there, they found the sepulcher empty. They could not find the body of Jesus, as John informs, and had the sorrow of the disappointment in their design of anointing his body added to their sorrow for his death. While they stood here, disappointed and sorrowful, not knowing what to do, two angels appeared to them, and told them that Christ was risen and was alive. This filled them with surprise and joy, for it did not only take away their concern for their disappointment in not finding the body of Jesus in the sepulcher, but brought them the unexpected and unspeakably joyful news that Christ, their dear Lord, was alive again. How suddenly did this turn them from the deepest sorrow to overflowing joy. It is said in the Matthew 28:8, "They departed quickly from the sepulcher with fear and great joy, and did run to bring his disciples

-- 878 --

word." How eager were they to impart the joyful news to their fellow disciples that were sharers in sorrow for his death. And as they ran, Christ himself met them, and in a friendly manner saluted them. And what a new surprise was this! Now they see with their own eyes the truth of what the angels had told them. How did it heighten their joy now to see their dear Lord himself, that they had so lately seen put to so cruel a death, and never expected to see more, meet them alive, saluting them in a sweet and cheerful manner. And how do they express their joy and love to their risen Lord? They come and hold him by the feet, and worshipped him. They express their joy and testify their respect to him in the most dear, humble, and adoring manner.

Matthew 28:18–19. "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations."] I have acquired a right to all mankind. Go therefore, and bring 'em home to me.MS: "be." This shows that it was in Christ's aim to assert his right over mankind, that he had acquired by the labors he went through, by actually bringing all nations into his kingdom. And therefore, inasmuch as this has never been accomplished, we may suppose that there is a day remaining in which it will be accomplished; and that that reward of his humiliation, spoken of, Philippians 2:9–10, of every knee's bowing, and every tongue's confessing to Christ, shall be accomplished by an universal conversion of the world to the Christian faith, and a bringing all into the visible kingdom of Christ, an admission into which baptism is a sign and seal of. And the place of the Old Testament, whence that clause in Philippians is cited, seems chiefly to intend an accomplishment in this, as is evident if we take them with the foregoing words. Isaiah 45:22–23, "Look unto me, and be ye saved, all ye ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is none else. I have sworn by myself: the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear," which is agreeable to what God the Father says to his Son in the Psalms 2. "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. I will declare the decree.… Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee" (i.e. especially on the day of his resurrection). "I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for thy possession" Psalms 2:6–8]. This is that which is to be accomplished on the pouring out of the seventh vial, when it is proclaimed, as in Revelation 11:15, "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ."

-- 879 --

Mark

Mark 1:24.] See no. 76.Works, 15, 72. The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. "I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God." This is one of the appellations given to the Messiah in the Old Testament. Psalms 16:10, "Nor suffer thy Holy One to see corruption."JE deleted "Isaiah 10:17, 'The light of Israel shall be for.'" And he is called "the most Holy," or the holy of holies, in Daniel 9:24. "Seventy weeks are determined… to anoint the most Holy."

Mark 2:4.] This teaches us after what manner we ought to seek spiritual healing. We must break though all difficulties, must be violent in the matter. Let it be never so inconvenient for us as to our temporal ease and comfort, never so costly and troublesome, our places of habitation and rest must be brokenJE deleted "down." up, yea, and utterly destroyed, rather than fail of this benefit.

Mark 2:26. "In the days of Abiathar the high priest."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 72–73.Kidder defends the Evangelist against the charge by Jewish critics that his text is in error by suggesting that Abiathar was also called Abimelech, and that the category "high priest" was generic or not specific to one individual only, the equivalent of a "chief priest." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 72–73.

Mark 2:27–28.] 'Tis given as the reason why the Son of man is made Lord of the sabbath day. Christ is the Son of man, and he is the head of mankind, especially of the elect part thereof. He is their surety, their Savior, their Lord, king, and mediator. And therefore God saw meet that he should be constituted Lord of all that was for man, of all that was for his benefit or any way concerned his welfare. He is constituted the great disposer and dispenser of all his benefits; all is committed into the hands of their head. God hath set him king in Zion, and therefore has committed into his hands all that he has made for the people of Zion, for him to order and dispose.

-- 880 --

Mark 3:6. "Took counsel with the Herodians."] "The Herodians were a sect" that were zealous "for the family of Herod," and in compliance with them were "zealous for the authority of the Romans," and were conforming to the Roman customs in some particulars as Herod did, that were [an] exceeding offense to most of the Jews and especially the Pharisees. They and the Pharisees were sects "most diametrically opposite one to another, so that the conjunction of their counsels against Christ is a very memorable proof of the keenness of that malice, which could thus cause them to forget so deep a quarrel with each other." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 312, n. f.

Mark 4:5.] See no. 23.Works, 15, 54.

Mark 4:21.] The light that is in Christians is put "under a bushel" when it is hid under their covetousness, and it is put "under a bed" when it is hid under sloth.

Mark 4:25.] See no. 24.Ibid., 54–55.

Mark 4:26–28.] See no. 25.Ibid., 55. The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. 'Tis not man that makes his corn to grow, for the earth brings forth of itself; and it grows he knows not how. It is the influence of the heavens and the blessing of God; so it is in the kingdom of God. Man uses the means, but don't produce the effect; it is produced he knows not how. Very commonly persons can't trace the footsteps of God in the work of conversion. 'Tis very mysterial, and God therein is not confined to any certain method wherein his footsteps can be traced.

Mark 4:37–38.] Christ was asleep because it was now in the night; it was evening when they embarked (Mark 4:35), so that this voyage and this storm was in the night, as well as that which we read of, John 6:16–21. And that great triumph of Christ over Satan in casting out a legion of devils, and delivering and converting the poor demoniac, was in the morning [Mark 5:1–20], well representing the great things that Christ will do against Satan and for the miserable captivated souls of men in the morning of the great day of God's grace. See note on Matthew 14:24–25.

Mark 6:7.] He sent them, "two and two." It was best on many accounts that two should go together, but this was probably one end: that their testimony might be valid, for the testimony of two witnesses is true.

-- 881 --

Mark 6:8. "Save a staff only."] See Numbers 21:18.

Mark 6:40. "They sat down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties."] I.e. they were disposed "in a long square, containing an 100 in a rank and fifty in a file," for fifty hundred makes 5000. So they sat down in ranks or rows by hundreds and by fifties, an 100 in a row one way and fifty in a row the other. "This was the shortest and exactest way of ranging them," and the most convenient way, there being room to pass between them to give everyone his portion. And this "reconciles Mark's account with Luke's," who speaks of their sitting down by fifty in a company [Luke 9:14]. "Thus disposed, they would wait more patiently till they were served in their turns. The number would appear at once, and they would see that Christ knew it" (Doddridge).Family Expositor, 1, 487–88, n. h. And the company thus regularly disposed was the fitter type of the church (that is fed by Christ with spiritual food), as the congregation in the wilderness in their regular orderly disposition were,JE deleted "a type of the." who were fed for so many years with bread from heaven.

Mark 6:44. "And they that did eat of the loaves."] See no. 26.Works, 15, 55.

Mark 6:45 ff] Christ commanded his disciples to go, and row, and endeavor to cross the sea to the other side. And they strove long, toiling in rowing in vain, for the wind was contrary to them; and there was a great storm, as appears by the account of other evangelists, so that they could not get forward, and instead of that were in danger of being swallowed up of the sea. Thus they continued all night. And then in the fourth watch of the night, which was about break of day (See Wilson's Christian Dictionary),Wilson writes in an entry entitled "Watch," "For of old the night was divided in certain spaces, called Watches… which is sometimes put for the whole night." The fourth watch extended until the rising of the sun (Complete Christian Dictionary [6th ed.], p. 735). Christ came to them; and then the wind ceased, and they were presently at land "whither they went." See John 6:21. Their greatest distress was just before their deliverance; when they saw Christ coming, they cried out for fear. This is a lively representation of what is spiritual, and may be a great encouragement to both saints and sinners earnestly to seek God in the use of the means that he has prescribed, and labor and toil therein, though the wind and tide is against them, and all seems in vain. In this way we must be willing to continue to the end, toiling all night.

-- 882 --

Christ will come atMS: "&." last, and then we shall have success. Though weeping continue for a night, yet joy will come in the morning [Psalms 30:5]. So it was in the morning, once and again, that Christ came to the disciples after they had been toiling all night with their nets, and had caught nothing; and still at his command they let down the net, and had success. So it was when the day brake that Jacob obtained the blessing, after wrestling for it all night [Genesis 32:24–28].

Mark 6:52.] See no. 27.Works, 15, 55.

Mark 8:24.] 'Tis from the great dimness of men's sight that man looks like so great a thing to them. If men saw clearly, man would look like a far less thing than he does.

Mark 8:32. "And he spake that saying openly."] "Plainly" and "freely"; so παρρησία evidently signifies, and is often rendered in our version (compare John 10:2 and John 11:14). And in this sense it is opposed to speaking in proverbs (John 16:25, John 16:29). Christ had before given only distant and obscure hints of this (John 2:19, and John 3:14, and John 6:51; Matthew 10:38, and Matthew 12:40; and elsewhere). He had just before more expressly acknowledged himself to be the Messiah than ever before; and having done that, and it being now but a few months to his crucifixion, he more expressly and plainly than ever before tells them of his sufferings.

Mark 9:12. "And how it is written of the Son."] The words told them are understood. Christ told them that "Elias verily cometh first, and restoreth all things," and told them "how it is written," etc.

Mark 9:30–31.] By these two verses it is evident that one great and main reason why Christ frequently forbid the publishing of his miracles abroad in his lifetime was that nothing might be done to prevent his being crucified. When it is said here, Mark 9:30, "he would not that any man should know it," reference is had to that miracle that we have account of in the preceding verses, for Christ said this while they were wondering at this (Luke 9:43). And the reason why he would have it concealed is given in the Mark 9:31, viz. that the Son of man was to be delivered, etc. The same is evident by the Mark 9:9, and by what he said to the man out

-- 883 --

of whom he cast the legion. He refused to let him go with him into his own countryI.e. Jesus' own country. to publish the miracle among the Jews, who were the people that were to crucify him, but suffers him, yea, commands him, to go and publish it in his own country [Mark 5:18–20].

Mark 9:33–34.] Their disputing and jarring by the way about "who should be the greatest" seems to be emblematical of the differences, heats, and contentions that are maintained in the Christian church, or among Christians while in the way towardsJE deleted "a future state or the H." heaven, or the house where Christ resides (typified here by what is called the "house"). For almost all strifes and jarrings among Christians, whatever various pretenses they are colored over with, are indeed about this, viz. "who shall be the greatest." 'Tis an affectation of being uppermost that is indeed at the bottom of most or all unchristian heats among Christians. And here is applicable that warning of Joseph, who was a type of Christ, to his brethren, Genesis 45:24, "See that ye fall not out by the way." See notes on that passage.

Mark 9:38–39.] See no. 30.Works, 15, 56.

Mark 9:42. "These little ones."] See no. 31.Ibid., 56–57. JE deleted this reference in front of the preceding three words, and then he rewrote it here when he composed the following entry. "It is better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he were cast into the sea." I.e. the natural tendency and consequence of it is much more dreadful, and a being thus cast into the sea is a much more eligible evil than that risk that they run who offend any of these little ones. Not that it will certainly prove worse for him in the event, for he may be forgiven; yea, it may be so that such a sin may be overruled for his greater happiness. There are three ways in which anyone may offend God's saints.

1st, by persecution. So did the apostle Paul, and yet he obtained mercy. The final event to him was not worse than being drowned in the sea, but great good was brought to him out of this evil. He was all his days the more humble and the more excellent saint for it.

2ndly, offending them by casting stumbling blocks before them, by false doctrines whereby their minds may be darkened, their faith shocked, and they for a while may be seduced. But pardon of this may be obtained by repentance, as is evident by Revelation 2:20–22. "Thou sufferest

-- 884 --

that woman Jezebel, that calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed to idols. And I gave her a space to repent of her fornication, but she repented not. Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds."

3rdly, casting a stumbling block before them by our practice. So did the apostle Peter in the instance the apostle Paul reproved him for. Galatians 2:12–13, "For before certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles; but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them that were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him, insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation."

Mark 10:24 and Mark 10:26. "And the disciples were astonished," etc.] The reason why they were so astonished seems to be twofold. 1. This was contrary to the notions they had of the Messiah's kingdom as a kingdom of great temporal wealth and glory. They wondered therefore how it should come to pass that riches should exclude men out of it. And 2. It was very contrary to the notions they had been brought up in among the Jews, who had an high esteem of rich men. They were their scribes; and others that were their great men that were rich were in highest esteem among them, and supposed to be highest in favor with God. As to the poorer, meaner sort of people, they were low in esteem in comparison of them. They thought none so likely to be admitted as these, and therefore when they hear that these are like to be excluded, they say, Who then can be saved?

Therefore Christ greatly contradicted the notions of the Jews in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, in representing a rich man and child of Abraham as going to hell and not to Abraham's bosom, but seeing there afar off Lazarus, a poor stranger [Luke 16:19–23]. See Poole's Synopsis on Matthew 11:5, at the place marked thus

.This paragraph is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, IV (London, 1674), Pt. 1, cols. 303–4.

Mark 10:29–30.] See no. 148.Works, 15, 92–93.

Mark 10:32. "Jesus went before them."] Manifesting a great forwardness and readiness to go to Jerusalem, notwithstanding he had from time to time,

-- 885 --

and especially the last time he was at Jerusalem, been in such great danger through the malice of the Jews there (See John 10:31, John 10:39, and John 11:7–8, John 11:16.), and notwithstanding the public resolution that the great Sanhedrin there had come into, that at the first opportunity they would seize him, and put him to death, and had accordingly published a mandate "that if any knew where he was, he should show it, that they might take him" (John 11:53, John 11:57). "And they were amazed." I.e. "at the spirit and ardor which he discovered" in this journey. "And as they followed him, they were afraid." For though Jesus discovered no fear, those threatening appearances very much terrified them. The apparent danger that there was in his going to Bethany to raise Lazarus [John 11:1–45], which was before this, made 'em wonder at Christ's going there, and apprehensive of their own danger in following him (See John 11:53, John 11:57) But since that, the apparent danger was greatly increased by what the Sanhedrin had done on occasion of his raising Lazarus, which occasioned Christ to flee to Ephraim. But now they are astonished at his returning so quick, and [the] resolution that he manifested to go even to Jerusalem where the Sanhedrin sat, and that at the feast of the Passover when all his enemies would be gathered together. And they were much afraid of their own lives because they were his disciples. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 263–65.

Mark 10:37.] See Doddridge, Appendix to vol. 3, note 76."Note 76 points to an allusion from Talmudic writers regarding two distinguished members who sat on the right hand and the left hand, respectively, of the Sanhedrin's presiding officer (Family Expositor, 5, Appendix, 17–18).

Mark 10:46. "And as he went out of Jericho."] Concerning the seeming inconsistence of this circumstance with Luke's account, see no. 233.Works, 15, 182–84.

Mark 10:50. "And he cast away his garment, rose, and came to Jesus."] Which probably typifies that when persons do truly come to Christ, they cast away their covering, their excuses and pleas, their fig leaves, and the filthy rags of their own righteousness, and come naked.

Mark 11:13. "For the time of figs was not yet."] See no. 226.Ibid., 175–76.

I.e. theJE deleted "fig harvest." time of gathering figs was not yet come. "Dr. HalletJoseph Hallet (1691?–1744), a Dissenting minister and popular preacher in England, published three volumes of notes and discourses on select texts of the Bible under diverse tides (1729–36). has proved

-- 886 --

from incontestable authority that the climate of Judea, being abundantly warmer than ours, the Passover, though never later than April, commonly fell at the beginning of their harvest, i.e. of their summer, which is there vehemently hot, not only in May, but in March and April (in which last this Passover probably fell). Compare Joshua 3:15, and Joshua 4:19, and Joshua 5:10–11, and 1 Chronicles 12:15. See also Leviticus 23:15–17, compared with Exodus 9 and Ruth 2:23. Now 'tis equally certain that one, and that the most delicate kind of figs, was ripe in Judea at the beginning of summer (as we have a fine sort in England which are ripe before our harvest). See Hosea 9:10, Micah 7:1, Nahum 3:12, Jeremiah 24:2, Canticles 2:11–13, and Isaiah 28:4. And the fig tree's opening its leaves, which everybody knows do not appear till after the fruit, is spoken of as a sign of approaching summer (Matthew 24:32). Our Lord therefore at this time might well expect to find fruit on this tree, since the time of gathering in these early figs was not yet come. That καιρὸς σύκων signifies the time of gathering them in, Bp. Kidder has abundantly proved. Compare Matthew 21:34, Mark 12:2, and Numbers 13:23." Doddridge's note on the place.Family Expositor, 2, 314, n. f. "See Bp. Kidder's exposition of this text, Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 38–39,"Ibid. and also the margin of pp. 40–41.This sentence and the following paragraph are a later addition. Kidder defends Jesus' action against the charge that he had cursed the fig tree without cause, for if he were a divine person, he would not have expected figs on the tree at that time. Kidder explains the phrase "the time of figs" to be equivalent to "the time of gathering figs." He also suggests a "mystical sense" for the passage, signifying "the approaching malediction and rejection of the Jewish nation. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 38–41.

Luke 20:10, "And at the season" (ὁν καίρω, i.e. at the time of gathering the fruit), "he sent a servant to the husbandmen, that they should give him of the fruit of the vineyard."This and the preceding paragraph are a separate entry.

Mark 11:17. "My house shall be called of all nations an house of prayer."] It was in that court of the temple that was called "the court of the Gentiles, that the Jews permitted to be kept a market of sheep, andThis and the preceding word destroyed by hole in MS. oxen, and doves, and the tables of the money changers to stand;This word destroyed by hole in MS. whereby the Jews showed the mean regard they had for the Gentiles, placing them in the same court with their cattle." Christ, who came to be the Savior of the

-- 887 --

Gentiles, and to bring them to the enjoyment of the same privileges with the Jews, and as the Apostle expresses it, Ephesians 2:14, to break down the "wall of partition" between them (the Apostle there alluding to the wall that separated this court from the court of the Jews; see notes),I.e. on Ephesians 2:14. fitly mentions on this occasion the passage out of Isaiah 56:7, where and in the context is a most plain prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles to be partakers of the same privileges with the Jews. This prophecy Christ was come to fulfill, and therefore it well became him, and this business on which he came into the world, thus to manifest his resentment for so unreasonable a contempt of the Gentiles, and such a treatment of them that was so directly contrary to that regard which God was now about to manifest to them. This wall of separation was first broken down by the admission of Cornelius and his family into the Christian church [Acts 10:1–33], who was a proselyte of the gate, or one of them that used to worship in this court. Wells' Sacred Geography, vol. 4, pp. 54–55.Historical Geography of the New Testament (2nd ed.). "Vol. 4" appears on the spine of the binding. See also no. 330.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 313–14.

Mark 12:7.] See no. 32.Works, 15, 57.

Mark 12:24.] See no. 33.Ibid.

Mark 13:22.] See no. 34.Ibid.

Mark 14:3. "There came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment," etc.] This woman'sJE deleted "anointing." pouring this precious ointment on Christ seems to be ordered as a type of the church's or believing soul's exercise of the grace of the Holy Spirit towards Christ, which does primarily and summarily consist in love. Oil is the principal type made use of in Scripture to represent the Holy [Spirit]; and grace in the soulMS: "Heart ‹Soul.›" is only the Spirit of God dwelling in it, and acting in union with its faculties as a vital principle. As this oil is first poured forth from ChristMS: "God ‹X.›" into the heart, so it is poured forth from the heart again upon Christ as the great object as well as fountain

-- 888 --

of it. This ointment was exceeding precious, and exceeding sweet and fragrant (In the John 12:4, it is said, "the house was filled with the odor of the ointment."), and therefore does more fitly represent the grace of his Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers, which is represented as so sweet and lovely to Christ, in Canticles and elsewhere, and which we are told is "in the sight of God of great price" [1 Peter 3:4]. This is one way in which Christ is the Messiah, or Christ, or the anointed, viz. as he is not only anointed by God, but by the church, by every believing soul. See note on Daniel 9:25. As Jacob anointed the stone on which he rested in Bethel, see notes on that history in the twenty-eighth of Genesis, the second part.

The box in which this precious ointment was contained and out of which it was poured represents the heart. The believer does as it were pour forth his soul in love to Christ. Its being an alabaster box represents the purity of the heart that contains this sweet ointment. They are the pure in heart (The most common color of alabaster is "extremely white, and shining." See Chambers' Cyclopædia.)This parenthetical remark is a later addition. Chambers describes alabaster as "a kind of stone, softer than marble, yet harder than plaister of Paris," which was used for making statues, figures, ornaments, vases, columns, etc., because it cut smooth and easily. "Some derive the word from the Latin albus, because of the whiteness of this stone." He also notes that some critics have questioned whether a vase made of alabaster would break "so easily, as is intimated by St. Mark" (Cyclopaedia, 2, no pagination). only that have that precious treasure; they that pretend to grace and ben't pure in heart, do but deceive themselves. Those offerings alone are acceptable to Christ, or as a sweet savor or odor to him, that are offered out of a pure heart. If we regard iniquity in our hearts, God will not hear our prayers or accept any of our offerings. Again the box in which this ointment was, was broken ("And she brake the box, and poured it on his head."); so true Christian grace and divine love flows only out of a broken heart. And the heart of a saint never pours forth such sweet ointment, never sends forth such a sweet savor to Christ, as when it is most broken and contrite, as is evident by Psalms 34:18 and Psalms 51:17, and Isaiah 57:15 and Isaiah 66:1–2. In the instance that we have in the Luke 7, of a woman that anointed Christ with an alabaster box of ointment, which is exactly parallel to this, if not the same, there was this very thing remarkably manifest in the woman in the time of her anointing Christ that I suppose is represented by breaking the box, viz. brokenness of heart. For we are told in the Luke 7:38, that she "stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head,

-- 889 --
