and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment." If this here was not the same instance, yet probably it was like it in that respect as it was in all others, for this woman did [not] only anoint the head of Christ, but the feet, and wiped them "with her hair," as we are told in the John 12:3. Her anointing his feet represents the exercise of the grace of love and charity that is in the saints, not only to Christ himself, the head of the body, but towards his members and even the meanest of them.See JE's application of themes from this entry in the exposition of the "Sixth Sign" in his Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, namely, "Gracious affections are attended with evangelical humiliation" (Works, 2, 339–40).

Her breaking the box seems also to represent the believer's devoting and making a sacrifice of his heart to Christ, as 'tis said in the Psalms 51, "The sacrifice of God is a broken heart" Psalms 51:7]. Mary did not only devote the ointment that was so precious, and spend it upon Christ, but she devoted the box that was also precious to him. She brake it, and made a sacrifice of it to him she looked upon worthy of it. So the true believer looks on Christ as worthy that he should devote his whole soul a sacrifice to Christ.

See sermon on the words.JE's sermon on Mark 14:3 (no. 611), preached May 1741, with the propositions, "I. I shall briefly take notice of the nature and circumstances of the external act of this woman. II. Observe how it was resented [i.e. received] by Jesus Christ, on whom the act was done. III. Give the reason why it was so resented" (Mary's Remarkable Act, in Works, 22, 381). See notes on Luke 7:38.These two references are later additions.

Mark 14:50. "And they all forsook him, and fled."] It is one thing that shows the wonderful freeness, strength, and constancy of the love of Christ,JE deleted "that it should remain steadfast." that hisJE deleted "readiness." willingness to die for his people,MS: "Sinners ‹his people›." and to go through that great, and difficult, and terrible work for them, not only when he came to look death in the face, and to have a most terrible apprehension of the near approach of it, and God had forsaken him and hid his face from him, and Satan buffeted him, and his cruel enemies laid hold on like a parcel of hellhounds; but also when his people, that he was going to die and suffer all this for, basely forsook him, and disowned [him], and hid themselves from him, andJE deleted "Peter who foll." one of 'em who followed after him denied him, and was ashamed of him, that under all this opposition his love should hold to go through this extreme disgrace and torment for his people,

-- 890 --

that in the very time of it could not show so much respect to him as to watch with him one hour, and when he was apprehended, forsook and disowned him.

Mark 14:51. "A linen cloth wrapped about his naked body."] Which seems to be the garment he was wont to wrap himself in when he lay down to sleep at their usual lodging place in the Mount of Olives.

Mark 15:25.] Concerning the time of Christ's crucifixion, see "Scripture," no. 445.Works, 15, 527–28.

Mark 16.] No. 220.Ibid., 154–56.

Mark 16:2. "At the rising of the sun."] Note on Luke 23:44.

Luke

Luke 1:13. "Thy prayer is heard."] I.e. especially "his prayers for the deliverance of Israel by the Messiah, whose appearance was then much expected and the more earnestly desired just at this time, as they suffered so many grievous things, by the oppression of the Romans and the tyranny of Herod, which, towards the close of his reign, grew more and more insupportable." We can't suppose he was praying for children, having evidently "given up all expectations of that kind." See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 14, n. d.

Luke 1:14.] See Doddridge's additional notes, Appendix to vol. 3, p. 2, n. 4.Note 4 is a digression regarding the centrality of the family of Aaron, i.e. the Levites, in the Jewish religion, and God's special care in maintaining the male members (Family Expositor, 3, Appendix, 2).

Luke 1:15. "And he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb."] Hence we learn that it is not needful that a man should himself have experience of the terrors of the law and that legal humiliation that is preparatory to conversion, or that he should ever remember the time when he was in a natural condition and sensibly under the misery of such a state, in order to his being eminently fitted to preach the law, or to preach so as shall tend to awaken sinners' consciences, and to humble them, and to lead them in a preparatory work, for this was eminently the office of John the Baptist above all men that ever lived, and yet [he] was sanctified from the womb.

Luke 1:34. "Seeing I know not a man."] Note on Isaiah 7:14.

Luke 1:35.] How the Virgin Mary herein was a type of the church and of the believing soul, see no. 314.Works, 15, 288–89.

"That holy thing which shall be born of thee." "That which was born of Mary was a first-born son, and holy to the Lord, as the true first-born. Luke 2:22–23, 'They brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the

-- 892 --

Lord; as it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb, shall be called holy to the Lord.' This is the true first-born, prefigured by all the first-born of Israel, and holy to the Lord in a peculiar and most eminent manner." Glas, Notes on Scripture-Text, No. 1, pp. 4–5.This paragraph is a separate entry. Glas' citation is part of a section on the "Import of these names of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and, the Word of God. With an account of the Image of God in Man." Works (2nd ed.), III, 12.

Luke 1:45. "And blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord."] Thus the Virgin Mary, though a pure virgin, conceived by faith, which [is] a much greater evidence of the power of faith than Sarah's conceiving seed "when she wasJE deleted "ninety years old." past age," which yet is mentioned as an extraordinary instance of the power of faith (Hebrews 11:11).

"It is worthy of our remark that Mary, though a young virgin, should so readily believe an event in itself so much more wonderful than that which Zacharias, though an aged priest, had found it so difficult to credit."Doddridge, Family Expositor, 1, 23, n. e. The blessed Virgin, in faith in God, resignedMS: "resign." her reputation and even her life to the divine care and providence, as well as her interest in Joseph, whom she was espoused to, and we may suppose, dearly loved, for all these were exposed by her by being found with child after she was espoused by another than her husband. But yet when the angel had delivered his message to her, she in humble faith and resignation says, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word" [Luke 1:38].

Luke 1:74. "Serve him without fear."] Exodus 4:23.

Luke 2.] Concerning the birth of Christ, see no. 204.Works, 15, 127–28.

Luke 2:26. "The Lord's Christ."] Or "the Lord's anointed," as it signifies.

Luke 2:44.] "They, supposing him to be in the company, went a day's journey" homeward before they missed him. And then, when they came to inquire for him, and "sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance" that were their fellow travelers, "they found him not" Luke 2:45].

-- 893 --

Luke 2:46.] "They found him in an apartment of the temple, where the teachers of the law used to lecture upon it to the people, and where young persons, in particular, were examined, and had liberty to ask what questions they thought proper for their further information (Which things are well illustrated by Dr. Lightfoot in his Horæ HebraicæHorae Hebraicæ et Talmudicæ (6 vols., 1658–78). on this place. See also Drusius'sJohannes Drusius (1550–1616), a biblical scholar, who published I. Drusii annotationum in totum Iesu Christi Testamentum (1612). excellent note on this place.). Here Jesus placed himself among others on this occasion, not that he was disputing with the doctors, but only asking some questions, and answering others, which was very usual in these assemblies, and indeed the very end of them. He might be said to be 'in the midst of the doctors,' as they sat on benches of a semicircular form, raised above their auditors and disciples." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 83–84.

Luke 2:49.] The more literal translation is, "'Do ye not know that I ought to be at my Father's?' In the Syriac version it is, 'in my Father's house.' So Josephus puts, ἐν τοῖς τοῦ Διός, for 'in Jupiter's temple.' Compare John 19:27, Esther 5:10, and Esther 6:12, and Esther 7:9. Gr." (See Doddridge.)Ibid., 84–85. The "Gr." appears to be Doddridge's abbreviation for "Grotius," who is one of three sources he identifies as following the Syriac version of the text. So that Christ does as much as say, How is it that ye spent so much time in looking for me at other houses in Jerusalem, and did not go in the first place to the temple, which is my Father's house, where you might easily think it was most likely that I should be found?

In Luke 7:25, ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις εἰσίν is translated "in kings' palaces."This sentence is a later addition.

Luke 3:4–5.] "Grotius has most elegantly illustrated the reference, that appears so plainly in this passage, to the custom of sending pioneers to level the way before princes, when they are coming with numerous attendants." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 1, 91, n. h.

Luke 3:10, Luke 3:12, Luke 3:14. "What shall we do?"] It confirms me that those remarkable stirs about eternal salvation that there are sometimes in our congregations are from the Spirit of God, for it seems to have been very much so in Judea in John's time by all accounts that we have of it. Christ observes that the kingdom of heaven suffered violence, and the violent took it by

-- 894 --

force, and that all men pressed into it. This stir in Judea, in a great measure, ceased before John's death, but many were savingly converted, had their natures changed, and so were prepared for Christ. They were prepared to embrace the gospel of Christ when it should be preached by him and his apostles, as many of them did before Christ's death, but more afterwards. Thus John made "ready a people prepared," as Luke 1:17. See Luke 7:29–30, Acts 19:3, and Acts 18:25.

Luke 3:23. "Which was the son of Heli."] "An ancient rabbi expressly calls Mary, the daughter of Heli."The father of Joseph in the genealogy of Jesus. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 48, n. 1.

Concerning the difficulties in the genealogies of Matthew and Luke, see Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 108–68.This sentence is a later addition. Demonstration on the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 108–68. See note on Matthew 1.

Luke 3:27. "Salathiel, which was the son of Neri."] See note on Jeremiah 22:30.

Luke 3:36. "Which was the son of Cainan."] This person is not mentioned in the genealogy of the Old Testament; and 'tis probable there was no such person in the line between Sala and Arphaxad, for Luke only reckons over the lineage as they in those days had it in the Bible that was in common use, which was the Septuagint. For Luke don't, as an historian, assert that Sala was the son of Cainan and that Cainan was the son of Arphaxad, but only that it was so supposed, as it was reckoned. For at the beginning of this genealogy he says, Jesus, "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, of Heli, of Matthat, of Levi, of Melchi, of Janna, etc.," as it is expressed in the original.ὤν υἱός, ὡς ἐομίζετο, ῎Ιωσήν, τοῦ ῎Ηλὶ τοῦ Ματθὰτ τοῦ Λευὶ τοῦ Μελχὶ τοῦ ῎Ιανναὶ. For 'tis all but one sentence to the end of the chapter, so that these words, "as was supposed," relate to all the remaining part of the sentence and not only to the next immediate link of the chain. And this is no forced, but a natural construction as the words stand in the original.

Luke 3:38. "Which was the son of God."]Here referring to Adam. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, latter half of the fourteenth paragraph.Works, 18, 287–88.

Luke 4:9.] The devil, finding by the unsuccessfulness of the foregoing temptation that "it was in vain to tempt Christ to a distrust of providence, he was for trying to persuade him to presumption." (Doddridge.)Family Expositor, 1, 111. Thus the devil often in his temptations goes from one extreme toJE deleted "another." the contrary.

Luke 4:18. "To preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind."] Here "seems to be an allusion to the wretched state of those prisoners who, according to the inhumaneMS: "inhuman." Doddridge: "inhumane." custom still retained in the Eastern countries, had their eyes put out." "And to set at liberty those that are bruised." I.e. bruised with their fetters. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 192.

Luke 4:25. "Three years and six months."] See Manton on James, p. 605.Thomas Manton cites a variety of commentators who attempted to reconcile Luke's reference to "three years and six months" with the dating in 1 Kings 18:1 where the text reads "in the third year" (Practical Commentary on James).

Luke 5:5. "We have toiled all night."] WhichJE deleted "signifies." represents the dark times of the church wherein Christ's ministers are wont to labor in vain. See "Scripture," no. 366,Works, 15, 356–57. and note on John 21:3–7.

Luke 5:8. "Depart from me."] See additional notes in the Appendix to Dr. Doddridge's third volume of Family Expositor, p. 9, n. 36.Note 36 glosses Peter's comment by citing the ancient tradition that it was "improper and unsafe" for "Good Men to be in the same Ship with Persons of an infamous Character."

Luke 5:11. "They forsook all."] See note on Matthew 4:21–22.

Luke 6:5.] See no. 500, second paragraph.Works, 15, 593.

Luke 6:9. "To do good, or to do evil? To save life, or to destroy it?"] While Christ was doing, these that found fault with him were plotting mischief. While he was saving life, they were on a murderous design, seeking an advantage against him to accuse him and have him put to death. This Christ seems to refer to in what he says. The murderous design of those

-- 896 --

that Christ speaks to appears by what followed. See Luke 6:11, and Matthew 12:14, and Mark 3:6. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 311–14.

Luke 7:13. "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her."] This we find given as a reason of many of Christ's miracles for the help and relief of others, that "he had compassion" on them. Matthew 14:14, "And Jesus went forth, and saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them, and healed their sick." Thus Christ, when he was about miraculously to feed the multitude in the wilderness, says to his disciples, "I have compassion on the multitude" (Matthew 15:32 and Mark 8:2). This is given as the reason of his opening the eyes of the two blind men (Matthew 20:34). So here Christ raises the widow's son from compassion to her. And when the distressed come to Christ, seeking that he would help them by some miracle, they come begging his mercy and compassion. Thus when the man brought his son to Christ that [was] possessed with a devil, he begs Christ to have compassion on 'em, and help them (Mark 9:22). And so the two blind men, they cry, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on us." And again, the other two blind men (Matthew 20:30). By this it evidently appears that he did not work miracles as other prophets, but as a divine person. It was a godlike way of working miracles, to heal the sick, to open the eyes of the blind, to cast out devils, to create bread for a multitude in the wilderness, and to raise the dead, from his own compassion, or because he had compassion on those that suffered. It shows that the works were properly his own, as he pretended them to be (John 5:17, and onwards, and in many other places), that they were properly the effects of his own power as well as his own mercy and inclination. It showed that he had nature properly at his own dispose, as the Lord of nature. Christ did professedly work miracles at his own will. John 5:21, "The Son quickeneth whom he will," and did set himself upon a level with God in working miracles, as may be seen in that verse and the context.

Luke 7:37.] This woman seems to have been before a common whore, and that precious box of ointment was what she kept to anoint herself with, to render herself agreeable to her gallants, and particularly used to anoint her hair with, which was accountedMS: "account." the special ornament of women, that she now makes use of as a towel to wipe Christ's feet. And

-- 897 --

having, now [that] she is brought to repentance, no further use for this costly box in that way, nor the precious ointment that is in it, she breaks the box, and pours the ointment on Christ.

See note on Mark 14:3.This reference is a separate entry.

Luke 7:38.] She anoints his feet and not his head, expressing her sense of her own unworthiness and her high and exalting esteem of Christ. She first washes his feet with her tears, and wipes them with her hair, to prepare them for being anointed. In this account is represented the manner of a sinner's closure with Christ. As this woman comes at Christ's feet, and first washes his feet with her tears, and then embraces, and kisses, and anoints them, so persons when they first come to Christ come in an humble manner, and ordinarily have first sensible exercises of contrition and repentance before they sensibly embrace Christ by faith and love, and rejoice in him. She wipes his feet with her hair, which is the ornament and glory with which nature hath crowned the head of the woman (1 Corinthians 11:15). Hair is the natural crown of the head, and hence baldness was looked upon so disgraceful. See notes on 2 Kings 2:23. But such an high esteem has this woman of Christ, and such a mean thought of herself in comparison of him, that she did [not] think her hair too good to be used to wipe Christ's feet. See notes on Mark 14:3 and John 12:3.

Luke 7:41–42 ff.] Christ plainly intimates that he is the creditor, or that he is the being against whom sin is committed, for he is the person that forgives the debtor (Luke 7:48–49), and he is the person the debtor loves for forgiveness of the debt (Luke 7:44–47). And if Christ be the creditor, he is God.

Luke 8:1–3.] This company of women that followed Christ from city to city, ministering to him of their substance, is a little image and resemblance of that blessed company of virgins that "follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth," spoken of in the Revelation 14:4.

Luke 8:6. "It withered away, because it lacked moisture."] In Matthew it is, "And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away" [Matthew 13:6], which is very agreeable with this, for that is the reason that it lacked moisture, viz. because the burning heat of the sun presently dried up all the moisture that was in the

-- 898 --

thin covering of earth on the rock, and turned it into dry dust. And then no wonder that the growth was scorched and withered!

Luke 8:23.] In all probability it was that legion of devils that possessed the man Christ was going to deliver that raised this storm, if possible, to prevent Christ's coming into the land. For 'tis evident by the sequel that they had a suspicion of his coming on a design against them, and therefore were dreadfully afraid. See Luke 8:28.

Luke 8:23 ff.] This story teaches us that when Christ rescues souls out of the hands of Satan, he comes through a dreadful gulf and stormy sea to their deliverance, in which he suffers death, as here he went over a stormy sea in which he was overwhelmed and covered with the waves, and was in the meantime asleep, which is the image of death. See observation on the story of the man possessed by the legion of devils, in my sermons beginning with Luke 8:27.JE's sermon on Luke 8:27 (no. 650c), preached Jan. 1742, with the doctrine, "Men as they are by nature are possessed with devils" (MS, p. 2).

Luke 8:28–31.] See no. 131.Works, 15, 87. The devil's praying to Christ so earnestly out of fear of misery when about to be cast out is a representation of whatMS: "when." commonly is in natural men when under awakenings. Before the devil is cast out, they will pray earnestly, for fear of torment from mere nature which, as it is in itself and as it is in them, is corrupt and is a devil. The voice of the devil in this case represents the voice of the sinner, as it does, Acts 8:7.

Luke 8:29. "And he brake the bands."] The devil's management of this possessed man is a lively image of his cruel, violent management of many that are spiritually under his dominion, as in other respects, so particularly in causing him to break the strong bonds, even chains and fetters of iron and brass. So the devil causes his servants to break the strongest bonds, and violate the strongest obligations and ties of duty, convictions of conscience, and their own interest.

Luke 8:31. "Go out into the deep."] Or "abyss," i.e. out of the man into hell. The "deep" or abyss, here mentioned, is the same with that "bottomless pit" in the twentieth of Revelation, into which Satan is to be cast and

-- 899 --

chained up in the beginning of the millennium. Hence we may argue that hell is in the interior parts of the earth.

Luke 8:39.] There is scarce any text in the Bible that seems so much to justify persons'JE deleted "telling or." publishing their experiences.

Luke 8:43–44.] See a note on this in "Miscellanies," no. 645.Works, 18, 178.

Luke 9:21–22. "And he straightly charged them, and commanded them to tell no man that thing, saying, The Son of man must suffer many things," etc.] I.e. he gave this as the reason why they should not tell that thing, viz. lest discovering of it should prevent his suffering. These verses may be a key to open to us the reason why Christ so industriously concealed himself, and so often gave charges not to make him known till after his resurrection.

Luke 9:28. "And it came to pass about an eight days after these sayings."] Matthew and Mark express themselves thus: "and after six days." Here is no disagreement between these, for Matthew and Mark reckon the days that were between the day when he said these things, and the day when this was accomplished. Therefore they express themselves so, "And it came to pass after six days." And the reason why they reckon only the six complete days that were between seems to be that these things that were spoken, mentioned in the preceding words, seem to have been spoken towards the evening or latter end of the day. And the transfiguration seems to [be] at the beginning of the day, according [to] the Jewish reckoning, for it was in the night, concerning which, see notes on Luke 9:32. But that these forementioned things were spoken at the latter end of the day, or towards evening, seems very probable, for, by comparing the accounts of the several evangelists, Christ had gone that day before from Bethsaida to the coasts of Caesarea Philippi, which by Prideaux's map was at a considerable distance.A fold-out map of Palestine, or the Holy Land, is attached after p. xxxii in Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1. But Luke reckons in both the day wherein these things were spoken, and also the day of his transfiguration, which with the six complete days between made eight days. See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, pp. 104d–e and 105a.Kidder reconciles different time references among the evangelists in this way. When Luke "says that happened about eight days after," he is supposing "six days complete," which allows him to say "about eight days after." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), 104–5.

-- 900 --

Luke 9:32. "But Peter and they that were with him were heavy with sleep. And when they were awake, they saw his glory, and the two men that stood with him."] Christ's transfiguration seems to have been in the night, for it was a very usual thing for Christ and his disciples to lodge abroad in the night in the open air in mountains and such like places. See notes on Luke 21:37. And this seems to be the reason why these disciples were heavy with sleep. They seem to have been there in the mountain all night. And therefore it is said to be the "next day, when he came down from the hill (Luke 9:37), when much people met him," etc., for these people met him as they were coming from this mountain, as seems plain by the accounts of the other evangelists (Matthew 17:14 and Mark 9:14–15).

"Peter and they there with him were heavy with sleep." It was not only in the night, but weary with the labor of ascending so high a mountain. And therefore while their Master was praying (as he sometimes was wont to spend the whole night in prayer in mountains and solitary places), they fell asleep. This was before his transfiguration, so that they did not see the beginning of it.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Luke 9:57–62.] These several instances that are here given are not to be supposed to have been all at one and the same time. They are set down together because they are all of the same nature, but doubtless happened atMS: "at difference." different [times]. One was when Christ was about to go to the other side of the sea of Galilee, and therefore Matthew sets down the account then (Matthew 8:18–19 ff.). Another of the instances was when Christ was going up to Jerusalem to suffer there, and therefore Luke sets down the account of them at that time. And another instance might probably be at some other time.

Luke 9:62. "He that puts his hand to the plough," etc.] Here the business of religion is compared to the business of an husbandman through the course of the year, which is begun with his ploughing his field in the spring, and is finished with his gathering in his harvest. The business of religion is in other places of Scripture compared to the business of an husbandman, as it most fitly may upon many accounts. It requires diligence, watchfulness, and constancy. The success of it depends on the divine blessing, on the showers, dews, and shines of heaven, like that.

-- 901 --

There is a great probability of success in a way of diligence, but yet it depends on God's sovereign blessing, without an absolute promise (Hosea 10:12, Jeremiah 4:3). It requires long patience in order to a receiving the harvest (James 5:7). And innumerable things in husbandry are lively images of things that pertain to the business of religion. See Psalms 126:5–6.

Furthermore, it is worthy to be observed that there is no employment that men are engaged in that more requires them to have their eyes always forward than plowing, in him that holds or puts his hand to the plow, that he may guide and direct the plow. His hand will be quickly out when his eye is off.

Luke 10:17. "Even the devils are subject to us through thy name."] This seems to be more than they expected, for when Christ sent them forth, he bid them heal the sick, but told 'em nothing of their casting out devils, as he did the twelve when he sent them forth.

Luke 10:28. "This do, and thou shalt live."] By which I would observe, that those same things that were under the old testament proposed as terms of acceptance with God are terms of acceptance now under the gospel.

Matthew 19:17–18.This reference is a separate entry.

Luke 10:30.] Mr. Maundrell, who visited these parts at the latter end of the last century, gives this account, "that the whole country between Jerusalem and Jericho is all rock and desert, and so apt to be infested with thieves." Wells' Sacred Geography, vol. 4, p. 121.Historical Geography of the New Testament (2nd ed.). "Vol. 4" appears on the spine of the binding.

Luke 10:36. "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbor to him?" etc.] Christ told him that if he would love his neighbor as himself, he should live. And "he, willing to justify himself, asked the question, Who is my neighbor?" [Luke 10:29]. He was willing to have it, that his love and beneficence had been extensive enough to answer this rule, and entitle him to life. It was the general opinion amongst the Jews that the rule extended no farther than to those of their nation, and that there was no duty nor loveliness in loving or showing kindness to a Gentile, and especially a Samaritan. Christ, therefore, having proposed this instance of a Samaritan's showing kindness to a Jew, convinces him that it was amiable

-- 902 --

in him, that he did a neighborly part. It was so proposed that he could not help acknowledging it, and so would convince him that the rule of loving our neighbor extended to such an action, and that it would be amiable in a Jew to extend kindness to a Samaritan, as well as in a Samaritan to show kindness to a Jew. For if the Jews were neighbors to the Samaritans, then the Samaritans by consequence must be neighbors to the Jews. Hereby Christ evidences two things to him, viz. that the Gentiles, those that were of another nation and religion, were his neighbors, and also that he ought to do the part of a neighbor to his enemy, for the Jews and Samaritans were bitter enemies, one to another. Both these were contrary to the received notions of their lawyers and scribes. They made a distinction between a man's neighbor and his enemy, and were wont to say, Thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy.

Luke 10:38–42.] No. 295.Works, 15, 266–67.

Luke 10:41–42.] As of old, God declared, 1 Samuel 15:22, that he had more pleasure "in obeying the voice of the Lord" than in sacrifices, and "to hearken" was better "than the fat of rams," better than the most sumptuous feasts they held for the honor of God. And God directs us to "be more ready to hear" than to offer sacrifice [Ecclesiastes 5:1]. So here Christ manifests that the behavior of Mary, who was ready to hear Christ's word, and hearkened to the voice of the Lord, was more acceptable to him than the behavior of Martha, who showed her respect to Christ in another way, viz. in making a feast for Christ.

Luke 11:16. "Sought of him a sign from heaven."] Though the discourse immediately before had been about the miracles he wrought, and particularly his casting out devils, but they insisted on something more remarkably convincing. And possibly by "a sign from heaven," they mean "some such celestial appearance" as several of the ancient prophets gave, "some miracle performed in the visible heavens, where, they seem to have thought, imposters had less power than on earth (See Matthew 16:1, Mark 8:11, John 6:30.). And they might probably conclude they had the better excuse for making such a demand, as Moses (Exodus 9:22–24, and many other places), Joshua (Joshua 10:12), Samuel (1 Samuel 7:9–10), and Elijah (1 Kings 18:38) had given such signs." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 383, n. a.

-- 903 --

Luke 11:24–26.] By comparing these verses with what goes before, it is confirmed that apostasy is one great ingredient or constituent of the unpardonable sin, for 'tis manifest Christ says this of those same Pharisees spoken of before, that said, "He cast out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of the devils" [Luke 11:15]. 'Tis more manifest still by comparing what is said in this place with Matthew 12:22–45. There, speaking of the unclean spirit being "gone out of a man" Matthew 12:43], and returning again, etc., he adds, "Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation" Matthew 12:45]. It seems there was a time when these Pharisees had much of the common influences of the Spirit of God, and the unclean spirit for a season seemed to be gone out of them. And this probably was a consequence of the awakening they were the subjects of by John [the] Baptist's preaching. But after the illuminations they then had, it seems that their religion greatly degenerated (though they were still very religious in their way). They were exceedingly lifted up with spiritual pride, and fell into the condemnation of the devil, and at last into the unpardonable sin. Hence 'tis manifest that we nowhere in Scripture have any description of the unpardonable sin, but that apostasy is one thing that constitutes it.

Luke 11:27–28.] See note on Luke 1:35.

Luke 11:30. "For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites."] Note on Jonah 3:5.

Luke 11:44. See no. 28.Works, 15, 56.

Luke 11:48. "Truly ye bear witness," etc.] Here are two things that Christ means when he speaks of their building the sepulchers of the prophets. First, he has respect to their literally building their sepulchers. They were exceeding superstitious and hypocritical in this, and hereby they condemned themselves in their own persecuting spirit and practice, for here was a pretense of great respect to the memory of the prophets, and a disapprobation of the act of their fathers in killing of saints. The language of it was, "If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets," as Matthew 23:30. And yet they did the like. Secondly, Christ has respect to their building their sepulchers allegorically, viz. in going on in the same kind of work, in adding other saints to their graves, whereby they did as it were garnish their sepulchers, as increasing a man's family, and adding to the number

-- 904 --

of the living of the family, and propagating and continuing the family, is called "building hisOr: "the." house," as Deuteronomy 25:9, Ruth 4:11. So adding to men's graves, and continuing the slaughter of men of the same generation or kind, is called "building their sepulchers." By this building the sepulchers of the prophets whom their fathers killed, they testified an allowance of the deeds of their fathers. 'Tis probable that this was a common expression amongst the Jews, and [a] metaphor that they used to signify this. If a man died, and any killed his children and relations, they built his sepulcher for him. If a king was slain, and many of his subjects were slain, they built his sepulcher. If a general was slain, and many of his army with him, they that killed his soldiers built his sepulcher. His soldiers are as it were gone to attend him. So if a man be slain, and his posterity and kindred are slain because of their relation, they are sent to the grave as it were to accompany him. So the saints that are slain for the same cause that the prophets were, are sent as it were to their graves to be company for them, and to build their sepulchers for them. See Ezekiel 32, beginning with the Luke 11:29–54, and Luke 11:31.

This is not the only instance wherein Christ is to be understood in two different senses when speaking of a thing, the one a literal sense, and the other mystical, in the continuation of the same discourse. There is very much a like instance with this. Luke 22:35–36 speaks of "purse and scrip," etc., in a literal sense in one verse, and mystical in the next.

Christ seems to explain himself in the verse following in this sense. "Therefore also said the wisdom of God," i.e. Christ, "I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute" Luke 11:49]. Thus they shall build and garnish the sepulchers of the ancients, and so bear witness that they allow the deeds of them that killed, and by this consent to their deeds, brought the guilt of them upon them, as it follows in the next verses, "That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation," etc. Luke 11:50].This and the following paragraph are a later addition.

Or these two verses may be thus paraphrased: "You seem to condemn the deeds of your fathers, and to honor the prophets whom they killed, in that you build the sepulchers of the prophets whom they murdered. But really and in truth, you honor not the prophets, but them that killed, and by your practice show that you approve of their deeds, and do rather

-- 905 --

build the sepulchers of the murderers that slew the prophets, than of the prophets themselves."

Luke 12:1–5. "Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell."] It seems plain from hence that the souls of wicked men, after they are dead, go to hell before the resurrection. Christ seems plainly to speak of their being cast into hell as a thing consequent upon their dying, and as a punishment that is inflicted upon them while they are in a state of death. The distinction that Christ here makes between body and soul naturally leads to this interpretation. Men can only kill the body; but God, after he hath killed the body, is able to cast the remainder into hell. And besides, Christ's saying, "Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do," seems to me plainly to imply that the soul lives in a separate state after the body is dead, that their power reaches only the body; it don't reach the soul, but that lives and acts as it did before. Whereas if the soul was not, or perceived and acted not, till the resurrection, it would not be so. The soul would cease for the present. It would cease as to any life it has with the body, and would [not] rise again to life till the body did. In short, the soul would suffer the same fate that the body doth.

Luke 12:36. "When he will return from the wedding."] Christ makes use of this comparison, because marriages used to be in the night, and the guests often were wont to return from the entertainments late in the night. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 120.

Luke 12:49. "I am come to send fire on earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?"] I am come to send that religion, that gospel and Spirit, that will prove in many respects like fire. "And what will I, if it be already kindled?" καὶ τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη, which Dr. Doddridge translates thus, "And what do I wish? O that it were already kindled!" And [he] says in his note on this place, "I think Sir Norton KnatchbullKnatchbull (1602–85), a scholar and member of the Long Parliament, published Animadversiones in libros Novi Testamenti (1659). has abundantly established this version. Dr. WhitbyDaniel Whitby (1638–1726), an English divine, the rector of St. Edmund's church in Salisbury, and author of A Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament (2 vols. London, 1703). (who here, as in many other places, transcribes from Grotius) seems fully to have proved, that εἰ sometimes has this force. Compare Luke 19:42, and Numbers 22:29; Joshua 7:7; Psalms 81:13

-- 906 --

Psalms 81:13, Septuagint. (Perhaps we may add Luke 22:49.)Doddridge reads Luke 22:42. Both verses contain εἰ. See Grotius, in loc."Family Expositor, 2, 125. 'Tis not unusual with Christ in his discourses in this manner to introduce something remarkable that he declares with an interrogation, as "What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yea, I say unto you, and more than a prophet" [Luke 7:24–26]. "Whereunto shall I liken the men of this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplace," etc. [Luke 7:31–32]. "Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God, or with what comparison shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed" (Mark 4:30–31). There seems to be an ellipsis in the words, "if it were already kindled!" There is something to be understood that is not expressed. It [is] as much as if Christ had said, O, if it were already kindled! How pleasing would it be to me, or How should I rejoice! Just such an ellipsis is there in Luke 19:42. The next words of Christ that follow do much confirm this sense. "But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!" Luke 12:50], signifying that though he so earnestly desired the immediate enkindling of this fire, yet it was necessary that he should suffer death in the appointed time; and therefore he was willing to wait. After this baptism had been accomplished, and he was ascended into heaven, and the Spirit was poured as fire on his disciples, and they were baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire, then this fire was kindled. And this was the joy that was set before [him]; this was the beginning of that glorious event for which his soul travailed. And therefore no wonder he expresses such eager desires of it in this text. Christ often signifies the necessity there was that his death and ascension should precede this event.

Luke 12:50. "But I have a baptism to be baptized with."] The baptism Christ here speaks of was in his own blood. He was washed from that guilt that he had taken on him, and those sins that were imputed to him, in his own blood. This bloody baptism cleansed him and delivered him.

Luke 12:57. "Yea, and why even of yourselves?"] I.e. without extrinsic signs mentioned in the foregoing verse. Why have ye not that sense of right and wrong, that spiritual taste of true excellency, whereby you can distinguish right from wrong, that which is holy and divine from that that is contrary? Why have ye not that savor of the things of God whereby you can distinguish 'em? Han't you that spiritual and holy nature within you

-- 907 --

that shall teach you what is excellent and from God, and what is sinful and from the devil?

'Tis spoken in the same sense as that of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 11:13–14, "Judge ye in your own selves: Is it comely?… Doth not even nature itself teach you?" Job 34:3, "The ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat." So Christ's question is to this purpose: Why have ye not such a savor and relish of what is divine as should dispose you to receive me, and believe my gospel, as well as the discerning the signs of these times?

Luke 13:1–5. "Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."] Christ in these words seems to have respect to something more than merely their perishing, as well as they, unless they repented. He seems also to have regard to the "remarkable resemblance between the fate of these Galileans, 'whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifice,' and of those 'on whom the tower of Siloam fell,' and that of the whole Jewish nation, the flower of which was slain at Jerusalem by the Roman sword, while they were assembled at one of their great festivals. And many thousands of 'em perished in the temple itself," as these Galileans were slain by the Roman sword while they were worshipping in the temple at a public feast. So [the] nation, in the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, as it were perished under the ruins of the holy city. Yea, "many thousands of 'em were literally buried under the ruins" of the temple (as Josephus represents at large), as those eighteen were buried under the tower of Siloam, a part of that city near the temple over a basin that received the water from the fountain of Siloam, where the Jews were wont to wash and purify themselves to fit themselves for the temple service, and therefore was especially frequented at the time of their festivals. 'Tis therefore probable that it was at some such time that the tower fell on eighteen that were there at once purifying themselves. See John 11:55. Doddridge.Ibid., 130, n. b and c.

Luke 13:20.] See no. 2.Works, 15, 49.

Luke 13:23–24.] Such saying as that few are "saved," etc., not meant of the glorious times of the latter day, see "Miscellanies," no. 1339.Ibid., 2, 356–59.

Luke 13:28. "There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham," etc.] Christ in these words probably alludes to those words,

-- 908 --

Psalms 112:10, "The wicked shall see it, and be grieved, and gnash with his teeth, and melt away. The desire of the wicked shall perish."

Luke 13:32.] A fox is remarkably subtile in catching his prey. It seems that Christ was aware that Herod had a design in some subtile and politic way to catch him and destroy him.

Luke 13:35.] "Your house is left unto you desolate."] I.e. I will leave your house. Your house shall be forsaken of me (As it follows, "You shall see me no more.");This parenthesis is a later interlineation. and the consequence shall be, that it shall be desolate. It shall be forsaken of your children, whom I would have gathered as a hen doth her chickens; they shall be destroyed out of it.

Luke 14:14–15. "Thou shalt be blessed, for thou shalt be recompensed," etc.] As much as to say, Though they can't invite thee to a feast again, yet thou shalt feast with the saints at "the resurrection of the just." One answers, "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God," consenting to what Christ said, as much as to say, They shall be blessed indeed that shall feast at the resurrection of the just, or in the kingdom of God. See sermon on Luke 14:17.No extant copy of this sermon has been located.

Luke 14:18. "Make excuse."] Or "reject."

Luke 14:22–23.] See no. 3.Works, 13, 49.

Luke 14:26.] We must hate these, considered as an exchange for Christ, or as offered to us as inducement to forsake Christ, in the same manner as a just judge is said to hate gifts (Proverbs 15:27). Not that is meant that he should hate gold, or silver, or goods simply considered, but considered as offered as a purchase and bias of his judgment. And in the same manner, as it is said in Canticles 8:7, "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned," not that it would be contemned simply and absolute, but as offered as an exchange for those things which love seeks and desires.This sentence is a later addition.

Luke 15:5. "Layeth it on his shoulders."] See note on Deuteronomy 33:12.

-- 909 --

Luke 15:15. "To feed swine."] If this prodigal son be considered as a Jew, the aversion of that nation for this unclean animal must render the employment peculiarly odious to him. And probably this circumstance was chosen by our Lord to represent him as reduced to the most vile and servile state that could be. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 161, n. c.

Luke 15:16. "And no man gave unto him."] It is not meant that no man gave him any husks, but, although he was reduced to such extremity as to eat husks, "no man gave him anything to eat."

Luke 15:22.] See no. 40.Works, 15, 58.

Luke 16:8. "The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light."] The meaning is that "the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light" are in theirs, i.e. "the children of this world are wiser" in the management of their secular affairs, to promote their worldly interest, andJE deleted "to manage their business amon." in contriving and disposing things that appertain to their generation, that is, to "the children of this world," than the children of light are in the management of spiritual affairs for their spiritual interest. That this is the meaning, and not that the children of this world are wiser in temporal matters than the children of light are in the same matters, is evident by the following, where Christ advises us to be as wise for ourselves in spiritual affairs as the children of this world are in temporal affairs.

Luke 16:9. "And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, that when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations."] I.e. make to yourselves friends in heaven of your earthly possessions and substance. Make God the Father, and Christ, and the other inhabitants of the heavenly world your friends by bestowing the earthly goods that ye are stewards of upon them, as the unjust steward made himself friends by bestowing the goods that he was steward of upon them. Bestow your earthly goods upon them by bestowing them on the poor, who are God's receivers. If it [is] bestowed on one of the least of Christ's brethren, 'tis bestowed on Christ. Thus we shall make God, and Christ, and heavenly angels our friends, which friends will receive us when we fail. 'Tis called "the mammon of unrighteousness," because 'tis

-- 910 --

that which in time past we have as it were stolen, and embezzled, and not improved them as God's stewards, but used them as if they were our own, as the unjust steward embezzled his lord's goods. 'Tis for the sake of these worldly goods that we have been unjust, as the steward was unjust for the sake of his master's goods, that he might have them for his own, and use them for his own private ends. Sin consists radically in the love of this world; and 'tis because this world is that which sin or the corruption of nature hath for its object that 'tis called "the mammon of unrighteousness." 'Tis by our thus using the world that we come to be turned out of it, and to be separated from those worldly enjoyments by death, as the steward was turned out of his stewardship, and was deprived of his lord's goods for his embezzling them. The sin by which man fell at first, and for which our first parents were turned out of the earthly paradise that God had committed to their care as stewards, to dress it and to keep it, was using it as unjust stewards, putting the goods committed to their care to an use contrary to the owner's command, and to serve their own private ends. This will therefore be a wise improvement of that mammon, by which we have lost our possession and enjoyment of all things here below, to make ourselves friends of it that may receive us when we are turned out of our stewardship, and taken out of the world. Note that that expression, "that when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations," thus explained, are a clear proof of the separate state of souls.This sentence is a later addition.

Luke 16:11. "If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?"] This "unrighteous mammon" is that which is intended by that which is "least," in the foregoing verse. One would be more backward to commit to an unfaithful man's trust that which is greatest than that which is least, because the damage of his unfaithful improvement of that which is least is less than in a misimprovement of that which is greatest. God does as it were try men's faithfulness by first committing to them this world's goods, which are comparatively poor, vile, worthless things, before he commits to them the true riches, for this may serve well for a trial. For he that is unfaithful in that which is least, will also [be] in that which is greatest. If these worthless things are misspent by his unfaithfulness, 'tis not so much matter; but God will never commit to him the infinitely precious treasure of true riches to be misspent by him.

-- 911 --

Luke 16:12. "If ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?"] By "that which is another man's" is represented this world's goods, the same with "the unrighteous mammon," as 'tis called in the foregoing verse. And by that which is our "own" is represented the blessings and enjoyments of heaven, the same that is called "the true riches," in the preceding verse. This world's goods ben't our own; they are but lent to us for a little while, and are to be taken from us again presently. We are but stewards of them, agreeable to the foregoing parable that gave occasion to these reflections. So the possession of the children of Israel in the earthly Canaan was represented as not their own, but only what they improve as God's tenants, and as sojourners with him who is their landlord, in Leviticus 25:23: "The land shall not be sold forever, for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me." So here, what we have in this world is represented as not our own, but God's, and we only as stewards.The last three sentences are a later addition. But heavenly blessings are given to us as our proper inheritance, and that wherein our happiness consists. 'Tis not lent to us, but is given to us, never to be taken from us, but to be ours forever. We are but sojourners with God on earth, but heaven is our proper home. Hence we may see the force of the argument. "If ye han't been faithful in that which is another man's, who will give you that which is your own?" If you ben't fit to have something only committed to your care for a little while that is quickly to be taken from you again, how much less are you fit to be be trusted with things forever, not only to have them lent to you, or committed into your hands for a little while, but to have them given finally into your everlasting possession. If you can't be trusted with something for only a few days, how much less can you be trusted with the eternal possession of a thing?

Luke 16:15. "Ye are they which justify yourselves before men."] They, as we are told in the foregoing verse, derided Christ's doctrine that showed the evil of covetousness; and the reason why they derided this doctrine before the people was to prevent the people's having mean thoughts of them, whose practice was so contrary. They condemned his doctrine "before men," that they might "justify themselves" before them. And therefore Christ says, "Ye are they that justify yourselves before men."

"That which is highly esteemed amongst men." See Hervey's Dialogue, vol. 1, p. 329.'This paragraph is a later addition. Hervey writes, "Whereas, whatever is high and lifted up, haughty and conceited; every Sentiment of Self-admiration, and all the Fruits that spring from this bitter Root; these are certainly and invariably Objects of the divine Abhorrence.—This Interpretation, I think, is most suitable, not only to Fact in general, but to the Import of this Word in particular.… It seems also best to quadrate with the Tenour of our SAVIOUR's Reproof; Ye are they that justify Yourselves before Men, but all such arrogant Attempts, and every such elated Air, the most holy GOD beholds with Detestation" (Dialogues, 1, 329–30, note).

-- 912 --

Luke 16:16. "And every man."] Here I would observe that when universal terms are used about redemption, they don't prove universal redemption, any more than the universal term here used proves that every man, in a strict and proper sense, did press into the kingdom of heaven since the preaching of John the Baptist.See JE's extended discussion of "Pressing into the Kingdom of God" in his sermon by that name on Luke 16:16 (no. 351), preached Feb. 1735, with the doctrine, "It concerns everyone that would obtain the kingdom of God, to be pressing into it" (Works, 19, 274–80).

"Every man presseth into it." Christ is not so much speaking of what had already actually come to pass since John's time, as giving a description of that new dispensation that John began, and showing wherein it differed from the old dispensation under the Law and the Prophets, as to the much greater numbers that are saved, and the multitudes that, under this dispensation that John's preaching was the dawning of, flock and press into the kingdom of God. The pouring out of the Spirit in John [the] Baptist's time was the beginning of a glorious harvest of souls that continued from that time to the end of that age, wherein multitudes of all sorts pressed into the kingdom of God.This paragraph is a later addition.

Luke 16:22–31.] This parable contains most clear evidences of rewards and punishments of souls in their separate state. For here Abraham is supposed to be yet existing, and in a state of action in another world, many ages after he was dead, for he speaks of Moses and the Prophets, referring to their writings, who were Abraham's posterity, and wrote many ages afterJE deleted "he was in this world." his death. And again Dives and Lazarus, when they die, go into another world before the resurrection, as is evident by two things, viz. that the five brethren of the rich man are yet alive, and also that Abraham speaks of Lazarus's returning into this world to warn those five brethren, as the rich man desired, as one's rising "from the dead." And then Abraham tells the rich man that he in his lifetime had his "good things," plainly implying that it was not his lifetime, that now his body was dead. And this evidently teaches us that there is a state of happiness and misery that is not in the lifetime, and before the lifetime shall return,

-- 913 --

by their rising again to life. See 2 Corinthians 5:10. And Christ plainly teaches in the Luke 16:26 that there are two opposite states and distant places of the departed spirits of godly and ungodly.

Luke 16:29–31.] These verses with the context imply that if Dives' brethren heard the commands and exhortations of Moses and the prophets, it would save 'em from that place of torment. And as this parable is for the use of Christians, or for the use of the church under the new testament, for whom the New Testament was written, so it teaches that Moses and the Prophets prescribed the same conditions of escape from God's wrath as Christ and his apostles.

Luke 17:7–8.] Christ, when he here speaks of a servant's "plowing or feeding cattle," seems to have a particular respect to the work of the ministry, the service they were to be employed in, which is often in Scripture compared to the business of an husbandman or shepherd. When they come from the field, having done their work, their good master will cause them to "sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them," as is promised, Luke 12:37.

Luke 17:20.] See no. 41.Works, 15, 58–59.

Luke 17:30–37.] See no. 42.Ibid., 59.

Luke 17:37. "And he said unto them, Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together."] This is an enigmatical answer to their question; but yet by giving diligent heed to this answer, with due care to understand it, together with a diligent observation of events, to be determined by it, Christ's answer is that these things that he speaks of shall be when and where they shall see the eagles gathered about the dead carcass. Now the Roman armies' bearing an eagle as their ensign, this might naturally lead them to think that the Romans were the eagles Christ spake of. But what should lead them to think that Jerusalem was meant by the dead body? I answer, because when Jerusalem was besieged by the Roman armies, the city was filled with dead carcasses. What innumerable multitudes were there that died in Jerusalem during that siege by famine and by killing one another! When the Roman armies were "gathered together" about Jerusalem, then was it remarkably fulfilled

-- 914 --

that the eagles were gathered together about the dead's carcasses. Or rather, by the carcass he means his own dead body that was killed at Jerusalem. And after this, the Jewish nation were like Christ's dead carcass, and not his living body, as the true church is, for his spirit thenceforward left that church. And the temple and typical ordinances of their worship thenceforward became as Christ's dead body. The church with its ordinances of worship is the body of Christ. The church with the presence and spirit of Christ is his living body, but when deprived of it, his dead body. The Jews therefore, by killing Christ's body, killed then their own church, by this means became a dead carcass and a fit prey for eagles. From the time the Jews killed Christ, the Jewish church was dead and putrefied, till they became a stinking carrion before the time of their destruction; and their stink called the eagles together upon them.

Luke 18:13. "And the publican, standing afar off."] For the Gentiles were not allowed so near an approach to temple.

Luke 18:35. "And it came to pass, that as he was come nigh unto Jericho, a certain blind man," etc.] How to reconcile this with the other evangelists, who say it was "as he went out of Jericho" [Mark 10:46], see no. 233.Ibid., 182–84.

"ἐν τῷ ἐγγίζειν only signifies 'when' or 'while he was near it' (Compare Luke 19:29.)." See Doddridge.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 2, 271, n. a.

Luke 19:8. "Taken anything by false accusation."] "ἐσυκοφάντησα, as HeinsiusDaniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a scholar of the classics, published Sacrarum exercitationum ad Novum Testamentum libri XX (Cambridge, 1640). has abundantly shown, may properly signify any kind of oppression, especially under pretense of law (Compare Ecclesiastes 4:1 and Ecclesiastes 5:7, Septuagint.). It seems therefore not so proper to limit it, as our translation does, to an injury done by a 'false accusation,' which implies something of a formal trial, and defense of the party accused; whereas many frauds and oppressions might be practiced by such a tax-gatherer, where nothing of this sort occurred." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 275, n. e.

Luke 19:12. "Went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return."] Such a representation in this parable was the moreJE deleted "natural." familiar to

-- 915 --

the Jews, because this had actually been the case with their late princes, Herod, Archelaus, etc. They, in order to receive their kingdom,JE deleted "first." left Judea for a sea, and "went into a far country," to Rome, to be invested with the kingdom by the Roman emperor, and then returned invested and in the exercise of their royal authority. So Christ "went into a far country" and a greater city than Rome, to be invested with the kingdom over the Jews and over mankind in this world, his own country, by one infinitely greater than the Roman emperor.

Luke 19:14.] They sent this message to that superior potentate that was to invest him.

Luke 19:17. "Over ten cities."] For now the nobleman was returned with kingly authority over the whole country, and had power to dispose of the government of cities.

Luke 19:21–23.] See notes on Matthew 25:24 ff.

"For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou laidst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow." "And therefore apprehending I might incur thy severity, if any accident should befall this money in trade, I was determined not to venture it out of mine hands, and now return it just as I received it. 'And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee.… Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down.… Wherefore then gavest thou not my money to the bank, that at my coming I might receive mine own with usury?'" I.e. if it be as you say,JE deleted "you are condemned out of." you might conclude that I should expect to reap where I had sown. "And why then didst thou not give my money into the bank" (where it would have been no more liable to accidents than in thine own hands), "that when I came to call for it at my return, I might at least have received it at the common interest, if not with the extraordinary improvement which might have attended a successful trade?" Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 2, 280.

Luke 19:37. "And the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen."] And especially for the great miracle of raising Lazarus from the grave after

-- 916 --

he had been dead four days, as we are told, John 12:18. This miracle, being at such a time as when they were flocking from all parts to the feast, greatly increased the number of his disciples, as John 12:11. And they had lately been in great numbers to see Lazarus after his resurrection, as John 12:9. And having come afresh from beholding the admirable sight, and their affectedness at the same was fresh and strong, and seeing [Jesus] entering into the city with more solemnity than usual, this was the cause of their being thus affected.

See notes on this solemn entry into Jerusalem, no. 324.Works, 15, 307–10.

"And when he was come nigh." See note on Isaiah 52:7.This reference is a separate entry.

Luke 19:40. "If these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out."] They had extraordinary reason to celebrate the praises of Christ at this time, especially because they had seen so many mighty works of his, and especially because they had so lately seen that great miracle of raising Lazarus from the grave (See note on Luke 19:37.), which was perhaps the greatest of all his miracles. "The stones would cry out." That is, they would cry out in God's praises on this occasion, and so bare testimony against them, that their hearts were harder than the very stones, as Balaam's ass testified against the madness of his rider, in that he would not go against a drawn sword, but yet Balaam would venture to go against the command of God. And the ass spoke, though he knew not what he said [Numbers 22:23–31]. Yet his speaking and reasoning with Balaam, and instructing him as he did, was a testimony of God that he was more brutish than an ass. See note on 2 Peter 2:16.

Luke 19:41. "When he beheld the city, he wept over it."] Though he foresaw "so circumstantially all the ungrateful and inhuman treatment he was to meet with in this nest of murderers, with the scene of his sufferings, and the very house of Caiaphas in his full view, for if we may credit the best accounts of Jerusalem which remain, this was the case." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 302.

Luke 19:45–46.] See note on Mark 11:17.

Luke 20:36. "Neither can they die anymore."] And therefore there will be no need of marriage to continue the species, as in this world.

-- 917 --

Luke 21:20–21.] See "Miscellanies," no. 972, [sec. 4., (2), 3, and 4., (3), 2].Works, 20, 259–60, and 265. The first of these paragraphs begins, "Fearful sights and signs from heaven." The second begins, "Another subsequent circumstance."

Luke 21:24. "And Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, till the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled."] I.e. till the "time, times, and half" a time, spoken of in Daniel 12:7, be fulfilled. See notes on Matthew 24:21–24 ff., no. 292, §10.Works, 15, 258–59. Hence we may infer that Antichrist will fall, and the Jews be called about the same time. See this also further confirmed from other parts of that forementioned note. See notes on "Revelation," no. 83.This reference is a later addition. Works, 5, 195–97.

"Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles." "Their land was sold, and no Jew was allowed to inhabit there (a rigor never used, that I know of, towards any other people conquered by the Romans). Nay, they might not come within sight of Jerusalem, or rather of Aelia,MS: "Elia." the name given to the new city when the foundations of the old were plowed up. A heathen temple was built where that of God had stood, and a Turkish mosque pollutes it to this day." Doddridge, in loc.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 2, 383–84, n. g.

Luke 21:37. "And in the daytime," etc.] By this it is evident that Christ was very commonly wont to lodge in the open field; he had not where to lay his head in Jerusalem. He had no friends there to invite him in, and he had not money to purchase entertainment at an inn. And therefore it was his constant manner to go and lodge at a certain place in the Mount of Olives, which was the place where he and his disciples were found when Judas betrayed him. And therefore 'tis said, in the Luke 22:39, that that night "he came out, and went, as he was wont, to the Mount of Olives." And hence also is that, John 18:1–2. "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden into which he entered, and his disciples. And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place, for Jesus oftentimes resorted thither with his disciples." See also John 8:1 with John 7:53. Hence we may learn that what is spoken of Christ figuratively in Canticles 5:2, "My head is wet with the dew, and my locks with the drops of the night," was often literally fulfilled while he dwelt here on earth, and that he often suffered greatly in being obliged to lodge abroad in the cold and rain.

-- 918 --

Luke 22:25. "Are called benefactors."] The word sometimes used for "prince" in the Old Testament is נָדִיב, that signifies "ingenuous, liberal, munificent." (See Buxtorf.) This is the word for "prince" (1 Samuel 2:8, Psalms 47:9).Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum (6th ed. London, 1646), 422. Buxtorf's reference, Psalms 47:10, is to the Hebrew Bible. In the KJV it is Psalms 47:9.

Luke 22:29. "As my Father hath appointed unto me."] The particle καθώς here is of the same force as ὡς in Revelation 2:27. "He shall rule them with a rod of iron, even as I received of my Father," implying that the same privilege or benefit is bestowed by Christ on his disciples as is bestowed by the Father on him.

Luke 22:31.] See no. 338.Works, 15, 323–24. In this entry JE deleted "no. 123" (Works, 15, 85), which is an earlier note on Luke 22:31. No. 338 reflects a change in his understanding of the text.

Luke 22:32.] Hence I infer that a principle of grace yet remains in the saints in the time of great falls. The sins they are guilty of, though great, yet don't destroy or extinguish grace. Peter's fall was such that he needed to be converted again, and yet his faith as to the principle failed not.

Luke 22:35–36.] 'Tis a spiritual purse, and scrip, and sword that Christ means. There was coming a great time of trial, wherein they should need all the stock they had, and all the spiritual forces they could make. These two verses imply as much as if Christ had said, When I sent you forth on a journey in which you was exposed to temporal evils and calamities, I directed you not much to concern yourselves in making provision for your preservation and defense from these, for these temporal evils are comparatively but trivial things, worthy of but little. But now a time of great spiritual danger is coming, wherein you are like to be remarkably exposed to spiritual calamities; your conduct should be far otherwise. These are so terrible that they are worthy of your utmost care and concern, to provide that you may be well defended from them, worthy that you should part with the most necessary of outward things in order to it. And 'tis probable that Christ, in mentioning a garment in particular, aimed at something special that was mystically signified by his garment, viz. his own righteousness, which men naturally trust in as their defense from spiritual evils. This we must strip off and utterly cast away in order to our obtaining a true and effectual defense from our spiritual enemies.

-- 919 --

Luke 22:39. "Went as he was wont."] See note on Luke 21:37.

Luke 22:44. "As it were great drops of blood."] The blood, being gradually forced through his pores, congealed in clotters before it fell to the ground, so that they were great drops, not properly drops, but rather clotters. The word in the originalθρόμβοι signifies lumps or clotters.

'Tis not to be supposed that Christ sweat mere blood. He was doubtless in a great watery sweat through his agony before the blood began to come, till at length the blood began to be mixed with the sweat, so that here was blood and water mixed, as that was that issued from his vitals on the cross, to signify the cleansing virtue of his blood. See notes on John 19:34.

"He prayed more earnestly." See no. 225.Works, 15, 172–75.

"His sweat was as it were great drops of blood." "A great many expositors have thought, as Mr. Le ClercJean Le Clerc (1657–1736), biblical scholar and Arminian theologian who taught at the Remonstrant College in Amsterdam. In his commentaries and annotations he adopted a rationalistic approach to the text. did, that the expression only implies that his drops of sweat were large and clammy like clots of gore. But Dr. Whitby observes that Aristotle and Diodorus SiculusSame as the Greek historian Diodorus. both mention bloody sweats as attending some extraordinary agony of mind; and I find Leti,Gregorio Leti (1630–1701), author of Vita de Sisto V (1669), translated in 1704. in his Life of Pope Sixtus V, p. 200, and Sir John Chardin,Chardin (1643–1712), the French-born traveler, who wrote Voyages du chevalier Chardin èn Perse, el autres lieux de l'Orient. in his History of Persia, vol. 1, p. 126, mentioning a like phenomenon." Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 2, 502, n. k.

Luke 22:50.] Peter in his zeal aimed not only at the ear, but the head of the man he struck. He intended to have split his head, but missing his aim, smote off his ear.

Luke 22:50–51.] This was a type of that circumcision, or cutting off of the ear, that we read of, Acts 7:51 and Jeremiah 6:10, which is effected by means of the ministers of Christ fighting for their Lord and Master with the word of God, the sword of the Spirit. The old ear was cut off, and a new one given by Christ. So in conversion the old, deaf, obstinate ear is cut off, and an hearing, obedient ear given. This is particularly typical of what often has

-- 920 --

come to pass in times of persecution, that has been stirred up by heathen priests and by the Pope, the great, false, high priest of apostate Israel. Their servants, that have been employed as instruments of their malice, have been converted by the word of God that they have heard from the persecuted. And the weapons of their warfare have proved mighty, and the word of God in their mouths sharper than a two-edged sword.

Luke 22:51. "Suffer ye thus far. And he touched his ear, and healed him."] The wordἐᾶτε. translated "suffer" signifies to "permit" or to "give liberty." "As they were binding Christ, he answered and said, Suffer me at least to have my hands at liberty thus far, and stay but for a moment, while I add one act of power and compassion to those I have already done. And calling Malchus to him, he touched his ear, and immediately healed him." Doddridge's Paraphrase.Family Expositor, 2, 511.

Luke 23:15. "Done unto him."] "πεπραγμένον αὐτῷ, 'done by him.' The words must here have this signification. For though this is something of an unusual construction, yet Raphelius has produced many instances of the like nature." Doddridge.Ibid., 540, n. c.

Luke 23:34. "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."] If they had known what they did, their sin would have been the unpardonable sin, for their malice, and persecution, and cruelty against Christ was principally for that Spirit that he spake and acted by. And in that abundant mockery and derision of him at this time, they doubtless had reproached that Spirit by which he taught and wrought [miracles]. We have an account, Luke 23:35, that they reviled his miracles; and doubtless they reviled the Spirit that he wrought miracles by, as the Pharisees did who said he wrought miracles by Beelzebub [Matthew 12:24], for that was the common say[ing] and pretense amongst the enemies of Christ. If they therefore had known what they did, and had done it against light, their sin would have been the unpardonable sin against the Holy Ghost.

Luke 23:43. "In paradise."] "The wordπαράδεισος. 'paradise' originally signified a garden of pleasure, such as those in which Eastern monarchs made their magnificent banquets." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 567, n. k.

-- 921 --

Luke 23:44.] He who made the sun to be a type of Christ saw meet that when Christ died, that should be darkened, that while Christ's sufferings on the cross continued, and he was deprived of joy and comfort, the sun should be deprived of light. That the sun is a type of Christ was probably one reason why Christ's resurrection was about the time of the rising of the sun, i.e. its first rising by its light, because the rising of the sun is a type of the resurrection of Christ, as the sun's setting is a type of the death of Christ. See note on Deuteronomy 21:23. And though the rising of the sun happens so often, 'tis no sign that it is not a type of the resurrection of Christ that is but once, for 'tis fit that the type should be repeated often, but that the antitype should be but once, as the daily sacrifices of old (Hebrews 9:12, Hebrews 9:25–28; Hebrews 7:27). See "Shadows of Divine Things," no. 54.Works, 11, 66.

"At Christ's birth the night was turned into day (Luke 2:9), and at his death the day was turned into night; nature as it were went into mourning, upon the death of the maker and heir of the world." Hurrion, Of the Knowledge of Christ Crucified, p. 291.This paragraph is a later addition. John Hurrion, The Knowledge of Christ, and Him Crucified, Opened and Applied; in Eight Sermons Preached at the Merchants Lecture at Pinner's-Hall (London, 1727). In some citations, JE identified this as "vol. 1," probably with an eye to the fact that two years later Hurrion (1675–1731), an independent minister in England, published The Knowledge of Christ Glorified, opened and applied in twelve sermons on Christ's resurrection, ascension, sitting at God's right hand, intercession and judging the world (London, 1729), which he also cited. See Works, 18, 363, n. 3. Neither publication carried a volume number.

Luke 23:51. "The same had not consented."] The Sanhedrin sat with Pilate in judging Jesus. Joseph of Arimathea, Joseph was one of the Sanhedrin, but "had not consented," etc.

"He was of Arimathea." Called in the Old Testament, "Ramathaim" (1 Samuel 1:1).This paragraph is a later addition.

Luke 24.] No. 220.Works, 15, 154–56.

Luke 24:11.] Thus it often is with regard to a believer's fellowship in Christ's resurrection, or his being risen with Christ, and Christ's being risen for him, and his partaking of the benefit of his resurrection by conversion and justification. He believes it not; it seems too great and too good to be true.

-- 922 --

Luke 24:30.] Christ now again on the day of his resurrection, the day of the Christian sabbath, administered the Lord's Supper, which thenceforward was the day of the disciples' coming together to break bread. Compare the Evangelist's expression here with those in Luke 22:19, and also with Acts 2:42, Acts 2:46; Acts 20:7, Acts 20:11; 1 Corinthians 10:16. See Erskine's Humble Attempt to Promote Frequent Communicating, pp. 10–12.From the fact that Jesus himself dispensed the Lord's Supper twice in the space of less than a week, the second time on the sabbath, John Erskine (1721–1803), a leader of the evangelical party in Scotland, argued that it "seems an Intimation that our Lord intended it should be a principal Part of the Sanctification of the Christian Sabbath" (A Humble Attempt to Promote Frequent Communicating [Glasgow, 1749], 12). JE and Erskine were frequent correspondents. See Works, 11.

Luke 24:49. "The promise of my Father."] The promise of the Father to him. The Holy Ghost was the great good which God the Father promised to Christ, to bestow on them that he was to die for in the covenant of redemption, on condition of his dying, and therefore was plentifully and abundantly bestowed soon after he had died. It seems to be upon this account that Christ calls it "the promise of his Father."

-- 923 --

John

THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN, written as a supplement to the other gospels. See "Scripture, no. 447."This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 529–30.

John 1:1–2. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God," etc.] In all likelihood the Evangelist has those expressions in the beginning of Genesis in his eye, Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image"; and Genesis 3:22, "Behold, the man is become as one of us."

John 1:1–3.] Of the notions of the ancient Jews concerning the "Word," see Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 3, Preface, p. 11c–e.Kidder cites the Targum by Jonathan as evidence that in many places in the Hebrew Bible "where the Memra, or Word of the Lord," is mentioned, the expression denotes "a divine person," references he interprets as predictions of the Messiah. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 11.

John 1:3.
