"All things were made by him."] See note second in the Appendix at the end of the third volume of Dr. Doddridge's Family Expositor, p. 1 of the Appendix.Note 2 cites Philo on the role of the Logos, or Divine Word, in "governing the whole Course of Nature both in Heaven and Earth," using the analogy of a charioteer who directs the chariot and is seated next to the rider, God the Father, "who commands the Charioteer how he is to manage the Reins" (Appendix, pp. 1–2).

John 1:9.] I.e. there is not, nor ever was, nor will be, any man in the world enlightened but by Jesus Christ. "Every man that cometh into the world" that ever is enlightened is enlightened by him. Or hereby is meant that this light is not only to enlighten the Jews, but that it enlightens indifferently every man, let him be of what nation soever. It was fit that the True Light, when he came, should be a general light. Moses enlightened only the nation of the Jews, because he was not the True Light.

See a very parallel expression, Colossians 1:23.This sentence is a later addition.

-- 924 --

John 1:16.] See no. 122.Works, 15, 85.

John 1:18.] God under the old testament gave the images of things, the substance and reality of which he gave in the new. And one instance of this was that Christ so often under the old testament appeared in human shape. This was an image and an earnest of his future incarnation. And 'tis still God's manner to give the images and earnests of the glorious things that are to [be] brought to pass for his church and in the spiritual world before he actually accomplishes them. And it was pleasing to him to appear in human shape, whose delights were with the sons of men, who delighted in the human nature, and in the thoughts of taking the human nature and an human body. He delighted in a human shape and in the resemblance of his future incarnation. See "Miscellanies," no. 777.This reference is a later addition. Works, 18, 427–34.

"No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him." This verse seems to be connected with the two preceding. The design of all is to show the preference of Christ to Moses or any prophet that had appeared in the world before. None of 'em had ever seen God. Even Moses, himself the greatest of the old testament prophets, desired to see God, but saw only his back parts. God told him no man could see him and live [Exodus 33:20], but Christ not only saw his back parts, but his face, yea, dwells in his bosom. And he is that great prophet or servant of God that among all the prophets is distinguished as the only begotten Son. He has the peculiar honor of at length declaring the Father, and bringing his people to see God, to see and know much more of him than ever any of the ancient prophets, yea, Moses himself, ever saw. Thus truth comes by Jesus Christ.This paragraph is a later addition.

John 1:31. "And I knew him not."] How it came to pass that John did not know him, see no. 446.Works, 15, 528–29.

John 1:32. "And John bare record, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven."] John seems to have been the only person that saw this sight, and heard that voice from heaven that accompanied it. The three evangelists, Matthew, and Mark, and John, tell us that he saw it. I believe that

-- 925 --

John was raised up in a great measure for this end, that he might be a witness of this anointing of Christ to his office, and this solemn testimony of God from heaven concerning him.

John 1:38. "Master, where dwellest thou?"] It seems that as Jesus attended the worship of the synagogue and attended John's baptism, so he likewise often attended other parts of John's ministry, and therefore often resorted to him to hear him preach the word with others, at least about that time that is spoken of in this verse and the context, and had therefore taken up a certain "private lodging" somewhere near the place where John was preaching and baptizing, and not in Galilee from whence he came to attend John's ministry "from day to day." It was this lodging that the disciples have respect to when they inquire where he dwelt or abode, they having a desire to visit him there and spend some time in conversation with him. And accordingly, they went with him to his lodging, and spent that evening with him, it being then, as is said in the next verse, "'about the tenth hour,' or about four in the afternoon." But there is no appearance in this account of their now beginning to be his constant followers. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 124–25.

John 1:45. "Philip findeth Nathaniel."] Nathaniel is supposed to be the same with Bartholomew; and that Nathaniel was his proper name, and Bartholomew his surname, from his father Tholmai (no uncommon name among the Jews), as Bar-jona was Simon's surname from his father Jonah. He is supposed to be the same with Bartholomew for these reasons. "John never mentions Bartholomew in the number of the apostles; so the other evangelists never take notice of Nathaniel. And as in John, Philip and Nathaniel are joined together, in their coming to Christ," and seem to have been from the first companions one with another, so the other evangelists constantly join Philip and Bartholomew. And "Nathaniel is particularly mentioned with the other apostles, to whom our Lord appeared at the Sea of Tiberias after his resurrection (John 21:1)." See "The Life of Bartholomew," in Reading's Evangelical History.Reading's "Life of Bartholomew," is pp. 515–19 in HISTORY of Our Lord and Saviour JESUS CHRIST (4th ed.). These citations are from pp. 515–16.

John 1:47. "An Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile."] We are told concerning Jacob or Israel, Genesis 25:27, that he was "a plain man." In the original,תָּם אִישׁ

-- 926 --

the word signifies "an upright or perfect man." Christ here seems to allude to that. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 129. See. Psalms 73:1.This reference is a later addition.

John 1:48. "When thou wast under the fig tree."] 'Tis very probable that Nathaniel, when alone under the fig tree at the time Christ refers to, had been employed in some secret religion, prayer, or pious and devout meditation. See Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 1, 129, n. e.

John 2:1–11.] Concerning Christ's turning water into wine, see no. 368.Works, 15, 358–59.

John 2:4. "Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee?"] This expression, as it was used in those times, carried nothing of disrespect. By what was then understood by the expression and the force that [the] words then bore, they were not looked upon unsuitable to be used towards one most superior. This is evident because the devil, when through the greatness of his fear he feigned himself an humble and earnest supplicant to Jesus Christ, used this expression. Luke 8:28, "When he saw Jesus, he cried out, and fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God most high? I beseech thee, torment me not."

John 2:6. "After the manner of the purifying of the Jews."] "That was made use of by the guests, and that was necessary for the washing of cups and other vessels that were used at the table, according to the Jewish custom of purifying, which in some instances was grown to such a superstitious nicety, as to require a considerable quantity of water to be ready on such occasions." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 1, 135–36.

John 2:11. "This beginning of miracles."] Jesus began his public ministry in a quite different manner from that wherein John the Baptist had performed.MS: "performed not." The "not" appears to be a mistake that JE did not cross out. John came, neither eating nor drinking, with great austerities with respect to food and clothing. Jesus, beginning his public ministry, works his first miracle at a wedding, an occasion of feasting, and banqueting,

-- 927 --

and rejoicing; and the miracle that was wrought was to furnish the table for the feast, to provide for the banquet, and increase the joy. Thus it became Christ to begin his ministry, who, after John had prepared the way by promoting conviction, humiliation, and repentance, came as the bridegroom of his church to introduce the consolation and joy of Israel, and provide for and give to his people a joyful feast and banquet, and the glorious entertainment of an eternal wedding.

John 2:14–16.] See note on Mark 11:17.

John 2:17. "Hath eaten me up."] See note on Psalms 69:2

John 2:20.] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. II, p. 872.The forty-six years during which the temple was being built extended from the beginning of the process under Herod till the time of this first Passover of Christ's ministry. There were vet laborers at work on out-buildings, according to Prideaux (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 4, p. 872).

John 2:21.] See no. 47.Works, 15, 63.

John 2:23–25.] See a remark from this text concerning judging or censuring, "Miscellanies," no. 998.Ibid., 2, 326.

John 3:5. "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit."] See Turretin, Tome 3, pp. 435–36.The thirteenth question in Turretin's nineteenth topic, De Sacramentis, asks "Is baptism absolutely necessary to salvation?" Turretin's answer in § XIX is negative, using this passage in John as evidence, where "water" designates "spiritual renovation, which is produced by the Holy Spirit." Thus the reference is to "'spiritual water' or the spirit washing and cleansing the heart." The cause of regeneration, namely, the Spirit, and the manner of the effect (viz. by spiritual washing) are designated by the passage. Turretin identifies this text as employing a hendiadys, a figure of speech that is confirmed by the fact "that the Holy Spirit is constantly designated by water, especially as he was about to be dispensed under the New Testament." This judgment is also reinforced by Christ's instruction of Nicodemus (Institutio Theologiae Elencticae). See Dennison, ed., Institutes of Elenctic Theology, III, 386, 390–91.

John 3:6.] See notes on Galatians 5:17, the first Corol.

St. Paul's words, Romans 8:5, confirm the true meaning of these words of our Savior. "For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit, the things of the Spirit." Such

-- 928 --

phrases, "they that are after the flesh," and "they that are after the Spirit," with the Apostle signify much the same thing with "those that are born after the flesh," and "those that are born after the Spirit," as appears by Galatians 4:29, where the last expression, "they that are born after the Spirit," in the originalτὸν κατὰ πνεῦμα is the same as in Romans 8:5, "they that are after the Spirit."

John 3:8. "And thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, or whither it goeth. So is everyone that is born of the Spirit."] Still Christ has respect to Nicodemus's question in the John 3:4. "How can a man be born again when he is old? Can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?"

This question, How is, or how can, a man be born again? may be asked either: 1. From a faultyJE deleted "and gross." ignorance. And so it was indeed asked by Nicodemus. And 'tis with respect to his ignorance and gross notions that heI.e. Christ. makes answer in the three preceding verses, teaching that what he means is not any external birth, but a being born "of the Spirit" (John 3:5); and then [he] proceeds, John 3:6, to give the reason why such a new birth is necessary, viz. because "that which is born of the flesh is flesh," etc. 2. This question, How is a man born again? may be asked out of a vain curiosity, and with a conceit of men's own wisdom and ability to trace the footsteps of the Spirit of God in this work, and a sufficiency to describe and mark out with exact limits the course that the Spirit takes, in order to bring this work to effect from the very first rise to the issue of its operations. For although Nicodemus did not now inquire in this manner, yet Christ foreknew that many masters in Israel hereafter would do so. And therefore, after correcting Nicodemus's mistake, and [having] told in general what kind of regeneration it was that he meant, he here instructs us that if any shall go about to inquire minutely concerning the particular method the Spirit shall take in producing this effect, they will be more curious than wise, because we know not what the way of the Spirit is in this, any more than we know the particular rise and course of the wind. We know the wind blows by hearing the sound of it, and by the sensible effects of it, but know not "whence it comes, nor whither it goes." So we ought to judge of the operations of the Spirit in regeneration by the sensible effects of it, and not by any precise order and sensible method and steps of its proceeding. Isaiah 40:13, "Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord, or being his counselor hath taught him?"

-- 929 --

John 3:12.] Intimating that "heavenly things" are far more mysterious. This doctrine about regeneration is earthly, because 'tis about man, who is on the earth and is of the earth. "Heavenly things" are things pertaining to God and Christ, who is in heaven and came from thence, as it follows in the next verse. Such are the doctrines of the Trinity, of Christ's incarnation, and satisfaction by his death and sufferings. What Christ speaks of in the John 3:14 is an heavenly thing. "Miscellanies," no. 839.This and the following reference are later additions. Works, 20, 54–55. See John 4:34.

John 3:13. "And no man hath ascended up to heaven."] I.e. in his understanding and acquaintance with God and divine and heavenly things, spoken of in the preceding verse, "no man hath ascended up" so high as to get a thorough and complete knowledge of heavenly things. See Deuteronomy 30:12 and Proverbs 30:4. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 153–54, n. d. See John 4:34.This reference is a later addition.

John 3:14–18.] In these verses Christ teaches Nicodemus those things that were very contrary to the notions of the Pharisees and rulers of the Jews at that day, one of which Nicodemus was. They expected to see the Messiah "raised on a magnificent earthly throne," but instead of that Christ intimates that he must be "lifted up on the cross." They thought that he would come to save their nation, and that being of their nation and conforming to the law of Moses would surely entitle men to the Messiah's benefits. But he teaches that he came not only to save the Jews, but all that believe on him through the world, and that God sent him not only from love to their nation, but love to the world, that he did not come to destroy the world as they imagined the Messiah would, but to save and bless it, and that they that did not believe on him—let 'em be who they would, of their nation or other nations—should certainly be condemned and destroyed. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 154–58.

John 3:17.] Note.The point of this reference is unclear. Perhaps it is unfinished. JE may have intended to reference the entry on John 3:18–19, which points back to this verse.

John 3:18–19.] "But he that believeth not is condemned already."] This is said to clear up what was said in the foregoing verse, viz. that Christ did not

-- 930 --

come "to condemn the world." For though they be condemned for not believing on him, yet Christ is only the occasion of it. That which is the foundation of their condemnation, which their condemnation arises from, is to be considered as antecedent to his coming, viz. the law of God, and their evil deeds and wicked hearts, whereby they hate that which is good, as in following verses. See notes on John 16:9.

John 3:23. "AenonMS: "Enon." near Salim, because there was much water there."] 'Tis not probable that the water here spoken of was that of the river Jordan, for if so, it is probable it would have been expressed, "because it was near Jordan," rather than "because there was much water there." It seems to have been other waters, and not the waters of Jordan, that are intended. Aenon, as Wells in his Sacred Geography observes, signifies "a place of springs" (vol. 4, p. 57).Historical Geography of the New Testament (2nd ed.). "Vol. 4" appears on the spine of the binding. And therefore by πολλὰ ὕδατα in this verse probablyMS: "probable." is not to be understood a great body of waters, as sometimes many waters in Scripture signifies, but more literally for many springs or streams of water.

John 3:30.] The new testament dispensation increased before and after Christ's resurrection; and the old testament decreased much after the same manner, as the ministry of Christ increased and the ministry of John the Baptist decreased. John the Baptist was a forerunner of Christ, much after the same manner as the old testament prepared the way for the new.

John 3:33–34.] See "Miscellanies," no. 764b.Works, 18, 411.

John 4:5. "Called Sychar."] "The city was originally Shechem or Sychem. But the Jews," out of hatred and contempt of the Samaritans, who now had it in possession, "called it 'Sychar,' which was a term of reproach, intimating that it was the seat of drunkards and liars, for 'Sychar' in the Syriac language signifies a drunkard and a liar."Doddridge, Family Expositor, 1, 171.

John 4:10–11, John 4:13–14.] Note on John 7:38–39, no. 263.Works, 15, 209–10.

-- 931 --

John 4:13.] The continual returns of appetite after often eating and drinking is an argument that earthly good is not men's true good, or that true happiness is not to be found in them. See Ecclesiastes 6:7, and note on Hebrews 10:1–3.

John 4:14. "Shall never thirst."] The spiritual joys and delights that are to be had in Christ are satisfying in these senses. 1. They are of such a nature that those that receive them desire no other kind of enjoyment; not that they won't desire more of the same, for 'tis the character of a godly man that he hungers and thirsts after righteousness. But they shall be satisfied with it as to kind; they never will desire any change. It is not so with temporal enjoyments. After a man has one enjoyment a little while, he can't be satisfied with it; he wants something new. But the soul is never cloyed or weary in perpetually giving up itself with all its powers to the enjoyment of spiritual joys in Christ so as to desire any change.

2. It is satisfying, as there is enough in it to satisfy the soul as to degree, were but obstacles removed, and the enjoying faculty duly applied. There is room enough here for the soul to extend itself. Here is an infinite ocean of it. If men ben't satisfied here in degree of happiness, the cause is with themselves. 'Tis because they don't open their mouths wide enough. There is enough of that which is enjoyed, viz. the glory and the love of God, did we but so apply our souls to it as to take our fill of it. And whenever obstacles are removed, the soul shall be satisfied in degree of happiness, though, indeed, I do not think that the soul will ever be so filled as to be cloyed, or so as not to desire and pursue after more. But it will be free from those uneasy longings and that painful hunger and thirsts that arises from those defects and those clogs and hindrances which persons have in this world. But they will ever have an appetite to further degrees, which shall keep employed in launching forth further and further into this ocean, and shall cause 'em to receive with relish those perpetual additions which they shall freely obtain, as they pursue without painful labor and without those hindrances and disappointments which pursuits are attended with in this world.

3. Spiritual enjoyments are satisfying also in a respect that worldly enjoyments are not, in this, that they answer the expectation of the appetite. When the appetite is high to anything, the expectation necessarily is so. Appetite to a particular object implies expectation in its nature. It is an expectation without reflection. When the man stands to reflect, his judgment may be otherwise. But as soon as ever the actual view of what reflection and consideration set before the mind ceases, the expectation is raised again. The appetite could not be upheld without expectation.

-- 932 --

'Tis this expectation that is not satisfied by worldly enjoyments. The man expected to have a great occasion of happiness, but he don't find himself much, if anything, more happy than he was before. But it is not so with spiritual enjoyments. They fully answer and satisfy the expectation. They find themselves as much happier as they expected.

Again, the gratification and pleasure of spiritual enjoyments are permanent. 'Tis not so with worldly enjoyments. They in a sense satisfy particular appetites. But the appetite, in being satisfied, is glutted; and then the pleasure is over. And as soon as ever that is over, the general appetite after happiness returns, and is as needy as ever. So the glutting of a particular appetite does but take away from and leave empty the general appetite and thirst of nature.

And moreover, Christ probably has here a principal respect to what shall be through the water that he shall give in another world, in heaven, the country of the church, where flows the river of water of life; they never thirst. See Revelation 7:16–17. "They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more, for the Lamb shall lead them to living fountains of water."

John 4:20. "Our fathers worshipped in this mountain."] See Genesis 12:6–7, and Genesis 33:18, Genesis 33:20.

John 4:22. "Ye worship ye know not what."] This spoken with reference to God's being a Spirit, which is observed in the next verse but one.

John 4:36–37.] "That both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together."] "He that soweth" is Christ. The ministers of the gospel, they do but reap the fruit of Christ's labors. 'Tis he that has as it were plowed the field, and tilledOr: "fitted." the ground, and sowed the seed; and he waters the seed sown. The Word, ordinances, and Spirit are of his purchasing and bestowing. Hence ministers are represented as laborers that are sent into the harvest, only to gather in the harvest, to gather in souls, the foundation of whose salvation is all already laid by Christ. He that sows is the owner of the field and Lord of the harvest. Ministers are only laborers or servants sent forth to gather in his harvest that grows in his field and sprang from seed that he has sowed. He that sows and he that reaps shall rejoice together, as Christ and the servants did when they returned and told him of their success (Luke 10:17–18, Luke 10:21). Luke 10:37, "And herein is that saying true, One soweth, and another reapeth." This was remarkablyMS: "remarkeable."

-- 933 --

verified with respect to Christ and those his disciples, for Christ, while he dwelt on earth, sowed, laid all the foundation of his future church; but the apostles and other ministers gathered in the harvest after his ascension.

John 4:43–44. "He departed thence, and went into Galilee, for Jesus himself testified, that a prophet hath no honor in his own country."] He went into Galilee and not Nazareth, where he had been brought up, because he knew that he should not meet with a good reception there. It was natural here to observe the reason why he did not now go to Nazareth, for this was soon after the beginning of his public ministry, and till then he had lived constantly at Nazareth, and he had made but one short visit to Galilee since his baptism till now, and then he returned to Nazareth, near to which was Cana. But now on this second return thither, after about eight months absence in Judea, he don't immediately return thither, as he did before, but goes into other parts of Galilee. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 185–86. JE marked this entry with a large "X" and deleted the reference to it.

John 4:46. "A certain nobleman."] "Supposed to [be] Chuza, Herod's steward,… whose wife Joanna afterwards became an attendant on Christ (Luke 8:3)." Reading's Evangelical History, Pt. 2, ch. 2.HISTORY of Our Lord and Saviour JESUS CHRIST (4th ed.), pp. 114–15. Part II contains an account of Jesus' "Discourses and Miracles, from the Imprisonment of John the Baptist, till the Great Week of his Passion."

John 4:54.] I.e. the "second miracle" which Jesus wrought in Galilee. The first was his turning water into wine at Cana [John 2:1–11]. This also was wrought at Cana, as that was, and agreed with that in this circumstance, that it was wrought as Jesus came out of Judea into Galilee. But this was not the second miracle that Christ had wrought in the whole, for this Evangelist himself gives account of many miracles he wrought before in Judea (John 2:23 and John 3:2).

John 5.] In the latter end of this chapter, and so in other places of this Evangelist, what Christ says is set down altogether, as though Christ spake it in a continued discourse. But it seems to me to have been otherwise. That the Evangelist writes together what Christ said at one time in talk with the Jews, and the Jews' speeches, to which Christ replies, are often

-- 934 --

omitted; and only what Christ said in the colloquy is set down, it being what the Evangelist chiefly aimed at, to give us the speeches of Christ.

John 5:1–4.] This of the pool of Bethesda seems to have been a miraculous dispensation of providence about that time when Christ was in the world, to be a type and representation of gospel ordinances and means of grace, and the way that persons are to seek spiritual healing by them, how that they heal not by any virtue in them, but only from a supernatural influence with them, as it was no intrinsic quality in the water of this pool whence it had its healing virtue, but from the angel's troubling the water. This troubling of the water was at no fixed period of time, but when God pleased, as 'tis just when God pleases that he gives the influences of his Spirit with his ordinances. The impotent folk seem to represent poor, impotent, diseased souls. The five porches where the impotent folk waited seem to represent wisdom's gates, as they are called in Proverbs 8. The way for the impotent folk to obtain healing was constantly to lie at the pool, for they knew not when the water would be troubled. And if they happened then to be absent when the water was troubled, they knew not whether they should ever have another. And while they lay there, the way was constantly and diligently to watch the water, because only he that first stepped in was healed. And if their eyes happened to be off, they soon lostMS: "loss'd." their opportunity, which represents the diligent and constant manner in which means for salvation are to be used in order to success. When the water was troubled, only the first that stepped [in] was healed, which seems to be to represent that when opportunities are given, the persons that are most earnest and make the most haste are commonly the persons that obtain. He that stepped in was healed of whatsoever disease he had. So there is encouragement for all sorts of sinners, and under all manner of circumstances, to seek healing in the ways of God's appointment.

See "Scripture," no. 448.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 530.

See also "Scripture," no. 449.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 531–32.

John 5:10–11.] See note on Joshua 6, "Scripture," no. 500, second paragraph.Works, 15, 593.

John 5:14. "Sin no more."] Referring probably to the sins of his youth, which the man that was healed knew in his conscience had brought his calamity

-- 935 --

upon him. These, "though committed before Christ was born (for he had labored, as we are told, under his disorder thirty-eight years John 5:5]), yet were perfectly known to him." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 287.

John 5:16. "And therefore did the Jews persecute Christ,KJV: "Jesus." JE often substituted "Christ" for "Jesus" in biblical texts. and sought to slay him."] He was accused before the Sanhedrin, who sought occasion to sentence him to death. Therefore we are to understand that the following discourse of Christ was before them, which is confirmed by John 5:33, where Christ puts 'em [in] mind how they had sent to John, and he had borne witness to him. But it was undoubtedly the Sanhedrin that sent. See John 1:19. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 1, 288, 297.

John 5:17.] "My Father worketh" at all times, on sabbath days as well as others. He heals the sick, and doth other works of power and goodness on sabbath days; and I do likewise. God the Father did not only work the six first days of the creation, but he has wrought from the beginning of the world till this time. He continually exerts the same power in upholding and governing the world which he did in creating it. And "what things soever the Father doth, these doth the Son likewise," as John 5:19.

Christ, in saying, "My Father worketh hitherto," may have respect to his miracles, as much as to say, The same works which I have wrought all along, I alone have not wrought them, but God has wrought them also, as John 5:19. And so it has been now in this work which I have done on the sabbath day.

"My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." The objection the Jews had against Christ's healing on the sabbath day was that this was a day of rest, a day wherein God rested from all his works, and wherein men ought to rest. But here Christ signifies that God did not yet rest from his great work, that work that was what he had mainly in view in the creation of the world, which he had carried on hitherto, and would continue to do so till the resurrection, spoken of, John 5:21, John 5:24–26. Though we read that on the seventh day God rested from the works of creation, yet the same is the case with respect to this rest on the seventh day that is true concerning the rest that Joshua gave the children of Israel in the land of Canaan; they are God's rest no otherwise than typically. The great rest of God yet remains, which is in the finishing and glorious issue of his work of redemption, the new creation, which as to the impetration was

-- 936 --

finished in Christ's resurrection, and as to its application will be finished in the general resurrection and day of judgment, spoken [of], John 5:21–30 (See Hebrews 4:1, Hebrews 4:10.). This great work of redemption the Father works by him who is the Redeemer. This work is carried on still on sabbath days and all days, God's rest from it not being yet come. And his healing or otherwise delivering of miserable men from their calamities on the sabbath was pursuant to the designs of this great work.This paragraph is a separate entry.

John 5:21.] By raising up and quickening the dead seems, by the John 5:24–25 which are exegetical of this, to be meant the conferring of eternal life on a fallen man, including all those divine works by which it is done, not only the raising the dead bodies at the last day, and translating and transforming the soul at death, but in renewing the soul in sanctification. Christ, in the exercise of that power which the Father hath given him as judge, begins to bestow eternal life on them that believe on him in this world, goes on so to do at death, and perfects it at the day of judgment, in all these things raising and quickening the dead.

John 5:27. "And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man."] Christ is the more fitted to be the judge of men for his being himself a man, one of the same race, having the same faculties, and senses, and organs, living in the same world under the same law, and the same circumstances and temptations, sin only excepted. It tends to confirm the faith of the saints that their near kinsman and elder brother, and himself being in the form of a servant, performed obedience for them, and wrought out the righteousness that they depend upon for justification in the judgment, and also suffered from the same unrighteous enemies. This tends to encourage and confirm their faith and hope that he will vindicate 'em in the judgment, and plead their righteous cause against their unrighteous enemies. And it tends also to the convictions of those that shall be condemned in the judgment. Christ, being in the same nature with them, and subject to the same law, under like weakness, frailty, and temptations, yea, infinitely greater temptations, will be the fitter to rise up in judgment against them, and condemn 'em.

John 5:37. "Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape."] "Ye," i.e. your nation. The nation of Israel, they never heard the voice of

-- 937 --

the Father, nor saw his shape; but he hath sent me, and has spoken and appeared by me, and so hath "borne witness of me" by sending me. See John 1:18 and John 6:46, and 1 John 4:12.

John 5:37–39.] As much as to say, 'Tis true ye have not heard his voice, and seen his shape, as you have often required when you have said, Show us a sign from heaven, desiring to hear his voice, and see some outward visible form or appearance, as your fathers did at Mt. Sinai. But my Father has borne witness of me in his word; and therefore ye would know that he has borne witness of me, if his word were abiding in you, which it is not. Therefore "search the scriptures" John 5:39], and there you will find that the Father testifies of me.

John 5:43–44.] They were ready to follow those false messiahs, mentioned in the John 5:43, because they promised them worldly honor, or the honor which was of men, to make 'em rulers of the world. But he came with no such doctrine or promises. He taught mortification and abasement. His doctrine and life, and all that was to be observed in him, tended to lead 'em away from the glory of this world. And therefore they who sought earthly glory could not find it in their hearts to close with him.

John 5:45.] See no. 43.Works, 15, 59.

John 6:26.] Hence learn that rational arguments, such as the miracles that Christ wrought, tend to a saving conviction. It is implied here that if the Jews had sought Christ because they were thoroughly convinced by his miracles, they would have sought him aright. And therefore that belief of gospel truth may be saving which arises from arguments that tend to convince the reason. The same is implied, John 10:37–38; and John 11:15 and John 11:42; and John 13:19; and John 14:29; and John 17:21; and John 19:35. John 2:11, John 11:45, and John 20:8, and John 12:37, and John 20:27, etc.

John 6:31. "Our fathers did eat manna."] As much as to say, Thou, indeed, has fed us miraculously in the wilderness with a few loaves and fishes, but that was but one meal. But Moses fedJE deleted "over six hundred thousand beside." that vast congregation in the wilderness for forty years together with bread from heaven. That was what these men that followed Christ for the loaves aimed at, constantly

-- 938 --

to be fed by Jesus without any labor or expense of theirs, that they might enjoy a fullness in ease and sloth.

John 6:31–33.] See no. 210, Corol. 1, in that part of it that is there noted in the margin.Works, 15, 138, n

John 6:39.] This verse proves perseverance, for all that believe on Christ are those that God has given him, as appears by the following verse.

John 6:63. "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing."] This is to explain in what sense they must eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, viz. not in a corporal and carnal manner, but by receiving those influences of his Spirit which he has purchased by his body and blood, and by the influences of that Spirit feeding on his body and blood by faith. "The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life." And this is to show how they must receive that "spirit that quickeneth," or how they must receive the spirit and life by the Spirit, viz. by his word. The Spirit of Christ is conveyed by the word of Christ and life by the Spirit. The way for them to eat the flesh of the Son of man, and to drink his blood so as to live by it, or to obtain that spiritual and eternal life that is given by his Spirit, is to receive and entertain his word. And therefore it was their not believing his word that cut them off from life, as in the next verse.

John 6:64–65.] See "Controversies," pp. 110e and 111b.JE interprets these passages from John as proof that "apostates never have the same kind of faith with true saints," for Jesus knew from the beginning that Judas would afterwards betray him. Though Judas had "a kind of faith in Christ," yet he was destitute of true faith and piety, being "wholly under the dominion of wickedness" ("'Controversies' Notebook," section on Perseverance, MS pp. 105–11).

John 6:70. "Jesus answered, Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?"] It is manifest by the history which the evangelists give us that Christ had been exceedingly admired and mightily flocked after by a very great part of the common people in Galilee, and especially the region round about Capernaum, from his first beginning to preach and work miracles there till now, being influenced by secular views and an expectation of great worldly advantages in the kingdom of heaven or kingdom of the Messiah, which they hoped that Jesus would introduce. And the

-- 939 --

multitude of his followers, and their great expectations from him, seemed rather to increase till this time. They seemed to be raised to their greatest height by the miracle of his feeding five thousand with five loaves and two fishes. But Christ did not at all cherish their carnal expectations, and that admiration and applause, and seeming friendship of theirs that was built upon it, but disappointed and confounded 'em exceedingly in this discourse of his that is related in this chapter. They hoped for a fullness of meat and drink, and an abundance of worldly good things, but he encouraged 'em with the hopes of no other meat and drink but his flesh and blood, telling 'em that he came down from heaven, assuring them that unless they eat the flesh of the Son of man and drank his blood, they had no life in 'em, and that he that eat his flesh and drank his blood dwelt in him, and he in him; signifying that instead of reigning in perpetua worldly glory here, he should in a little time leave this world and ascend up where he was before, also teaching them that the blessings of his kingdom were not of a temporal or carnal, but spiritual nature. These things were very unintelligible to them, and appeared to 'em strange absurd doctrines; but yet they understood so much of the tendency of 'em that they perceived nothing of that sort of plenty and glory [that] was to be expected from him, the expectations of which were raised so high just before. Therefore a very great part of that multitude that used to throng him from this time forsook him and followed him no more. And the number of his followers seems to have been diminished for some time after this.This sentence is a later interlineation. And now was the faith of the twelve also remarkably tried more than ever it had been before by the doctrine Christ had now taught, and by the great alteration that appeared in the multitude that followed him, and the example of so many that forsook him, which occasioned Christ to say to 'em, as he does, John 6:67, "Will ye also go away?" It seems that the faith of them all stood this trial, excepting Judas. But now it is highly probable that the faith of Judas began to fail. And though he did [not] for shame openly forsake Christ till about a twelve-month after, and was silent when Christ put this question and Peter answered as he did, in the name of the rest, yet that now his expectations of that worldly wealth and glory that he aimed at in following Christ began to fail, and that he was inwardly much offended by this mysterious spiritual discourse of his master, and began to be alienated from him, and to have within him secret workings of disgust and enmity (though he said nothing when Christ asked them whether they also would go away, and hypocritically by his silence

-- 940 --

allowed Peter's answer to go for them all), yet Christ, who searched all hearts, perceiving how it was, saw fit to let it be known that he knew that there was one of 'em that did not cordially join in Peter's answer, which Judas knew in his conscience was his case.

John 7:27. "When Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is."] See Isaiah 53:8. The Jews probably took this apprehension concerning the Messiah from thence.This sentence is a later addition.

John 7:29. "I am from him."] "παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, 'I am with him.'" So Doddridge renders it.Family Expositor, 2, 52, n. d.

John 7:34.] This is what Christ says to the Jews that sought his life, and particularly the officers that the Pharisees had sent to take him. They now sought Christ to take him and kill him. Now Christ was here; now they could find him and could kill. But he shall rise again, and then shall live forevermore. And he shall not remain here to be any longer in their reach, for he shall go to him that sent him, shall ascend up to heaven to sit down on the right hand of the throne of God. And though they shall seek him then, as they do now, they shall persecute him in his members, and endeavor to destroy his interest in the world, and kill his church, but they shall not be able to do it. For Christ being then ascended to glory, this will be the safety of his interest in the world, for all power shall be committed to him in heaven and in earth. He shall ascend as the church's head; and therefore as he will be out of the reach of his enemies,MS: "Church." so will his church. The gates of hell never shall prevail against [him]. This may be the comfort of his people, that however they are persecuted, Christ is alive forevermore, and is for them at the right hand of the throne of God. So the man-child that the woman brought forth,MS: "forth is." that the dragon persecuted and sought to destroy as soon as it was born, is said to be "caught up to God, and to his throne" (Revelation 12:5), i.e. that it might be out of the reach of the dragon that persecuted it. So the two witnesses that had been persecuted and slain are said, when they come to life, to ascend into heaven in the sight of their enemies, that is, for the time to come to be out of their reach [Revelation 11:12]. The church shall come to such a state that Antichrist by his persecutions shall not be able to suppress or destroy her. See John 8:21.

-- 941 --

John 7:37. "In the last day."] This feast of tabernacles represents the glorious state of the church in the latter age of the world; and this "last day" of it, which was commanded to be kept as a sabbath, represents theJE deleted "eternal rest." glory of the church which shall be at the day of judgment, represented in the Revelation 21-22. See note on Zechariah 14:16 ff. And therefore this invitation of Christ is attended with circumstances parallel with those in the Revelation 22.

John 7:38–39.] No. 263.Works, 15, 209–10.

John 8:1.] See note on Luke 21:37.

John 8:6. "This they said, tempting him, that they might have whereof to accuse him."] Their question was exceeding subtile and ensnaring. They seem to suggest the strongest reasons against his determining that they might not stone [her], for they tell him of the most direct evidence of her guilt, for she was taken in the very act, and also tell him that Moses commanded that such should be stoned, which could not be denied. But if he answered that she ought to be stoned, then they stood ready to accuse him to the Roman government of sedition, for the Romans had taken away the power of life and death from the Jews. And if he said that they should not stone her, then they would accuse him to the Jews of expressly contradicting Moses. Therefore we are not to understand Christ's answer as though he disapproved of such a law of Moses, but only that he would not so concern himself in this matter as to do anything against the Roman authority they were now under. It was one thing that rendered the Jews exceeding uneasy under the Roman government, that the Romans had taken away the power of life and death from them, whereby they were incapable of inflicting those kinds of punishments that the law of Moses directed to. Christ knew their hearts, and knew those secret acts that they themselves were conscious to, and how far they had been guilty of things of a like nature, and therefore knew how to answer 'em.

See Doddridge, note 68, p. 16, of the additional notes in the Appendix to third volume of Family Expositor.This paragraph is a later addition. Note 68 points to the "snare" laid for Jesus by his questioners. If Jesus pronounced a "Capital Sentence" on the adulterous, for which "he had no Authority from the Romans," they might accuse him to Pilate, the Roman governor. Even Jewish authorities, who had the right to try such cases, were obligated to have their sentence "recognized and allowed by the Romans."

-- 942 --

John 8:12. "I am the light of the world."] This probably was spoken on occasion of the sun's being "lately risen, and shining" on the people that he was speaking to as they stood in the court of the temple, for it was now in the morning. See John 8:2.JE deleted "Doddridge." See Family Expositor, 2, 60, 65.

And it may be observed that this was the morning after the feast of tabernacles, probably before the morning sacrifice, after which no doubt many of the people would be setting out for their habitations in the country. And as to the light of this natural sun that was now risen on the earth, it would quickly fail 'em. The sun would be set, and leave 'em to travail in the dark. For it could not be otherwise than a common thing for the people, coming from all parts to the three great feasts at Jerusalem, to travel in the night in their going and returning, for there could not be accommodations for the convenient lodging such vast multitudes in houses by the way. See Isaiah 30:29.

John 8:15.] See no. 43.Works, 15, 59. Christ did not now appear in the quality of a judge, but a Savior. Hereafter he shall appear in the quality of a judge. See John 3:17.

"I judge no man." John 12:47.This reference is a separate entry.

John 8:21. "Whither I go, ye cannot come."] Note on John 7:34.

John 8:33.] The Jews have reference to that law in Leviticus 25:39–46, where God appoints that the children of strangers might be made bondmen, but not those that were of the seed of Israel; and to what Solomon did that we have account of in 1 Kings 9:21–22, who levied "a tribute of bond service" of the children of strangers, "but of the children of Israel he made no bondmen, but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen"; and to the prophecy of Isaiah 14:1–2, where it is foretold that other nations should be joined to the children of Israel, and they should possess them "for servants and handmaids." They therefore took in disdain that Christ should tell them of being "made free," as if now they were bondmen, and especially that he should speak of himself as being the means of their being

-- 943 --

made free, who supposed that as they were the children of Abraham [they] were as free as he himself, and needed none of his good offices in that respect. They looked upon it that he magnified himself too much in so saying, as well as debased them, which is more evident by the reply they make to what Christ says in the John 8:51, as further pursuing this same doctrine. This thought of theirs seems to be the occasion of what Christ says in the John 8:35–36, showing of them that he hath greater honor and privilege in the house of God than they, and that true liberty in that house must be by him.

John 8:36. "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."] "In which our Savior seems to allude to a custom which was in some of the cities of Greece, and perhaps in other places, whereby the son and heir had a power to adopt brethren, and to give the liberty and privilege of the family." Tillotson's Works, vol. 3, p. 578.This is taken from Tillotson's sermon 193, "True Liberty, the Result of Christianity" (pp. 578–85).

John 8:40. "This did not Abraham."] But was most remote from it, and did what was very contrary to it. Instead of having a mortal hatred to me as you have, he "rejoiced to see my day, and saw it, and was glad," as John 8:56. Instead of being so opposite to the truth which is revealed from God, 'tis written of Abraham that he believed God [Genesis 15:6], and so is the father of the faithful and believers, and not of malicious unbelievers.

John 8:44.] Christ proves that they are not the children of Abraham, in the John 8:40, and that they are the children of the devil, in this verse, viz. by their works, particularly in seeking to kill him, and in their enmity against the divine truth that he declared. He, in the John 8:40, observes that these are not the works of Abraham, and in this verse he shows that they were both the works of the devil. He shows first that they did the works of the devil in seeking to kill him, in that "heI.e. the devil. was a murderer from the beginning." And then he shows that they did the lust of the devil also in their enmity against that divine truth that heI.e. Christ. taught, in that the devil "abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him, and when he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own," he being "a liar, and the father of it."

-- 944 --

John 8:51. "Verily, verily, I say unto you, If a man keep my words, he shall never see death."] This Christ says, as still insisting on and pursuing the same doctrine, in the John 8:32, John 8:34, and John 8:35, which were the occasion of this controversy that he had with the Jews, and which he reproves them for not believing, in the John 8:45–47.

John 8:56. "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day; and he saw it, and was glad."] What Christ probably refers to here in the history of Abraham, at least in part, was Abraham's laughing when Isaac was promised, and those great blessings which God promised to and by his seed (Genesis 17:17), for that laughter of Abraham's was not like that unbelieving laughter of Sarah, that we read of the next chapter, for which she was reproved. For God never reproved Abraham, but rather manifested his approbation of it in ordering that his son's name should be Isaacיִצְחָק, יִשְׂתחָק on that occasion, which signifies "laughter, or "he shall laugh." It seems to [be] a laughter occasioned by the joy and gladness of his heart, arising from his belief of God's promises, and the prospect of their fulfillment, and particularly some inward discovery he had then made to him of the glorious things of Christ that was his seed, and the consideration of the strangeness and wonderfulness of it that such blessings should be granted to him who was so unlikely to receive them, and almost past hope of having it in the way now spoken of, by reason that he and Sarah were so old, which Abraham had consideration of when he laughed, as in that forementioned verse in Genesis.

The occasion of Christ's mentioning this is to show the Jews that the honor that he had was not of himself, but that both God and their father Abraham honored him. They had been boasting that Abraham was their father (John 8:33, John 8:39, John 8:53), and also that God was their Father (John 8:41). And therefore here Christ shows that he don't only honor himself, but first that God, that they said was their God and Father, honored him (John 8:54), and that Abraham, that they also boasted so much of, honored him, as in this verse.This paragraph is a later addition.

John 9:6–7.] As Christ spit on the ground, so he puts the word and spirit of his mouth into earth, into ministers that are but clay, and with them opens men's eyes.

-- 945 --

John 9:7. "Siloam,Σιλωάμ which is by interpretation, Sent."] From this I observe two things. 1. That the facts related in the history of Christ in the New Testament are typical or mystical, as well as the facts of the history of the Old Testament. 2. That the Holy Spirit makes account of the signification of names in order to instruct the church in divine matters.

John 10:3. "To him the porter openeth."] I.e. either Christ's true minister, or the Holy Spirit.

John 10:10.] The words "more abundantly" refer either to what man would have had if he had stood by the first covenant, or to what the people of God were wont to have before Christ came into the world, and probably to both.

John 10:11–12.] The "good shepherd" standeth between the wolf and the sheep, and himself is slain by the wolf to save the lives of the sheep.

John 10:12. "Hireling."] See note on Micah 3:11.

John 10:14–15.] Our translation here darkens the sense and connection. These two verses are connected together as the words are in the original.καὶ γινώσκο τὰ ἐμὰ καὶ γινώσκουσί με τὰ ἐμὰ, καθώς γινώσκει με ὁ πατὴρ κἀγὼ γινώσκο τὸν πατέρα. "Thus I know my sheep, and am known of mine, even as the Father knoweth me, and I know the Father." (See Doddridge.)Family Expositor, 2, 214. These words in the latter part of John 10:15, "and I lay down my life for the sheep," are connected with the foregoing verse, the former part of this verse coming in as a parenthesis. Concerning the import of the word "know" here, see Matthew 25:12, Deuteronomy 33:9, Job 9:21, Psalms 31:7.

John 10:17. "Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again."] By this it seems not an unscriptural way of speaking to call that favor of God that is consequent on the righteousness the creature hath, his "love," for God here is said to love Christ for his righteousness, or that great act of obedience, his laying down his life. See next verse. By that Christ purchased the love of God for himself, and therefore for all that are in him. God loves Christ for his own righteousness, and therefore he loves all to whom his righteousness is imputed

-- 946 --

for the same righteousness. The love of God is consequent on the righteousness of Christ in two respects. 1. A love of complacence is consequent. 2. The exercises, and communications, and fruits of a love of benevolence, and manifestation of it. See John 14:21, and also Proverbs 8:17.

John 10:18. "Of my Father."] Isaiah 50:5–6.

John 10:22.] Of this "feast of dedication," see Prideaux, Connection, Pt. II, p. 278.This eight-day festival, during which candles were set up at every door, was called the Feast of Lights (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, p. 278).

Concerning the feast of dedication. When the temple was finished in Ezra's time, they kept the feast of dedication with great solemnity under the direction of persons divinely inspired (Ezra 6:16–17). And 'tis very probable that they kept the same from year to year by the same direction, and that this, having been long their custom, led the Jews, on the restoration of the temple by Judas Maccabeus, to keep it from year to year in like manner, looking on the divine direction by Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah as an implicit direction annually to keep the dedication of the temple in a restoration after it had been desolate. And 'tis not likely they would have gone into this custom of such an annual feast to commemorate the restoration of the temple if it had not been an usage before, for they could not look on this restoration greater than that after the Babylonish captivity.This paragraph is a separate entry.

John 10:26–29.] These verses afford two arguments for perseverance. First, the John 10:26–27 show that only those that are Christ's sheep hear his voice, that is, none but those that are elected. Christ calls all those his sheep that are elected, and not only those that are actually called, as is evident by John 10:16. Those Christ calls "his" that are those whom God has given him. But men are given to Christ before they are called (John 17:6).

John 10:35. "If he called them gods."] Nos. 234 and 482.Works, 15, 184–85, 578–80.

John 10:36.] See "Miscellanies," nos. 624 and 709.Ibid., 2, 154, 333–35. The second reference is a later addition.

-- 947 --

John 10:41. "John did no miracle, but all things that John spake of this man was true."] The verifying of the things that he said concerning Christ was good evidence of his being a prophet sent from God, though he had not the evidence of miracles.

John 11:16. "Let us also go, that we may die with him."] I.e. that we may die with Jesus, for Thomas has respect to that danger which the disciples objected against, his returning to Judea (John 11:7). But since their objection did not prevail, but they perceived that Christ persisted in his resolution to go notwithstanding, Thomas says as he does here.

John 11:33–38.] Christ wept, and groaned in spirit, and was troubled, as we have here an account. His soul was as it were in travail for Lazarus when about to raise him from the dead. His raising Lazarus was a remarkable type of the spiritual resurrection, regeneration, and salvation of a soul. The salvation of souls is through the travail of Christ's soul, as Isaiah 53. Here is a representation of that, and here is an example set for ministers and others, how they ought to seek the spiritual renovation and salvation of other souls. They should as it were travail in birth with them.

John 11:51.] See no. 53.Works, 15, 65.

John 11:52. "But that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad."] That is, that he should also die for the people of God that are "scattered abroad," that should be by means of his death gathered together with the Jews to be one nation, to be all one spiritual Israel. The meaning of the Evangelist is this, that when Caiaphas spoke of Christ's dying "for that nation," the mind of God, who purposely directed Caiaphas to these words, was by "that nation" to signify the whole true Israel, so that the prophecy included allJE deleted "believers." the elect, for they were all by the death of Christ to be gathered to Israel to be one nation.

John 12:3. "And wiped his feet with her hair."] She esteemed it an honor to have her head anointed with the ointment of Christ's feet. See note on Luke 7:38.

Mary at this time anointed both the head and also the feet of Jesus with the precious ointment out of her broken alabaster box. So divine

-- 948 --

love issues out of a pure and broken heart not only to Christ, the head of the church, but towards the meanest of his members. And 'tis brokenness of heart that brings persons to so humble a disposition as to put honor on the meanest Christians, and this is signified by Christ's feet's being anointed with tears. 'Tis tears of repentance that brings the heart to so humble a frame.This paragraph is a later addition.

"Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard." See note on Mark 14:3.This reference is a separate entry.

John 12:24.] The corn of wheat falling into the ground, and rising again, and being so greatly increased, represents two things. [1.] It represents Christ's dying, and rising again, and being greatly increased, both in the exaltation and glory of his person, and by his thereby bringing forth the church, whereby Christ is as it were multiplied into thousands. This is what Christ has respect to in the John 12:24. And 2. It represents the great increase the saints have by their death, especially those that lay down their lives for Christ's sake. They exchange this mortal life for life eternal. This is spoken of in this John 12:25.

John 12:27–28.] It was meet that the natural weakness of the human nature of Christ should appear in his last and greatest conflict with the powers of darkness, which was in his last sufferings, for the power of God appears the more glorious in the victory that he obtained by that weak instrument, the human nature of Christ. God was pleased to make use of [a] tender plant, a babe to overthrow that mighty, proud enemy, the devil. It was a little babe that bruised his head, that trampled him underfoot, and gloriously triumphed over him. God strengthened the human nature of Christ so that it overcame when its strength seemed ready to be overpowered. See Matthew 26:38–39.

John 12:34. "How sayst thou the Son of man must be lift up? Who is this Son of man?"] Everything in the gospel is darkness and confusion to the ungodly. Christ is a gin and snare to them. They are ignorant both of his person and of his design. They know not who he is, nor what he came for, nor to what purpose. Christ crucified is "to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness" [1 Corinthians 1:23]. Though Christ "had done so many miracles, yet believed they not on him" (John 12:37). They were

-- 949 --

not the children of light, but walked in darkness, and knew not whitherMS: "whether." they went (John 12:35–36). They could not believe; their eyes were blinded, that "they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart" (John 12:39–40).

John 12:47.] See no. 43.Works, 15, 59.

"I judge him not, for I came not to judge," etc. Christ intermeddles not with judging in the world till his mediation for sinners is over, till pardoning sin is done, and no more sin shall be forgiven. Then Christ's business will be to judge; but till all that work is done, Christ concerns not himself with judging.This paragraph is a separate entry.

John 13:2. "And supper being ended."] "δείπνου γενομένου. It should have been rendered, 'supper being come,' which is the sense in which the word is often used elsewhere. Thus John 21:4, πρωῖας γενομένης, is 'when the morning was come.' Acts 12:18 and Acts 16:35, ἡμέρας γενομένης, 'when day was come.' Acts 21:40, σιγῆς γενομένης, 'when silence was made.'" Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 423, n. a.

John 13:4.] This action of Christ is typical, for Christ in coming to die for us, does as it were make himself our servant. He is "least in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 11:11). He greatly humbled himself, and suffered shame, and was made a curse, that he might minister to us, that he might wash and cleanse us from the filthiness of sin. This washing is that which is here signified. And therefore Christ says to Peter, John 13:8, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part in me," i.e. if he did not wash him from his sins, which was the thing signified by his washing his feet. See Luke 22:25–27.

"He riseth from supper." I.e. from "the antepast that had been taken, which is mentioned by the Jews as preceding the paschal lamb. The master of the family began the feast with a cup of wine which, having solemnly blessed, he divided among the guests, and afterwards washed his hands. And if I am rightly informed, the Jews continue this custom still." But Christ now, besides this, washes his disciples' feet. Doddridge, in loc., and on Mark 14:17.This paragraph is later addition. Family Expositor, 2, 424, n. c.; 420, n. e.

-- 950 --

John 13:10. "He that is washed,MS: "washeth." needeth not save to wash his feet."] Christ here seems to allude to their having just bathed themselves, after the manner before the Passover. Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 425–26. And probably Christ may have some respect to the legal washings of the priests, who at their consecration were washed all over (Exodus 29:4), but afterwards were required only to "wash their hands and their feet" at the laver (Exodus 30:19–21).This sentence is a later addition.

John 13:14–15.] 'Tis especially the duty of the disciples as ministers that Christ intends to teach them here; and what that duty is, is explained by that practice of the apostle Paul, which he speaks of in 1 Corinthians 9:19.

John 13:34. "A new commandment."] Called "a new commandment" in contradistinction to that, Leviticus 19:18. The old commandment required us to love one another as ourselves, but the new commandment requires that we love one another as Christ hath loved us.

John 13:35.] "It is well known that the founders of new societies appoint some peculiar ornament, sign, or mode of living by which their followers may be known from others. This seems to be here alluded to." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 440, n. c.

John 14:2. "In my Father's house are many mansions. If it were not so, I would have told you."] Christ had told his disciples that he was going away. They were troubled and concerned to think that he was going to leave them, and that henceforward they should be separated from him, as they took it. It was contrary to their expectation, who expected to be with Christ, and to reign with him in a kingdom. Christ, to remove their concern and doubts, tells them that in his Father's house where he was going, there was room for them too. There was more mansions than one. Though he was God's only begotten Son, yet other children might be admitted into the family. There was not only a mansion for him there, but for many other children, and room enough for them to be admitted, that they might be there in his Father's house along with him. "If it were not so, I would have told you," says Christ. The disciples, though they had not right notions of Christ's glorified state, and did not know that it was in heaven and not on earth that he was to have his residence and throne, yet they had always expected that their master would ere long be in a

-- 951 --

more glorious state than that that he was in at present, and that there would be a time when he would take the possession of a kingdom and they all along expected to be with him in this his exalted state, never thought of any such thing as being separated from him, and therefore seem surprised now Christ tells them of going away. They had often manifested such an expectation, and Christ never discountenanced it in them, which he certainly would have done if this was not a privilege designed for his disciples. If there had not been more mansions in heaven than one, if there had been no room for them there to be there with him, if they were to be kept separate from him in his glorified state so contrary to their expectations, he certainly would have told them. He never would have led them on in the blind, and have nourished in them a groundless expectation of a higher privilege than ever they were like to obtain. Christ desired not that they should think that they were like to get more by being his disciples than they were.

"I go to prepare a place for you." What must most naturally be understood by this speech of Christ is that he was going to prepare or make ready a place for them, in that sense in that he was going to alter the place that was to be the place of their future abode, so as to make it better for them, more fit for the reception and entertainment of those that were Christ's friends and the objects of his dear love, and those that he delights to honor, as persons, when they expect a dear friend from far to be their guest, will prepare his house, and adorn it against [when] he comes, that it may be the fitter for his convenient, comfortable, and honorable entertainment. So if a person was fitting his house for the reception of a beloved bride, it would be by putting it in every respect under such circumstances as should be most for her delightful entertainment. Thus Christ, that loved the church and gave himself for her, after he had redeemed her, went to heaven to prepare the palace of his eternal abode for reception by beautifying and adorning it, and increasing its glory. Hence [we] may argue that at Christ's ascension the glory of heaven was greatly increased, and made a more happy and blessed seat, and put under vastly superior circumstances for the entertainment and delight of its inhabitants than what it was in before, and so will probably receive a still further accession of glory at Christ's second ascension.This paragraph is a separate entry.

John 14:4. "And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know."] Christ means, Ye know the Father to whom I go, and ye know me that am the way to

-- 952 --

the Father, the way by which ye also may come whither I am now going, viz. to the Father. This appears to be the meaning by the context.

John 14:6. "I am the way, the truth, and the life."] In the foregoing verses there are three things spoken of, viz. 1. The place or blessed state to which Christ was going; 2. The way to it; and 3. The knowledge of it. About each of these the disciples are here inquiring of Christ. And therefore Christ in this verse tells them that he himself is virtually each of these. He was the life or happiness to which they desired to know the way. And he was also the way to it. And he was the truth by which they might come to the knowledge of both the life and the way to it. There was everything in him that they needed; in him all fullness dwelt.

John 14:7. "If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also."] This Christ says with respect to what Thomas said in the John 14:5. "Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?" But Christ here intimates that if they knew him, they also knew whither he went, or to whom he went, viz. God the Father. They knew the Father to whom he went, if they knew him. This is to confirm what Christ said in the John 14:4, "Whither I go ye know."

John 14:10. "The words that I speak unto you, I speak not of myself."] "The words that I speak" are the Father's words; and the Father is plainly to be seen in my word, as 'tis a divine word. And then it follows, "But the Father that dwelleth in me, he doth the works." This proves the foregoing sentence, viz. that the words that he spake [were] not of himself, but of the Father, because the Father did the works. 'Tis taken for granted that he that confirms Christ's word by miracles, that does those works to confirm them, that they are his word. This shows how that he that sees Christ, sees the Father, in that he hears the word, and sees the works of the Father.

John 14:11. "Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me."] I.e. from the evidences there are of divinity in me and in my word, from what is plainly to be seen in my person of my union with God and God's union with me, or of my being a divine person. "Or else believe me for the very works' sake." The foregoing verse confirms this interpretation.

John 14:12. "Because I go to my Father."] To receive the gift of the Holy Ghost, and send it down upon you. For if I go not to the Father, the Comforter

-- 953 --

will not come [John 16:7]. This is said to comfort them about his going away, and to make them sensible of the benefit of it.This sentence is a later addition.

John 14:13. "And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do," etc.] Christ speaks especially of those works or miracles spoken of in the foregoing verse. And therefore 'tis said, "that will I do," and not, "that will I give."

John 14:21. "He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them."] He that hath Christ's commandments is he that now professes Christ's name, and observes his religion. He that keepeth them is he that perseveres therein. See note on Hebrews 2:1.

"Shall be loved of my Father." See John 10:17.This reference is a separate entry.

John 14:22. "How is it that thou wilt manifest thyself to us, and not unto the world?"] Christ told them in the John 14:19 that "yet a little while, and the world should see" him no more, but they should see him, and in the John 14:21 [he] tells 'em that he would manifest and show himself to them that loved him. However, the world saw him not. This was [a] matter of difficulty unto Judas, for Christ hitherto was seen not only by them, but by others.

John 14:23–24. "If a man love me, he will keep my words."] Christ manifests himself and is seen now since his ascension by his word made effectual by the Spirit. And therefore they that love him will see him, when the world doth not, because they keep his sayings. And the world that don't love him don't keep his sayings, by which he is seen; and therefore they see him not.

John 14:24.] 'Tis added, "And the word which you hear is not mine, but the Father's that sent me." This is to explain how not only he, but the Father, shall abide with him that keeps his word, because 'tis his Father's word as well as his.

John 15:1. "I am the true vine."] Christ may probably here have reference to what is said, Psalms 80:8–19.

-- 954 --

John 15:2. "Every branch in me that beareth not fruit."] See Luke 5:18, Matthew 13:12.

John 15:3. "Now ye are clean," etc.] Christ here refers to the purging spoken of in the preceding verse. "Every branch in me that beareth [not] fruit he purgeth," and he hath purged you "through the word that I have spoken."

John 15:10. "If ye keep my commandments," etc.] A persevering in a holy life is here and elsewhere made the condition of continuing in Christ's love. But this no more proves a possibility of falling from grace than the latter part of this verse proves the possibility of Christ's failing of continuing in obedience to his Father.

John 15:15.] The word "henceforth" has respect to the old testament dispensation when Christ's people were treated as servants, and had the spirit of bondage (the son, while a child, differs nothing from a servant), as well as to the reserve with which he taught them the mysteries of his kingdom before his ascension.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. And the latter part of the verse, "all things that I have heard of my Father have I made known unto you," have a more especial reference to that more plain and clear revelation Christ was about to make to them of the great doctrines of the gospel by his Spirit after his ascension, he speaking of that which certainly would be, and that quickly, as if it were past, as is frequent in Scripture, and even in Christ's own discourses. A most evident instance of it will appear by comparing John 17:12 with John 18:9.

John 15:16.] See note on John 16:16.MS: "See next page." Or the "16" may point to the John 16:16 entry.

John 15:19. "If ye were of the world."] Numbers 23:9.

John 16:7. "It is expedient," etc.] The Comforter here spoken [of] is the sum of all that Christ procured for his disciples in his redemption. His dying and ascending was needful in order to a procuring this benefit these ways, viz. as it was by his death that this benefit was purchased, for in this context he speaks of his going away as his "righteousness" (John 16:10). And then his going to heaven, and entering into the holiest of all with his own

-- 955 --

blood, was needful in order to a procuring it by his intercession. And then it was needful that he should be instated in his kingdom, wherein he was made head over all things to his church by being set down at the right hand of God in heaven, that he might himself, according to his own will, dispense purchased benefits, and send forth the Comforter, which he had purchased.

John 16:8–11.] See no. 134.Works, 15, 87–88. See John 3:18.This reference is a later addition.

"He will reprove the world of sin," etc. "The word ἐλέγξει properly signifies 'convince.' Compare John 8:9, John 8:46; 1 Corinthians 14:24; Titus 1:9; and James 2:9.'" "Of sin, because they believe not on me" John 16:9]. "He will convince the world of that aggravated sin which they are guilty of, because they do not believe in me, to the truth of whose mission he will bear an unanswerable testimony by his enlightening influences and miraculous operations." "Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more" John 16:10]. "He will convince the world of my righteousness and innocence, because it will evidently appear, that I go to my Father, and am accepted of him, when I send the Spirit from him in so glorious a manner (Compare Acts 2:33 and Romans 1:4.), and that my righteousness may therefore be relied on for the justification and acceptance of my people, since you see me no more appearing among you in the form of a servant, but are assured that having finished what I was to do on earth, I am taken up to heaven, and received into glory." "Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged" John 16:11]. "And he will convince of my being invested with the power of executing judgment, because the prince of this world, the great head of the apostasy, is now as it were already judged and condemned, and shall then be triumphed over in a very remarkable manner, when his oracles are silenced, and he is cast out of from many persons, and countries too, which he before possessed. (Compare John 12:31.) And Satan being thus divested of his power, my gospel shall be propagated through the world, and a full proof at length be given of my sovereign authority, in my coming to execute judgment upon all ungodly sinners." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 2, 474–75. See "Scripture," no. 498.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 588–92. See Poole's Synopsis, in loc., at the place marked in the margin.This paragraph is a separate entry, and this reference is a later addition. Synopsis Criticorum, IV (London, 1674), Pt. 1, cols. 1339–42.

-- 956 --

John 16:9.] The guilt of that part of the world that live under the gospel, it chiefly arises from unbelief, and rejecting and contemning Christ. This, the guilt that arises, hence is more than what arises from all other sins. Not but that the guilt of one that lives in grossly vicious practices under the gospel may be manifold more than another unbeliever that also rejects Christ, because presumptuously perpetrating vice under the gospel is an high act of contempt of Christ,JE deleted "in all his offices, prophet, priest, and king." and of the glory and grace of God appearing in him and his redemption.

John 16:10. "Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more."] 'Tis his death that Christ chiefly respectsMS: "Respect." when he here speaks of his going to the Father, and their seeing him no more, though not excluding his ascension. It was his death by which Christ left the world. Though he appeared from time to time a little while to his disciples here below after his death, yet it was by his death that his union with the world was broke, and by which he was translated out of a terrestrial or worldly state. Christ had [been] telling the disciples of his approaching death under those expressions of his "going to the Father" and their "seeing him no more"; and he still uses the same expressions, aiming hereby to hint to them the necessity and importance of that which they appeared full of concern about (See John 16:6 and John 16:7.), and to suggest that which should be comforting and encouraging to them about his going away. 'Tis the death of Christ that is the principal thing that is the foundation of that righteousness that the Holy Ghost convinces the world of. His being obedient to death was the highest act of his righteousness, and the main foundation of justification.

But his ascension is not unconcerned in this affair, for as Christ died for our sins, so he rose again and ascended for our justification. As by his death he wrought righteousness and procured justification, so he ascended, entered into the holiest of all, with his blood to plead his satisfaction and righteousness to our actual acceptance with God as righteous, and in order to the application of it to us by faith in our justification, and our having the fruit of it in our inherent righteousness by his sending down the Holy Ghost to work faith in us, and sanctify us.

John 16:13. "And he will show you things to come."] This had its chief accomplishment in the revelations which God gave to John in the isle of Patmos.

-- 957 --

John 16:16.] See no. 66.Works, 15, 68.

"A little while, and ye shall not see [me]; and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to my Father."
