In "a little while," they should not see him, because he was going "to the Father," and was going out of the world. "And again, a little while," and they should see him spiritually, because he was going "to the Father," to send down the Holy Spirit upon them, who should manifest him to them. See John 16:7.This paragraph is a separate entry.

John 16:20. "That ye shall weep and lament."] See Matthew 9:15.

John 16:27. "For the Father," etc.] This verse argues that love is a thing included in justifying faith. For the love here spoken of is not electing love, for God don't love us with that love because we love Christ, but it must be that love of favor and acceptance that is consequent on believing. Now to say that the Father loves us because of anything else but faith, implies full as much as to say, that he justifies us for something else. Therefore if we are accepted and justified by faith alone, love to Christ is included in faith in Christ. But if you answer, That though God loves us because we love Christ, but 'tis not in the same sense that he loves us, because we believe on him, the words of the verse don't allow of that, for 'tis said, "the Father loves you, because ye have loved me, and have believed," etc. Loving and believing would not thus have been coupled together, if it was not because of one in the same sense as the other. But this, in general, is what Christ would signify to them, viz. that the Father loved them because of their union to him, and so he loved them for his sake. See John 14:20–21, John 14:23. See also 1 Timothy 1:14.This reference is a later addition.

John 16:29–30.] "Christ's 'disciples,' [who] were struck with the correspondence of what he said to what was secretly passing in their own minds, 'said to him,' Lord, behold, 'now thou speakest' very 'plainly' to us, 'and usest no parable' or obscure form of expression, so that we clearly understand thy meaning, and rejoice in it. 'And now we know' by this further token, even thy discerning our inmost doubts on this head, 'that thou knowest all things, and hast no need that anyone should ask thee' any particular questions to inform thee of those scruples, which thou seest when first rising in their minds. 'On this account' therefore 'we'

-- 958 --

firmly 'believe that thou camest out from God.'" Doddridge's Paraphrase.Family Exposition, 2, 148.

John 16:30. "And needest not that any man should ask thee."] I.e. thou not only knowest all things, but art gracious and free to communicate to us, without our asking, agreeably to what Christ said, John 16:23.JE marked this entry with a large "X" and boxed it off on the MS.

John 17:3.] Concerning that saving knowledge of God and Christ here spoken of, see "Miscellanies," no. 1204.Works, 23, 126.

John 17:6 ff.] This chapter is exceeding evidential of the truth of the doctrine of perseverance. By the John 17:6–8, it seems evident that Christ manifests God's name, and gives faith only to those that the Father had given him. Christ prays for all such as God had given him, by which he means all such as had believed on him, as is evident by the John 17:20. He prays that God would keep them; doubtless, he means, keep them from falling away. He explains himself in the John 17:15, and declares that he means that they should be kept "from the evil." When he prays that God would keep them, he means the same sort of keeping as he means when he says that he himself had kept them (John 17:11), where he evidently means, keeping from falling away. He tells the Father that while he was with them in the world, he kept them; and now he is coming out of the world, he prays that the Father would keep them, meaning a keeping in the same respect. In the John 17:24, he prays that they may all be with him. Doubtless, these prayers of Christ shall be answered. This was one end why he prayed this prayer, that the church might have comfort in, assurance of, obtaining the things that he prayed for. Christ here prays concerning the church in general, as he did concerning Peter in particular, who he foresaw a great temptation that he was to meet with. Luke 22:32, "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not."

John 17:12. "Those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition."] See my papers on "Predestination," no. 50.JE initially wrote "34" and then later "50, " This reference to his "papers on 'Predestination'" points to a section of the "Controversies" Notebook where he has copied a citation from Doddridge, Family Expositor, 2, 487, n. f. Doddridge criticizes "learned divines," including Bishop Gilbert Burnet, whom he openly admired, who attacked the notion of election on the basis of this text. Doddridge argues that the mistaken translation of εἰ μὴ as "but" accounts for a mistaken inference. He suggests that similar mistranslations would lead to ridiculous conclusions in a number of scriptural contexts. His suggested translation is, "Those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, unless it be the son of perdition." He makes his case by arguing that εἰ μὴ here and elsewhere "is not used strictly as an exceptive particle" ("Controversies" Notebook, p. 285, section on Predestination, MS pp. 273–91).

-- 959 --

John 17:15. "But that thou shouldst keep them from the evil."] The same, I suppose, is meant here by "the evil" with that which Christ directs us to pray God to keep us from, in the seventh petition of the Lord's Prayer. See note on Matthew 6:13.This reference is a later addition.

John 17:22.] See "Miscellanies," no. 1084.Works, 20, 467.

John 17:24. "That they also."] Query. What doth this particle "also" refer to? Ans. Christ had before prayed for his own glory. This he begun with in the John 17:1. "Father (says he), the hour is come; glorify thy Son." This he repeats in the John 17:5. "And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was" John 17:5]. And this he speaks of in the verses immediately preceding (John 17:22–23); he speaks of the glory which God had given. Here he prays that God would not only glorify him, but the disciples also with him, and in his glory. He here explains his request that God would glorify him, signifying that he meant not himself singly, but with his disciples.

John 17:26.] See "Miscellanies," no. 1084.Ibid.

John 18:2. "Jesus oft times resorted thither with his disciples."] See note on Luke 21:37.

John 18:4–8.] Christ seems to have "blinded the eyes" of those that came to apprehend him "so as they did not know him," as Mr. Hurrion observes in his Knowledge of Christ Crucified, p. 225. "It could not be the darkness of the night that concealed him, for they had lanterns and torches; and besides Judas was with them, and gave them the sign agreed upon; and also Christ told them, that he was the person." But yet they seem to be confounded and lost, as not knowing where to find the person they sought. This Christ seems to have done, as also "causing them to go backward,

-- 960 --

and fall to the ground," to show that it was not for want of power in him to defend himself that he was apprehended by them, but that "he voluntarily yielded himself" up into their hands.Hurrion, Knowledge of Christ, and Him Crucified, pp. 225–26.

There were two things that Christ's enemies were afraid of and used precautions against. 1. They were afraid that it being in the night, that Christ, when he sees 'em coming, would get away before they should lay hold of him. There was Christ and his disciples, so many of 'em together, that they were afraid that while they were at a loss which was he, he would get out of their way. And to prevent this, they bring lights and torches with them, and also contrive with Judas, who knew him better than they, to direct them to the person. And he gives 'em this sign, that he go directly up to the person they sought, and kiss him; and then they should speedily lay hold on him, and hold him fast. And 2. They were afraid of resistance from him or his disciples, and therefore bring swords and staves to prevent it or suppress it. But Christ, before he delivers himself up into their hands, lets 'em know that it was none of their precautions, contrivance, or weapons that prevented his either getting away, or resisting and overcoming them. He lets them know that he could easily get out of their way if he pleased, notwithstanding the sign Judas had given them, by blinding their eyes so that they boggled, and were greatly at a loss, and knew not who to take, notwithstanding Judas's sign, till Christ himself asked them, whom they sought, and told 'em that he was the person once and again, and so after they had been thus confounded for some time, delivered himself up into their hands. And then he showed them that he could easily resist them, for all their swords, and staves, and numbers, by throwing them backwards to the ground by an invisible power, before he delivered himself up to them.This paragraph is a separate entry

John 18:8. "If therefore ye seek me, let these go their way."] Here is contained in this saying of Christ some shadow and typical intimation of that eternal deliverance from judgment and condemnation that Christ's disciples have by Christ's being substituted in their room, and being apprehended and bound as a prisoner, and condemned and executed as a malefactor in their stead.

John 18:19. "Of his disciples, and of his doctrine."] I.e. what he had taught concerning himself, whom he pretended himself to be, and with what

-- 961 --

view he had gathered so many followers, whether he had not pretended that he was the Messiah, and whether it was not with a view, as such, to set up a kingdom, that he gathered disciples?

John 18:30. "If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up to thee."] If he were not guilty of a capital crime, we would not have brought him to thee that hast the power of life and death; but we would have punished him ourselves, as we have power to inflict lesser punishments.

John 18:37–38.] Pilate inquires into the charge of taking on him the title of king, and perceiving that he intended not by it any worldly government, but that he had some mysterious scheme of a spiritual kingdom which he calls the truth, Pilate inquires of him, what was that truth that he so called, that is, what his scheme or doctrine about himself was?

John 19:2. "And the soldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put it on his head; and they put on him a purple robe."] By comparing the accounts of the several evangelists, it seems probable that this same purple robe was first put on by Herod and his soldiers (for we read, Luke 23:11, that they "arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him again to Pilate"), and that he wore this henceforward, till they led him away to crucify him, except when they stripped [him] to scourge him. And then the soldiers that were concerned in scourging him put it on again, and added the crown of thorns; and that after Pilate had delivered him to be crucified, that then they made a set business of mocking him, striking him, and spitting in his face, and the like. Matthew and Mark give no account of the soldiers dressing him in his mock robe, and putting on the crown of thorns, till they come to give an account of that last spell of mocking and deriding; and then they give an account of all under one.

John 19:5. "Behold the man!"] As much as to say, You see what a poor creature he is. Is it worth the whileMS: "which." to crucify such an one for fear of his making head against Caesar?

John 19:14.] Concerning the time of Christ's crucifixion, see "Scripture," no. 445.Works, 15, 527–28.

-- 962 --

John 19:20–22.] See "Miscellanies," no. 601.Ibid., 2, 142.

John 19:34. "And forthwith there came out blood and water."] We don't read of Christ's sweating blood on the cross, though the suffering of Christ's soul was doubtless vastly greater than in the garden, for it was the forethought of this cup that was the occasion of his agony there. But there is this very good reason for it, viz. his blood, though now in a greater ferment than before, yet now had vent otherwise, viz. through his wounds. And this was probably the reason that he died so soon that "Pilate marveled if he were already dead" [Mark 15:44], and that he died sooner than the thieves, viz. that his blood, being in a great ferment through the amazing suffering of his soul, issued through his wounds faster and was sooner gone. And though Christ did not sweat blood outwardly, yet it seems that through the extremity of the agonies of his soul, which operated on his vital parts, his blood issued out of its proper vessels inwardly. Those parts being affected with either joy or grief more than the other parts of the body, the blood in extreme exercise of mind is agitated and pressed in them. Christ's heart did as it were break, and his vitals were rent with torment and amazement. And his heart's blood issued out immediately from his heart, and was shed out of his vitals into the cavity of his body. Hence when the soldier pierced his side, which seems to be done against the upperJE deleted "region." apartment of the trunk of his body where his vitals were contained, "there forthwith came out blood and water." This don't seem to [be] any blood that then issued out of its proper vessels, but some that was lodged in the cavity of his body that had issued out there. It seems that all his blood was shed either inwardly or outwardly; none remained in the vessels. And what was shed inwardly now was shed on the ground, as the rest had before been, and through the extreme torment, having as it were boiled with God's wrath, was turned into a wateryJE deleted "substance." fluid matter. Thus Christ's blood became water, and received its cleansing virtue by being shed in such extreme suffering. This was a kind of literal fulfillment of that, Psalms 22:14. "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint. My heart is like wax in the midst of my bowels." And Christ's bones were probably literally out of joint when he hung on the cross. See notes on the text.

Or possibly the case might be thus. That the spear piercing Christ's

-- 963 --

heart, the fountain of the blood, might with the blood that was in the heart, let out the water that is contained within the pericardium. For as is observed in Chambers' Dictionary under the word "Pericardium," there is contained in the pericardium a very thin watery humor, which some think natural, others that it is "forcibly separated by the convulsive agonies supervening in the article of death. Dr. KeilMS: "Keil." James Keill (1673–1719). a physician and anatomist, who wrote An Account of Animal Secretions, the Quantity of Blood in the Human Body, and Muscular Motion (London, 1708). represents this liquor as the most fluid of any that is separated from the blood."Cyclopaedia, II, 785–86. If that be the case that this liquor, which is always found there, be forcibly separated by the agonies of death, 'tis probable that the extraordinary agonies Christ was in caused an extraordinary quantity of it in him.This paragraph is a later addition.

John 19:39–40.] The sweet perfumed ointments, with which they of old used to anoint and embalm dead bodies as ordered in providence, betokened he happiness of departed souls of saints by being anointed with the Holy Ghost, especially the anointing and embalming the bodies of Jacob and of Jesus. The body of Jesus represented the whole church of saints, which is his body, who when they are in the fate of the dead are in Hades, are perfumed, are in a state of sweet rest by the anointing of the blessed Spirit. By this embalming, the nature of death is as it were changed; that dead body, that by the nature or natural tendency of a state of death, sends forth an horrid stench, and turns soon to putrefaction, but by this embalming the body is preserved from putrefaction. Death is defeated in that respect, and the dead body, instead of a stench, sends forth a sweet savor. Thus as "the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot" [Proverbs 10:7] and stink like the rotten corpse, so the soul of the just is blessed and perfumed, but the soul of the wicked perishes in an horrible spiritual stench and putrefaction. As the rotting and loathsomeness of dead unburied bodies signifies the misery of damned souls at the latter end, and Ecclesiastes 6:3. Therefore it was carefully ordered that Christ's body should not see corruption.), so the permanence and sweetness of the embalmed body signifies the happiness of the departed soul.

John 20.] No. 220.Works, 15, 154–56.

-- 964 --

John 20:10. "To their own home."] The original is πρὸς ἑαυτούς, which, says Dr. Doddridge, "seems here evidently to signify their own companions."Family Expositor, 2, 598, n. 1.

John 20:17. "Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father."] She was going to embrace Jesus Christ, as 'tis said, Matthew 28:9, that she and the other Mary "came and held him by the feet." But Jesus repelled her with the words we have in this verse, and gives this as the reason why he did not allow of those embraces now, because he was not yet ascended to his Father. That familiarity and full enjoyment of Christ is not allowed before his ascension, for this great blessedness of the saints in the enjoyment of Christ, though it be purchased by Christ's death, is obtained to be bestowed by his ascension into heaven, and entering into the holiest of all with his own blood, by his there appearing for us before God, and representing his satisfaction and obedience. When Christ ascended, then was the reward given to Christ into his hands, to be bestowed on his disciples. Then he received the promise of the Father to bestow on those that are his. Christ aims in all his discourses with his disciples before his death, and still his aim is the same after his death, to possess his followers with an apprehension that it will be profitable for them for him to go away, and go to his Father. He had told them before, that if he went away, he would come again, and take them to himself, that where he was, there they might be also [John 14:3]. And here he would suggest to Mary Magdalene that she may then, when that time comes, have a more intimate and full enjoyment of him than now. Possibly it was partly on the account of her sex. Christ might not see it upon all accounts meet to suffer a woman to embrace him in this world.

"When Mary would have come, and familiarly have embraced him, whether his feet or otherwise, saith he, 'Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended.' 'Tis not reproof, so much as a staying her from the present enjoyment, with the hint of a time wherein kindness was to be shown yet to come, and is as if he had said, There is time enough; we shall be familiar in heaven." Dr. Goodwin's Works, vol. 1, Pt. 2, p. 271.This paragraph is a separate entry. This is from Goodwin's sermon, no. 20, on Ephesians 2:7 (Works of Thomas Goodwin).

John 20:22. "And he breathed on them, and saith," etc.] By this it appears that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Son as well as the Father, for the Holy Ghost is the breath of Christ.

-- 965 --

John 20:26. "After eight days."] Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, pp. 104d–e and 105a.Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 104–5. See note on Luke 9:28.

John 20:29.] This verse very evidently teaches degrees of blessedness among the saints in their state of reward, in their fixed and eternal state.

John 21:3–7 ff. "And that night they caught nothing."] During the dark season of the church, ministers labor in vain (See Luke 5:5.); but when the morning, the appointed time of the church's light and glory comes, then Christ will wonderfully appear. (See "Scripture," no. 366.)Works, 13, 356–57. The disciples at first knew not that it was Jesus. When Christ begins gloriously to appear at the dawning of the glorious times, the sight will be so unusual that many of his own disciples will for a while be at a loss about, and will hardly know what to make of, so new and extraordinary a thing till they are convinced by the success of the gospel, the great draught of fishes. The disciples were found by Christ hungry. He asks them whether they have any meat. They answered, No. When Christ comes at the beginning of the glorious times, he will find his own disciples in a pining, languishing condition, many of them not fed with the pure doctrines of the gospel, and those that are having it preached to them without life and power. But Christ comes; he will soon spread a table before them.

Their being without meat and pining with hunger at the conclusion of this dark night represents two things. 1. It represents the unsuccessfulness of Christ's ministers during the dark season of the church. And 2. It represents the pining state of Christians for want of being suitably fed with spiritual food by their pastors. And this seems to be the special reason why Christ, after he had provided food for them, and was feeding them after they had been hungry, asks Peter whether he loved him more than that food, and upon his answering that he did, bids him, feed his sheep and his lambs. For if we understand their hungry empty state of ministers' unsuccessfulness, then Peter's loving Christ better than that outward food might well be urged upon him as a reason why he should diligently and earnestly preach the gospel, and seek success. For if he loves Christ better than those fishes, then he will desire success in his ministry more than his necessary food, as Christ loved the work of his ministry more than his food (John 4:34), and it will be more irksome to him to labor in vain in his ministry without catching souls than to labor

-- 966 --

in vain in his fishing, and to go hungry. Or ifThis is a later insertion by another hand, perhaps JE, Jr. we understand it the other way, that their being without meat represents the pining, starving state of Christ's flock for want of being suitably fed by their pastors with Christ, the proper food of their souls, then Peter's loving Christ better than outward [food] was a strong argument why he should feed Christ's flock with Christ, and not suffer their souls to go empty for want of this spiritual food, as they had done for want of this outward food, for Peter, being one of Christ's flock, knew the heart of one of his sheep. He knew that they loved and needed Christ, more than he, when he had now gone so long without outward food, needed that; and therefore he must take care that he did not withhold that food from them. If he did, he would be condemned out of his own mouth.This paragraph is a later addition.

John 21:11.] By the sale of so many large, fine fishes, a seasonable provision was made for their subsistence at Jerusalem while they were waiting for the descent of the Spirit.

John 21:13.] The bread that Christ gave them signifies the spiritual nourishment and strength that ministers receive in their own souls. The fish signifies the success they have in their ministry as fishers of men.

John 21:15.] From this verse we may note that they only are fit to be set about the work of the ministry, or the work of feeding Christ's sheep, that love Christ better than their maintenance. See notes on John 21:3–4 ff.I.e. John 21:3–7 ff.

John 21:19. "Follow me."] Christ, by thus bidding Peter to follow him, intimated to him that it was his will he should follow him in his sufferings, and so to give evidence of that love that he had professed. And Peter, by this action of following Christ, testified his readiness so to conform to Christ's death.

John 21:20.] Peter, seeing John also following, inquires whether he were also to follow him in his death, or what was to become of him? John 21:21].

-- 967 --

John 21:25.] By these it appears that the life of Christ was filled up with action. He was not idle, but was perpetually doing the work that God sent him to do, doing something that tended to further the design that he came into the world upon. See no. 313.Works, 15, 286–87.

-- 968 --

Acts

Acts 1:3. "Forty days."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstratio n. p. 110b–c.Kidder finds two issues of significance relating to the "forty days." That amount of time was sufficient to provide "abundant proof" that it was the same body that had been crucified and buried "that was risen from the dead." And "forty days" was the time between Christ's birth and his presentation in the temple, the same amount of time after his resurrection before his presentation "in heaven, or the temple above." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 110.

Acts 1:9.] See note on Psalms 68, no. 319, the whole of it, but especially the third paragraph of that note.Works, 15, 297–302, especially 299–300.

Acts 1:11.] "Why stand ye gazing up into heaven," as lamenting his departure, and being astonished at it, that he should leave the world without setting up that glorious kingdom in it that you expected? For he is not finally gone, but will come again. "This same Jesus will come again in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven," i.e. he will come again in his human nature, and by his bodily presence. And then he will take you forever to himself; and then he will appear in that glorious kingdom; and then you shall receive those rewards and that honor in his kingdom that he has promised you, and you have expected.

Acts 1:15.] See no. 70.Ibid., 69.

Acts 2:1. "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come."] Isaiah 51:4.

Acts 2:3. "Cloven tongues."] Or "tongues divided," so as to be two or more tongues in one, to represent that extraordinary gift that they were then endowed with by the Holy Ghost of speaking diverse languages, so that they had as it were two or more tongues in one, or one tongue that could speak diverse languages, as if they had all been their mother tongue.

See Doddridge's note here.This reference is a later addition. Family Expositor, 3, 15–16.

-- 969 --

Acts 2:18–21.] See Doddridge, in loc.Doddridge interprets these prophecies of the last days as applying to the impending destruction of the Jewish nation and the city of Jerusalem (Family Expositor, 3, 19–21).

Acts 2:42. "And fellowship."] The originalἦσαν δὲ προσκαρτεροῦντες τῇ διδαχῇ τῶν άποστόλων καὶ τῇ κοινωνία, τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄροτου καὶ ταῖς προσευχαῖς. shows plainly that "the apostles' doctrine, and the fellowship," or communication (as it should have been rendered), "and the breaking of bread, and the prayers," are mentioned as four distinct parts of the public service of the church. And by "the communication" is doubtless meant communicating to the poor, which was a part of the stated service of every sabbath. See the use of the word κοινωνία (Romans 15:26; 2 Corinthians 8:4, and 2 Corinthians 9:13; Hebrews 13:16; 1 Timothy 6:18, κοινωνικός). See the meaning of the wordκοινωνέω (Romans 12:13, Galatians 6:6, Philippians 4:15).

Acts 2:47. "And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved."] Or "such as were to be saved," i.e. such as God had ordained to be saved were daily brought in and added to the church. Or "God daily brought in the elect," agreeable to Acts 13:48, "And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed."

Acts 3:19.] Doddridge renders it,ὅπως ἂν ἔλθωσιν καιροὶ ἀαψύξεως. "That times of refreshment may come." See his reasons in his exposition.Doddridge links "times of refreshment" with the conversion of the Jews, which will be attended with extraordinary prosperity and joy (Family Expositor, 3, 42, n. e.).

Acts 3:21. "The restitution of all things."] Or "regulation." See Doddridge.Doddridge links this "regulation" with "the present Disorders in the Moral World, and the seeming Inequalities of Providential Dispensadons" (Family Expositor, 3, 43, n. g.).

Acts 4:2. "The resurrection of the dead."] This peculiarly provoked the Sadducees who denied any resurrection, etc. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 3, 47. See Acts 5:17.

Acts 4:6. "John and Alexander."] See Doddridge.Doddridge suggests that these two were "Persons of great Note among the Jews at that time," perhaps even the celebrated scholar Rabban Jochanan Ben Zaccai and Alabarch, the governor of the Jews in Alexandria (Family Expositor, 3, 48, n. e.).

-- 970 --

Acts 4:32–37.] Concerning the reasons why it was requisite that they should have "all things common," see no. 333.Works, 15, 316–18.

Acts 5:9. "To tempt the Spirit of the Lord."] I.e. to try the Holy Spirit, to try the omniscience of the Holy Ghost, that had lately been poured out on the apostles, and that the apostles were now full of. They would try if they could not impose upon 'em, for all their having this, which implicitly [is] a trying if they could not impose on the Spirit himself, or lying to the Holy Ghost, as the apostle Peter charges them (Acts 5:4).

Acts 5:13. "And of the rest durst no man join himself unto them."] "Of the rest," i.e. of those that were unbelievers, or not Christians, or of that sort that Ananias and Sapphira were. They durst not do as Ananias and Sapphira did, for the sake of their temporal interest, or the advantage of sharing equally with the rest in the common stock, [who] came in the disguise of Christians, and offer to join themselves to the company. Many would have been under temptation so to have done, for many that were very poor hereby might have had a competent subsistence for them and their families. And others might have kept back great part of their own estates secretly, and have thrown into the common stock a part that was of far less value than their equal share of the whole. And probably the church would have been in this manner greatly infested with cheats, had not they been effectually deterred by the example of Ananias and Sapphira.

Acts 5:24. "Whereunto this would grow."] In the Greek, τί ἄν γένοιτο τοῦτο, "what this could be." See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 3, 69.

Acts 6:13–14. "Shall destroy this place."] See Jeremiah 26:9.

Acts 7.] The drift of this whole rehearsal of Stephen is to show how their nation had of old resisted the Holy Ghost in the revelations and promises that he had made of good to them. They resisted the accomplishment of those promises of their own good. The Holy Ghost was resisted in it two ways, viz. 1. as they resisted those promises that the Holy Ghost had revealed; 2. they resisted the operation of the Holy Ghost in accomplishing those promises, or in what he did in order to it, and seeking

-- 971 --

their good. They resisted him in Moses and other instruments, which God raised up and by his Holy Spirit furnished, and sent, and assisted, and wrought in and by them, for the accomplishment of those promises.

Stephen particularly insists on the promise that God made to Abraham, that he would give unto his seed the land of Canaan "for a possession" Acts 7:5]. And therefore he begins by giving an account of that promise and the circumstances with which it was given to Abraham: how God called Abraham from his own country in order to the making this covenant with him, and the bestowment of this blessing on him; and what circumstances there were that rendered the promise wonderful, and commended Abraham's faith in resting in it, viz. that for the present, God "gave him none inheritance in the land, no, not so much as to set his foot on," and that the promise was made "when as yet he had no child" Acts 7:5]; and gives an account how God confirmed this promise by the seal of circumcision.

And nextly he proceeds to the steps that God took in order to the accomplishment of this promise, first by sending Joseph into Egypt in order to the keeping them alive in famine Acts 7:9], lest Abraham's posterity should be extinct, and so the promise fail. Joseph was the first instrument that the Holy Ghost wrought by, and that they resisted. See notes on Genesis 37:4.This reference is a later addition. And then Stephen takes notice by the way of their fathers' being buried in Canaan, in the piece of ground that Abraham had bought there for the possession of a burying place Acts 7:16], as an earnest of the fulfillment of the promise. That possession of a burying place was all that Abraham and the patriarchs had in the land, and it was an earnest that hereafter they should have the whole. And their being buried there was in token that their posterity should possess that land. It was in faith of this that Joseph gave commandment concerning his bones.

Then he proceeds to give an account of the miserable circumstances the nation was in just before the accomplishment of the promise, and then relates the wonderful steps that God took to accomplish it, and how they resisted him therein. The next instrument that the Holy Ghost wrought by for the bringing about the fulfillment of the promise was Moses, who was, as Stephen observes from Moses' own words, an eminent type of Christ Acts 7:37], and particularly observes how they resisted him, and then gives an account of their being brought into Canaan by Joshua, whereby the promise was in great measure fulfilled, and then finishes with the complete accomplishment thereof in David's

-- 972 --

and Solomon's time Acts 7:45–47]. The promise never was fully accomplished till then. The state of Israel in Canaan was never fully settled till then, never before had the full and entire possession of Canaan, never till then had the land in the extent that it was promised, viz. from the river of Egypt to the river Euphrates, etc., and never had the quiet and peaceable possession of it till Solomon's time. Then first God took up his settled abode among them in the land he had given them, by walking no longer in a movable tabernacle like a wayfaring man, but in a fixed temple, in token that Israel should remain God's people, and that accordingly God would continue them in that his land. See 2 Samuel 7.

And then Stephen observes that, notwithstanding, God don't dwell "in temples made with hands" Acts 7:48], that Solomon's temple was not the true temple of God by the account of their own prophets, whereby he justifies himself in what they accused him of, in the Acts 6:14.

Acts 7:9. "And the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph," etc.] Stephen mentions this to show the perverseness of the Jews, for this is very much the design of Stephen in this rehearsal, as appears by Acts 7:51–53. The patriarchs, their first fathers, sold Joseph, their brother and their savior, and a type of Christ, out of envy, as they had sold Christ himself, their brother of the same nature and nation, and the great Savior, out of envy.

Acts 7:9–10. "But God was with him," etc.] Though your fathers thus evil entreated him, yet God exalted him to be a prince and a savior, as he hath also done Christ whom ye have sold and crucified.

Acts 7:14. "Threescore and fifteen souls."] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 86–88.Kidder provides an elaborate defense of the number of persons cited by Stephen as part of Jacob's kindred, who are elsewhere numbered as 70, not 75. The issue raised by Jewish critics involves the fact that Stephen is declared to be "full of the Holy Ghost," and yet mistaken in this count. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 86–88.

Acts 7:15–16.] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 88–90.Kidder answers a series of charges leveled against the accuracy of Stephen's account in these verses, using linguistical and historical arguments to defend parts of the account, and conceding other charges as of little or no significance. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 88–90.

-- 973 --

Acts 7:16.] The field that Abraham bought for a possession of a burying place was the only land that he owned in Canaan, as 'tis said in the Acts 7:5, that God "gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on." And Abraham, when he is about buying it, he gives this as a reason why he would buy it to the sons of Heth,A reference to the Hittites. viz. that he was "a stranger and a sojourner" with them (Genesis 23:4), by which he would be understood that he had no land of his own. The patriarchs' being buried there, and being carried up out of Egypt to Canaan after they are dead that they may rest there, seems to typify that the saints, when they die, go to heaven, the true Canaan, and have rest there, which if it be so (we may observe, by the way), confutes the notion of the souls of saints not going to heaven when they die, both of those that hold that they sleep till the resurrection, and of those that hold that they go to some other abode, i.e. the Hades, prepared for them. Jacob's body being carried up to Canaan and buried there was an earnest to his posterity that they should have Canaan for a possession. Even so Christ, the true Jacob, his entering through death or through his own blood into heaven, was an earnest to his spiritual posterity that they should have that for a possession. The children of Israel entered into Canaan with Joseph's bones; so the spiritual Israel enter into heaven by Christ's death.

Acts 7:22. "Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians."] 'Tis probable that this wisdom of the Egyptians consisted much in three things. 1. In traditional knowledge of ancient history. Before writing was known, very much of the learning of the world must consist in traditional history. Greater care was needful then to keep up the knowledge of ancient facts, and to deliver 'em down from one generation to another. Dr. Winder shows this to be exceeding probable (History of Knowledge, pp. 48–49).Winder discusses the role of oral teaching and spoken narration in the period before "writing was discovered." Critical and Chronological History (2nd ed.), II, 48–49. And probably the affair, as being of great importance, was then committed to the priests, of whom Moses learned it. 2. In the knowledge of their hieroglyphical figures. And 3. In understanding of their enigmatical speeches, wherein 'tis evident ancient learning very much consisted. Moses' learning in these things might in some respects fit him for writing the history of the world from the beginning, and being the instrument of introducing the typical worship and administration of the Old Testament.

-- 974 --

Acts 7:25–27 ff.] Their fathers' treatment of Moses was another instance of that unbelief and perverseness of that nation that Stephen observes in the conclusion of this rehearsal (Acts 7:51–53). Their treatment of Moses was very parallel to their treatment of Christ that Moses was a remarkable type of. They did not understand that God by his hand would deliver them. They "thrust him away, saying, Who made thee a ruler and judge over us?" And so was their treatment of him in the wilderness, as Acts 7:39–41. But [God] exalted Moses, notwithstanding, to be a prince and a savior, as he did Christ (Acts 7:35–36), and punished them for it, as he did the Jews for rejecting Christ, by giving them up to hardness of heart, as Acts 7:42–43. This Moses was like to Christ, or a type of Christ, as God and Moses himself by him taught, as Stephen observes, Acts 7:37. And therefore their treatment of Moses was the more parallel to their treatment of Christ.

Acts 7:36. "In the land of Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness forty years."] This is observable that Moses was in Pharaoh's court, before he visited "his brethren the children of Israel," forty years (Acts 7:23). And that again he was forty years in the land of Midian before God sent him to deliver the children of Israel out of Egypt (Acts 7:30). And again he was with the children of Israel, leading of them out of Egypt forty years, and then resigned to Joshua to lead the people into Canaan. It seems to me that each of these forty years represents that 4000 years before Christ came into the world, putting each year for a century, and each ten for a thousand. After four thousand years, Christ left the court of the heavenly King, and visited his brethren here on earth, as Moses did when he was forty years old. He was sent by God to redeem them out of their spiritual bondage, as Moses was after forty years' stay in Midian. And then Moses, or the Mosaic dispensation, resigned to Jesus, the true Joshua, who brings the church into Canaan, as Moses resigned to Joshua after he had been forty years with them. The same is signified by his stay in the mount forty days and forty nights, as we have elsewhere observed.See note on Exodus 34.

Acts 7:37–38.] The things which Stephen observes of Moses in these verses serve the more to show the comparison that he makes of the Jews' treatment of Christ with their fathers' treatment of Moses to be apt and pertinent, and to render the application he makes, Acts 7:51 ff., the more convincing. For here [Stephen] observes that Moses himself compares the

-- 975 --

Messiah to him, and says that he shall be a prophet like to him Acts 7:37]. And besides, their fathers, in rejecting Moses, rejected Christ, for Moses spake and acted in the name of Christ, and as his messenger and instrument. And Christ was with him in what he did and said, as Stephen observes, Acts 7:38, that Moses was "with the angel" (i.e. Christ) "in Mt. Sinai, who spake to him," etc., so that Moses spake his word. So that in rejecting Moses, they rejected Christ's own words; and their murmurings against him, and opposition of him, was really opposition to Christ.

Acts 7:38. "The lively oracles."] In the original,λόγια ζῶντα. "the living oracles," not oracles that shall be struck dumb, as the heathen oracles long since are, but the oracles of the living God, oracles that shall live in their force and effect forever.

Acts 7:43. "Beyond Babylon."] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, p. 18.Prideaux explains how this reference in Stephen's sermon was an appropriate and true citation of Amos' prophecy of a captivity that was "beyond Damascus" (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 18). See also note on Amos 5:27.

Acts 7:44–49.] What is here said about the tabernacle and temple seems to be in answer to that part of the accusation, viz. that he, Stephen, had spoken blasphemous words against the temple.

Acts 7:52.] 'Tis a great confirmation of the truth of the history of the Old Testament that it all along gives such an account of the perverseness of that nation. 'Tis not to be supposed that so proud and self-righteous a nation would forge such a history of themselves, or if forged by any other, would universally receive it that gives such an account of 'em as should give occasion for their being thus upbraided.

Acts 8:20.] Simon Magus seems here to be a type of hypocrites and self-righteous professors. His money that he offered seems to be a type of men's own righteousness that they offer to purchase divine gifts. And what Peter says to him in this verse teaches us the damning nature of self-righteousness, that it is a damning error for anyone to think that the gift of God can be purchased with their price, and that such person's price is like to perish with them. When we come for spiritual blessings, we are directed to come "without money and without price" (Isaiah 55:1).

-- 976 --

"Thy money perish with thee." This intimates that he was in great danger of perishing; and they signify that his money should remain with him, and perish with him, before they would take it.

Acts 8:20–22.] By what is here said it is evident that a man may contract fearful guilt, and may undo himself to all eternity, by that which he has no great sense of the badness of. In the time of it, when he commits it, it don't seem heinous to him. For Simon the Sorcerer seems to have had no great sense of any hurt in his proposal of buying the gift or power of conferring the Holy Ghost with money. He was very bold in his proposal, and in all likelihood it was very unexpected to him to meet with such a rebuke.

Acts 8:23.] It was an evidence of his being in a natural condition that he should entertain such a mean and dishonorable thought of God, that he should imagine that he could as it were buy God for his money, so as to have his power and his Spirit at his disposal to give it to whomsoever he would. No man that had the saving knowledge of God could have entertained such a thought.

Acts 9:3.] See concerning the circumstances of Paul's conversion, "Miscellanies," no. 645.Works, 18, 176–79.

Acts 9:14. "That call on thy name."] By this it appears that Christ is the proper object of prayer. See also the places quoted in the margins of the Bishop of Worcester's Bible.This reference is to an edition of the Authorized Version of the Bible commonly ascribed to William Lloyd (1627–1717), the Bishop of Worcester. The marginal citations JE points to at Acts 9:14 are Acts 9:21, Acts 7:59, and Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 1:2; and 2 Timothy 2:22, all of which speak of calling on the Lord. See The Holy Bible, Containing the Old and New Testaments, Newly Translated out of the Original Tongues and with the Former Translations Diligently Compared and Revised (Oxford, 1701), p. 1310, n. k. Concerning the cross references and parallel passages in Lloyd's edition, see A. Tindal Hart, William Lloyd, 1627–1717: Bishop, Politician, Author and Prophet (London, 1952), p. 238.

Acts 10:4–6.] By this it appears that almsgiving is a way in which those that are concerned for their soul'sJE deleted "good ought." salvation ought to seek saving mercy, and that 'tis a likely way to obtain not only temporal rewards, but spiritual blessings and eternal life.JE preached a sermon on this text in 1741 (no. 587) with the doctrine, "To be much in deeds of charity is the way to have spiritual discoveries." See Wilson H. Kimnach, Kenneth P. Minkema, and Douglas A. Sweeney, eds., The Sermons of Jonathan Edwards :A Reader (New Haven: Yale Univ. Press, 1999), pp. 197–211.

-- 977 --

Acts 10:34.] See Mr. Dickinson's Five Discourses, beginning with the second paragraph, p. 39.Jonathan Dickinson argues that election does not make God a "respecter of persons," because God will "adopt, justify, and finally glorify all penitent Believers, whatever their external circumstances," whether Jew or Gentile, in "A Discourse on the Decree of Election" published in The True Scripture-Doctrine Concerning Some Important Points of Christian Faith… in Five Discourses (Boston, 1741), 39–40.

Acts 13:2.] It is probable that Barnabas and Saul were not accounted apostles till now. It was now first that Saul's name was changed, and henceforth is called Paul (see Acts 13:9, Acts 13:13). This was soon after James' death. See Acts 12:2. And possibly some other apostle might be now dead, so that the number twelve was now filled again a second time, the first time by the appointment of Matthias.

Acts 13:20. "About the space of four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet."] These words don't only refer to the words immediately foregoing, viz. "after that he gave unto them judges," as showing the space of time in which that was done; but they refer to the whole that is by the Apostle before declared of God's dealings with Israel, in this and the three foregoing verses. To show the space of time in which all these things were done, the Apostle first reckons up several things that were done, viz. God's exalting the people while they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with an high arm bringing them out, and suffering their manners in the wilderness, and destroying seven nations of Canaan, and dividing their land to them by lot, and appointing judges over them; and then at the conclusion [he] tells us for what space of time these things were transacting, or how long the state of Israel had continued under various changes before the establishment of kingly government among them. As if I were to recount the several remarkable changes of the state of the English nation from the time of the Reformation to the Revolution, and should rehearse one thing after another, and at the end of all should add, "for the space of about 140 years." This would be understood not only as referring to the last clause, or as signifying the continuance of the state of the nation under the last change mentioned, but the space of time including all the changes rehearsed.

Acts 13:33. "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee."] See Revelation 1:5.

See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 1, pp. 98–100, and Pt. 2, p. 88a–b.These references are a later addition. Kidder defends the Apostle's use of these words of the Psalmist with reference to resurrection of Christ, citing ancient sources that speak of the earth as a "mother" and Old Testament writings that call the grave a "womb." Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 98–100. The reference in Pt. 2, p. 88, does not relate to this passage.

-- 978 --

Acts 13:39. "From which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses."] This is true in two senses. 1. The law of Moses made no provision for the expiation of presumptuous sins. There were no sacrifices appointed for such sins (Numbers 15:30–31). It was so ordered on purpose that men, being kept in doubt, and their consciences not fully satisfied about their presumptuous sins, that when Christ came, and the gospel, which declared the forgiveness of all sin through him, [it] might be the more joyful tidings. The forgiveness of sin never was fully revealed till Christ came. 'Tis probable that the forgiveness of presumptuous sin had been a matter of great question and controversy amongst their doctors, and therefore now Paul tells them that 'tis by Christ that they are justified from those sins. And 2. The sacrifices of the law of Moses could not truly take away the guilt of any sin.

Acts 13:41. "Behold, ye despisers," etc.] The aggravated misery of many unbelievers appears in that they hear of God's great works of salvation, and behold much of them, have 'em set before their eyes, yet through their pride, self-sufficiency, and leaning to their own understandings and self-exalting disposition, despise those things that are so spiritual, mysterious, and abasing, and always stumble at them, and never know what to make of 'em, and so never have any benefit of them, and in the end perish eternally. Christ is set for their fall. He is "a stone of stumbling and rock of offense" to them [1 Peter 2:8]. They go backwards, and are snared and taken. These things are all in parables to them. Hosea 14:9, "Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? Prudent, and he shall know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them; but the transgressors shall fall therein."

Acts 15:10.] They that won't admit persons into the society or to the privileges of saints, or that refuse to receive 'em into their charity, without certain conditions or qualifications that God has not fixed as necessary, tempt God, and do what in them lies to oblige God to admit none into his church unless he admits 'em in that way, because if he admits 'em in any other way, they will be in danger of failing of some of those privileges God has designed for them, viz. the privileges of visible Christians, and

-- 979 --

the charity and society of God's people. So those that insistMS: "Inst." such a manner of experience is necessary to godliness that is not necessary are guilty of tempting God.

Acts 15:11.] See Doddridge.Doddridge's comments on this verse strike the theme of salvation by grace, and underscore the apostles' refusal to accept the burden of observing the ceremonial precepts of the law (Family Expositor, 3, 235).

Acts 15:17.] See note on Amos 9:12.

Acts 15:28–29.] We can't certainly conclude that all these things are of a moral nature because some of 'em are, or that all were necessary things on the same account, and of like perpetual obligation because they are all mentioned together, for the Scripture don't observe such a kind of accuracy in ranking things together. Sometimes things are ranked together that are of a very diverse nature. As in Romans 12:6–8, showing mercy, a duty that Christians were to perform by offices, is ranked with the duties of officers themselves. Sometimes things are mentioned together that, indeed, are not distributively distinct, as Hebrews 6:1–2. There "the doctrine of baptism, and laying on of hands," i.e. the doctrine taught persons at their first initiation into Christianity, are ranked with the doctrines of faith, and repentance, and the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment, whereas these are not distinct from the doctrines that they were taught at their baptism and when the apostles laid their hands on them. Prayer, a moral duty, is connected with anointing with oil (James 5:14). See Doddridge, note on Acts 16:4.This reference is a later addition. Doddridge's note asserts that the decrees of the Council at Jerusalem were "intended for all Gentiles Christians living among Jews" (Family Expositor, 3, 251, n. b.

"No greater burden," etc. Which burden was afterwards lessened. The burden, which consisted of four prohibitions, were reduced to two, viz. the first and the last, eating things offered to idols, and fornication, which were the two moral prohibitions which were to be perpetual, and to remain in force till Christ comes. See Revelation 2:20, with Revelation 2:24 and Revelation 2:25. See notes on Revelation 2:24.This paragraph is a separate entry. This reference is a later addition.

Acts 16:3. "Circumcised him."] See Doddridge.Doddridge explains that Paul, who thought circumcision unnecessary, circumcised Timothy in order to avoid offense to Jews and thereby enhance his prospects for preaching successfully in the synagogues (Family Expositor, 3, 249–50).

-- 980 --

Acts 16:13.] See Doddridge.Doddridge describes the Jewish custom of erecting places of public prayer near water, either by the sea or by rivers, "for the Sake of Purifications" (Family Expositor, 3, 255, n. a.).

Acts 17:16. "Wholly given to idolatry."] See Doddridge.Paul, according to Doddridge, strongly moved by the superstition and idolatry in Athens, attacked it not with rage, but with serious and "rational Remonstrances" (Family Expositor, 3, 276–77).

Acts 17:18. "Strange gods."] See Doddridge.Doddridge discusses the tradition of interpretation that suggested both Jesus and the resurrection, when preached by Paul, were thought to be deities by the Athenians (Family Expositor, 3, 279, n. f.).

Acts 17:22. "Too superstitious."] See Doddridge.Doddridge argues for reducing the offense of the text by translating δεισιδαιμονεστέρους with "exceedingly addicted to the worship of invisible powers" rather than "too superstitious," a strategy more consistent with the purpose of Paul's discourse (Family Expositor, 3, 280, n. i.).

Acts 17:23. "Your devotions."] See Doddridge.Doddridge asserts that there is no English equivalent for σεβάσματα, which he paraphrases as "Objects and Instruments of your Worship" (Family Expositor, 3, 280).

"To the Unknown God."] See Doddridge.In an extended scholarly note, Doddridge enumerates the opinions of commentators, both ancient and modern, on the identity of the "Unknown God." He concludes that Paul linked the Lord he preached with the deity who was responsible for sending and removing a great pestilence some 600 years before Christ (Family Expositor, 3, 281, n. 1.).

Cudworth in his Intellectual System, pp. 473–74, says, "Both PhilostratusPhilostratus (170–245), a Greek prose writer. and PausaniasPausanias, a Greek traveler and topographer in the 2nd century. write, that there were at Athens 'Altars of Unknown Gods.' But their meaning in this might well be, not that there were altars dedicated to unknown gods plurally, but that there were several altars which had this singular inscription, 'TO THE UNKNOWN OF GOD.' And that there was at least one such, besides this Scripture record, is evident from that dialogue in Lucian'sLucian, a Greek satirical author of the 2nd century. works entitled Philopatris, where Critias useth this form of oath, 'No, by the Unknown God at Athens.' And Triephon, in the close of that dialogue, speaketh thus. 'But we, having found out that Unknown God at Athens, and worshipped him, with hands stretched up to heaven, will give thanks to him, as having been thought worthy to be made subject to this power.' Which plainly implies that this Unknown God was the supreme governor of the world, probably

-- 981 --

so called not only because he is invisible, but incomprehensible by mortals, of whom Josephus against Appion writeth, that 'as to his own essence he is unknowable.' And when in Dion Cassius,Dion Cassius (155–240), Bithynian historian of Rome. the God of the Jews is said to be 'invisible and ineffable,' the reason hereof seems to have been, not only because there was no image of him, but also because the TetragrammatonThe term for the four-letter name of God in Hebrew יהוה (i.e. YHWH), which because of its sacred character Jews did not utter beginning around 300 B.C.E., substituting instead the Hebrew word for "Lord." was religiously forborn as to common use."This paragraph is a later addition. Ralph Cudworth, The True Intellectual System of the Universe: The First Part; Wherein All the Reason and Philosophy of Atheism is Confuted; and Its Impossibility Demonstrated (London, 1678). Cudworth (1617–88) was an Anglican divine and professor of Hebrew. For more on him, see Works, 23, 15–16.

Acts 17:26–27.] No. 387.Works, 15, 369–72.

Acts 17:27–28. "If haply they might feel after him, and find him."] Alluding to the darkness in which the heathen world is represented. Miscell. Sacra.Herman Witsius, Miscellaneorum Sacrorum Libri Quatuor (2 vols. Rhenum, 1692–1700), probably I, 565–617. In two chapters on these pages, Witsius (1636–1708), a Dutch theologian who taught at the universities of Utrecht and Leyden, discusses the evil and impiety of the religious views of the "heathen world," including those of the Babylonians, Romans, Goths, Vandals, and Muslims, as well as the ancient cult of Moloch, drawing on a variety of ancient sources.

Acts 17:28. "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."] See Doddridge.This clause, Doddridge declares, summarizes "the continual and necessary Dependence of all derived Beings… on their First and Almighty Cause" (Family Expositor, 3, 283, n. p.).

"For we [are] also his offspring." See Doddridge.Doddridge links this text with Aratus, a poet from Cilecia, Paul's native country, and with the hymn of Cleanthes to Jupiter (Family Expositor, 3, 283, n. q.).

Acts 17:29.] See Doddridge.Paul disparages all attempts, according to Doddridge, to imagine deities resembling anything inferior to humans, such as idols (Family Expositor, 3, 283–84).

Acts 18:3. "Same craft."] See Doddridge.I.e. tent makers. Doddridge inserts a long note on the Jewish tradition of teaching their children a trade, even when they were trained in the liberal sciences (Family Expositor, 3, 288, n. c.

Acts 18:15.] See Doddridge.Doddridge applauds the action of the wise magistrate Gallio who did not use Roman law to declare Paul a criminal on religious grounds (Family Expositor, 3, 293, n. 1.).

-- 982 --

Acts 18:17.] See Doddridge.Doddridge constructs a hypothetical set of circumstances whereby Gallio appears less responsible for the beating of Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue (Family Expositor, 3, 294, n. m.).

Acts 18:25.] See Doddridge.Doddridge speculates about the manner in which Apollos the Jew had been baptized by John the Baptist and instructed by him in the need for repentance and faith in a coming Messiah (Family Expositor, 3, 299).

Acts 19:13. "Exorcists."] See Doddridge.Doddridge cites several authorities, ancient and modern, to support the contention that there were Jews during this period who pretended to cast out demons by arts and charms derived from Solomon (Family Expositor, 3, 306, n. g.).

Acts 19:19.] See Doddridge.Doddridge supplies an explanation for the high price attributed to the books on magical arts burned in Ephesus (Family Expositor, 3, 307).

Acts 19:37. "Nor yet blasphemers of your goddess."] They said that they were no god which were made with hands; but they supposed the image of Diana was not made with hands, but fell down from Jupiter. See Doddridge.Family Expositor, 3, 315.

Acts 20:35. "The weak."] See Doddridge.Doddridge points out that ἀσθενούντων is used of persons who are disabled in some way by either poverty or sickness (Family Expositor, 3, 331, n. p.).

Acts 21:16. "Brought with them one MnasonAn aged disciple with whom Paul lodged. of Cyprus."] See Doddridge.Doddridge suggests the text should be paraphrased "brought [us] to the House of one Mnason a Cyprian, an old Disciple" (Family Expositor, 3, 337).

Acts 21:32. "Left beating of Paul."] See Doddridge.As an explanation of Paul's situation, Doddridge cites John Lightfoot's observations on the Jewish practice called the "Beating of the Rebels," by which Jews attacked persons who profaned the temple, some of whom died from the beatings (Family Expositor, 3, 346, n. o.).

Acts 21:35. "And when he came upon the stairs."] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. II, p. 468.Prideaux identifies these as stairs leading to the southeast turret of the adjacent fortress of Antonia (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, 468).

-- 983 --

Acts 21:37. "Canst thou speak Greek?"] See Doddridge.Paul's ability to speak Greek, according to Doddridge, kept him from being falsely identified as the Egyptian prophet who had led a rebellion against Roman authority (Family Expositor, 3, 348).

Acts 21:38.] Josephus tells us of an Egyptian prophet that came to Jerusalem about twenty-two years after Christ's death, in the time that Felix was governor of Judea, "and persuaded the people to follow him to Mt. Olivet, persuading them, that from thence they should see the walls of Jerusalem fall down, and so might enter into the city. Which Felix understanding, sent soldiers, and slew and took several of them, but the Egyptian impostor himself made his escape." To this the chief captain here refers. Tillotson's third volume of Sermons, p. 529.Sermon no. 182, in a series entitled "The Evidences of the Truth of the Christian Religion" (Works, 3).

"Madest an uproar." See Doddridge.This reference is a separate entry. Doddridge cites sources and details concerning the uprising led by the Egyptian prophet.

Acts 21:39. "No mean city."] See Doddridge.Doddridge explains that Paul's claims for Tarsus, which had a reputation for learning, commerce, and wealth, established his right as a Jew to be in the temple (Family Expositor, 3, 349, n. h.).

Acts 22:3. "In this city."] See Doddridge.Doddridge details Paul's education in Jerusalem, in accord with the traditional practice of devout Jewish parents who desired more extensive religious instruction for their children (Family Expositor, 3, 350).

Acts 23:3. "God shall smite thee, thou whited wall."] Soon after this "Agrippa the SecondMarcus Julius Agrippa (28–c. 100), a king who served at the pleasure of Rome and sided with Rome in the Jewish war of 66–70. took away his priestly dignity from him."I.e. from the high priest Ananias. And afterwards his own son Eleazar "pulled down his house" where he was hid in an upper chamber, and some of his son's company murdered him. See Basnage's History of the Jews, p. 39.

See Doddridge.This reference is a separate entry. Doddridge cites Josephus' account of Ananias' crimes and his violent death (Family Expositor, 3, 362–63, n. c).

Acts 24:6.] See Doddridge.Doddridge addresses Tertullus' charge that Paul profaned the temple, and discusses the legal restrictions on executions under Roman rule (Family Expositor, 3, 375).

-- 984 --

Acts 24:14. "The God of my fathers."] See Doddridge.Doddridge asserts that αἵρεσις, which is translated as "heresy," refers appropriately to a sect or party, and need not be of "bad signification." He suggests Paul's use of the term allowed those who professed Christ and yet accepted the law and the prophets, to be distinguished from adherents of the national religion (Family Expositor, 3, 379).

Acts 24:16. "And herein."] It should have been rendered, "on this account." See Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 3, 379–80, n. e.

Acts 24:22. "Knowledge of that way."] See Doddridge.Doddridge probes the motivations of Felix's inquiries concerning Paul's preaching (Family Expositor, 3, 381–82, n. f.).

Acts 24:26. "He hoped also that money should be given him."] See Doddridge.Doddridge points to the collection of money by Paul for Jerusalem and his standing among the Christians as possible sources for ransom funds to buy his liberty (Family Expositor, 3, 385).

Acts 24:27.] Concerning the things which happened among the Jews during those two years of Paul's confinement at Caesarea, see Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 3, 385–86.

"Willing to show the Jews a pleasure." See Doddridge.This reference is a separate entry. Doddridge interprets Felix's decision to leave Paul in prison as a move to ingratiate himself with the Jews (Family Expositor, 3, 385–86).

Acts 25:10.] See Doddridge.Doddridge notes that provincial tribunals were regarded as "Caesar's tribunal" (Family Expositor, 3, 388, n. h.).

Acts 25:11. "I appeal unto Caesar."] See Doddridge.Roman law, Doddridge records, allowed every Roman citizen such an appeal before being sentenced (Family Expositor, 3, 389, n. k.).

Acts 27:9. "The fast was now already past."] See Doddridge.The fast in reference, according to Doddridge, was the Day of Atonement, which he dated around September 25 (Family Expositor, 3, 411, n. e.).

Acts 27:31. "Except these abide in the ship."] See Doddridge.Doddridge interprets Paul's counsel to mariners as applicable to other affairs, namely, the fulfillment of God's promises often require "prudential Measures to secure them" (Family Expositor, 3, 417).

-- 985 --

Romans

Romans 1:12.] See Taylor's Paraphrase.John Taylor writes, "I speak not this, as if you only were to be Receivers from me; I expect my Share of Benefit from you; and please myself both Parties would be refreshed and strengthened, I by your spiritual Attainments, as well as you by mine" (Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 213).

Romans 1:16. "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ."] That I should be ashamed to preach it at Rome, the metropolis and mistress of the world.

"It is the power of God to salvation to everyone that believeth, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Ques. How is the gospel "the power of God to salvation to those that believe, to the Jew first?" And so it is said in the Romans 2:10, that God will render "glory, honor, and peace to every man that worketh good, to the Jew first." Arts. God was ready to justify all that believed in Christ, and to reward all that work good, but especially the Jews, for the peculiar favor he bore to that nation for their forefathers' sakes, as Romans 11:28, and because they were born in covenant, or were his covenant people by descent. See Romans 2:25, "For circumcision verily profiteth," etc.

Romans 1:16–18.] No. 318.Works, 15, 294–96.

Romans 1:21. "Glorified him not as God, neither were thankful."] The respect we owe to God consists in two things, viz. a supreme regard to God for what he is in himself as his divine glory, and that respect we owe him for his goodness to us. Both are here mentioned.

Romans 1:27.] See Taylor's note on this verse.Taylor's commentary on the Apostle's discussion of men lusting after men cites Cicero who, "without any Mark of Disapprobation," refers to a man of high rank who practiced "this worse than beastly Vice," and also notes that other men and philosophers were "Admirers of young men." This Taylor called a "most detestable Vice" (Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans, pp. 320–21).

-- 986 --

Romans 1:31. "Without natural affection."] ἅστοργη may include the absence both of parental and filial affection. The custom of exposing newborn infants, which prevailed so generally in the heathen world, and that among polite nations and persons in other respects not destitute of humanity, is a most striking instance of the truth of this assertion, as that of killing their aged parents also was of the counterpart.Doddridge, Family Expositor, 4, 24, n. t.

Romans 1:32-2:1.] It seems to be a mistake of many that the Apostle, in what he says of men's wickedness in the Romans 1, has respect only to the Gentiles, and that in what he says in the Romans 2, he has respect only to the Jews. 'Tis true that in the Romans 1 he evidently has his eye chiefly on the wickedness that prevailed [in the Gentile] world. But that is not his professed design in it, only to describe the sin of the pagan world, but the wickedness of the world of mankind. 'Tis all unrighteousness and ungodliness of men that hold the truth in unrighteousness. And in the Romans 2 he has his eye chiefly on the Jews, but it is not his professed design to speak only of them, as appears by his beginning in the Romans 2:1, the universal terms that he uses in it. "Therefore thou art inexcusable, o MAN (not O Jew). WHOSOEVER thou art (of mankind, whether Jew or Gentile) that judgest," etc. In the Romans 1:32, the Apostle speaks of the wickedness of mankind in general, and shows how they "hold the truth in unrighteousness," as he had said before (Romans 1:18). And the special design of that verse is to set forth how they are all alike, and all agreed in wickedness, and in the same kind of wickedness. Though they all have that light that is sufficient to teach them that those that commit such things deserve the condemnation and wrath of God, and so death and destruction, which they are very ready to acknowledge and declare in the case of others when they see their wickedness, their unrighteousness, covetousness, maliciousness, envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity, etc.: I say, though when they see others guilty of such things, they can easily see that they are worthy of death, and are forward to express it, yet they do the very same things, and not only so, but they show plainly that they have just such hearts. They show a full practical consent to all the wickedness of others that they are forward to condemn and to declare worthy of death. Thus unreasonable are they, and inconsistent with themselves. Thus the beginning of the Romans 2 comes in. "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest." Thou that art forward to condemn others as worthy

-- 987 --

of death, "for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." Thou art very unreasonable and exceeding inconsistent with thyself, "for thou that judgest dost the same things," and showest that thou hast pleasure in their practice. There is at the same time that you judge them, a full practical consent to and good liking of the very same practices. So God of old condemned the Jews for that in their practice they had justified Samaria and Sodom, and were a comfort to 'em, and yet had judged them (Ezekiel 16:51–52, Ezekiel 16:54).

Romans 2:1. "O man."] This is spoken emphatically, a poor, weak, fallible, sinful man, in opposition to God, mentioned in the next verse.

Romans 2:1–2 ff.] The Apostle has a special eye to the Jews when he speaks of them that judge others, for it was very much their manner of that day to trust in themselves that they were righteous, and to condemn others. See note on Matthew 7:1.

Romans 2:2.] The Apostle's words here do doubtless imply that he was sure that their punishment would be terrible, in that it would be "according to truth," i.e. would be such a punishment as their crime deserves, which implies that if the sin was not punished according to its desert, God's judgment would not be according to truth. Otherwise what does the Apostle build his confidence and sureness upon, that they shall be punished, if God's judgment may be according to truth and justice, and yet not punish them as they deserve, or if God be under no necessity in honor to his truth or justice to punish sin according to its desert? Why was the Apostle so sure, from the truth or justice of God, that sin would be punished as it deserves? This text shows plainly that God is obliged to punish sin as it deserves.JE deleted the following sentence with a large "X." "And it shows that God is obliged to fulfill his threatenings, that 'tis contrary to his truth not to do it, for by truth here respect must be had to something of the nature of a threatening, either the explicit threatening of his word, or the signification and manifestation of his will in this matter in the nature and constitution of things."

When it is said, "the judgment of God is according to truth," the meaning is that God's judgment will be a true judgment; he will judge things as they be, or that his judgment will be conformed to the nature of things. Now the act of judging with regard to any crime is twofold, viz. declaring the guilt, and sentencing to punishment. God shall do these according to truth. His declaration of guilt shall be as the case is indeed,

-- 988 --

and his sentence to punishment shall be that which shall be agreeable thereto. His declaration of guilt and his sentence to punishment shall both have the same language, and the language of both shall be true. They shall both speak true, or as the thing is. The Apostle has evidently respect to both these, not only declaration of guilt, but sentencing to punishment, as is evident by the context. Hence it follows that if God did not sentence to that punishment that sin deserves, his judgment would not be according to truth; and therefore God is obliged to punish sin as it deserves.This paragraph is a later addition.

Romans 2:3–5.] Dost thou think "that thou shalt escape the judgment of God," because judgment is not yet executed? Do you flatter and encourage yourself in your wicked ways from God's goodness, and forbearance, and long-suffering, and so improve the time of God's forbearance to treasure up wrath, and aggravate your condemnation, against the time of God's judgment?

Romans 2:5.] Isaiah 5:18.

Romans 2:8. "But unto them that are contentious."] The Apostle in this word has respect to the perverse spirit of the Jews' quarreling with the gospel that revealed justification by faith alone, and abolished their ceremonial law, and admitted the Gentiles to equal privileges with themselves, etc.

Romans 2:8–9. "Indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish."] Here seems to be a reference to these words, Psalms 78:49, when speaking of the Egyptians, it is said, "He cast upon them the fierceness of his anger, wrath, indignation, and trouble."Doddridge, Family Expositor, 4, 28, n. e.

Romans 2:10. "To the Jew first, and also to the Gentile."] See Romans 1:16.

Romans 2:13. "For not the hearers," etc.] By this verse it appears that the apostle Paul and the apostle James were of the same mind in the matter of justification, however their expressions seem to be opposite. Here the apostle Paul says the same thing that the apostle James means, when he says a man is justified by works, and not by faith only. It is doubtless the same thing that the apostle James meant, if we would explain him by himself,

-- 989 --

for he expresses himself elsewhere almost in the same words that Paul does here (James 1:22–23, James 1:25).

Romans 2:15.] See Taylor.Taylor observes that "Jews and Gentiles, if wicked, shall equally perish; if virtuous, shall equally be saved in the Last Day." His note on Romans 2:15 underscores that the Gentiles have a "rule of action" in their hearts (Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans, pp. 220, 326–27).

Romans 2:21–22.] The Apostle in these verses seems to allude to those words in Psalms 50:16–18.

"Thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal? Thou that sayst a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?" "Grotius on this text proves from Josephus, that some of the Jewish priests lived by rapine, depriving others of their share of the tithes, and even suffering them to perish for want; that others were guilty of gross uncleanness. And as for sacrilegiously robbing God and his altar, it had been complained of as early as Malachi's days (Malachi 1:8, Malachi 1:12–13). So that the instances here are given with great propriety."Doddridge, Family Expositor, 4, 34, n. e.

Romans 2:22. "Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?"] Sacrilege was violating the temple of God, and to a high degree profaning it, especially robbing God of the sacred things. But one of the visible professing people of God was to regard his own body and soul as the temple, and all within him as God's property devoted sacred to him. And therefore by such an one's living in wickedness, God's temple was defiled and altogether violated, and God robbed of all its sacred treasures, vessels, and utensils, which are wickedly taken from him, and devoted to idols, and used in their service. What the sin here intended by the Apostle is we may learn by 1 Corinthians 6:15–20, and 1 Corinthians 3:16–17; Ezekiel 16:15–19; Ezekiel 20:39. There is a sacrilege in the wicked lives of the professors of religion far more aggravated than the idolatry of the heathen.

Romans 2:23.] Thou that gloriest in the law as thine honor, art thou so inconsistent with thyself as at the same time, by breaking the law, to dishonor the lawgiver? Dost thou expose the God to contempt that thou gloriest in?

Romans 2:25. "For circumcision verily profiteth, if thou keep the law."] A profession or visibility of religion profiteth, if we live according to our profession;

-- 990 --

otherwise it only aggravates our condemnation. See note on Romans 1:16.This reference is a later addition.

Romans 2:28. "For he is not a Jew."] Psalms 125:5.

Romans 2:29. "Whose praise is not of men, but of God."] No. 365.Works, 15, 351–56.

Romans 3:1. "What profit is there of circumcision?"] This inquiry has reference to what the Apostle had said before, Romans 2:25.

Romans 3:2–4 ff. "Chiefly, because unto them were committed the oracles of God."] They had greater advantage for faith, because they had the ground of faith more fully and clearly set before them, viz. the word or truth of God. This ground of faith he, in the next verse, calls "the faith of God." This can be a just ground of faith, as it relies on the faithfulness of God whose word or truth it is. 'Tis this strength of the ground of faith that makes it an advantage to have this ground. The unbelief of some don't argue that the ground is vain and insufficient so as that it's no advantage to have it. If "the oracles of God" ben't true, then it's no advantage to have 'em committed to us; but the unbelief of some don't argue that for the word of God or oracles of God to be without effect, or vain, or no advantage, is for 'em not to be true, or not to be a good ground for faith. But the unbelief of some, that have had the abundant enjoyment of these oracles, don't argue thatJE deleted "See Taylor on the Romans 3:3." Taylor's paraphrase of Romans 3:3 is at Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans, pp. 223–24. His note argues against the prevailing pattern of linking Romans 3:3–4 with Romans 3:2 (pp. 335–36). τά λόγια, or "the oracles of God," which the Apostle speaks of, especially intends the promises and prophecies of Christ and his salvation that he made to Abraham and others.

Romans 3:4. "God forbid," etc.] So far from that, that man's unbelief shall be made to commend the faith of God. God's truth will shine the brighter for men's opposition to it. The Romans 3:5 and Romans 3:7 refer to this.
