All that had those extraordinary gifts thereby became a kind of extraordinary officers in the exercise of those gifts, and so far as that extended, and accordingly used to officiate in the church. This is evident by this, and the Romans 14, and also the Romans 12. So far as any person had a miraculous gift by the immediate and extraordinary influence of the spirit of Christ on their minds, so far were they (as Christ, who is the head and fountain of all church office power, and therefore when they were in the exercise of that gift) to be submitted to by the church, as if Jesus Christ himself spake and acted, for it was not they indeed that spake and acted, but Christ in them. Christ, by giving of them such a miraculous gift, marked out a person for such work in the church.

But it can't be argued from hence that there are so many distinct standing offices in the church as there were extraordinary gifts.

A spirit of government, or an extraordinary and miraculous qualification for the exercise of that part of the pastor's office which consists in judging, reproving, rebuking, admonishing, etc., he that had this gift was authorized to do this part of a pastor's work; and the church submitted to him herein that they discerned had this gift, for they had a discerning of spirits (among other gifts of the Spirit) among them. But this no more argues that government was a distinct standing office than that exhorting was, for some that had a gift of exhorting were in the exercise of that gift to do the part of a pastor, and no otherwise (Romans 12:8). One had an extraordinary gift of the Spirit in doctrine, another in counseling and exhorting, another in reproving, admonishing, and judging of offenders. But these are only so many different parts of a pastor's office,

-- 1055 --

and may indeed all be referred to preaching and declaring the word of God. All this is confirmed from Romans 12:6–8. The spirits of Christians,JE deleted "in those days." which they had in an extraordinary manner dwelling in them, sometimes directed in judging offenders. Thus the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 5:4, directs the Corinthians to excommunicate the incestuous person in the name of his spirit.

1 Corinthians 12:31. "But covet earnestly the best gifts."] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus. "Ye contend earnestly about the best gifts," and says, "I doubt not but this is the just rendering of ζηλοῦτε τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα. For it seems contradictory to suppose, that after the Apostle had been showing them that these gifts were not at their own option, and that they ought not to emulate the gifts of each other, nor aspire to superiority, he should in effect unsay all again, and give them contrary advice."Family Expositor, 4, 352, n. h. JE marked this entry with a vertical line near the left margin.

1 Corinthians 13:8.] See sermon on this verse, throughout the doctrinal part and First Inference.JE's sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 (no. 897), preached May 1748, with the doctrine, "The extraordinary influences of the Spirit of God imparting immediate revelations to men were designed only for a temporary continuance while the church was in its minority, and never were intended to be steadily upheld in the Christian church. "JE identifies prophesying, knowledge, and tongues as extraordinary gifts of the Spirit that are the product of immediate revelation, by contrast with the graces of the Spirit—faith, hope, and charity. The former gifts are no longer needed because the means of grace are available. "It is not to be expected that any of those gifts that imply divine revelation should be bestowed in these days because the canon of the Scripture has long since been complete." See Works of Jonathan Edwards, 25, Sermons and Discourses, 1743–1758, ed. Wilson H. Kimnach (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 2006), 275–311. See also no. 305, notes on this and three following verses.Works, 15, 277–79.

1 Corinthians 13:12. "For now we see through a glass darkly."] The word in the original signifies a looking glass, and what we translate "darkly" would have been literally translated, "in an enigma or dark saying." Such are those sayings by which God reveals himself to us in this world, and tells us what manner of being he is. That he might speak to us in our manner, he represents him [self] by such words as we use about other things, which indeed are applicable to God only figuratively, or dark shadows and distant resemblances, as 'tis in the words of an enigma or riddle. See "Miscellanies," no. 710.Ibid., 18, 335–39.

"The exact rendering of δι᾽ ἐσόπτρου is 'by means of a mirror.' And

-- 1056 --

the Seventy use this word for the women's looking glasses, or mirrors of metal (Exodus 38:8)." Doddridge, in loc.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 4, 359, n. i.

1 Corinthians 13:13. "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; and the greatest of these is charity."] "Charity is the very grace and ornament of heaven, the employment and the pleasure of blessed spirits. Nor can faith and hope ever be parted from true religion. For there is no being so great as not to depend on faith in God, and trust in his power and wisdom, or to be above hoping anything from his goodness and benevolence. And therefore the Apostle says expressly of faith and hope, that they shall remain, with charity, the greatest of the three. Other gifts are bestowed for the service of the church, such as tongues, miracles, and the like; and they may well cease, when the occasion which required them ceases. But faith, hope, and charity are not occasional gifts, but are essential to religion, and must continue as long as religion itself." Dr. Sherlock's Several Discourses Preached at Temple Church, p. 268.Thomas Sherlock, Several Discourses Preached at the Temple Church (4 vols. London, 1756–61), I, 268. This selection is drawn from Discourse XIV, Pt. I, which concerns the topic of faith. Vol. I does not have a volume number on it.

"Hope." Note on Hebrews 6:19, no. 284; no. 304.This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 15, 240–42, 276–77. No. 304 is a later addition.

1 Corinthians 14:13. "Wherefore let him that speaketh in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret."] He that had the gift of tongues understood what he himself spake, as is evident by several passages in the chapter. But a person might have the understanding of an unknown tongue, and yet not be well able to interpret, i.e. he might not be able to render what he spake into another tongue readily so as fully to express the same sense, and maintain the purity of the idiom of the tongue into which what he says is rendered. See Miscell. Sacra, vol. 1, pp. 55–56.Herman Witsius, Miscellaneorum Sacrorum, I. Bk. I, entitled "Prophetis et Prophetia," the section from which JE draws these comments, discusses various modes of revelation, including ecstasy, visions, soothsaying, divination, and communication through angels.

1 Corinthians 14:14. "My understanding is unfruitful."] I.e. though I understand myself (See 1 Corinthians 14:4.), yet my meaning is unprofitable to others.

1 Corinthians 14:15. "With the understanding also."] I.e. in an intelligible manner so as to communicate my understanding. See verse preceding and following, and 1 Corinthians 14:19.

-- 1057 --

1 Corinthians 14:20. "Brethren, be not children in understanding."] He that speaks in an unknown tongue, and don't interpret, don't speak with the understanding, talks like a child that repeats words after others, and don't understand what he says. This is to enforce the advice that the Apostle had given before, that he that speaks in an unknown tongue should pray that he might interpret, and that they might speak with the spirit and with the understanding also, that they might speak words that the Holy Ghost dictates, as children do after their parents, and know not what they say.

The Apostle adds this, "Howbeit in malice be ye children," because it seems they must be as little children, as Christ taught; but the Apostle would let 'em know that this should not be in understanding, but in malice.

1 Corinthians 14:24. "He is convinced of all; he is judged of all."] I.e. of, or by, all of you by your prophesying.

1 Corinthians 14:24–25.] There are many instances of this inward conviction of the conscience that happen by the preaching of the word of God faithfully and skillfully when it is done without inspiration. But when the preacher is inspired, and speaks by a spirit of prophecy, which directly reveals the most secret things and often the secrets of men's hearts, the preacher may be under infinitely greater advantage thoroughly and effectually to convince the hearer, as Christ often convinced his hearers by telling them the secret things they were conscious of in their hearts, as the woman of SamariaJE deleted "and others." [John 4] in particular.

1 Corinthians 14:32. "And the spirits of the prophets."] 'Tis diverse spirits considered as in them, i.e. as it becomes a principle in them. It is diverse principles in diverse persons. One has a spirit of prophecy; another has a spirit of knowledge, another a spirit of faith, another spirit of working miracles, etc. Thus these different principles are called spirits in the 1 Corinthians 14:12, but considered in himself, he is but one Spirit, as the Apostle teaches, 1 Corinthians 12:8–11. The Apostle, in the 1 Corinthians 12:14, calls the Spirit of God in him his spirit. So again the Apostle directs them to cast out the incestuous person in the name of his spirit, because the Spirit of God miraculously dwelling in him directed to it (1 Corinthians 5:4).

1 Corinthians 15:4. "Rose again the third day according to the scriptures."] Particularly according to that scripture, Psalms 16:10, "which intimates that he should

-- 1058 --

not see corruption in the grave," because commonly "bodies begin to corrupt on the fourth day, agreeable to John 11:39." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 4, 379.

1 Corinthians 15:11. "Therefore whether it were I or they," etc.] There was no such thing as any difference among the Apostles in the doctrines that they preached, or as one's finding fault with what another taught; but all acknowledged each other's doctrine. It appears by this and several other places, as 2 Peter 3:15–16; Jude 3 and Jude 17; Galatians 1:17–19, Galatians 1:22–24; Galatians 2:7–9; Galatians 2:9 of this context; Romans 16:7; 1 Corinthians 4:9, and 1 Corinthians 9:5, and 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 2:20; 2 Peter 3:2; Revelation 18:20; Revelation 21:14. And it appears by the history of Paul's life in the Acts, that he owned the doctrine of the other apostles, and that his was agreeable to theirs, so that there was no difference between him and them, or amongst Christians that had been converted and taught by them about doctrines that were taught and received. Paul at his first conversion was sent to Ananias, a disciple of the other apostles, of him to be baptized and have his eyes opened. And Paul relates of himself, Galatians 1:23, that then he preached "the faith that once he destroyed," and that was the doctrine of the other apostles. And after he was converted, he assayed to join himself to the disciples at Jerusalem, and that he was with the apostles, coming in and going out at Jerusalem. The disciples at Antioch, where the church was first established by the other apostles, send Paul and Barnabas, who carried their charity to the church at Jerusalem, which was founded and taught by other apostles. Those who had not their Christianity of Paul were chosen by him to be his companions in his labors, to assist him in preaching the gospel, as Barnabas, and Mark, and Silas, etc.

Paul and Silas were separated and sent forth from Antioch by disciples of other apostles, and [Paul] is sent by them again to Jerusalem about circumcision. He goes to the other apostles for their determination, acknowledging their authority to teach and determine as the apostles of Christ, and then carries their determination. Thus he is acknowledged by the churches of Antioch and Jerusalem that were founded by other apostles, and by the other apostles themselves, for they send him with their determination, with a commendation (Acts 15:26). And other like instances might be mentioned. The apostle Paul acknowledges the church of Jerusalem to be the mother of other churches, and that they were indebted to them as having received their faith from them (Romans 15:25–27). Again Luke, who was the companion of Paul, his writing so

-- 1059 --

much in honor of the other apostles in his gospel and history of the Acts of the Apostles, is an argument that Paul gave 'em all that honor that he did. The Apostle, in the 1 Corinthians 15:9 of the context, owns the church that was built only on the foundation of the other apostles to be the church of God. Jesus Christ, when he first appeared to Paul, called the church that Paul persecuted himself, saying, "Why persecutest thou me?", and "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest" [Acts 9:4–5]. Also see Acts 22:19–20.

Now if the apostles had not the doctrine they taught by revelation, it was a strange thing there should be no difference among them, for they taught a multitude of strange and wonderful things that were never before in any such manner so plainly, particularly, and expressly taught by anyone whatsoever. If all was of their own invention, it was strange they did not differ in their schemes.

1 Corinthians 15:17. "And if Christ is not risen, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins."] Because his not being risen: 1. Would be an argument of his insufficiency as a Savior. If he were unable to deliver himself from death, it would have been an argument that he was not able to deliver us. If he was a physician that could not heal himself, there would be cause to apprehend that he was not sufficient [for those] whose diseases were so much worse. And then this was the appointed way of his restoring us, viz. by his restoring himself. We were to be saved no otherwise than in him and with him as members of him, and so to be justified in his justification, which was his resurrection, to be delivered in his deliverance, to have victory in his victory, to triumph with him, to be raised up together with him, and made to sit together in heavenly places in him. And then if God the Father had not thus opened his prison doors, it would have been an evidence that he was not satisfied. And besides, if he had not risen, he would not have been alive to intercede for us, and fulfill the work of salvation he had laid a foundation for in his suffering in his kingly office. So were things constituted in the affair of our redemption, that these things were to be done by Christ as God-man and the head of the human nature. And, 2. If Christ were not risen, it would be an evidence that he was an impostor, for the grand evidence of his mission and appointment as our Savior was his resurrection, which Christ foretold as such, and the determination of that grand point was put on that issue.

1 Corinthians 15:19. "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable."] "It is quite foreign to the purpose, to argue from this text,

-- 1060 --

as some have done, that 'if there were no future state, virtue would make men more miserable than they would otherwise be.' It is evident St. Paul speaks, not here of the case of good men in general, if their hopes of future happiness should after all be disappointed, but of the case of the apostles and other preachers of Christianity, if amidst all their hardships and persecutions, they were not supported by their hope. Destitute of this amidst the extremest sufferings, they must have been perpetually subjected to the upbraidings of their own minds, for sacrificing every view of happiness in this world or another, to advance what they knew to be a pernicious falsehood. Perhaps there never were men on earth so criminal and so wretched as they must on this supposition have been." Doddridge, in loc.Ibid., 385, n. c.

1 Corinthians 15:20. "But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the first fruits of them that slept."] "Where he refers to the law concerning the first fruits. When the harvest was ripe, they were to bring a sheaf of the first fruits for a wave offering, with a burnt offering at the same time (Leviticus 23:9–11). Nor might they eat bread, parched corn, or green ears, till they had made their offering of first fruits. But having done this as the law required, the whole mass and substance of the harvest was hallowed, this offering of the first fruits being instead of all the rest, to which he alludes, Romans 11:16. 'If the first fruits be holy, the lump is holy.' Now with reference hereto, the Apostle calls the resurrection of Christ the 'first fruits'; it having as it were hallowed the dead bodies of the saints, and consecrated them to a new life. He rose not only as first in order, but his resurrection was a representation and figure of ours; showed not only that it might be, but that it should be; he rose as our head; when the natural body was raised, the mystical was raised also. 'By his resurrection he dissolved the tyranny of death,' saith one of the Fathers, 'and raised the whole world or church.' Which is no more than what the Apostle intimates in these words, 'He hath raised us up together with Christ' (Ephesians 2:6). He rose for us, went into heaven for us, as our 'forerunner' (Hebrews 6:20)." Bennet's Christian Oratory, p. 165.Benjamin Bennet, The Christian Oratory: Or, The Devotion of the Closet Display'd (2nd ed. London, 1728), pp. 165–66. See Isaiah 26:19.

1 Corinthians 15:21–23. "Since by man came death," etc.… "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."] I.e. all that are in Christ. The

-- 1061 --

words impart no more, for the Apostle speaks of no more being made alive in Christ than are in him. The Apostle in these words has respect only to the resurrection of the saints, as is evident by the words that follow in the next verse. "But every man in his own order: Christ the first fruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming." Indeed, this resurrection only can well be called a "being made alive," for this only is in Scripture called a "resurrection to life." John 5:29, "And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life, and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation." Daniel 12:2, "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." This "resurrection to life" is alone meant by the word "resurrection" elsewhere, as Luke 20:35. "But they which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection of the dead." And Philippians 3:11, "If by any means I might attain to the resurrection of the dead." And 'tis this "resurrection to life" the Apostle evidently has a special respect to, in the foregoing verses, and indeed throughout this whole chapter, as appears by 1 Corinthians 15:14, 1 Corinthians 15:17–20, 1 Corinthians 15:23, 1 Corinthians 15:29–32, 1 Corinthians 15:35, and all the following part of the chapter, especially the 1 Corinthians 15:45, taken with the foregoing and following, and compared with these words we are now treating of. Therefore those that would argue from hence that Christ, as the Second Adam or as men's surety, procures the resurrection of the wicked as well as of the just, argue without foundation.

1 Corinthians 15:24.] See "Miscellanies," nos. 86 and 609.Works, 13, 250–51; 2, 143–45. See Mastricht, p. 1096b;This sentence is a later addition. Mastricht writes, "Sextus hujus dispensationis passus, qui erit in traditione regni, de qua textus loquitur Revelation 11:15. dicens regna mundi futura, Domini & Christi ejus, & Dominus Deus omnipotens, ut Rex regnaturus vs. 17. quod etiam distinctius repraesentat Apostolus 1 Corinthians 15:24–29" (Theoretica-Practica Theologia [Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715], p. 1096, col. 2). and note on v. 28. See "Miscellanies," no. 736;Works, 18, 360–63. Pfaffius, p. 439.This sentence is a later addition. Christoph Matthew Pfaff's comments on this text are cited in Works, 18, 363, n. 4. His observations on Christ's continuing heavenly reign include this closing note: "Regnum denique gloriam, quod Christo competit, sequentibus effatis biblicis indigitatur" (Institutiones theologiae dogmaticae et moralis).

1 Corinthians 15:25–26. "For he must reign till he hath," etc.] These two verses confirm me in it, that those great enemies of Christ—Antichrist, and Mahometanism, and heathenism—shall be overcome and subdued under

-- 1062 --

Christ's feet, and the whole world be brought into a visible subjection to Christ before the resurrection and last day. That is intimated here and in the Psalms 110:1, that is here referred to, that that shall be the design that shall be carried on all the while that Christ sits at God's right hand, all the while that he reigns, that is, in his mediatorial kingdom, viz. the subduing all Christ's "enemies under his feet." And as soon as this is done, he shall resign up the kingdom to the Father, as having done his work. We shall therefore doubtless see this work gloriously carried on before that time comes and the last stroke is given.

1 Corinthians 15:28.] See no. 158.Works, 15, 95–96.

1 Corinthians 15:29.] See no. 20.Ibid., 53–54. The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. "Baptized for the dead." 'Tis no objection against supposing that by "the dead" here the Apostle has respect to Christ, who those that he wrote against supposed to be a dead man, that the word is in the plural number, as is evident, Matthew 2:20, "they are dead"; by Matthew 9:8, "and glorified God, which had given such power unto men"; and also John 4:38, "other men labored, and ye are entered into their labors," where by "other men" Christ means himself, as seems plain by the context. John 3:12, "Earthly things," when only one thing is intended. ὑπέρ is used in such a sense as here, in John 11:4, Romans 1:5, Philippians 1:29, Acts 5:41, 2 Thessalonians 1:5.

The Apostle uses the third person plural, "What shall they do that are baptized for the dead?" and "Why are they then baptized for the dead?" because he has a special respect to those heretics themselves that infested the church of Corinth, and taught that there was no resurrection of the dead. They themselves had baptized for Christ. And if Christ be yet dead, what will they do? And if this be what they believe, that Christ is still dead, why would they go to be baptized for the dead? How inconsistently did they act with themselves in it! For if this be the case, their baptism did 'em no good. Their faith is vain, and they are yet unwashed from their sins. Matthew 21:7, the plural number is twice used for the singular. See the original,ἤγαγον τὴν ὄνον καὶ τὸν πῶλον, καὶ ἐπέθηκαν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῶν καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια, καὶ ἐπεκάθισεν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν. and compare it with the other Evangelists.The last two sentences are a later addition.

There are instances also in the Old Testament of the plural number being put for the singular: dried up mighty rivers, whereas it was but one

-- 1063 --

river, viz. Jordan. So Habakkuk 3:8. "Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? Was thine anger against the rivers?" And another instance in the New not mentioned before, Matthew 26:8. "But when the disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste?", when but one disciple is meant, viz. Judas. (See this text more fully spoken to, in answer to a question proposed to be answered before the Association,I.e. the Hampshire County Association. The Hampshire County Association Minutes (MS, Forbes Library, Northampton, Mass.), contain no identifiable reference to such a question or discussion, nor is the MS to which JE refers extant. in one of my drawers.)I.e. the drawers of JE's scrutore, or writing desk. For a photograph of the desk, see the frontispiece in Works, 13. Mark 1:21, "Immediately on the sabbath day"; in the Greek it is τοῖς σάββασιν, in the plural number. So the plural is in like manner put for the singular in Matthew 12:2, and Matthew 28:1; and Acts 13:14. See also Matthew 27:44, Genesis 19:29, Judges 12:7, Psalms 137:1, 1 Samuel 28:13, Genesis 21:7, Exodus 32:31, 1 Samuel 10:12, Genesis 27:29. See 1 Samuel 17:43, "That thou comest to me with staves." 1 Samuel 28:13. 2 Chronicles 24:25, "And for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest," when only one son is meant, viz. Zechariah, whom we read of, 2 Chronicles 24:20–21. (See SSS on 2 Chronicles 24:25, where are quoted several instances from heathen writers.)Poole, Synopsis Criticorum, I (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 852. Genesis 21:7, "Who would have said that Sarah should have children suck?" Genesis 46:1, "All the souls of his sons and his daughters," when he had but one daughter, viz. Dinah. See also Genesis 46:7. Genesis 36:25, "The children of Anah were Dishon." Genesis 46:23, "And the sons of Dan, Hushim."This and the preceding paragraph are a later addition.

1 Corinthians 15:33. "Evil communications corrupt good manners."] What the Apostle had said in the verses immediately preceding showed how this doctrine of no resurrection tended to "corrupt good manners." Such a principle removes the main enforcement of Christian self-denial, and opens a door for all manner of licentiousness. For if it be so, men will be mere Epicures, and say, Let us enjoy our pleasures, for tomorrow we die.

1 Corinthians 15:34.] Seeing that it is so that these heretical doctrines tended to corrupt the practice, such as were tainted with them needed this advice to awake to righteousness, and forsake their corrupt practices. They denied the resurrection of the body, but they stood in need of the resurrection of the soul to rise or awake to righteousness. "For some men have not the knowledge of God." They were not aware that they needed advice to

-- 1064 --

awake to righteousness. They supposed that that was done already when they became Christians and were baptized. They supposed that all that turnedJE deleted "to Christianity and were baptized had the." from idols to Christianity had now the knowledge of the true God, and were holy. But the Apostle informs them otherwise, that some men have not the knowledge of God, even of them that profess Christianity.

1 Corinthians 15:35. "But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? With what body do they come?"] The objection against the resurrection that the Apostle here supposes to be made is this: What body will the dead rise with? Will they rise with such parts as our bodies are now constituted of, the end of many of which is only to subserve to the purposes of the animal life, and we can conceive of no use for 'em in such a world as you say the resurrection world is? What use will the blood and bowels, etc., be of? Such vainly curious questions as these were more likely to be started at Corinth or Athens than in most other places.

1 Corinthians 15:39. "All flesh is not the same flesh," etc.] "The scope of the place makes it evident, that by 'flesh' St. Paul here means bodies, viz. that God has given to the several sorts of animals bodies in shape, texture, and organization very different from one another, as he hath thought good, and so he can give to men at the resurrection bodies of very different constitutions and qualities from those they had before." Locke.Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians, 98, n. i.

1 Corinthians 15:42. "So also is the resurrection of the dead."] The stop that is made between the two foregoing verses makes the meaning of this a little more difficult to be perceived, for it refers to what is said in those verses together. 'Tis indeed only the first of those verses that is directly to the argument the Apostle was upon, which was to answer that objection, 1 Corinthians 15:35, "How are the dead raised up, and with what body do they come?" In answer to which, he insists that their body will be exceedingly more glorious than the body that dies. And to illustrate this, he mentions in the 1 Corinthians 15:40 the great difference there is between terrestrial bodies, such as bodies, and plants, and animals, and celestial bodies, such as the sun, moon, and stars, in these words, "There are also celestial bodies and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another." And having mentioned this, he goes on to observe

-- 1065 --

the difference there is even among celestial bodies themselves, signifying the different glory there will be among the bodies of the resurrectedMS: "resurrection." themselves, though not directly to the argument that the Apostle was upon, which is very agreeable to this Apostle's way of writing, who exceedingly overflowed with matter. "There is," says he, "one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars" (and not only so, but), "one star differs from another star in glory" 1 Corinthians 15:41]. And these words, "So also is the resurrection of the dead," refer to both these verses. So is "the resurrection of the dead" in both these respects, viz. that the glory of their bodies greatly differs from the glory of their bodies that fell, as the celestial bodies differ in glory from the terrestrial, and the resurrection bodies also differ in glory one from another, as the celestial bodies do, though the former being most directly to the Apostle's argument, he does but only occasionally mention the latter, and returns and goes on to insist only on the former in the following verses. Among the celestial bodies the glory of the sun well represents the glory of Christ's resurrection body, the glory of the moon the glory of the bodies of the apostles, and prophets, and other great lights of the church that have been improved by God to reflect and convey the light of the sun, i.e. of Christ, to the world,JE deleted "The diverse glory of the stars represents the diverse glory of the bodies of other saints, and perhaps also the glorified body." not to exclude all women, especially the blessed Virgin Mary, who was so highly favored to beJE deleted "the instrument of conveying that light to the world." the mother of Christ, and conceived and brought him forth by her faith (Luke 1:45). 'Tis said that all generations shall call her blessed for this [Luke 1:48]; and 'tis probable that as the church in this world will call her blessed in this world in all ages of the world, so they will to all eternity, as seeing of her to be peculiarly blessed when she is called blessed, that is, peculiarly blessed among women (Luke 1:42), blessed above other women, blessed in an eminent sense. 'Tis not with [out] cause. She is really still peculiarly blessed and exalted in glory, not merely because she was the mother of Christ, for "Rather, blessed is he that hears the word of God, and keeps it" [Luke 11:28], but for her eminent holiness that this was a reward of, and as this was a fruit of her extraordinary faith (See notes on Luke 1:45.), and for the good she did in nursing and bringing up Christ.JE deleted "Herein she perhaps did more good than ever any other woman did." Persons are rewarded not merely in proportion to the degree of their faith and holiness, but for the fruits of it, and the good that is done by it. The

-- 1066 --

fruits of the exercise of the Virgin Mary's faith in conceiving and bringing forth, and her faith and love in bringing up Christ, is the greatest good to the world. Herein she did more good than ever any other woman did, and to her that hath, shall be given. She was the instrument of conveying this light to the world, in a way to which the way in which the apostles and other ministers do is compared, for they travail in birth till Christ is formed and brought forth, and are the great instruments of bringing forth the man-child, in the sense spoken of Revelation 12:5. See notes on Canticles 2:11, the second part of that note. That these should be thus distinguished in this representation of the resurrection state from other saints, by that which differs so much as the moon does from the stars, is no more than is agreeable to other scriptures, particularly where Christ says that when he "shall sit on the throne of his glory, they also shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel" [Matthew 19:28], and Abraham's being called the father of the faithful, and the saints being carried into his bosom, and sitting down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and there being so often represented in the Revelation by the four and twenty elders that are next to the throne in heaven, and especially the apostles being represented as the twelve foundations of the New Jerusalem, or the church in her glorified state. See Turretin, Tome 3, p. 701, §12.This reference is a later addition. The tenth question in Turretin's twentieth topic, De Novissimis, "Will there be degrees of glory? And will the glory in heaven be equal or unequal and unlike?" Turretin uses a variety of passages, including Matthew 19:28, to argue that "the patriarchs, prophets and apostles" are described as "the commanders and leaders of believers in glory." There is therefore "a certain disparity between their glory and that of all believers." Although all the saints will shine in glory, nevertheless, some will be "distinguished by order and degree of light" (Institutio Tlieologiae Elencticae). See Dennison, ed., Institutes of Etenctic Theology, III, 621, 626–27.

The diverse glory of the stars represents the different degrees of the glory of the other saints.

Christ and his saints in heaven will be all one family. But in this family Christ will be as it were the father; and prophets, and apostles, and other saints that have been great lights in the church and eminent blessings to it, will be as it were the wife and the mother; and other saints will be as the children in the family. And of these children some will be elder, others younger, which is a like similitude with that in this verse in which Christ is compared to the sun, the saints who have been great lights and blessings in the church to the moon, and other saints to the stars, though some greater and others lesser. The church is often spoken of as a mother; but when it is so, it is especially with respect to the teaching part of the church. See notes on Canticles 3:11, and Hosea 4:5. The whole

-- 1067 --

church is very often called the spouse or wife of Christ, but yet we often find a distinction made in the church of wife, or mother and children (Isaiah 49:14, Isaiah 49:17–18, Isaiah 49:20–23, Isaiah 49:25; and Isaiah 54:1, Isaiah 54:3–6, Isaiah 54:13; Isaiah 60:1, Isaiah 60:3–5; and in other places). Sun, moon, and stars are made use of in Scripture to represent father, and mother, and children in Scripture, as particularly in Joseph's dream [Genesis 37:9].

1 Corinthians 15:44–45.] See notes on Galatians 5:17, Corol. 3.

1 Corinthians 15:55.] The sting of death is the misery that is in the tail, or last end and issue of death. This misery properly belongs to death. The sting of death is in its tail; and Christ, in taking away the misery of hell, has taken away the worst part of death, and almost all that is terrible in death.

1 Corinthians 15:58. "Forasmuch as ye know that your labor shall not be in vain in the Lord."] As it would be if there was no resurrection. But ye know that there is a resurrection wherein you shall be rewarded. See 1 Corinthians 15:17, 1 Corinthians 15:19, 1 Corinthians 15:30–33.

1 Corinthians 16:21–24.] See no. 120.Works, 15, 84.

1 Corinthians 16:22. "If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha."] "The lower kinds of excommunication among the Jews were attended only with separation from the synagogue worship, and from familiar converse (Luke 6:22), or in cases of greater guilt, with confiscation of goods, and forfeiture of all their substance (Ezra 10:8). The highest kind of it was a capital sentence (Leviticus 27:29), the execution of which, when regularly pronounced, was indeed an act of duty and obedience to God, while they had the power of life and death in their hands. But after it was wrested from them, they had a dependence upon the interposition of providence, to add that efficacy to their censures, which their power, infringed as it was, could not give. In reference to which, this highest sentence of excommunication was in the decline of their state called 'Anathema Maranatha,' or a sentence which 'the Lord would' remarkably 'come' to execute, though they themselves could not carry it into effect. St. Paul therefore, with a beauty and propriety, so far as I can find, never full explained, applies it to a crime not capable of conviction before any human judges, even the want of sincere love to Christ, though under a Christian profession." Doddridge, on John 16:2.Family Expositor, 2, 472–73, n. a.

-- 1068 --

II Corinthians

2 Corinthians 1:1. "By the will of God."] No. 268.Works, 15, 222–23.

2 Corinthians 1:13. "But what you read or acknowledge."] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "But what you know and acknowledge," and says, "The word ἀναγινώσκω is ambiguous, and may signify either to acknowledge, or to know, or to read; but, I think, the sense here plainly determines it to 'knowing.'"Family Expositor, 4, 428 and n. a.

2 Corinthians 1:14. "In part."] I.e. a part of you. See 2 Corinthians 2:5. See Taylor's note on Romans 15:15.Taylor explicitly links this text with the explanation given of ἀπὸ μέρους at Romans 15:15. See JE's entry on the latter text.

2 Corinthians 1:24.] This verse is to be joined to the fourteenth.

2 Corinthians 2:5. "Grieved me in part."] I.e. according to Dr. Doddridge, he has not grieved me only, but me as one of a considerable number among yourselves, who have been united with me, as of the same company of mourners for this offense. I have been grieved only as a part of the company, who with one heart have mourned.Family Expositor, 4, 435–36.

2 Corinthians 2:6. "Inflicted of many."] If thisὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων. be rightly translated "of many," rather than "before many," as Dr. Hammond, yet it might be "of many," and not by the whole congregation, by virtue of any power vested in the brethren. See note on 1 Corinthians 12:28.The translation by Henry Hammond (1605–66), an Anglican divine and biblical critic, allows a distinction to be made by the Apostle, so "that the whole Church may not be afflicted, as if they had all grieved" him, or incurred his censure. This interpretation implies the transaction is to be carried out "in the presence of the whole congregation." Hammond's note on 1 Corinthians 12:28 identifies the chief officers of the church and their respective responsibilities (A Paraphrase, and Annotations Upon all the Books of the New Testament: Briefly explaining all the difficult places thereof [London, 1653], pp. 584, 604–5).

-- 1069 --

2 Corinthians 3:3. "Forasmuch as ye," etc.] The Corinthian converts were a sort of epistle from Christ in commendation of the faithfulness and efficacy of the Apostle's ministry. This efficacy was upon their hearts, so that the epistle was written there, though the characters that were written on their hearts wereJE deleted "read by the manifestation of them in their lives." made visible in their lives.

2 Corinthians 3:6.] See notes on Galatians 5:18, Ans. to 2nd Inq., "Scripture," no. 196.Works, 15, 113–15. See also "Miscellanies," no. 1353.This reference is a later addition. Works, 23, 495–99. This portion of no. 1353, an entry entitled "THE TWO DISPENSATIONS COMPARED, THAT UNDER MOSES AND THAT UNDER CHRIST," focuses on the ways "wherein the two dispensations differ." JE pointed to this section of the entry using specific page references.

2 Corinthians 3:9. "Ministration of righteousness."] Here we may be convinced that the apostle Paul often uses the word "righteousness" for justification, and in opposition to condemnation.

2 Corinthians 3:14–16.] No. 363.Works, 15, 349–50.

2 Corinthians 3:15.] St. Paul possibly here alludes to the custom of the Jews, which continues still in the synagogue. When the law is read, they put a veil over their faces. Locke.A Paraphrase and Notes on the Second Epistle of St. Paul to the Corinthians (London, 1706), 18, n. n.

2 Corinthians 3:16.] "Nevertheless when it," i.e. their heart, "shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away," in allusion to Moses' taking off the veil when he turned away from the people to the Lord (Exodus 34:33–35).JE deleted "The heart of the people is compared to Moses, in the foregoing verse, with a veil over his face. Moses herein perhaps is a type of the people. As Moses had a veil over his face, so they had a veil over their heart. Moses herein perhaps is a type of that people who are called the body of Moses." Moses, while absent from the Lord, was blinded and hoodwinked; but when he turned to the Lord, the veil was taken away. So it is with the hearts of men.

2 Corinthians 3:17. "That Spirit."] See 2 Corinthians 3:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:8.

-- 1070 --

2 Corinthians 3:17–18.] See nos. 89 and 96.Works, 15, 76, 78. "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," because the Lord is the Son of God; and so those that have "the Spirit of the Lord" have a filial spirit, and therefore a free spirit, a "Spirit of adoption," which is opposite to a "spirit of bondage" [Romans 8:15]. If the Son gives us his own Spirit, we shall have a free spirit indeed; for whom the Son makes free, he shall be free indeed. See notes on Galatians 5:18, Ans. to Inq. 2, no. 196.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 113–15.

2 Corinthians 3:18.] See "Miscellanies," no. 370; and "Scripture," nos. 335 and 341.Works, 13, 441–42; 2, 319–22, 325. The two "Scriptures" references are later additions.

2 Corinthians 4:2. "But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty."] The Apostle in this has reference to what he had said before, 2 Corinthians 3:12, "We use great plainness of speech." Dr. Doddridge renders the wordsπολλῃ. παρρησίᾳ χρώμεθα. thus, "We have renounced the hidden things of shame," and supposes the Apostle has reference to the practices of the heathen priests [in which they] dealt "so much, in order to impose on the people over whom they presided, practicing in their mysteries so many impure and so many foolish rites."Family Expositor, 4, 450.

2 Corinthians 4:3. "But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost."] Here is reference to what was said, 2 Corinthians 3:12–13, "We use great plainness of speech, and not as Moses, who put a veil over his face." Dr. Doddridge renders these words thus, "But if our gospel be under a veil too, it is veiled to them that are perishing," and says this is literally agreeable to the words, εἰ δὲ καὶ ἔστιν κεκαλυμμένον τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἡμὼν.Ibid., 451, n. c.

2 Corinthians 4:5.] It might have been better rendered, "We preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus Lord, and ourselves your servants," etc. I.e. we don't preach ourselves lords, but Jesus Christ, and ourselves servants, etc.

2 Corinthians 4:10–11. "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body," etc.] For the Apostle's yet living, though "always delivered to death," as it is expressed in the next verse, his flesh, which was in itself marked and very liable to dissolution, being so wonderfully preserved, though continually

-- 1071 --

so exposed and often so greatly suffering, made the life of Christ manifest, or made it manifest that Christ was alive, and took care of him, and preserved him by his power. Christ's power was manifest in his infirmities, as the Apostle elsewhere calls 'em, or exposedness and suffering.JE deleted "See 2 Corinthians 4:7. 'Tis evident that this is the Apostle's meaning by the preceding verses." (See 2 Corinthians 4:8–10.) But more especially in his being not only so preserved under such great infirmities and sufferings, but in being made in his ministry so successful, victorious, and triumphant, in being the instrument of so much good, even spiritual and eternal life to others, while I as it were am dying myself; for, says the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 4:12, though death works in me, yet life works in others, in those in whom appears the success of my ministry. While I am dying as it were, I am not only preserved, but bring life to others. So the life of Christ is manifested in my death.

2 Corinthians 4:12.] See note on 2 Corinthians 4:10–11.

2 Corinthians 4:13. "We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written."] Dr. Doddridge renders the words thus. "We having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written," i.e. the same spirit of faith that the Psalmist had, which he expressed in the words quoted.Family Expositor, 4, 455–56.

2 Corinthians 4:15. "For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving," etc.] AllJE deleted "these former times instances of the power and mercy of God toward me when troubled on every side and not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, etc. This is for your sakes that I might be preserved to benefit your souls." my sufferings I expose myself to for your sakes. "That the abundant grace." I.e. this God's abundant grace towards me in so remarkably upholding, preserving, and assisting me, mentioned. The 2 Corinthians 1:10–11 confirm this exposition.

2 Corinthians 5:1 ff.] See nos. 57 and 60.Works, 15, 66, 67.

The Apostle seems to wish that he might be "clothed upon" at once with immortality in soul and body "without dying," but since things are otherwise determined, then in the next place, he would rather choose absence from the body, that he might "be present with the Lord" 2 Corinthians 5:9] (Dr. Watts).Here JE is paraphrasing a discussion of 2 Corinthians 5:1–2 (p. 521) in Isaac Watts, An Essay Toward a Proof of a Separate State of Souls Between Death and Resurrection, and The commencement of the rewards of Virtue and Vice immediately after death, published as a preface to The World to Come (pp. 511–752), in Works, 1. Later in Discourse VIII entitled "A soul prepared for heaven," Watts writes, "We know, saith he in the 2 Corinthians 5:1 of this chapter, we know that as soon as our mortal tabernacle, in which we now dwell, is dissolved, we have a building ready for us in the heavens" (p. 635). He intimates, in the 2 Corinthians 5:4, that to be in a separate state is in itself undesirable. But yet he, in the 2 Corinthians 5:6 and 2 Corinthians 5:8,

-- 1072 --

signifies that though it must be so, that he, when he died, and if persecution destroyed the union between soul and body, and caused him to be in a separate state, that notwithstanding he was confident his hope and comfort was still supported, because, though being in a separate state was undesirable, yet to be in a separate state with the Lord was far better than to be in the body and absent from the Lord.This paragraph is a later addition. JE's "A Sermon Preached on the Day of the Funeral of the Rev. Mr. David Brainerd," struck the theme "True saints, when absent from the body, are present with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). For the text, see Works, 7, 543–54.

In the 2 Corinthians 5:4 and following verses, the Apostle intimates that he did not long to put off this tabernacle for the sake of being unclothed, or being in a separate state, which was in itself undesirable. But here are two things that the Apostle mentions as what supported him under apprehensions of death, and dangers of it by persecution, though death would put him into a state of separation, viz. 1. That the time surely would come when he should be "clothed upon," and "mortality would be swallowed up of life," because he that had wrought him for this selfsame was God, who has given the Spirit as an earnest of it 2 Corinthians 5:5]. 2. That in the meantime, though he should be in a separate state, yet he should be present with the Lord, which was better than to be absent from the Lord in the body.This paragraph is a separate entry.

2 Corinthians 5:6.] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus, "While we are sojourning in the body, we are in a state of exile from the Lord," and says, "ἐνδημοῦντες properly signifies 'sojourning,' and that it is wrong to render it, 'at home,' since it is the Apostle's design to intimate that this is not our home."Family Expositor, 4, 461 and n. f.

2 Corinthians 5:10.] This verse and the context very plainly declare the existence of the souls of both good and bad in a state of separation. If it be the day of general judgment when men shall appear before Christ in their bodies, yet it implies that such as have died before have been [in] a state wherein they have not been in the body. See notes on Luke 16:22 ff.

-- 1073 --

2 Corinthians 5:12. "Which glory in appearance, and not in heart."] I.e. glory outwardly, but their own consciences reproach and condemn them, it being herein otherwise with their false teacher than he had been declaring that it was with him, in this and the preceding chapter.

2 Corinthians 5:14–16.] The Apostle in these verses would signify how that in glorying, he did not act in his own name, or on his own behalf, but as one that lives to Christ, and acts for him, and knows and has respect to men and things not after the flesh, or as having respect to himself as a private person, or as relating to his own separate interest, but as related to Christ. He acts towards all as a member of him, and as one that acts for him, and not for himself. For when a man is "in Christ, he is a new creature," as it follows in the 2 Corinthians 5:17. He is cut off from his own separate root, and is engrafted into Christ, and knows all things. All things influence him and affect him now as they stand related to Christ, and not as they stand related to himself separately.

2 Corinthians 5:15. "That they which live."] οἱ ζῶντες, which is a name for true Christians, they only being those that are spiritually alive. "Should not henceforth live unto themselves." I.e. from the time that they are quickened and begin spiritually to live.

2 Corinthians 5:16. "Wherefore henceforth."] The word "henceforth" in this verse relates to the same time with the same word in the preceding verse, viz. from the time of spiritual quickening, or the beginning of spiritual life, i.e. from the time of conversion.

2 Corinthians 5:17.] See sermon on the words.JE's sermon on 2 Corinthians 5:17 (no. 1005), preached Sept. 1751, with the doctrines: "1. What is meant by being in Christ. 2. How he that is in Christ is a new creature. 3. How old things are passed away in him that is in Christ and all things are become new" (MS, p. 1).

2 Corinthians 7:8. "Though I did repent."] Dr. Doddridge renders these words thus: "However anxious I might before have been" (i.e. before Titus came). In his note on the place, he says, "So I choose to render εἰ καὶ μετεμελόμην as μεταμέλεια strictly expresses an after-care and anxiety for anything that has been done, whereas the word "repent" always signifies a wish it had not been done. Now as what St. Paul did, in writing the former epistle, was proper, and done under the direction of the divine

-- 1074 --

Spirit, it does not seem reasonable to suppose that he really repented of it. It may also signify a kind of misgiving of heart, natural, when the reproof, however necessary, is given to a person one tenderly loves, where the event is dubious, as in this instance it might be."Family Expositor, 4, 481 and n. c.

2 Corinthians 7:10. "Not to be repented of."] This refers to those foregoing words in the 2 Corinthians 7:8, "For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent."

2 Corinthians 7:12.] "I did it not" so much out of regard to him "that had done wrong," or him "that suffered wrong," as out of regard to the well-being of the church, the state of religion, and the welfare of the souls of the people in general.

2 Corinthians 8:10.] See no. 162.Works, 15, 97.

2 Corinthians 8:18. "The brother whose praise is in the gospel," etc.] This brother Dr. Doddridge supposes to be St. Luke, and says most commentators are of this mind. He observes St. Luke "certainly attended St. Paul in this journey to Jerusalem," as he says in the next verse. He was chosen of the churches to travel with him. What is said of him in this and the three next verses implies a very high commendation of him indeed. And that expression of his praise being "in the gospel in all the churches" must imply that he was everywhere, among Christians that knew him, esteemed very eminent in his knowledge in the gospel, and his faithfulness, zeal, great labors, and success in promoting it. And perhaps his writing the gospel of Luke may especially be referred to, and its being everywhere received with great "applause," as (Dr. Doddridge says) "many ancient Christians" supposed.Family Expositor, 4, 491.

2 Corinthians 9:10. "Now he that ministereth," etc.] The Apostle here alludes to that which [is] found in the course of God's common providence by them that till and sow the ground. Of the crop they receive, he gives them seed to sow the ground again, over and above a sufficiency for bread for their food (And that part of the grain they sow is no more lost to 'em than that which they eat.), but more so, as God multiplies their seed sown, so that

-- 1075 --

from thence they have their future supply for bread to eat, and more seed than ever to sow, as well as more bread to eat.

2 Corinthians 9:12. "This service."] The word is λειτουργία, which intimates that their charity "was to be considered as an act of religion most pleasing to God, and suitable to the nature of the gospel dispensation." Doddridge.Ibid., 497, n. d.

2 Corinthians 9:15.] 'Tis a confirmation that the "unspeakable gift" here mentioned is Christ, that the Apostle had before, in the preceding chapter, put 'em in mind of the grace of God in this gift as a proper motive to incite them to charity (2 Corinthians 9:9).

2 Corinthians 11:2. "For I have espoused you to one husband," etc.] "This is much illustrated by recollecting that there was an officer among the Greeks, whose business it was to educate and form young women, especially those of rank and figure, designed for marriage, and then to present them to those who were to be their husbands. And if this officer permitted them, through negligence, to be corrupted, between the espousals and consummation of the marriage, great blame would naturally fall upon him." Doddridge, in loc.Ibid., 507–8, n. a.

2 Corinthians 11:3. "The simplicity that is in Christ."] ἁπλότητος τῆς εἰς Χριστόν, which Dr. Doddridge renders "simplicity towards Christ," and says, "The phrase implies an entire undivided devotedness to Christ as the great husband Christians should desire to please, and from whom they are to receive law, and is with peculiar propriety opposed to that mixture of Judaism which some were endeavoring to bring in among the Corinthians."Ibid., 508 and n. d.

2 Corinthians 11:4.] See no. 164.Works, 15, 97–98.

Dr. Doddridge, agreeably to Poole's Synopsis,Synopsis Criticorum, IV (London, 1676), Pt. 2, cols. 636–37. paraphrases this verse thus. "If he, that cometh among you with such extraordinary pretenses, preach another Jesus, or can point out another Christ, who shall equally deserve your attention and regard, or if ye receive by his preaching another spirit, which can bestow upon you gifts superior to those which we have imparted, or another gospel, the tidings of which shall be equally

-- 1076 --

happy, evident, and important, ye might well bear with him; and there would be some excuse for your conduct."This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 4, 508–9.

2 Corinthians 11:12.] The sense of the verse is: That which I do and will do, in not taking of you any temporal reward for my labors, is not because I don't look on you as my entire friends, and so durst not trust you so far as I do the Christians of Macedonia (of whom I take wages), but that I may cut off from your false teachers (that take large sums of you, and "devour you"; see 2 Corinthians 11:20) that occasion they would be glad of, to justify them, and glory in what they do, in this respect, viz. that therein they are found, do other than we do.JE deleted "They desire this occasion to glory or boast." Their great gains was their glory, their outward wealth, and worldly advantages, which they obtained by what they took from the Corinthians, was that which they were puffed up with, and set their hearts much upon. And they desired to have it to appear that in this making a gain of the Corinthians, they were found even as the apostle Paul.

2 Corinthians 11:21. "I speak concerning reproach, as though we had been weak."] In order to understand what the Apostle's meaning in these words is, it must be observed that they have reference to the words following, and not the foregoing, as much as to say, In what I am now going to say, I have respect to the reproach your false teachers cast upon me, as though I were weak, and cowardly, and mean-spirited (Compare 1 Corinthians 2:3.), and ascribe my not taking wages, and working with mine own hands, and other parts of my conduct, to that.

2 Corinthians 12:2–4.] The privilege that Moses was admitted to makes what the Apostle here relates of himself the more credible. See note on the Exodus 34. When the Old Testament saints and prophets have been admitted to so great a privilege, 'tis not unreasonable to suppose that New Testament saints and apostles should be admitted to as great and greater of the like kind, considering how much more glorious the dispensation is that the latter are ministers of than the other, and how much more honorable the ministers. John the Baptist, that was only the forerunner of Christ, was greater than the greatest of the Old Testament prophets; and Christ tells us the "least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he" [Luke 7:28]. But Paul was the greatest minister in the kingdom of heaven. The glory of the dispensation that Moses was minister

-- 1077 --

of, and that shining of his face was a signification of, was no glory in comparison of the glory of that dispensation that Paul was minister of, as he himself particularly declares, in the 2 Corinthians 3 of this epistle, magnifying his office. Paul was the principal minister of the New Testament, as Moses was the principal minister of the Old. Paul was the great apostle of the Gentiles, and revealer of the gospel to them, and founder of the Gentile church, as Moses was the greatest prophet of the Jews, and revealer of the law to them, and founder of the Jewish church. It is probable that when Paul ascended into heaven, that he there received his gospel, that he preached to the Gentiles, that he so often speaks of, of Jesus Christ. And it was suitable there should be such a difference, that Paul should receive his gospel in heaven, as Moses did the law on Mount Sinai, that that dispensation, which was earthly and contained only an image of the heavenly, should be communicated on earth, only on a mountain where was an image of heaven, but that the heavenly things themselves should be communicated in heaven itself. As the glory of Moses' dispensation was no glory in comparison of Paul's, so the glory of Mount Sinai was no glory in comparison of the glory of the third heaven.

2 Corinthians 12:3. "Whether in the body, or out of the body, I can not tell."] By this it appears that it was no strange, unheard of, unthought of notion, in the apostolic age and amongst the apostles themselves, that the soul of man should live, perceive, and act in a state of separation from the body.

2 Corinthians 12:4. "Paradise."] Note on Luke 23:43.

2 Corinthians 12:7. "And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure."] Dr. Doddridge, in loc., saysMS: "Says Signifies." that he falls in with Dr. Whitby and the author of Miscell. Sacra, "that the view the Apostle had of celestial glories affected the system of his nerves in such a manner, as to occasion some paralytic symptoms, and particularly a stammering in his speech, and some distortion of his countenance, referred to elsewhere in the phrase of the 'infirmity in his flesh' (Galatians 4:13–14, 1 Corinthians 2:3). Compare Daniel 8:27." And this case of St. Paul's, Dr. Doddridge compares to Jacob's, "when he had been so successfully wrestling with the angel," and went

-- 1078 --

away "halting on his thigh" [Genesis 32:31].Family Expositor, 4, 524, n. f., and 525. If such an infirmity followed those extraordinary visions, and so was sent by God, yet Satan might have a hand in it, as he had in Job's grievous and painful diseases, which yet are often spoken of as from the hand of God. 'Tis observable that Satan seems peculiarly to have advantage by disorders that immediately affect the system of the nerves and animal spirit to work, and with such disorders greatly to affect and afflict men's bodies and minds. See Luke 13:16, concerning the "woman that had a spirit of infirmity" Luke 13:11]. And this infirmity might be called the messenger of Satan, so far as Satan had a hand in it, as well as diseases be represented as God's messengers, subject to his command, as the soldiers under the command of their captain (Matthew 8:7–9). Waters and lightnings are represented as God's messengers (Job 38:34–35). See also Psalms 104:4.

2 Corinthians 13:1. "In the mouth of two or three witnesses."] No. 425.Works, 15, 504–5.

2 Corinthians 13:14. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ."] What is signified in each part of this benediction is the sum of all that good that the elect have by the redemption of Christ. This is called "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ," having respect to the way that we have this good through him, viz. by partaking of the fullness of that our head. He is full of grace, and we partake of his fullness, and grace for grace. The gift is first bestowed on our head, given into his possession as our head; and we partake of the gift or grace in him. "The love of all." All is of the love of the Father as its first spring, as he is the first mover, and head, and fountain of all in the affair of our redemption. And the gift that is received, that is the great benefit of the Father's love, that is first given to Christ, and is his fullness, and that we receive from him, or receiving his grace, is the Holy Spirit. We receive it by having a communion or participation of the Holy Ghost.

-- 1079 --

Galatians

Galatians 1:7.] "Which is not another."] I.e. indeed, no gospel at all.

"Pervert." Mr. Hervey says it should have been translated "overthrow." See Dialogues, vol. 2, p. 10, margin.This paragraph is a separate entry. Hervey writes, "St. Paul says of those Preachers, who taught Justification by the Works of the Law, They would pervert, or (as the Original μεταστρέφαι may be translated) subvert and overthrow the Gospel of CHRIST.—To pervert, give a wrong Turn, or a false Colour, seems not to express fully the Apostle's Idea, nor to preserve the native Energy of his Argument" (Dialogues, 2, 10, note).

Galatians 1:10.] "Πείθω, translated 'persuade,' is sometimes used for making application to anyone to obtain his good will or friendship; and hence Acts 12:20, πείσαντες Βλάστον, is translated, 'having made Blastus their friend.'" Mr. Locke.Paraphrase and Notes on Galatians (3rd ed.), 7, n. m.

Galatians 1:17. "Into Arabia."] No. 272.Works, 15, 228–29.

Galatians 2:5. "To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour."] In the original it is, οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ω]ραν εἴξαμεν, "nor did we yield to them an hour." "οὐδὲ, 'neither,' in the Galatians 2:3, according to the propriety of speech, ought to have a 'nor' to answer it, which is the οὐδὲ, 'nor,' here. 'Neither was Titus compelled to be circumcised, nor did we yield to them a moment.'" Mr. Locke.Paraphrase and Notes on Galatians (3rd ed.), 11, n. b.

"'By subjection.' The point those false brethren contended for, was that the law of Moses was to be kept. See Acts 15:5. St. Paul, who on other occasions was so complaisant, that to the Jews he 'became as a Jew, to those under the law as under the law' (1 Corinthians 9:19–22), yet when subjection to the law was claimed as due in any case, he would not yield the least matter. Where compliance was desired of him, upon the account of expedience, and not of subjection to the law, we do not find him stiff and inflexible, as may be seen, Acts 21:18–26, which was after the writing this epistle." Mr. Locke.Ibid., 11, n. c.

-- 1080 --

Galatians 2:18.] By believing and trusting in Christ as a Savior from eternal death, we destroy sin, and that because there is repentance necessarily implied in the nature of this faith. He that truly believes in Christ to save him from sin or the guilt of sin, he sees the evil of sin, and so is made sensible how justly God is provoked, and that his sin deserves death and hell. But he that thus sees the evil of sin and its desert of hell, he destroys it; his heart is divorced from it. A seeking "to be justified by Christ" (mentioned in the foregoing verse), or a seeking to be delivered from the guilt of sin by faith in him, implies in it a hatred of sin itself, which is a destroying of sin, for he that depends on Christ for deliverance from guilt is sensible of the guilt of sin. But he that is rightly sensible of sin is sensible of its hateful nature, for from its hateful nature its guilt or desert ofJE deleted "hell." the wrath of God arises. See "Miscellanies," no. 504.Works, 18, 51–52.

Galatians 3:8. "And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed."] That saying or promise implies that the nations shall be justified by faith two ways. 1. As it means that they shall be blessed and so justified "in" the great seed of Abraham, or by being "in" him, or united to him, which is "by faith," which is no other than the active union of the soul to him. 2. It is by their having the faith of Abraham, or such a faith as he had, spoken of here in the Galatians 3:6, that they are in Abraham, or become "the children of Abraham," as is observed in the foregoing verse. "Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham." And so by being his children, they are blessed in or blessed with him, as it follows in the next verse. "So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham."

Galatians 3:13. "Being made a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone that hangeth on a tree."] The place is Deuteronomy 21:23. "He that is hanged is accursed of God." In the Hebrewתָּלוּי אֱלהִים קִלְלַת it is, "is the curse of God." See SSS on Deuteronomy 21:22–23.Synopsis Criticorum, I, Pt. 1, cols. 829–31.

Galatians 3:14. "The promise of the Spirit."] The Spirit from time to time was promised of old by the Prophets as the great privilege of the happy gospel days which they foretold, but this promise was made to the seed or children

-- 1081 --

of Israel and Abraham. See Isaiah 44:2–3. "Fear not, O Jacob, my servant, and thou Jesurun, whom I have chosen. For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground. I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring." Here the Prophet puts the spirit and the blessing together, as the Apostle does in this verse. Again in that great promise of the Spirit, Joel 2:28, "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Isaiah 59:20–21, "And the Redeemer shall come to Zion, and unto them that turn from transgression in Jacob, saith the Lord. As for me, this is my covenant with them, saith the Lord. My spirit that is upon thee, and my words which I have put in thy mouth, shall not depart out of thy mouth, nor out of the mouth of thy seed, nor out the mouth of thy seed's seed, saith the Lord, from henceforth and forever." So from time to time the great promises of the Spirit in other places in the Prophets are to God's people Israel, or Israel's and Abraham's posterity. Hence a being endowed by the Spirit is by the Apostle spoken of as an evidence of being "the sons of God," as Romans 8:14, and in and "of Abraham," in this chapter.

Galatians 3:15.] This verse Mr. Locke well paraphrases thus. "Brethren, this is a known and allowed rule in human affairs, that a promise or compact, though it be barely a man's covenant, yet if it be once ratified, so it must stand. Nobody can render it void, or make any alteration in it."Paraphrase and Notes on Galatians (3rd ed.), 21.

Galatians 3:16. "He saith [not], And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed."] The passage in Genesis here referred to is doubtless that, Genesis 22:17–18, "And thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies; and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," for the promise made to Abraham, that the Apostle is here speaking of, is that all the families of the earth should be blessed [Genesis 12:3]; and this is expressly predicated of his seed in anything that God says to Abraham nowhere else but there. And the "seed" that is there spoken of is spoken of in such a manner that it is most naturally understood not as a noun of multitude, or as containing a plurality, but only an individual, because the singular verb "possess," and the singular pronoun "his" is used. "Thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies," where the same seed is doubtless to be understood, as in the words immediately following, "and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." It is not usual in Scripture that a

-- 1082 --

singular pronoun is thus annexed to the word "seed" when it is a noun of multitude. And the seed of Abraham, in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed, is spoken of elsewhere in the Old Testament as a single person, as in Psalms 72:17. "His name shall be continued as long as the sun, and men shall be blessed in him." And the word "seed," as used in the Old Testament, is sometimes understood of a particular person. Thus Eve says on occasion of the birth of Seth, Genesis 4:25, "God hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew." So Hannah says, 1 Samuel 1:11, "If thou wilt give thine handmaid seed of man," as 'tis in the original,אֲנָשִׁים זֶרֵע לַאֲמָתךָ נָתַתָּה meaning a man-child. See note on Genesis 3:15.

See no. 421.This reference is a later addition. Works, 15, 500–501. See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 2, pp. 85–86.This reference is a later addition. Kidder defends Paul's stress on the singularity of the word "seed," as referring to Christ, against Jewish critics who argued that it should be taken as a collective. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 85–86.

Galatians 3:17–18.] See no. 422.Works, 15, 501.

Galatians 3:18.] See notes on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Galatians 3:19. "Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made."] "When God brought the Israelites out of Egypt, true religion was almost perished from the face of the earth. Men in all nations were greatly corrupted both in faith and manners. Hereupon God was pleased to choose to himself the house of Jacob, to be a peculiar treasure unto him above all people. And he revealed himself unto them, and gave them a law, to recall, and preserve them, from going after the heathens to learn their ways, 'until the seed should come,' and to shut them 'up unto the faith, which should afterwards be revealed' Galatians 3:23]." Shuckford's Connection, vol. 3, p. 134.Sacred and Prophane History (2nd ed.).

Galatians 3:20.] See no. 423.Works, 15, 501–3.

Galatians 3:21–23.] These verses might be paraphrased thus, by which the Apostle's reasoning in them will be understood: Is God's giving of the law to the children therefore any way contrary to or inconsistent with the

-- 1083 --

constitution he had before established with Abraham, that was by free promise? No, by no means. Indeed, if the law that had been given at Mt. [Sinai] could have given life, so that justifying the children of Israel could have been the real design of it, the children of Abraham would have been justified that way; and so it would have been inconsistent with the preceding constitution with Abraham. But this is not the case, for the design of the law was not to justify the children of Israel, but on the contrary to conclude 'em under, to prepare 'em by faith to receive, the promise made to Abraham, etc., and so was not a constitution inconsistent with the preceding gracious constitution with Abraham, but subordinate to it.

Galatians 3:28. "Neither bond nor free."] Here is probably reference to the distinction that was made between bond and free in Abraham's family, where the son of the bondwoman might not be heir with the son of the free woman.

"Neither male nor female." Here is probably reference to the distinction made between male and female in circumcision, which was not made in Christian baptism, spoken of in the preceding verse, and the distinction made between male and female in the temple worship, which the males only were required to attend, whereas there is no distinction in Christian assemblies.

Galatians 4:3. "Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements" (or rudiments) "of the world."] "We were employed, in a way suited to the imperfect circumstances of an infant state, about worldly elements, or about those inferior things which are but like the letters of the alphabet." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 5, 60.

Galatians 4:6. "And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father."] "The learned Mr. SeldenJohn Selden (1584–1654), lawyer and orientalist, who authored De successionibus ad leges Ebraeorum in bona defunctorum (1695) cited by Doddridge. hath brought a very pertinent quotation from the Babylonian Gemara,The Babylonian Gemara contains commentary on the Mishna from Babylonian rabbinic academies from the third century through the fifth. to prove that it was not allowed to slaves to use the title of 'Abba' in addressing the master of the family to which he belonged, or the correspondent

-- 1084 --

title of 'Imma,' or mother, when speaking to the mistress of it." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 5, 61, n. b.

Galatians 4:9.] The law is here called "weak," because it could not give righteousness and life. See Romans 8:3 and Galatians 2:21. And it is called "beggarly," because it kept men in the poor estate of pupils from the possession of the inheritance. See Galatians 4:1–3.

Galatians 4:12. "For I am as ye are."] κἀγὼ ὠς ὑμεῖς, "I was as ye are." So Doddridge, in loc.Ibid., 64, n. g.

Galatians 4:25. "For this Agar is Mount Sinai."] This Mount Sinai and all other mountains in Arabia were called Hagar, for hagar is a word that in the language of the people of that country, or in the Arabic language, signifies "mountain." See Bedford, Scripture Chronology, p. 643, §88.

See note on this whole verse, in my answer to that question, "Whether any prophecies have respect to more events than one?," p. 9.This sentence is a later addition. The MS JE refers to has not been identified or located. However, in the "Table" to the "Miscellanies," under the entry "Prophecy," one subcategory is "respecting several events." JE lists "Miscellanies," nos. 251, 1227, 1287, 1316, and 1332b, as well as a "paper in the drawer." Perhaps this last item, which has also not been identified, is the document mentioned in this entry. See Works, 13, 143.

Dr. Doddridge observes that the name "Sarah"שָׂרָה signifies "a lady or princess," but "Hagar"The Arabic "hajar" means "stone." signifies "a rock," and that the Hagarenes, or descendants of Ishmael, were settled in the deserts of Arabia, in which Mt. Sinai was.This sentence is a later addition. Family Expositor, 5, 71–72.

Galatians 4:25–26.] Here are two Jerusalems spoken of. One is the literal Jerusalem, or the people of the Jews. And the spiritual Jerusalem, or the true church of God, this is called "Jerusalem which is above," for heaven is the proper city and dwelling place of the church. Here they have no abiding place, no city of their own, but are strangers and pilgrims. See Hebrews 12:22–24; Philippians 3:20, in the original; Hebrews 13:14; Ephesians 2:19.

Corol. If the spirits of just men departed were not in heaven, and so a great part of the church there, but either asleep, or in somewhere else, in Hades, 'tis not probable that the church would be called "Jerusalem which is above."

-- 1085 --

"Jerusalem which is above is free." Alluding to the freedom of the city of Rome, and of all that had the privileges of the city.This paragraph is a later addition.

Galatians 4:27. "Rejoice, thou barren."] Sarah had long been barren.

Galatians 5:2. "Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised" (as yielding to them who say that without it "ye cannot be saved"; see Acts 15:1), "Christ shall profit you nothing."] 'Tis a trusting in circumcision for salvation that the Apostle speaks of as being fatal, as is most evident, for he, in the Galatians 6:15, and often elsewhere, expressly declares that a being circumcised is nothing. So a "not being circumcised" is nothing, of no avail, and so neither of them to be trusted in.

Galatians 5:2–4.] See "Miscellanies," no. 637, Arg. 3.Works, 18, 166–69.

Galatians 5:6. "Worketh by love."] See Hebrews 6:10.

Galatians 5:17. "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh."] By this, with the context, it seemsJE deleted "evident." that grace in the heart is no other than the Spirit of God dwelling in the heart, and becoming a principle of life and action there, acting and exerting its nature in the exercise of man's faculties, for: 1. By the Spirit here spoken of, that lusteth "against the flesh," seems plainly to be meant grace in the heart, or the gracious nature in man, or man's regenerate and renewed part, which is opposite to the flesh or to the corrupt part, for that by the flesh is meant the corrupt nature is most evident by the Galatians 5:19–21, and Romans 7:5, Romans 7:19. By the Spirit therefore is doubtless meant the spiritual or gracious nature that is begun in man in his regeneration. Doubtless by the flesh and Spirit, that the Apostle says lust one against another, he means the same as by the law of the members and law of the mind that, he says, war one against another, in the Romans 7:23, which is further evident in that the Apostle there, in the continuation of the discourse of the same things, he uses these very terms of flesh and Spirit, as in the beginning of the Romans 8, where he speaks of the flesh and Spirit so much after the same manner as in this context, as may be seen by comparison, that 'tis most evident that he means the very same things.

-- 1086 --

2. The Spirit spoken of here and in other parallel texts, as signifying the gracious or holy nature in the regenerate, is the Spirit of God.
