For if this and the next verse be compared with Habakkuk 2:3–4, it will be exceeding manifest that the Apostle refers to what is there said, where God says by the Prophet, "The vision is for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it, because it will surely come, it will not tarry. Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him, but the just shall live by his faith." The thing that it is there said will come and not tarry is God's people's deliverance from the oppression of their enemies, especially from the Babylonish captivity, as appears by the context.

Hebrews 10:38. "Now the just shall live by faith; but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him."] This whole verse is a quotation of or reference

-- 1156 --

to Habakkuk 2:4, "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him, but the just shall live by his faith." "We render the phrase in Habakkuk, 'lifted up.' And it is observable, that the alteration of a single letterעפלה to עפל changes the reading into this sense, in which the Seventy have taken it." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 100, n. k.

Hebrews 11:1.] See no. 107.Works, 15, 81. The word ὑπόστασις here used signifies "confidence" in 2 Corinthians 9:4, and 2 Corinthians 11:17, and Hebrews 3:14. Concerning the meaning of the word "substance," or ὑπόστασις, in this, see Owen, in loc., pp. 3–5, at places marked in the margin.This sentence and the preceding sentence are later additions. The term ὑπόστασις, according to Owen, rendered "substance," refers more properly to a "real subsistence (of nature)… in contradiction unto appearing Phantasms." The result is confidence without fear in the believer who is the subject of justifying faith, which is the saving faith of the elect. The "things hoped for" are "all things of present Grace and future Glory" promised by God. They have real subsistence for the person of faith (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 11:3.] See Owen, in loc., p. 12 and p. 14, at places marked in the margin.Owen asserts the instrumental role faith plays in assuring believers that the world was created "out of nothing, which is contrary to the most received Principle of Natural Reason," i.e. that "nothing comes of nothing." The believer gains this understanding by assent to divine revelation in the word of God. Owen denies any "preexisting material Cause" involved with creation, identifying the power of God as the only "efficient Cause," responsible first for producing the chaotic mass of substance out of nothing, and men framing all things in beauty and order (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 11:4.] See note on Genesis 4:3–4, "Scripture," no. 453.Works, 15, 533–34.

"And by it he being dead yet speaketh."JE applied this text to David Brainerd in the Appendix to the "memoirs of his life" derived from his "private writings." He hoped that Brainerd might "still be as it were the instrument of much promoting the interest of religion in this world." See Works, 7, 540. See Owen, in loc., pp. 20–21, at the place marked in the margin.Owen ascribes multiple consequences to the declaration concerning the faith of Abel, who "yet speaketh" after his death. Many interpreters point to Abel's fame and reputation in later generations as the meaning. Owen, however, maintains that the Apostle intends that the blood of Abel speaks from the ground. "There is a Voice in all innocent blood shed by violence." Thus murders are avenged "sooner or later by God himself." This statement is also a pledge that God, "in due time," will punish "murderous Persecutors" of the church, which is "instructive unto Faith and Patience in suffering" for believers (Hebrews 11–13). Agreeable to the Doctor's exposition is Revelation 6:9–11 and Revelation 8:3–4.

-- 1157 --

Hebrews 11:5–6. "Before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God, for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."] The Apostle refers to that testimony which the Scripture gives of Enoch, that he "walked with God" [Genesis 5:22], which expression implies friendship, and friendly intercourse, and mutual complacence. For how can two walk together, except they be agreed? And therefore the Apostle might well say, that "he had this testimony, that he pleased God." And he most properly observes that there is no pleasing God in this sense, no maintaining friendship and mutually complacential intercourse, without believing that God is, and without believing "that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him," in the sense explained in my distinct note on Hebrews 11:6. When the Apostle says, "he that cometh to God," he may be well understood to mean, "he that comes to him to walk with him." He unites himself to him in friendly complacential union and intercourse. Dr. Doddridge here says in his note, "Raphelius hath shown, that the original word προσερχόμενον is applied in the Greek classics, to coming to God by prayer; and it is used in Hebrews 10:1, Hebrews 10:22, and Hebrews 12:22–23, for approaching to God in any act of divine worship. He therefore justly observes, that it may here be taken in a larger sense, and refer to that steady course of piety and virtue which is implied in pleasing God, or walking with him."Family Expositor, 6, 105, n. h.

Hebrews 11:6. "He that cometh to God."] I.e. he that has real access, admittance, and acceptance, comes so as to be truly united to God, and walk with him. "Must believe that he is." I.e. "must believe that he is" as God, which implies his having supreme glory, all-sufficiency, and dominion, a believing those things concerning God which are implied in that name of God, I AM. "Diligently seek him." Seeking God in Scripture commonly implies trusting in God, or the exercise of true faith. The word is ἐκζητεῖν, which is a strong expression. And what the Apostle means seems to be "seeking him with the whole heart," as the phrase is, Psalms 119:2, seeking him in reality, in earnest, and with a true fervor of soul. See Poole's Synopsis, in loc., p. 1358, right column, d, place marked in margin.Synopsis Criticorum, IV (London, 1676), Pt. 2, col. 1358. "Must believe that he is a rewarder." I.e. that it is not in vain to seek him and trust in [him], that one may do it with safety and just confidence of success, and a firm persuasion that he is sufficient, faithful,

-- 1158 --

and ready to bestow the benefit we trust in him for. The wordμισθαποδοσία is used to signify success and benefit (Hebrews 10:35). There is forgiveness with God that he may be feared [Psalms 130:4]. He hath not said to the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain. Blessed are all they that trust in him.

Hebrews 11:7. "Noe… became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.] "He was pronounced by God a righteous person, though his character was not absolutely free from imperfections.… Bp. CumberlandRichard Cumberland (1631–1718), Bishop of Peterborough, author of Origines Gentium Antiquissimœ; or Attempts for Discovering the Times of the First Planting of Nations (London, 1724). observes, that Noah is the first to whom the name of 'righteous man' [Genesis 7:1] is applied in Scripture." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 106 and n. k.

Hebrews 11:10. "Looked for a city which hath foundations."] This is here said because tabernacles, mentioned in the foregoing verse, hath no foundations, and because 'tis a movable thing, and is designed for no settled abode, but is such as travelers are wont to lodge in, who are traveling through a strange country amongst a people they are disunited from, and that are inhospitable to them, and therefore don't lodge in their houses. But the "city that has foundations" is that wherein they shall dwell in a fixed manner as the proper citizens.

"For he looked for a city…"]JE deleted this unfinished entry.

Hebrews 11:14. "Declare plainly that they seek a country."] "The original word, πατρίδα, is very emphatical; it signifies as it were a native country, or country in which their father dwelt, and is opposed to that in which they were strangers and pilgrims." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 109, n. n.

Hebrews 11:16. "God is not ashamed to be called their God."] Note on Matthew 22:31–32, no. 379.Works, 15, 363–65.

Hebrews 11:21. "Leaning on the top of his staff."] See Numbers 21:18. The passage in Genesis here referred to seems to be Genesis 48:2, or probably those two passages, Genesis 47:31, and Genesis 48:2. See note on Genesis 47:31. See also note on Numbers 21:18.

-- 1159 --

"Leaning on the top of his staff." "This agrees with the Greek and Syriac translation of Genesis 47:31. And WolsiusJohann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), evangelical theologian and orientalist in Wittenberg, author of Curae philologicae et criticae in IV. SS. Evangelica et Actus apostolicos (1725). adds, that the Seventy always render the Hebrew word מִטָּה, 'a staff.' Mr. HalletJoseph Hallet (1691–1744), a Nonconformist minister, published A Paraphrase and Notes on the Hebrews 11-13 (1733). therefore, in a learned note upon this place, is of opinion that the Hebrew word signifies either a bed or a staff, and that our English translators too implicitly followed the modern Jews, and supposed it here to signify a bed, in opposition to the authority of the Seventy and of the Apostle." Doddridge, in loc.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 113, n. e.

Hebrews 11:23.] See Dr. Owen, in loc., pp. 106–108, at the places marked in the margin.Owen discusses the actions of Moses' parents when they saw that God had given the infant "a peculiarly gracious promising Countenance." They were motivated in faith to take steps to preserve Moses from the king's edict that all male Hebrew children be drowned. They trusted God's promise to preserve and deliver the Hebrew nation. Though they had no special revelation concerning the matter, when they placed the child Moses in the ark in the river, they were committing him to the providence of God (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 11:24.] See note on Exodus 2:11.

Hebrews 11:27. "He endured."] In the original, ἐκαρτέρησεν, which Dr. Doddridge translates, "he was strengthened."Family Expositor, 6, 115.

Hebrews 11:35. "Women received their dead raised to life again; and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection."] A resurrection is twice mentioned in the verse. Once in the first part of it, "women received their dead raised to life" (or "by a resurrection," ἐκ ἀναστάσεως), and then again in the latter part of the verse, "that they might obtain a better resurrection," κρείττονος ἀναστάσεως. The resurrection last mentioned is said to be "better" than the other.

Hebrews 11:37. "They were tempted."] I.e. in the midst of their torments their cruel persecutors added earnest solicitations, persuasions, fair tempting promises, and the like, if they would desert the cause they suffered for, which was verified in Antiochus Epiphanes.

-- 1160 --

Hebrews 12:1. "Cloud of witnesses."] Isaiah 60:8, "Who are these that fly as a cloud?" A multitude is compared to a cloud (Ezekiel 38:9). An heavenly multitude is especially fitly represented by a cloud, for clouds have their place in heaven. They are dark in themselves, but receive brightness and glory from the sun. So is it with the saints in heaven. See note on Psalms 68, no. 319, the third paragraph of that note.Works, 15, 299–300.

"Wherefore being compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run." As when the Apostle speaks of Christians' running the race set before 'em, he undoubtedly alludes to the races in the Olympic games, so when he speaks of their being "compassed about with a great cloud of witnesses" in running this race, he evidently alludes to the vast crowd of spectators that stood about the racers in the Olympic games. Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it thus. "In the meantime we may consider this glorious triumphant assembly as looking down from the peaceful and blessed state at which many of them are already arrived, observing the manner in which we endeavor to follow them,… who surround us on every side in a vast innumerable assembly, the spectators of our trial, let us lay aside, etc." And in his notes he says, "The word 'witnesses' certainly alludes to the Olympic race, where persons were appointed to stand at the mark, to observe who first came thither, and give evidence in favor of the conqueror, upon whom therefore a crown was bestowed, according to their testimony."This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 115–16 and n. n.

Hebrews 12:2. "Looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith," etc.] The Apostle, having mentioned a great number of eminent examples of faith from the beginning of the world down to Christ, at last comes to him who is the "author and finisher of faith," of that faith of which those Old Testament saints had given such eminent examples of. In the preceding verse, the Apostle recommends perseverance as the fruit of faith. Being the author of faith respects the giving of faith at conversion; being the finisher of faith respects the upholding faith unto final perseverance, for believers "are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation" [1 Peter 1:5]. This perseverance of faith the Apostle had been recommending in the end of the Hebrews 10, and to enforce his exhortation brought in those examples, that "cloud of witnesses" in the Hebrews 11, spoken of in the foregoing verse. The words in the original translated "author and finisher," or ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν, the first word is

-- 1161 --

from ἀρχή, the "beginning," and the latter from τελειωτής, the "end." Christ is the beginner and finisher, the author and end of our faith. He is the finisher or consummator of our faith, not only as the completing effect, but as the object and end that terminates our faith, and in whom it is completed in what it seeks and aims at.

Hebrews 12:17.] The word "inherit" is used because the blessing was what would have descended to him from his father Isaac as the inheritance that belonged to the first-born, if he had not "sold his birthright" Hebrews 12:16]. He otherwise would have been Isaac's heir in those special promises made to him and to his seed, that he would give him the land of Canaan, and that in him and in his seed all the families of the earth should be blessed. Isaac thought that this blessing most properly descended to him, being the first-born, and therefore directed him to go and get him some venison that he might bless him before he died [Genesis 27:3–4].

Hebrews 12:18. "For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched," etc.] This comes in as an enforcement of the precept that the Apostle had given to the Christians, to look diligently, or take earnest heed, that their assemblies and worship was not polluted and profaned by such persons as Esau. For he would here teach us that Christians had more need to take heed to themselves now under the gospel, that they did not profanely and irreverently draw near to God in his worship, than the children of Israel had at Mt. Sinai, where God appeared so terribly, and where such strictness was required, and great care in the congregation in their waiting on God, lest for their error they should be immediately destroyed (See Hebrews 12:20.). That this is the drift of the Apostle appears by the application he makes of what is here said, Hebrews 12:25–29.

Hebrews 12:21.] See no. 135.Works, 15, 88. "Moses said." I.e. he wrote this of himself, as he gives an account in the Exodus 19:16, "that all the people that was in the camp trembled," including himself, for he was then in the camp. This is something after the same manner as God is said, in the Hebrews 1:8, to say unto his Son, "Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever," etc., i.e. David, speaking by the spirit of God, said so of the Son.This and the preceding two sentences are a later addition.

Or the Apostle may perhaps more probably have reference to what

-- 1162 --

Moses says in Deuteronomy 9:18–19. "And I fell down before the Lord, as at the first," etc.… "For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure, wherewith the Lord was wroth against you to destroy." 'Tis pretty manifest by the context of that place that Mt. Sinai burnt with fire afresh on that occasion of the children of Israel's making the golden calf (See Deuteronomy 9:15.), and probably in a very terrible manner, and that so terrible was the sight that Moses did exceedingly fear and quake, and that this is the fear Moses speaks of, Deuteronomy 9:19, and which the Apostle here has reference to.This paragraph is a later addition.

Hebrews 12:22–24. "But ye are come unto Mount Zion," etc.] "There seems to be throughout this whole period a reference to the manifestation God made of himself upon Mt. Zion, as being milder than that upon Mt. Sinai. And the heavenly society with which Christians are incorporated is considered as resembling the former (that is, Mt. Zion), in those circumstances in which it was more amiable than the latter. Zion was the city of God. In the temple, which stood there, cherubim were the ornaments of the walls, both in the holy and most holy place, to signify the presence of angels. There was a general assembly and congregation of the priests, which were substituted instead of the first-born, of whose name catalogues were kept. There was God, as the supreme judge of controversies, givingMS: "giveth." forth his oracles. The high priest was mediator between God and Israel (Compare Luke 1:8–10.), and the blood of sprinkling was daily used." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 137, n. h.

Hebrews 12:23. "And church of the first-born."] "The priests of God, the denizens of that city, and ministers of God's temple there.… Saints are called the first-born, because under the law the first-born were peculiarly appropriated to God, and heirs of a double honor and inheritance." Doddridge, in loc.Ibid., 137 and n. k. See note on Hebrews 12:22–24.

"To the spirits of just men made perfect." There are two things that evidence that 'tis the saints in their separate state the Apostle means. First, that he says "the spirits of just men." Why does he speak of the spirits distinctly? 2. That they are saints "made perfect." The saints ben't reckoned to be perfected till dead. Christ, when speaking of his death, Luke 13:32, says, "The third day I shall be perfected," the same word in the

-- 1163 --

original.τελειόω. So Revelation 6:11. The saints are said to "be fulfilled" when dead. 3. That these spirits are spoken as being in Mt. Sion Hebrews 12:22], by which the Apostle means heaven, as is evident by [the] Hebrews 12:25. See note.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. 4. The Apostle probably is led to mention these the rather from his having so lately spoken so largely of the faith of the Old Testament saints, in [he preceding chapter, who, he observed, labored under great difficulties, had not obtained the promises, nor were perfected while alive, but were now made perfect, especially since Christ's ascension. See Hebrews 11:39–40.

"The first-born." See notes on Exodus 4:22.This paragraph and the following two are separate entries.

"Church of the first-born." The first-born in Israel were those that God claimed as he did the first fruits of the field. He challenged the first-born of men and beast as consecrated to himself. See Dr. Owen, in loc., pp. 262 and 263, places marked in the margin.Owen takes issue with commentators who equated "the church of the first-born" with the apostles, evangelists, and others in the early Christian church. Rather, he asserts, the reference points to "all Elect Believers," both Jews and Gentiles, gathered into one assembly. This insight was a gospel mystery hid from the Jews under the institutions of the law in the Old Testament (Hebrews 11–13).

"And to God the judge of all." This in a special manner is the economical office which God the Father sustains in the society here spoken of, consisting of God and Christ, saints and angels.

Hebrews 12:24. "And to the blood of sprinkling, that speaks better things than the blood of Abel."] The blood of Abel brought great guilt; the blood of Christ removes it. The blood of Abel cried for vengeance; the blood of [Christ] cries for the removing of vengeance, and the exercise of mercy. The blood of Abel cried for vengeance on him that shed the blood. We all are as it were crucifiers and murderers of Christ. 'Tis our sins that have slain him, for he bore our sins. And the sin that is in all our hearts is of that nature and tendency to slay Christ, if there were opportunity for it; but this blood cries for the forgiveness of them that shed it, saying, as Christ said while his blood was shedding, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" [Luke 23:34]. The sin of the crucifying of Christ was a representative of the sin of all the elect. See "Miscellanies," no. 762.Works, 18, 407–9.

-- 1164 --

Hebrews 12:25–26. "See that ye refuse not him that speaketh."] Ye are come to Mt. Zion. "See that ye refuse not him that speaketh" from thence. There is a voice that speaks to us from both of these mountains forementioned, Mt. Sinai and Mt. Zion. "For if they escaped not who refused him who spake on earth," etc. He that spake at Mt. Sinai spake on earth; Sinai was an earthly mountain. He that speaks to us from Mt. Zion speaks from heaven, for this is not an earthly mountain, but a heavenly. 'Tis "the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:22); the Mt. Zion that Christians are come to is heaven. "Whose voice then shook the earth," etc. (Hebrews 12:26). The voice that spake on earth shook the earth, but the voice that speaks to us from heaven shakes both heaven and earth. Moses may perhaps be intended by him that spake on earth, for [he] spake from Mt. Sinai. He brought the law from thence, and Korah and his company be intended by them that refused [Numbers 16]. See "Miscellanies," no. 664a.Ibid., 201–2.

Hebrews 12:26–27.] See Bp. Kidder's Demonstration, Pt. 3, pp. 17–18.Kidder identifies the shaking of the heavens and the earth with the destruction of Jewish ritual and political institutions at the coming of the Messiah. Demonstration of the Messias (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 17–18. See note on Revelation 21:1.This reference is a later addition.

Hebrews 13:3. "As being yourselves also in the body."] Which implies that there is a state wherein souls exist out of the body. See 2 Corinthians 5:10.

Hebrews 13:7–8. "Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God, whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation."] The former part of this verse Dr. Doddridge translates thus, "Remember those, who having presided over you, have spoken to you the word of God," and says in his notes, "Our English version is far from being justifiable, 'Remember them who have the rule over you,' whereas they were now dead." And the rest of the verse he paraphrases thus. "Though all your intercourse with them for the present is cut off, do not however forget their instructions and examples; but be mindful of that faith which they taught and which they exercised. And let it be your great care to imitate them, 'considering the end of their conversation.' Reflect on the happy manner in which they quitted life, etc." And [he] observes in his note, that "Bp. LloydMS: "Wilkins." JE misread Doddridge who wrote, "Bishop Lloyd (Funeral Sermon for Bishop Wilkins, page 7, 8) thinks." John Wilkins (1614–72) was the Bishop of Chester. William Lloyd (1627–1717) was the Bishop of Peterborough. thinks this may

-- 1165 --

refer to James the Apostle, and to James, commonly called the first bishop of Jerusalem, both of which had been put to death there before this epistle was written." The next verse he renders thus: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever," i.e. "though your ministers die, Jesus Christ lives and remains the same, immutable."Family Expositor, 6, 145–46 and n. f.

Hebrews 13:9. "Be not carried about with diverse and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace, not with meats, which have not profited them which have been occupied therein."] The latter part of this verse Dr. Doddridge renders thus. "For it is a good thing that the heart be established in grace" (i.e. the grace of the gospel), "not in meats, etc."Ibid., 146–47.

Hebrews 13:9–10.] Owen, in loc., pp. 239–242, places marked.Owen discusses the rise of foreign doctrines that turn believers from the truth and work ruin in the church. Safety lies in adhering to the "Revelation of Divine Truth in the word of God." The contrast for the Apostle is between grace and meats. The Jews' concern with distinctions among meats (clean and unclean) and with the observance of Mosaic rites contrasts with "Grace as the only means to Establish… peace with God." Owen links foreign and false doctrines in his day with "the Papal church" and its "superstition" concerning "an unbloody Sacrifice of the Flesh and Blood of Christ… offered by Priests every Day" (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 13:11–12.] The letter of the law of the sin offering is that the bodies of the beasts offered shall be burnt "without the camp" [Leviticus 4:11–12]. But that was to be understood, according to the words, only during the continuance of the children of Israel in a camp in the wilderness. But after the children of Israel came to dwell in cities, and the sacrifices were offered at the temple, then they were to be burnt "without the gate."

Hebrews 13:12–14.] See no. 289.Works, 15, 248–49.

Hebrews 13:14. "For here we have no continuing city, but we seek one to come."] The Apostle gives this as the reason why he said, in the Hebrews 13:13, "Let us go forth to him without the camp," rather than "without the gate," for as he had said in the Hebrews 13:12, Christ "suffered without the gate." The church in this world is more like a camp, like the congregation in

-- 1166 --

the wilderness, moving to and fro, than like a people settled in a city as a fixed habitation.

Hebrews 13:15. "By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise."] Ephesians 5:20.

Hebrews 13:17.] Because "they watch for your souls, as those that must give an account," they must be faithful, must reprove sin wherever they see it, and must correct iniquity in the exercise of the discipline of God's house, without favor or fear. And therefore don't find fault with them for so doing, but "submit yourselves."

"That they may do it with joy, and not with grief." I.e. that they may perform that work of watching "for your souls," or that they may rule over you "with joy, and not with grief." Thus Dr. Doddridge understands it.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 6, 151.

-- 1167 --

James

James 1:10–12.] The rich man had reason to rejoice that he was "made low" by poverty of spirit, because that prepared him to part with all this outward glory, which surely would pass away "as the flower of the grass." And especially were those that were rich among Christians in those days liable to be deprived of all their worldly glory by reason of those persecutions that Christians were then exposed to. This trial of persecution is what seems here to be especially intended in the James 1:11 when the Apostle speaks of the sun's being "risen with a burning heat." This trial is compared to the same thing in Matthew 13:6. The Apostle, having spoken in the James 1:11 of the trial of persecution, therefore proceeds in the James 1:12 to speak of the blessedness of "the man that endureth temptation." Of those temptations he also speaks, James 1:2.

James 1:14. "Drawn away of his own lusts, and enticed."] ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος which Dr. Doddridge renders "allured and ensnared," and says the words have a peculiar "beauty and elegance, containing an allusion to the method of drawing fishes out of the water with a net,Doddridge reads "hook." concealed under the bait which they greedily devour."Family Expositor, 6, 170 and n. h.

James 1:16. "Do not err, my beloved brethren."] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "be not deceived," i.e. by your own lust, or by that bait alluded to in the foregoing verse. See note on that verse. Dr. Doddridge observes that in the Alexandrian manuscript,I.e. an early form of the Greek text of the New Testament. after μὴ is inserted οὖν, which makes the connection "more apparent."Family Expositor, 6, 170 and n. k.

James 1:17.] This verse has reference to what was said in the foregoing verses. In them it is asserted that evil is not from God. But here it is asserted that all good is from him.

"Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down

-- 1168 --

from the Father of lights," etc. The kind of gifts which the Apostle probably has respect to, that he calls perfect gifts, are what we call spiritual and saving gifts, or benefits. The word τέλειος is pretty often used in the New Testament to signify truly and absolutely good, that which appears good in the most perfect and complete view of things, and is found to be so on the most thorough trial and view of all circumstances, attendants, and consequences. So James 3:2, "The same is a perfect man." Matthew 19:21, "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell all." Romans 12:2, "That ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God." Philippians 3:15, "Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in anything ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you." The context confirms this sense. He is speaking of true thorough piety in opposition to that which is hypocritical, unstable, and temporary, and overthrown by temptations. See James 1:6, James 1:8, James 1:12–15. But here he shows the great difference between true grace and every perfect gift, and that temporary religion and virtue which comes to nothing. It is of divine original; it is from God not only as the author, but fountain, comes immediately from him, and is a communication of him, as light comes down from the sun, but only with this difference, that whereas the light of the sun has a shadow by turning, or by its revolution ceases, and is succeeded by darkness, this is a constant and everlasting light (So that this text is very parallel with Isaiah 60:20.), and the perfect gift, therefore abiding, and not temporary and overthrown by temptation, as the other sort before spoken of. It is said to be "from above," ἄνωθέν. Dr. Goodwin (first volume of his Works, p. 342) says, this "phrase is applied to none but to Christ, and to grace, in the whole Scripture."Works, I (London, 1681), Pt. 1. The following verse seems to confirm that the Apostle speaks of those gifts which are saving, divine, and supernatural, and belong to the new creation, that are wholly from God, of his mere sovereign gift and operation. "Of his own will begat he us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures" [James 1:18].This paragraph is a separate entry.

James 1:18. "Of his own will begot he us."] This is probably here mentioned after the preceding verse where the Apostle is speaking of the Father, because begetting is the proper act of a father.

James 1:19–21.] "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak."] "Guarding solicitously against every rash, and especially

-- 1169 --

every proud and dictatorial, expression; and slow to wrath." "It is well known that the Jewish doctors were apt to contend very fiercely about their different opinions." See James 3:1, James 3:13. James 1:20, "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." "Even where it may be most ready to assume the title of religious zeal, but on the contrary greatly obstructs the righteousness of God; instead of promoting the cause of true religion, it is a reproach to it, and a means of exciting the prejudices of mankind against it." James 1:21, "Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness" ("overflowing of malignity"), "and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls." "Laying aside all inward and outward filthiness, on the one hand, and all overflowing of malignity, on the other, compose yourselves with meekness, etc." "The engrafted word." "That word which is implanted in our minds by the influence of divine grace.… The version here given is undeniably justified by BosLambert Bos (1670–1717), author of Exercitationes philologicae, in quibus Novi Foederis local nonnulla ex auctoribus graecis illustrantur & exponuntur (1713). and Eisner,Jakob Eisner (1692–1750), author of Observationes sacrae in Novi Foederis libros, quibus plura illorum librorum loca ex auctoribus potissimum graecis & antiquitate exponuntur & illustrantur (1720–28). who illustrate this whole clause by some apposite and elegant quotations from the classics. The word of God is frequently compared to a seed or plant, particularly 1 Peter 1:23, 1 John 3:9, in which sense 'tis here said to be ἔμφυτος, engrafted or implanted in their minds." So Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 174–75 and nn. d. and f.

James 1:23–24.] As a man that looks "in a glass" beholds his own face no longer than just while the glass is before him, so those whose impressions and affections vanish as soon as they are gone from sermon have no sight of their own hearts, their own wants, and their own obligation or duty, no longer than while the glass of the word is before 'em, or while they are hearing of it. Men in the glass of the word may behold what they are, or what they ought. They have that image exhibited that is theirs, or that should be theirs.

James 1:25. "Law of liberty."] The Apostle has in this an eye to some that perverted the doctrine of Christian liberty, which the apostle Paul insists on, as they did his other doctrine of justification by faith alone, like the antinomians in these days. See 2 Peter 2:19. The law of liberty is the law of love, the love of God and man, called "the royal law" (James 2:8).This sentence is a later addition.

Galatians 5:18.This reference is a separate entry.

-- 1170 --

James 1:27. "Visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction."] By which is intended not merely to go to see them, but to visit them with kindness and help, as the expression is often used in Scripture.

"Pure religion and undefiled." "Archbishop Tillotson has justly observed, that there seems here to be an allusion to the excellence of a precious stone, which consists much in its being καθαρὰ καὶ ἀμίαντος, clear and without a flaw or cloud." Doddridge, in loc.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 177, n. k.

James 2:2. "A man with a gold ring."] χρυσοδακτύλιος. "Perhaps this compound word might have been rendered, 'having his fingers adorned with gold rings.' The learned AlbertAlbertus Magnus (d. 1280). hath observed, that those who valued themselves upon the richness and luxury of their dress, were accustomed to deck their fingers with a considerable number of costly and valuable rings, frequently wearing several upon one finger." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 180, n. c.

James 2:4. "And are become judges of evil thoughts."] Dr. Manton in his Exposition on James, p. 234, says that "from the running of the words in our translation, he should have guessed the sense to be this. That by these outward appearances of meanness and greatness in the world, they judged men's hearts. But," says he, "this κριταὶ διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν is to be taken in quite another sense. The meaning is, You judge altogether perversely, according to the rule of your own corrupt thoughts and intentions, in esteeming outward pomp above spiritual graces."Thomas Manton, Practical Commentary on James.

"Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?" Dr. Doddridge renders it, "'And distinguish not in yourselves,' i.e. according to the different characters of these two men, but only regard their outward appearance. 'You even become judges who reason ill.'" And in his notes, "'And distinguish not in yourselves,' καὶ οὐ διεκρίθητε ἐν ἐαυτοῖς. This I take to be the exact rendering of this clause, as the verb is of the middle signification, and that it should not be read as in our English version, with an interrogation. 'Judges who reason ill.' Beza'sTheodore Beza (1519–1605), Calvinist theologian, leader in the reform movement in Geneva, and editor of the New Testament. observation is a just one, that the phrase in the originalκριταὶ διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν. is a Hebraism, and is accordingly rendered by him, 'Judices male ratiocinantes.'" This agrees with Dr. Manton.Practical Commentary on James. See above.This paragraph is a separate entry.

-- 1171 --

James 2:5. "Hath not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith?"] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith," and says, "The ellipsis in these words of εἰς τὸ εἶναι or γινέσθαι is common, as Bos, and after him, Albert, hath observed."Family Expositor, 6, 181 and n. f.

James 2:8. "The royal law."] Probably so called because the law of love was by way of specialty the law of Christ, the king of the church. See Galatians 6:2, John 13:34 and John 15:12, 1 John 4:21.

James 2:13. "Mercy rejoiceth" (or, as it is in the margin,I.e. margin of the KJV. "glorieth") "against judgment."] I.e. mercy in us greatly tends to prevent it. It tends to prevent condemnation and punishment, and as it were overcomes judgment, agreeable to what the Apostle says in the following verses, of our being justified by works. Judgment or condemnation is the opposite to justification. So Daniel advised Nebuchadnezzar to prevent the judgment threatened to him [Daniel 4]. So when John the Baptist told the people that judgment was impending, that the axe was laid "at the root of the trees," and the people were awakened with fear and cried out, "What shall we do then?" he answereth, "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that has none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise" [Luke 3:9–11].

James 2:14–26.] The error of those whom the Apostle opposes, in what he here says about faith and works, consisted in three things. 1. They mistook the nature of justifying faith, and supposed that that mere assent of the understanding to doctrines [of] Christianity that were opposite to heathenish infidelity, such as that there is but "one God," etc. (James 2:19), was the faith the apostles meant when they said that we are justified by faith.

2. They did not understand the connection between justifying faith and works, and that the working nature of faith was the life and soul of it. When they heard that men are justified by faith alone, without the works of the law, they understood it that a man that was without works, or that had not works, might be justified by faith.

3. They did not distinguish between the first and second justification. The first justification, which is at conversion, is a man's becoming righteous, or his coming to have a righteousness belonging to him, or imputed to him. This is by faith alone. The second is at judgment, which is that by which a man is proved and declared righteous. This is by works, and not by faith only.

-- 1172 --

James 2:19.] See no. 52.Works, 15, 65.

James 2:20.] The apostle Paul, as well as James, held good works to be essential to true faith. See 1 Timothy 5:8.

James 2:21 ff.] By these verses it appears that there was the same way of salvation and the same conditions of acceptance with God as now under the new.

James 2:24.] Concerning a reconciliation of St. James and St. Paul, see "Miscellanies," no. 1130 [a].Ibid., 2, 508–509. See also Mr. Glas's Notes on Scripture-Texts, No. 2, p. 24.In a section entitled "Concerning Predestination; The Imputation of Sin and Righteousness; and, The Nature and Effects of Justifying Faith," Glas writes with reference to Abraham, "Thus we see, that as man who is justified or made just by faith, is justified or declared just by his works wherewith his faith works, and not by his believing without these works." Works (2nd ed.), III, 80–81. This sentence and each of the following two sentences are later additions. And Mr. Davies of Virginia, in his sermon on James 2:20.Samuel Davies' sermon on James 2:20 has not been located. On Davies (1723–61), an American Presbyterian minister, see George William Pilcher, Samuel Davies: Apostle of Dissent in Colonial Virginia (Knoxville, Univ. of Tennessee Press, 1971). See Pfaffius, pp. 497–500, and 540–44.Pfaff's discussion in Pt. II, ch. VII, entitled "De Justificatione, Adoptione et Libertate Christiana," features the figure of Abraham in his reconciliation of James and Paul. He writes, "Quod restat, notamus, exemplum Abrahami ad utramque justificationem tum eam, quae ex fide, tum eam, quae ex operibus contingit, probandam & quidem praeeuntibus Jacobo & Paulo utique adhiberi posse. Ubi enim Jacobus ex verbis: Credidit Abraham DEO & hoc imputatum ipsi fuit in justitiam justificationem ex operibus probat, cum fide ista, quam promissioni divinae Abraham adjecit, signum ipsius & effectum jungit, aitque, ex his omnibus Abrahamum a DEO pro justo declaratum fuisse. Ubi vero Paulus ex eodem loco probat, quod nonnisi fide Abraham corum DEO fuerit justificatus, innuit, uti ex Romans 4:10. patet, Abrahamum jam justificatum fuisse, antequam circumcideretur adeoque ex operibus caerimonialibus (ad quae quippe immediate hic Paul respicit,) haud justificatum fuisse" (Institutiones theologiae dogmaticae et moralis, p. 499). In ch. IX entitled "De Conversione, Poenitentia et Fide," Pfaff adds, "Et de hac justificatione, quae est justi corum DEO, & quae utique hac ratione ex fide & operibus simul fit, fit enim secundum veritatem, Apostolus Jacobus in epistolae suae capite secondo agit" (p. 541).

James 2:25.] Had Rahab the harlot said to the spies, "I believe God is yours, and Canaan yours, but dare not show you any kindness," her faith had been dead and unactive, and would not have justified her. But by receiving the spies, etc., she brought herself into the utmost peril of her life through her faith. She feared not the wrath of men, yea, of a king, the king of Jericho.

-- 1173 --

James 2:26.] The working acting nature of anything is the life of it; that which makes men call anything alive is because they observe it has an active nature in it. This working or acting nature in man is the spirit that he has in him. Therefore "as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without" a working nature "is dead also." This working nature, or active fruitful spirit that there is in faith, is love, as the apostle Paul tells us. Galatians 5:6, "For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith that worketh by love." Without love or charity, faith is nothing. 1 Corinthians 13:2, "And though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have no charity, I am nothing." So that love is included in the nature and essence of saving faith, yea, is the very life and soul of it, without which it is dead, as the body without the soul.

James 3:2. "If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body."] Agreeable to this are those words of Christ, "By thy words shall [thou] be justified, and by thy words shalt thou be condemned" [Matthew 12:37]; and those of the wise man, "Life and death are in the power of the tongue" [Proverbs 18:21]; and the Psalmist's making use of his bridling his tongue as a special argument of his sincerity (Psalms 17:3).

James 3:13–18.] How meekness and peaceableness is a great part of true wisdom, see Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 28:9, and Proverbs 19:11, and Proverbs 14:29; Ecclesiastes 7:8–9; Proverbs 14:16–18; Proverbs 20:3.

James 3:14. "But if ye have bitter envying."] Dr. Doddridge translates it "bitter zeal," which seems more agreeable to other things said in this epistle.Family Expositor, 6, 195. See notes on James 1:19–21.

James 3:18.] In these words the Apostle seems to have a plain reference to those words in Isaiah 32:17, "And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance forever." The former part of the verse declares what is the genuine exercise or work of righteousness, viz. peaceableness or peacemaking. The latter part expresses the effect, consequence, and reward of righteousness to those who have it, in this its genuine nature, and who exercise it, in this its genuine work.

-- 1174 --

James 4:5–6. "Lusteth to envy."] The words, according to Mr. Glas, ought to have been translated, "Do ye think that the Scripture saith in vain, The

-- 1175 --

spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth against envy? Wherefore it saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble," referring to the text in Proverbs 3:34, immediately cited. The Scripture in effect says, So there, in saying God resisteth the proud, etc. See Glas's Notes on Scripture-Texts, No. 5, pp. 7–8.Works (2nd ed.), III, 222.

James 4:6. "But he giveth more grace."] I.e. they to whom God has given some true grace, the grand note of which is humility, he rewardeth it with more grace, which is agreeable to what Christ says so often, To him that hath, shall be given [Matthew 13:12].

James 4:8. "Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you."] To him that hath "shall be given, and he shall have more abundance" [Matthew 13:12]. If your soul comes to God, and so you are near to him, he will come to you, and you shall be yet nearer, for "he gives more grace," as Hebrews 4:6.

James 4:11.] He that judgeth another don't act like "a doer of the law," or like one that is subject to law himself, but rather like a lawgiver and judge. He is not content to be a fellow servant. He refuses to own himself, so he casts off the yoke; he finds fault with it. He is not contented with it. In this sense he "speaks evil of the law, and judges the law." He withdraws himself from subjection to the law as a fellow servant, and so finds fault with it as his law, or a law by which he is obliged. He speaks by his actions; he expresses his dislike of it by his acting as a judge. He finds fault with the law as it makes God the only judge, and himself a fellow subject.

James 4:14. "It is even a vapor, that appeareth," etc.] Here seems to be an allusion to that vapor that appears in the breath (that is as it were man's life), sometimes while the breath is warm, but as soon as it is cool, vanishes away as it were in a moment. See Job 7:7, and Psalms 78:39, and "Images of Divine Things," no. 141.Works, 11, 100.

James 5:1–6.] Dr. Doddridge supposes that in these verses the Apostle has respect to those dreadful calamities on the Jewish nation which were then just at hand. The James 5:1 he translates, "Come now, ye rich men, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you," and says in his notes, "Josephus particularly observes how much the rich men suffered

-- 1176 --

by the Romans in the Jewish war. I have rendered ταλαιπωρίαις ταῖς ὲπερχομέναις, 'miseries which are coming upon you,' and I think it more agreeable to the original than our English version, ἐπερχομέναις being a participle of the present tense." "For the last days." "This phrase does not merely signify, for the time to come, but that period when the whole Jewish economy was to close, and when those awful judgments threatened in the Prophets to be poured out upon wicked men in the last days, are just coming (Acts 2:17, Hebrews 1:2, 2 Peter 3:3, and the like). Compare Matthew 24:33–34, 1 Corinthians 10:11." 1 Corinthians 10:5, "You have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter." Dr. Doddridge renders this thus. "Ye have pampered your hearts for a day of slaughter," i.e. as beasts fed for a day of slaughter, and observes, "That there are some who render ὡς ἐν ἡμέρα σφαγῆς 'as in a festival,' when many sacrifices are slain, but WolsiusJohann Christoph Wolf. observes that the word is always used in the Seventy to signify not a day of feasting, but of slaughter." 1 Corinthians 10:6, "Ye have condemned and killed the just." Dr. Doddridge renders it, "Ye have condemned and murdered the righteous one," supposing Christ especially intended by the righteous or just one.Family Expositor, 6, 204–6 and nn. b and c.

James 5:9. "Grudge [not] one against another."] "Justin MartyrJustin Martyr (c. 100–c. 165), an early Christian apologist. represents the Jewish converts as the worst sort of Christians, who were apt to be impatient of the Gentile yoke, and to retain their attachment to the views of a temporal kingdom." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 208, n. a.

James 5:12. "But above all things, swear not," etc.] "This the Jews were very apt to do upon trifling occasions." Doddridge, in loc.Ibid., 209, n. d.

James 5:16. "The effectual fervent prayer of the righteous man."] Dr. Doddridge translates it, "The prayer of a righteous man wrought by the energy of the Spirit," and says in his note, "The word ἐνεργουμένη, as Bp. HopkinsEzekiel Hopkins (1634–90), Bishop of London-Derry in Ireland, whose writings were collected in The works of the Right Reverend and Learned Ezekiel Hopkins (London, 1701). observes, seems to imply this sense."Family Expositor, 6, 211 and n. g.

James 5:17. "Three years and six months."] See Manton on James, p. 605.Manton draws on a variety of commentators to reconcile the time reference here and in Luke 4:25 with that in 1 Kings 18:1 (Practical Commentary on James).

-- 1177 --

I Peter

1 Peter 1:2–8, 1 Peter 1:13.] No. 264.Works, 15, 210–11.

1 Peter 1:3.] See sermon on the verse, the exposition of the text.JE deleted this entry. This undated sermon on the resurrection of Christ (no. 104, spring-fall 1729), is not extant, but is cited in "Miscellanies," no. 409. See Works, 13, 470; 2, 548.

"Hath begotten us." 'Tis probable that the Apostle uses this expression the rather because he was speaking of the work of God the Father as agreeing with his paternity. Begetting is the proper act of a father.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 Peter 1:4. "To an inheritance," etc.] This is probably here mentioned because those that the Apostle wrote this epistle to were strangers scattered abroad (1 Peter 1:1), out of their own land, the land of Canaan, not possessing that earthly inheritance of old promised to Israel, and cast out by their brethren according to the flesh for being Christians. See Dr. Goodwin's Works, vol. 1, p. 44.(London, 1681), I, Pt. 1.

1 Peter 1:9. "Even the salvation of your souls."] The salvation of the soul's being so often mentioned distinctly as here…JE marked this unfinished entry with two small "x's."

1 Peter 1:10–12. "Of which salvation the prophets," etc.] It is probable that the Apostle, in what he says in these verses, has a special respect to the prophet Daniel, and particular[ly] to what is said, Daniel 9:23–24 ff. And in that expression, "Unto whom it was revealed, that not unto themselves," etc., 'tis probable he has an eye to Daniel 12:9, Daniel 12:13.

1 Peter 1:14. "As obedient children."] In the Greek, τέκνα ὑπακοῆς, "children of obedience." The word ὑπακοῆ is often in the New Testament put for that compliance and yielding to the gospel that appertains to true faith. So it is in two other verses in this chapter, as 1 Peter 1:2 and 1 Peter 1:22, and in other parts of the New Testament, as Romans 1:5, and Romans 15:18, and Romans 16:26, II Cor.

-- 1178 --

1 Peter 10:5, and other places, τέκνα ὑπακοῆς, "children of obedience," are in the language of the apostles opposite to υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας "children of disobedience" (Ephesians 5:6). These two sorts of persons are spoken of together, and set in opposition one to another, in the 1 Peter 4:17. "And if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?" And again, 1 Peter 2:7–8, "Unto you therefore which believe he is precious, but unto them which be disobedient," etc.

1 Peter 2:1–2.] Lay "aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and evil speaking," and thereby become "as newborn babes" or little children, agreeable to Matthew 18. And then as such, "desire the sincere," or rational, "milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby."

1 Peter 2:2. "As newborn babes."] Referring to what had been said in the 1 Peter 1:23. "Desire the sincere milk of the word." Referring to what was said, in the 1 Peter 2:23–25, of "the word of God," its being the incorruptible seed, etc. It is not only the seed by which the newborn babe is begotten, but the milk by which it is nourished.

"Sincere milk." ἄδολον, "without guile," i.e. not counterfeited, unsophisticated, genuine, and unadulterated.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Peter 2:3. "If so be ye have tasted."] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "Since ye have tasted," and says, "This is the proper rendering of εἴπερ, and not, according to our translation, 'If so be.'"Family Expositor, 6, 235 and n. b.

1 Peter 2:5. "Acceptable to God by Jesus Christ."] See note on Colossians 3:17.

1 Peter 2:7–8.] See "Scripture," no. 480.Works, 15, 577–78.

1 Peter 2:8.] See Taylor's Key, pp. 39c ff.Taylor criticizes the KJV translation of this passage, suggesting that the Apostle's proper sense is restored by placing a period after "offence" and then beginning a new sentence that reads, "They stumble at the word," etc. (Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 39).

1 Peter 3:7. "Giving honor," etc.] A weak vessel must be taken more care of, and more tenderly used than another. The stronger must give honor to the weaker in respect of service; the weaker has the greater need of being

-- 1179 --

served, needs to have more done for it. As the Apostle says with respect to the members of the body, "God has so tempered the body together," that "we bestow more abundant honor" upon those members that seem to be more feeble by taking more care of them, and causes the stronger and more active parts to serve them (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).

1 Peter 3:18.] Christ suffered, or was "put to death in the flesh," "that he might bring us to God," or that we might die as pertaining to the flesh, and "live according to God," as the expression is, 1 Peter 4:6.

1 Peter 3:19.] By the same Spirit by which Christ himself was quickened, he strove with the men of the old world to bring them to a spiritual resurrection, or to "live according to God," as 1 Peter 4:6. This resurrection Spirit strove to bring them to condemn and judge themselves, to judge and condemn the corrupt part, that they might live to God, and escape that awful judgment of God, whereby they were slain and cast into the prison of hell. See 1 Peter 4:6. Here the Apostle, speaking of Christ's preaching to 'em by his Spirit, has reference to that expression in Genesis, "My spirit shall not always strive," etc. [Genesis 6:3], which is quoted in other words.

1 Peter 3:19–21.] The Apostle, bringing in these things as he does in this place, seems to signify that the destruction of God's visible church of old by the flood, and the wonderful preservation of Noah and his family, and the revival of the church afterwards from thence, is a type of the death and resurrection of Christ, as our baptism is. See next verse. By the flood, the old world was cleansed of its wicked inhabitants; so Christ, by his death, purged away our sins imputed to him, as 1 Peter 4:1. So we by baptism have our sin purged away, that we might live unto God.

"The like figure whereunto baptism doth now save us." This that follows [is] from Cudworth's Intellectual System, p. 328, where these words are cited from the Asclepian Dialogue.A Hermaic and Trismegistic text translated into Latin by Apuleius. For more, see Works, 23, 647, 649, 711. "When the world becomes thus degenerate, then the Lord and Father, the Supreme God and only Governor of the world, beholding the manners and deeds of men, by his will, which is his benignity, always resisting vice, and restoring things from their degeneracy, will either wash away the malignity of the world by water, or else consume it by fire, and restore it to its ancient form again."This paragraph is a separate entry. Part I (London, 1678).

-- 1180 --

1 Peter 3:20. "Saved by water."] This can be understood in no other sense than that water was the means of their salvation. That which was the instrument of the destruction of the old world was the instrument of the salvation of the church, for thereby it was saved from that deluge of wickedness that was likely to overflow it; but the water washed away that wickedness and filthiness, and delivered them. So the children of Israel were baptized in the Red Sea, and they were saved by water. The water washed away their wicked, filthy enemies that were ready to swallow 'em up, and set them at liberty (1 Corinthians 10:2).

1 Peter 4:6.] See no. 150.Works, 15, 93. See notes on Galatians 5:17. I.e. that they might be convicted, judged, and condemned as they are in themselves, or as they are naturally, or by mere human nature. For what men are by mere human nature without the spirit or without supernatural principles, they are said to [be] flesh, or "in the flesh." For mere human [nature] is often called flesh, and is also called the natural man, as that which is supernatural is the spirit. "They are judged according to men in the flesh," i.e. they are judged and condemned as they are and live according to mere, unassisted human nature, or those that are in flesh, and so escape the judgment of God spoken of in the foregoing verse; but they "live according to God in the spirit," by being according to God, or conformed to a divine supernatural principle. The old man is condemned and slain, but the new man lives to God, as the apostle Paul says, "If ye live after" or according "to the flesh, ye shall die; but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the flesh, ye shall live" [Romans 8:13]. The word "according" is used in the same sense that it [is] in Ephesians 4:22 and Ephesians 4:24.This sentence is a later addition. This verse is to be connected with the 1 Peter 4:1–4, which speak of our dying unto the flesh, as we are according to the flesh, and living spiritually and unto God. And it also has respect to what was said in the 1 Peter 3, especially 1 Peter 3:18–20. Preaching the gospel of old to the old world before the flood is here spoken of as parallel to the preaching of the gospel to men now, because as then, the end of the old world was at hand by the deluge; so now "the end of all things is at hand," as in the next verse, viz. 1 Peter 4:7, and also foregoing 1 Peter 4:5. The Apostle brings in these things about the antediluvians for that reason chiefly, because the state of the Jews at this day a little before the destruction of Jerusalem was very parallel with that of the old world at the time when the longsuffering of

-- 1181 --

God waited, and his Spirit was striving or preaching, while the ark was preparing.JE reworked this entry extensively.

1 Peter 4:7.] "Miscellanies," no. 842.Works, 20, 57–64.

1 Peter 4:14.] Called "the Spirit of glory" because the beauty, excellency, and happiness of Christians here, and their glory hereafter, is by the communion of this Spirit. The glory of God himself, his excellency and happiness, consists in the Spirit of God. This is the light by which the fountain of light shines, and by which, communicated and reflected, the saints shine. This is a suitable encouragement to them under the reproach that they suffered for the name of Christ. Glory is opposite to reproach and disgrace. That the Apostle, when he calls the Spirit of God "the Spirit of glory" means in this sense, is confirmed by the foregoing verse where he is speaking of the glory of Christ, and their glory and happiness in him, of which they had now the earnest and first fruits, in that they had the same Spirit now resting upon them which was "the Spirit of glory," or in partaking of which their future glory would consist.

"On their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified."JE deleted this last part of 1 Peter 4:14.

1 Peter 4:15. "As a busybody in other men's matters."] See Lardner's Credibility, vol. 1, pp. 425–26.Nathaniel Lardner explains the reference to a "busybody" by detailing Peter's intention a point to "very offensive conduct." He writes, "A meer prying into, or medling with the concerns of private families or particular persons would not have ranked with crimes that exposed the severest censure of the civil magistrate. The word, I think, intends one that affects the spection and direction of the affairs of other men: and in this place relates to the public affairs of other people" (The Credibility of the Gospel History: or, The Facts Occasionally mention'd in the New Testament; Confirmed by Passages of Ancient Authors… With an Appendix concerning the Time of Herod's Death (2 vols. London, John Chandler, 1727), I, 425–26.

1 Peter 5:4. "A crown of glory that fadeth not away."] Here is reference to the crowns or garlands given to conquerors in the Olympic games, and others on other occasions, in reward for extraordinary merit, or as betokening some high attainment, which crowns were made of leaves or flowers that quickly faded.

-- 1182 --

II Peter

2 Peter 1:1. "The righteousness of God and our Savior Jesus Christ."] The words in the original are τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος ῎Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ, and ought to have been rendered, as Mr. Hurrion observes, "the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ." Hurrion's Knowledge of Christ, and Him Crucified, p. 353, in the margin, this that follows. "Dei nostri et servatoris, τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος ita necesse est conjunctim legamus, quia unicus est articulus—itaque continet etiam hic locus manifestum divinitatis Christi testimonium. BezaTheodore Beza (1519–1605), a Calvinist theologian who translated the New Testament into Latin. in loc. τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος, ex Graeco apparet, haec duo de uno et eodem dici, non autem de duobus diversis ita scilicet ut vocabulum (Dei) intelligendum sit de patre, (servatoris) vero de Christo, sed utrumque de Christo dicitur, quoniam ante nomen Σωτῆτος abest articulus τοῦ. Piscator,Johannes Piscator (1546–1625) was professor of theology at Strassburg and author of Analysis logica septem epistolarum Apostolicarum, qua catholicæ appellari solent (London, 1593). Schol., in loc.The Hurrion citation, p. 353, n. e., reads, "So it is necessary that we read in conjunction, 'of our God and Savior,' τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος, because there is a single article—and so even this passage contains a manifest witness of the divinity of Christ. Beza, in loc. τοῦ θεοῦ ήμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος: from the Greek it appears that these two [nouns] are said about one and the same person, not, of course, about two different things, so that the noun (God) is to be understood about the Father, but (Savior) about Christ. But rather each is said about Christ, since before the name Σωτῆρος the article τοῦ is missing (Piscator, Schol., in loc.)."

The construction of the words here, where Christ is called "our God and Savior," is the very same as in 2 Peter 1:11, where he is called "our Lord and Savior." Here the words are τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος ῎Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ; there the words are τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος ῎Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ. And the words, according to Mr. Glas (Scripture Notes, No. 4, p. 14), instead of faith "through the righteousness," should have been rendered "in the righteousness," ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ.This paragraph is a later addition. Works (2nd ed.), III, 174–75. See also Dr. Doddridge, in loc.This reference is another later addition. Family Expositor, 6, 283–84.

2 Peter 1:3. "Hath called us unto glory and virtue."] διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀρετῆς, "by glory and virtue." "This is the proper rendering of διὰ, as several critics

-- 1183 --

have rightly observed. Dr. Whitby supposes these words to [be] an hen-diadys,I.e. an idea expressed by two nouns connected by "and." and understands them of the glorious and powerful effusion of the Spirit, ἀπετή may very properly be understood of that powerful energy, which God exerts on the human mind, which appeared in so extraordinary a manner in the apostolic age." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 284–85, n. c. These things are much confirmed by the first part of the verse: "According as his divine power hath given us all things that pertain unto life and godliness."

2 Peter 1:4.] The word "whereby" relates to those things that are given "that pertain to life and godliness," in the foregoing verse, viz. the merits, satisfaction, righteousness, of Christ, etc. 'Tis by means of these that room is made for the "great and precious promises" of the gospel.

2 Peter 1:5. "Add to your faith virtue."] "The word ἐπιχορηψήσατε properly signifies 'to lead up, as in a dance,' one of these virtues after another in a beautiful and majestic order." Doddridge.Ibid., 285, n. g.

2 Peter 1:10.] See no. 140.Works, 15, 90.

"Make your calling and election sure." 1 Corinthians 9:26.This reference is a separate entry.

2 Peter 1:11–21.] See no. 265.Works, 15, 212–18.

2 Peter 1:16. "But were eyewitnesses of his majesty."] See sermon on the words.JE deleted this entry. JE's sermon on 2 Peter 1:16, n. d. (no. 134, summer-fall 1729), with the doctrine, "That seeing the glory of Christ is what tends to assure the heart of the truth of the gospel" (MS, p. 3).

2 Peter 1:19. "A light that shines in a dark place."] Where 'tis night. "Until the day dawn, and the daystar shall arise in your hearts." When the night shall begin to cease, and the time comes on wherein you shall cease to be in a dark place.

2 Peter 1:20. "Private interpretation."] I.e. it is not men's speaking their own sense of things, or interpreting their own minds, but the mind of God.

-- 1184 --

That which is their sense is not always the sense or interpretation of Scripture. But that which was the sense of the Holy Ghost, the prophets did not always perceive the meaning of in their prophecies.

2 Peter 2:1. "Denying the Lord that bought them."] See "Miscellanies," no. 689, especially §6.Works, 18, 255–56.

2 Peter 2:16.] The ass's avoiding the sword of the angel while Balaam his master would rush on, and his speaking and rebuking Balaam [Numbers 22:21–31], seems to signify that wicked men are more sottish even than the brute creatures in rushing on upon the point of the sword of divine justice. Wicked men are in Scripture represented as more stupid than the brute creatures, and particularly than the ox and the ass (Isaiah 1:3). The Apostle seems to have an eye to this in this verse when he says, Balaam "was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet." God herein rebuked his madness, and signified that he was more mad and stupid than a dumb beast. Balaam's ass also testified against the madness of his rider another way as well, as by his reasoning with him and instructing him, viz. by his refusing to go forward against the angel's drawn sword, when yet Balaam went forward against God's command. Thus the ass rebuked his madness both by his speech and behavior. And it proved accordingly that Balaam, by going contrary to God's command, though not in cursing the people in words, yet bringing a curse upon them by his advice, viz. by teaching Barak to lay a stumbling block before them, as Revelation 2:14, he run himself on the sword of divine vengeance, and was slain by the children of Israel.

2 Peter 2:19. "For of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought into bondage."] The Apostle alludes to the law of nations, by which 'tis lawful to make slaves of those that are overcome and taken in war.See Kenneth P. Minkema, "Jonathan Edwards's Defense of Slavery," The Massachusetts Historical Review, 4 (2002), 23–59.

2 Peter 3:3–4. "Mockers… saying, Where is the promise of his coming?"] "Archbishop Tillotson explains this of the Carpocratians,Followers of Carpocrates, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher. a large sect of the Gnostics, who denied the resurrection of the dead, and the future judgment, and appeared quickly after the writing of this epistle." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 307, n. c.

-- 1185 --

2 Peter 3:6–7. "Whereby the world that then [was], being overflowed with water, perished (ἀπώλετο). But the heavens and earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition (ἀπωλείας) of ungodly men."] That it is here intended that that fire shall be for the everlasting final destruction of ungodly men is not only manifest by the words themselves of the 2 Peter 3:7, but is also manifest by the plain comparison of these two great and general destructions of the wicked inhabitants of this wicked world, one with the other, the destruction of the ungodly world by a deluge of water, and the far more dreadful and final, everlasting destruction of all the ungodly, impenitent inhabitants of the earth that ever have been or shall be by a deluge of fire. I might also observe how many ways 'tis evident that that destruction of the world by the flood was a type of the eternal destruction of the wicked by God's wrath, and particularly that which shall come upon them at Christ's coming to judgment. Both are prophesied under one by Enoch, and one is compared to the other several times by the apostle Peter in these two epistles (1 Peter 3:19–21, and 1 Peter 4:5–7). But 'tis most manifest by these verses that it was a type of the general conflagration. The burning of Sodom and the cities of the plain is also spoken of as a type of the eternal destruction of the wicked, but how evidently was it a type of the conflagration.

2 Peter 3:8. "One day," etc.] "This was, as many have observed, a proverbial expression among the Jews, to signify that no finite duration bears any proportion to the eternity of God. PlutarchPlutarch (46–120), a Greek biographer and moralist. has a passage exactly parallel to it in his Discourse on the Slowness of Divine Vengeance." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 309, n. f.

2 Peter 3:9.] Mr. Gill, in his fourth volume, against Whitby, pp. 28–29, cites a passage from Justin Martyr in these words. "God introduced Christ into heaven, after his resurrection from the dead, and detains him there until he has smitten his enemies the devils, and the number of them that are foreknown by him to be good and virtuous is completed, for whose sake he has not yet made the determined consummation. Which" (says Mr. Gill) "perfectly agrees with the doctrine of the apostle Peter, and gives light into the sense of his words in 2 Peter 3:9, where the same reason is given for the deferring of Christ's coming to judgment."JE cites the discussion of the English Baptist minister John Gill (1697–1771), "Of Predestination," which examines Daniel Whitby's use of ancient writers. In vol. 4 entitled The Cause of God and Truth. Being the Judgment of the Ancient Christian Church, or the Sense of the Christian Writers of the first Four Centuries after Christ, and before Austin, Concerning Predestination, Redemption, Original Sin, Free-Will, Efficacious Grace, The Perseverance of the Saints, And, the Case of the Heathens, Gill says that Justin Martyr asserted God's "eternal and universal prescience of future events" (p. 23), that God foreknows the saved and damned and prepares salvation for some and punishment for others (p. 26), and that the people of God are "the Elect" (p. 27). The general title for the volumes is The Cause of God and Truth: Being an Examination of the Principal Passages of Scripture Made Use of By the Arminians, in Favour of their Scheme, Particularly By Dr. Whitby, in his Discourse on the Five Points: In which the Arguments founded on the said Passages of Scripture, are answer'd; the Objections taken from them removed, and the genuine Sense of them given (4 vols. London, 1735–38).

-- 1186 --

2 Peter 3:15. "Even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given unto him, hath written unto you."] 'Tis Paul's epistle to the Hebrews that Peter refers to, for in that only had Paul directly written to them that Peter writes to. Peter writes to the Hebrews. His first epistle is directed to them, as appears by 1 Peter 1:1; and this second is directed to the same with the first, as appears by 2 Peter 3:1.

The passage in that epistle of Paul that Peter most probably refers to is that in Hebrews 10:34–36. See Bishop of London's Third Pastoral Letter, p. 41.Edmund Gibson (1669–1748), the Bishop of London, argues for the Pauline authorship of Hebrews, pointing to internal textual evidence, namely, the accent on the theme of the "just living by faith," and to parallels with other writings by the apostle Paul. The Bishop of London's Third Pastoral Letter to the People of his Diocese; Particularly, to those of the two great Cities of London and Westminster. Occasion'd by the Suggestions of Infidels against the Writings of the New Testament, consider'd as a Divine Rule of Faith and Manners (London, 1731).

"And account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation, even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given unto him, hath written unto you." Dr. Doddridge supposes that this epistle was written both to Christian Jews and Gentiles, as well as the former epistle, and that "the passage referred to is in his epistle to the Romans (Romans 2:4), where he testifies 'that the goodness of God leadeth to repentance.'"This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 312.

2 Peter 3:15–16.] See 1 Corinthians 15:11.This reference is sewn into the binding at the margin.

2 Peter 3:16. "As also in all his epistles."] By this it seems manifest that the epistles of the apostles, though written many of them to particular churches, were public things through the Christian church in general, even then presently after they were, for the apostle Peter here speaks of Paul's epistles not only as things that he was acquainted with, but they also to whom he wrote, though the apostle Paul wrote but one epistle to them, viz. that to the Hebrews.

-- 1187 --

I John

1 John 2:1. "An advocate."] "The word 'advocate' in our language commonly signifies one who is to plead for a person in a court of judicature. But Dr. Samuel HarrisSamuel Harris (1682–1733), a professor at Cambridge University. has taken great pains to show, that it properly signifies the same with 'patron' among the Romans, or עוֹוֵר in the Hebrew, a great person who used to patronize the cause of some of inferior rank, and who was also a sponsor for their good behavior. By this he imagines several scriptures may be illustrated, and particularly Isaiah 50:7–9, Job 29:12, Psalms 72:12, Job 33:23 ff. And in confirmation of this sentiment he brings some remarkable quotations from the ancients. Perhaps there is nothing that illustrates the matter more, than the residence of some eminent persons from distant provinces, in the courts of great princes or states, whose business it was constantly to negotiate with them the affairs of those whom they represented, to vindicate them from any unjust aspersions, and to advance their interest to the utmost of their power." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 329, n. a.

1 John 2:8. "Again, a new commandment I write to you, which thing is true in him and in you, because the darkness," etc.] I.e. this is true that 'tis "a new commandment" betwixt him and you, or as it is from him to you, for though it be no new duty, yet the revelation of it is new, for you before was ignorant of it, being in darkness. But now the darkness is past, and "the true light shines." The light therefore is new to you, and this duty as revealed by this light is new to you.

1 John 2:16. "The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life."] See Mastricht, p. 1158, at top.In Bk. 3, ch. 8, of Theologiae Moralis, Mastricht identifies the Johannine tripartite description of concupiscence with food and sexuality, external delights and pleasures, and the inclination toward glory and pomp respectively (Theoretico-Practica Theologia [Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715), p. 1158. See also notes on Genesis 3:6.

-- 1188 --

1 John 2:17. "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof."] I.e. the objects of "the lust thereof," the objects wherewith "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" 1 John 2:16], shall all pass away.

1 John 2:18. "It is the last time."] See "Scripture," no. 484.Works, 15, 581–82.

1 John 2:19. "Because they were not of us," etc.] As it was of Simon Magus, of whom we are told, Acts 8:13, that when others believed, he "believed also," but yet he was then "in the gall of bitterness, and bond of iniquity" Acts 8:23]; and he remained and not only became so, by his apostasy, as is evident by the manner of the apostle Peter's expressing himself.

1 John 2:22.] How the Pope doth what is said in this verse, see History of Popery, vol. 2, pp. 78–79.Henry Care declares the popes are the Antichrist because they deny that Jesus is the Christ, overthrowing through their lies both the person and offices of Christ. The doctrine of transubstantiation denies the truth of Christ's human nature by making the body of Christ lack "the Properties of a true Body." The popes oppose his prophetical office by inventing new doctrines necessary for salvation. They challenge his priestly office by setting up "innumerable other Intercessors, Advocates, and Mediators." They usurp the prerogatives of his kingly office by assuming titles and the jurisdiction that belong to Christ alone (History of Popery). Vol. 2 includes A Supplement, carrying on the History to the end of the Council of Trent. Containing a large Account of the Reformation, and of the Persecution in Queen Mary's Reign.

"Some are of opinion, that this was written against Cerinthus,Cerinthus was a Gnostic heretic who flourished around 100. who in his doctrine separated Jesus from Christ, maintaining them to be two distinct persons, and denied him to be the Son of God. See Dr. Berriman's History of the Trinity.William Berriman (1688–1750), an Anglican divine who wrote An Historical Account of the Controversies that have been in the Church, concerning the Doctrine of the… Trinity: in Eight Sermons (London, 1725). Compare Dr. Whitby's preface to this epistle. Rev. BaxterRichard Baxter (1615–91), a Puritan minister and prolific author; his works include The Practical Works of the Late Reverend and Pious Mr. Richard Baxter (4 vols. London, 1707). also takes in the Simonians, Menandrians, and Carpocratians."These were heretical movements breaking out of early Christianity. Simon Magus, the sorcerer, was linked to the Simonians who were Gnostic as were the Menandrians and the followers of Carpocrates, a second-century Gnostic teacher. Doddridge.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 6, 338, n. e.

1 John 2:23. "He that acknowledgeth the Son hath the Father also."] "These words are generally printed in our version in italic characters,Editorial additions introduced by the translators printed in italics. but they

-- 1189 --

are to be found in so many good manuscripts, that I cannot but believe they made a part of the original, by whatever accident they were omitted in some early copy, to which it seems, too much regard has been paid. See MillMS: "Mills." John Mill (1645–1707), editor of the Greek New Testament published in 1707. and Wetstein,Jean Jacques Wetstein (1693–1754), a Dutch theologian and editor of the Greek New Testament. in loc." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 339, n. f.
