1 John 2:27. "But the same anointing teacheth you of all things."] Probably here is an allusion to ointment with which they used to anoint eyes that were defective and their sight impaired, to restore a clear sight to them, which is spoken of in the Revelation 3:18.

"And ye need not that any man teach you." See Jeremiah 31:34.This reference is a separate entry.

1 John 3:2–3. "We shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure."] 'Tis as much as to say, As the perfect sight of Christ hereafter will make the saints like him in perfect holiness and glory, so a true faith in Christ, and hope of this future blessedness, with that knowledge of Christ from whence this faith and hope arises, will make men like Christ now in universal and increasing holiness and purity, will cause in them inclinations and endeavors after progress in holiness, and a coming nearer to that sinless perfection that is in Christ. See 1 John 3:6, with note as follows.

1 John 3:3. "Every one that hath this hope in him."] I.e. "in God," or in Christ. The person spoken of in the foregoing and following words, ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ. The preposition ἐπί expresses not the relation of hope to the subject of it, but to its object, as in many places of the New Testament. It signifies the relation of faith, trust, and hope to their object, as Matthew 27:43, "He trusted in God"; Luke 11:22, "wherein he trusted"; Luke 18:9, "trusted in themselves"; Luke 24:25, "to believe on all the Prophets," etc.; Acts 9:42, "many believed in the Lord"; Acts 11:17, "who believed in the Lord"; Acts 16:31, "Believe on the Lord Jesus"; Romans 4:24, "believe on him"; Romans 9:33, "believeth on him"; Romans 10:11, "believeth on him"; Romans 15:12, "in him shall the Gentiles hope"; 2 Corinthians 1:9, "should not trust in ourselves, but in God"; 2 Corinthians 2:3, "confidence in you all"; 1 Timothy 1:16, "believe on him"; 1 Timothy 4:10, "hoped in the living God"; 1 Timothy 5:5, "hoped in God"; 1 Timothy 6:17, "hope not in uncertain

-- 1190 --

riches"; Hebrews 2:13, "trusting in him"; Hebrews 6:1, "of faith in God"; 1 Peter 2:6, "he that believeth on him"; 1 Peter 3:5, "hoped in God."

1 John 3:6. "Sinneth not."] See Psalms 119:3, John 8:34, Ezekiel 33:13, John 5:29.The last three references are later additions. See Romans 7:17, Romans 7:20; Galatians 5:19–21; 2 Chronicles 32:31.This sentence is a later addition. See 2 Chronicles 32:9 note.This reference is a later addition.

"Whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him." This latter part of the verse, as well as the former, is an irrefragable argument of the truth of the doctrine of perseverance, for there is no force nor truth in what the Apostle says, if he that has seen or known God may fall from grace. For doubtless if so, he that is fallen from grace may sin in any sense the Apostle can intend. See to the same purpose, 3 John 11. The argument from this place against the falling away of one that it is born again is confirmed by Ezekiel 33:12–13, Ezekiel 33:18, where sinning is put for turning away from righteousness.This paragraph is a later addition.

"Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not; whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, nor known him." See 2 Samuel 12:13. "And David said to Nathan, I have sinned against the Lord. And Nathan said unto David, The Lord also hath put away thy sin." By this it appears that though David was so holy a man, a man after God's own heart, yet his deed was properly called sin. Yea, it was mortal sin, sin that deserved death, as is implied. See also the terms used, Psalms 51:1–5, Psalms 51:10, Psalms 51:16. So Job was a man that God gloried in, that was a "perfect and an upright man, one that feared God and eschewed evil" [Job 1:1], or which is the same thing, one that sinned not. He held fast his integrity to the end, "and eschewed evil," and made good God's boast of eschewing evil under his temptations. And yet Elihu, who spake by inspiration, was in God's stead, and the forerunner of God, and did not answer as his three friends did, but spake that which was right, and was not reproved by God, charges him with sinning. Job 34:37, "For he addeth rebellion to his sin," etc. See also note on 2 Chronicles 32:31.

It won't do to go about to solve the argument from these instances with the doctrine of falling from grace. This verse that we are now upon won't allow of that. (See note on latter part of the verse.)

And if any should imagine that the kind of operation on the hearts of the saints in the new testament, which the apostle John calls a being born again, is some [thing] peculiar to them, and what God's people under the old testament were not the subjects of, and that regeneration is a

-- 1191 --

thing peculiar to new testament times (Though that may be easily disproved: The old testament saints were circumcised in heart, and had a right spirit renewed in them, etc., and therefore were born again.), yet we have a remarkable instance in one that was said to have followed Christ in the regeneration (See Matthew 19:27–28.), viz. Peter, who denied his Lord with oaths and curses. Yet he was one that had been born again, and therefore was one of them that Christ called little children, and one that he spoke of, Matthew 18:6. "Whoso shall offend one of these little ones that believe in me," which he called so on the account of their new birth, as is manifest by the foregoing words, particularly the Matthew 18:3 of the chapter. "Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of God," which is parallel with what Christ says to Nicodemus, "Verily I say unto you, Except a man be born again, he shall not see the kingdom of God" [John 3:3]. The apostle John says in the latter part of this verse, "Whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, nor known him," but Peter had seen and known his Lord. And therefore Christ says to him, "Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona, for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven." And Christ, in his prayer in the seventeenth of John, speaks of him, with other of his disciples, expressly as having seen and known, John 17:3, "This is eternal life, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent"; and then says in the John 17:6–8, "I have manifested thy name to the men which thou gavest me out of the world.… Now they have known that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee. For I have given unto them the words which thou gavest me, and they have received them, and have known surely that I came out from thee; and they have believed that thou didst send me." These last words show, by what the apostle John himself says in this epistle, that Peter was born of God. 1 John 5:1, "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God."

Ecclesiastes 7:20, "There is not a just man upon earth that doth good, and sinneth not." 1 Kings 8:46, "If they sin against thee (for there is no man that sinneth not), and thou be angry with them," etc. So 2 Chronicles 6:36. Proverbs 20:9, "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?" Job 9:30–31, "If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean, yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch; and mine own clothes shall abhor me." And Job 9:20, "If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me. If I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse." And Job 9:2–3, "But how should man be just with God? If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand." Psalms 19:12,

-- 1192 --

"Who can understand his errors? Cleanse thou me from secret faults." Psalms 130:3, "If thou, O Lord, shouldst mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?"

There is sin in the new testament saints as well as the old. The wise virgins "slumbered and slept" [Matthew 25:5]. Romans 7, The thing "that I hate, that I do" Romans 7:15]. Hebrews 12, "Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin that easily besets us" Hebrews 12:1]. James 3:2, "In many things we offend all." And this apostle John him [self], even in this very epistle, several times speaks of those that are born again as liable to sin. 'Tis by the new birth that they become as little children. But the Apostle says, 1 John 2:1, "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." And this is a confirmation that the Apostle has not only respect to sins that were committed before regeneration, in the verses immediately foregoing. "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us," etc. Again, it is by the new birth, by which Christians are born of God, and so are begotten of the same Father, that they are brethren; but the Apostle in this epistle speaks of the brethren as liable to sin. 1 John 5:16, "If any man see his brother sin a sin which is not unto death, he shall ask," etc. And yet in the next verse but one, he repeats that saying that we are upon, "We know that whosoever is born of God sinneth not," which confirms that what the Apostle means when he says, he "sinneth not," is not that [he] never is guilty of any sinful act. See of the sins and failings of God's children in the Common Place-Book to the Bible.The running head for ch. 13 in John Locke's A Common Place-Book to the Holy Bible: or, The Scripture's Sufficiency Practically Demonstrated. Wherein the Substance of Scripture, respecting Doctrine, Worship, and Manners, is reduced to its proper Head, Weighty Cases are resolved, Truths confirmed, and difficult Texts illustrated and explained (3rd ed. London, 1725), entitled "The Children of God themselves may be overtaken with Faults, and are not free from sinful Dispositions and Inclinations in this Life, and therefore may deserve to be chastised of God," reads "Of the Sins and Failings of God's Children" (pp. 91–97). Locke filled these pages with particular instances of sins by God's children recorded in the Bible.

Such expressions in Scripture as this in the text, "sinneth," and "sinneth not," are not always to be taken for committing a particular act of sin, as that in Job. "The drought and heat consume the snow waters: so doth the grave them that have sinned" [Job 24:19]. By "them that have sinned" is not intended them that are guilty of a particular act of sin.

That in Ephesians 2:3, "fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind," in the original is ποιοῦντες, "doing the desires of the flesh," i.e. making a trade of this. 1 Peter 3:11, "If thou wouldst see good days, eschew evil, and do good." 'Tis not meant that to do one good action is the way to be

-- 1193 --

happy, but a man's setting himself in such a course, making a practice and business of doing good.

How often is the wickedness of the kings of Israel and Judah expressed by that, that they "did evil in the sight of the Lord."This and the preceding paragraph are a separate later addition.

"Sinneth." The words of the next verse are a full confutation of them that from hence would argue sinless perfection. "He that doth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous." There is no more reason to understand the Apostle of committing only one act of sin by the expression "sinneth," or "committeth" or "doeth sin," than to understand of one single act of righteousness by the expression "doth righteousness," and so to understand the next verse thus: "He that doeth any righteousness at any time is righteous, even as God is righteous." Whereas by "doing righteousness" the Apostle plainly means practicing righteousness, or making that his practice in the course of his life. So there is equal reason, when he speaks here of "committing sin," to understand him of practicing sin, or making wickedness his trade or practice. See doing righteousness and committing sin again set in opposition to each other, in 1 Peter 3:10.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"Whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him."] The Apostle has still in his eye what he had said of the transforming influence and tendency of seeing Christ, in verses second and third.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 John 3:7. "Little children, let no man deceive you."] The Apostle still has respect to those seducers that he spoke of in the latter end of the foregoing chapter. He is here insisting on the same rule, whereby they might discern them that were wolves in sheep's clothing, that Christ gave (Matthew 7:15–16), and which this Apostle gave to Gaius, in his 3 John 11.

That true saints are not perfectly free from sin, see note on Psalms 143:2.This sentence is a later addition.

1 John 3:9.] All that can justly be understood by these expressions is that no sin is his practice. They that are "born of God" have forsaken sin; they have left off the practice of sinning. In the 1 John 3:7–8 the Apostle says, "He that doth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous; but he that committeth sin is of the devil." It seems to this naturally no more is signified by these expressions here than of he that "doth righteousness,"

-- 1194 --

and "he that committeth sin," than he that lives righteously and is of a righteous behavior, and he that lives wickedly and in sinful practices. And doubtless the same is signified by other expressions of the context. By committing of sin is here meant one that may be called a committer of sin, that is, whose practice is the commission of some sin. If it should be said of any person that such an one trades, he don't work in the field, or that such an one is a husbandman, he don't trade, we should understand no more by it than that one and not the other was his practice. So when it is said here that he that "is born of God" doth righteousness, he don't commit sin, what we are to understand by it is that he that is born of God makes doing righteousness his practice, and not the commission of sin. In this sense he cannot sin, because he is born of God. See an excellent exposition of this whole verse in Turretin, Tome 2, p. 660, §23.The sixteenth question in Turretin's fifteenth topic, De Vocatione el Fide, asks "Whether the true believer can ever totally or finally fall from faith?" Turretin's negative answer rests in part on his exposition of this passage in § XXIII. He declares that the true believer does not "commit sin," which is the situation when sin rules over the believer. This is true because the Holy Spirit remains in the believer permanently. The act of regeneration creates an "eternal bond." That does not mean the believer does not ever sin, but rather that sin does not rule over or control the individual (Institutio Theologiae Elencticae). See Dennison, ed., Institutes of Elenctic Theology, II, 593, 603–604. See no. 287.This reference and each of the following two are later additions. Works, 15, 247. See note on 1 John 3:10. See 1 John 3:6 note.

1 John 3:10. "He cannot sin."] By such expressions here is doubtless meant the same as by "turning aside to crooked ways" (Psalms 125:5), and by erring from God's statutes. Psalms 119:118, "Thou hast trodden down all them that err from thy statutes, for their deceit is falsehood." The expressions "sinneth," and "sinneth not," and doth righteousness," in this context are parallel with "committeth iniquity," and "doth that which is lawful and right," in the Ezekiel 18, and other places of that book. See many parallel instances of the use of such expressions in the Common Place-Book to the Holy Scripture under the head of "Departing from Sin," pp. 167 ff.Locke's ch. 16 in A Common Place-Book to the Holy Bible (3rd. ed.) is entitled "Of the Duty of Believers, especially such as would excel" (pp. 108–97). The section of this chapter to which JE refers is subtitled "Depart from Sin, and all Appearance of it; hate it, and avoid the Occasions of it: The reasons thereof." It contains manifold biblical examples of individuals avoiding sin and of scriptural exhortations to forsake evil (pp. 167–71). Sinning is used here in the same sense as in Ezekiel 33:12.This sentence is a later addition.

-- 1195 --

1 John 3:11. "This is the message that ye heard from the beginning."] I.e. early recommended, and the contrary condemned by God's dealings with Cain, as in the next verse.

1 John 3:13. "Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you."] As you need not, if you consider that early instance of enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent, mentioned in the preceding verse.

1 John 4.] Here in the former part of this chapter the Apostle gives the primitive Christian three rules or distinguishing marks whereby they should try the spirits.1 John 4:1 is the biblical text for JE's commencement address, The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God, delivered at Yale College in 1741. See Works, 4, 226. 1. The spirit's confessing that Jesus Christ was come in the flesh, or that he that had already appeared in the flesh, whose name was Jesus, and was born of the Virgin Mary, and was crucified, etc., was the Christ or anointed of God, come from God, was sent by him, and was a divine person. By the spirit's confessing this is not meant merely allowing or not contradicting it, or not dissuading the person that had the spirit from that belief of it that he had before, but positively declaring, testifying, and confirming this to his mind, for so the word "confess" is commonly used in Scripture, as John 9:22, John 12:42, and Acts 23:8. This is here mentioned as an infallible sign of a true spirit, for a false spirit would never confirm that great foundation of Christianity, especially at that day when it was so much disputed, and all the powers of the heathen world by Satan's influence were engaged against it. This is agreeable to the apostle Paul, who says "that no man can say that Jesus is Lord, but by the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 12:3). And it may be questionable whether a false spirit could reveal this truth to the mind, if he would.

2. Another mark or rule by which they were to try spirits was their causing those that had them to hearken and yield to the teaching of the apostles as in all things the truth of God and the rule of the Christian church. False spirits would never incline those that they influence to hearken and cleave to the apostles, but on the contrary would, if possible, draw them off from them, and set them against them (1 John 4:6). What the apostle John here teaches is agreeable to the words of the apostle Paul, Galatians 1:8–9, "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached, let him be accursed," etc.

3. Another mark is that the true spirit is a spirit of love, which no false spirit is (1 John 4:8–13). 'Tis evident that this last is also given as a distinguishing

-- 1196 --

mark of a true spirit by 1 John 4:13, and also because this whole discourse of the trial of spirits was introduced on occasion of the Apostle's observing, in the last verses of the 1 John 3, love's dwelling in us to be an evidence of the Spirit of God dwelling in us.

1 John 4:2–3. "Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God, and every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God."] Dr. Doddridge translates it thus, "Every spirit that confesseth Jesus Christ, who is come in the flesh, is of God; and every spirit that doth not confess Jesus Christ, who is come in the flesh, is not of God," and says, "So the words, ὅ ὁμολογεῖ ῎Ιησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα, may very well be rendered." Or it may signify confessing Christ as come in the flesh, or as incarnate, humbled, suffering, and crucified, for his humiliation, infirmities, trials, and sufferings were all by his taking on him flesh, the likeness of sinful flesh. And Christ being in the flesh, or being manifest in the flesh, according to Scripture phraseology, implies Christ's appearing in his low suffering state. And the word "confess," ὁμολογέω, as used in the Scripture, don't only ownMS: "owning." a thing to be true, but implies the sincere, respectful, andJE deleted "adoring." joyful respect, acknowledgment, honor, and praise of heart, mouth, and practice, and a being devoted to. See Hebrews 13:15. In Matthew 14:7, it signifies vowing or promising to God. It has a like signification in the Septuagint, Jeremiah 44:25.The LXX reads, "ποιήσομεν τὰς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν ἅς ὡμολογήσαμεν," translated "we shall perform our vows that we have vowed." In the LXX this text is Jeremiah 51:25. ὁμολογία is put for voluntary offering (Deuteronomy 12:6, Deuteronomy 12:17; Ezekiel 46:12; Amos 4:5), for avow (Leviticus 22:18, Jeremiah 44:25). ὁμόλόγως signifies "with freedom of heart" (Hosea 14:4).I.e. in LXX. ἐξομολογέω is used for praise, and extol, and the like (Romans 15:9), and to adore and glorify (Romans 14:11, Philippians 2:11), and abundantly in the Septuagint.In the "Catalogue" (MS, p. 14, no. 474), JE lists Abraham Trommius, Concordantiae Graecae Versionis Vulgo Dictae LXX Interpretum, as mentioned in the preface of Cruden, Complete Concordance. Trommius' volume would provide the kind of information found in this entry. There is no evidence that JE owned Trommius.

1 John 4:3.] How the Pope doth what is said in this verse, see History of Popery, vol. 2, pp. 78–79.Care details the variety of ways in which an "antithesis" exists between the pope and Christ, thereby identifying the pope as the Antichrist, an opinion he associates with "all the Reformed Divines" and the "most Learned of the Church of England" (History of Popery). For details of Care's argument, see the first note on 1 John 2:22.

-- 1197 --

1 John 4:17. "Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment; because as he is, so are we in this world."] Dr. Doddridge translates it thus. "Herein is love perfected in us that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, in that as he is, so are we in this world."Family Expositor, 6, 361–62. The meaning seems to be this. We, while in this world in our state of trial, shall be delivered from fear of that judgment which is to be when our trial is at an end, and shall have boldness to appear before our judge at that [day], in that we now, while in a state of trial, are in some good measure as he is, our judge is, as he is love, whose love appears in Christ's dying for us, when we had no love to him. So we have love in some good measure like his love, are ready to lay down our lives for Christ and for his church, and to labor and suffer for our enemies. In thus being conformed to God and Christ in our love, our love will be made perfect, and we shall have that perfect love that casts out fear, spoken of in the next verse. Or more briefly, thus: Herein is our love brought to be that perfect love that casts out fear, and gives boldness to appear before God at the day of judgment, that we in our spirit of love are here in our state of trial like unto him who is to be our judge.

The sense seems to be this: Our love is made perfect to give us boldness before him (i.e. before Christ) in another world, even by our being "in this world as he is." Like him in love, then "is our love made perfect," when we love one another as he hath loved us. For it, that love that the Apostle is speaking of in the preceding verse, "we have known and believed the love that God hath to us." And what that love is "that God hath to us," the Apostle had observed in the preceding verses, 1 John 4:9–10, viz. God's sending his Son into the world to die for us, and then says, 1 John 4:11, "Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought to love one another," i.e. we ought to love one another as God hath loved us, and as Christ hath loved us, and so we shall be as he was. And hereby we shall have assurance, as it follows, 1 John 4:13. "Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit," made us to be of the same temper with himself. And then the Apostle, in the 1 John 4:14 and 1 John 4:16, further insists on this love of God to us in giving his Son, and in this 1 John 4:17 repeatedly mentions our conformity to him in this love as what will give assurance, and observes particularly, that it will give "boldness at the day of judgment," when we appear before Christ, that

-- 1198 --

in this world we have been like him, and behaved ourselves as he behaved himself in the world.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 John 4:18. "There is no fear in love," etc.] Love is the evangelical, fear the legal, principle. Love is the spirit of adoption; servile fear is the spirit of bondage. The evangelical principle gives boldness, as it is said in the foregoing verse. Servile fear keeps at a distance, prevents boldness of access.

"Perfect love casts out fear," or much of a spirit of adoption casts out fear, because it naturally assures the person of his good estate, of his being a child of God, and loved and accepted of him, as the apostle Paul (Romans 8:15–16).

This Apostle had much experience of this heavenly principle of divine love. His writings show how his heart abounded with that grace; and he had particular experience of this tendency of love here spoken of, viz. to cast out fear, and to open the way for boldness and nearness of access. He had experience of it when he leaned on Jesus' bosom [John 13:23]. His great love opened the way to such freedom and boldness, and drew him to such nearness and intimacy.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 John 5:3.] Herein the obedience of natural man and a gracious obedience differs: that the one is merely forced—they are drove to it by fear; it is grievous to them—but the other obeys from love with delight; he is drawn to obedience. He obeys freely, and not merely as being forced; he obeys from choice and with cheerfulness. Such an obedience as that is an evidence of love to God.

1 John 5:8.] See "Treatise on Faith," p. 7, at the bottom.JE writes, "This is the third of the Three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit bears witness by discovering the divine glory and stamps of divinity that are in the gospel; the water bears witness, that is, the experience of the power of the gospel to purify and sanctify the heart witnesses the truth of it; and the blood bears witness by delivering the conscience from guilt" ("Notebook on Faith," Works, 21, 430).

1 John 5:20. "This is the true God and eternal life."] That the Apostle means that Jesus Christ, the person last spoken, is the true God and eternal life, is confirmed from 1 John 1:2.

-- 1199 --

II John

II John and III John.] THE SECOND AND THIRD EPISTLES OF JHON. The reason why such expressions are so often used in these epistles as have the word "truth" in them, as "whom I love in the truth," "all that have known the truth," "for the truth's sake," "walking in the truth," etc., is that at that time there was a great defection from the truth to gross heresies among those that formerly had professed the truth.

-- 1200 --

III John

3 John 1. "Gaius."] Dr. Doddridge thinks it probable that this was the same person with "Gaius of Corinth, who hospitably received the apostle Paul when he went forth to preach the gospel gratis," whom he calls his "host" (Romans 16:23).Family Expositor, 6, 391, n. a.

3 John 2. "I wish above all things that thou mayst prosper."] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus, "I pray that in every respect (περὶ πάντων) thou mayst prosper," and says in this Erasmus SchmidiusErasmus Schmidius (1570–1637) compiled a concordance of the Greek New Testament which was published in Wittenberg in 1638. agrees with him.Family Expositor, 6, 392, n. b.

3 John 5. "Dost faithfully."] I.e. dost in the exercise of a true Christian faith. The Apostle thus expresses his holy conversation, because all evangelical obedience, Christian holiness of life, is in the way of believing in Christ. All the fruits of Christian obedience are but the various exercises and expressions of faith.

3 John 5-6. "Beloved, thou dost faithfully whatsoever thou dost to the brethren and to strangers, which have borne witness of thy charity before the church, whom if thou bring forward on their journey after a godly sort, thou shalt do well."] Which last words Dr. Doddridge renders thus. "'Whom thou dost well in bringing forward in their journey, in a manner worthy of God,' ἀξίως τοῦ θεοῦ, proceeding from a principle of divine love, and correspondent to the relation in which you, and they, stand to him. "And in his notes [he] says," This may possibly be understood in a spiritual sense, for assisting them in their travels through this wilderness to the heavenly world. Or it may have a literal signification, and then one kind of charity and hospitality is put for the rest. But I rather prefer the former sense."Ibid., 393 and n. e.

-- 1201 --

Jude

Jude 1.] The apostle mentions their being "preserved in Christ" because the occasion of the epistle is the apostasy of some.

Jude 4. "Before of old ordained to this condemnation."] "Before ordained," προγεγραμμένοι, which Dr. Doddridge supposes to signify, before "registered to this condemnation,"Ibid., 405. which is probably what the Apostle truly means in this place, having respect to the instances or examples which he mentions in the three next verses, like them whose crimes and dreadful condemnation is registered, or put on sacred record, as examples of that which is God's common manner of dealing with such men through all ages. And thus these men were of old registered for condemnation, in the same sense that Enoch is said to prophesy of such as these (Jude 14), even in prophesying of the destruction of the wicked of the old world, in many respects like these, and whose destruction by the flood was a type of the perdition that is coming on these.

Jude 9.] See no. 104.Works, 15, 80.

Jude 10.] They were guilty of unnatural lusts, left that way of gratifying their animal appetites, which nature taught them, and which nature teaches even the brute beasts, for those that were unnatural and monstrous.

Jude 12. "Trees whose fruit withereth."] "It seems toMS: "to be me." me, that φθινοπωρινὰ is much more exactly rendered, 'whose early buddings are withered'; and in this version the appearance of tautology is avoided." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 411, n. b.

Jude 14-15.] See no. 188.Works, 15, 104–5. Inspired writers of the Old Testament, sometimes when speaking of things recorded in Scripture history many ages

-- 1202 --

after those histories were written, do mention particulars not recorded in those histories, as particularly Asaph mentions thunder and lightning that there was in the time when Israel passed through the Red Sea, as Psalms 77:15 and following verses. So David mentions a great shower of rain that there was when God appeared on Mt. Sinai (Psalms 68:8). So the prophet Habakkuk mentions thunder that arose at the conclusion of the twelve hours that the sun and moon stood still. See notes on Habakkuk 3:11.

And we must allow the same to the inspired writers of the New Testament.

This prophecy of Enoch is probably the rather mentioned as applicable to those heretics and apostates he speaks of, because they strenuously denied and contemptuously ridiculed the doctrine of Christ's second coming, and pretended that it was only a cunningly devised fable of his, as appears by what the apostle Peter says of them in his second epistle (See notes on 2 Peter 1:11–21.). Therefore this prophecy is suitably applied to them, that foretells that Christ would come to convince 'em of their hard speeches that they had spoken against him, for that was hard speaking against him, indeed, to say that he only lied in pretending he would come a second time, and his second coming would most directly tend to convince 'em to the contrary of this above all. See no. 357.This paragraph is a later addition, and the reference is even later. Works, 15, 342–43.

Jude 19. "These be they who separate themselves."] The Apostle uses this form of expression because he has reference to some spoken of in the Old Testament, that are spoken of as separating themselves, either Ezekiel 14:7, or Hosea 4:14, or Hosea 9:10.

-- 1203 --

Revelation

Revelation. Concerning the authority of this book, see no. 291 of "Notes on Scripture."Works, 15, 249–51.

THE BOOK OF REVELATION, ITS AUTHORITY. "Though the authority of this book was called in question in the beginning of the third century, yet… perhaps no part of the New Testament, though of unquestionable authenticity and credit, was more universally acknowledged or mentioned with higher respect, during the two preceding centuries.

"Its canonical authority being debated so late as the third century, when it had been universally admitted before, appears to have arisen from the opposition made to those absurd opinions, which it is well known were entertained by several Fathers, concerning the millennium. These being entirely grounded upon an injudicious and mistaken interpretation of some prophecies contained in this book, Caius,Caius, or Gaius, an early third-century orthodox Roman presbyter. with some others, to end the controversy as speedily and effectually as possible, weakly and indiscreetly ventured to deny the authority of the book." Doddridge, in his introduction to his exposition of this book.This and the preceding paragraph are a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 419–20.

Concerning the method of the visions and prophecies of this book, see at the latter end of notes on the Revelation 11.JE writes, "For the method of these visions is first, to give a more general representation of things, and then afterwards, a more distinct description of the particular changes and revolutions that are the subjects of them." See Works, 5, 106–7.

Concerning the canonicalness of the book of Revelation. 'Tis a great evidence that there was some book that the Christian Catholic church had in possession under the name of the Revelation, or the Apocalypse, that the Christian church received as of great value and authority, and esteemed sacred, that there were so many spurious pieces published under that name of the Apocalypse or Revelation. Nothing but the great repute of a certain book under that name could have many, so many, so fond of counterfeiting it, and publishing pieces under its name. Mr. Jones, in his Canon of the New Testament, Pt. 1, ch. 3, gives account of these

-- 1204 --

following, mentioned by the writers of the primitive church: by the writers of the second century, the Revelation of Peter, "the Revelation of Cerinthus, pretending to be apostolical"; in the writers of the fourth century, the Revelation of Paul, the Revelation of Thomas, the Revelation of Stephen.This paragraph is a separate entry. Jeremiah Jones, New and Full Method, I, 36–44.

See remarks on what Mr. Lowman says about synchronisms in this book. See "Revelation."This reference is a later addition. Works, 5, 251–52.

Revelation 1:4. "To the seven churches in Asia."] See "Revelation."Works, 5, 97.

"And from the seven spirits." See note on 1 Corinthians 14:32. See also "Revelation."This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 5, 97–98.

Revelation 1:8. "I am Alpha and Omega."] Here is reference to the words that are written in this book, mentioned before (Revelation 1:3), as much as to say, Of all the things that are written in this book, I am the very first and the very last letter, as Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. This emphatically and livelily signifies that God is the beginning, and end, and the sum total, of all the things that are written of in this book, even from the very first to the very last event, and also of all the whole series of events, and revolutions, and dispensations that are written of in the whole Bible, from the first beginning of the creation to the end of the world and consummation of all things. Therefore these words are repeated again when John had seen the end of the world (Revelation 21:6 and Revelation 22:13), in each of which places the writings of this book are spoken of (See Revelation 21:5 and Revelation 22:9–10.), as they are, Revelation 1:11 of this chapter.

Revelation 1:10. "On the Lord's day."] See note on Ezekiel 1:2.

Revelation 1:13. "And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle."] As the high priest of old, when ordering the lamps in the seven branches of the golden candlestick in the temple and in other sacred ministrations, was "clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about" with the curious girdle of the ephod.

-- 1205 --

Christ's appearing thus on the Christian sabbath is a representation of what he does spiritually in his church, or among the golden candlesticks, on the sabbath. How then especially he walks in the midst of the candlesticks, and holds the stars. And how then especially the sharp sword of his word goes out of his mouth. How then he appears as he that is risen from the dead, or "was dead, and is alive" [Revelation 2:8], etc.

Revelation 1:15. "And his feet were like unto fine brass."] To signify the strength of those pillars on which he stands, and the sureness and immovableness of his steps, and how impossible it is for any to overthrow him, or remove him from the place where he stands, or the way that he pleases to go.

"As if they burned in a furnace." Signifying several things. 1. His going through the furnace of his Father's wrath for sinners. 2. His treading down the wicked in the furnace of his Father's wrath, for he will tread them in his anger. 3. His going against his enemies as a consuming fire when they set themselves as briars and thorns against him in battle. He will go through them, and burn them together.

Revelation 1:18. "Have the keys of hell and of death."] "Have the keys of the unseen world and of death." "Mr. HoweJohn Howe (1630–1705), a Puritan divine and author whose works were published in two volumes (London, 1724). has largely proved that the interpretation I have here given is most reasonable.… According to Grotius, the word 'Hades' always denotes either death or the state after death. And they who are of opinion that Luke 16:23 is an exception, may consult this learned author's judicious notes on the place. Our English, or rather Saxon, word 'hell,' in its original signification, exactly answers to the Greek word 'Hades,' and denotes a concealed or unseen place." Doddridge, in loc.Family Expositor, 6, 438 and n. b.

Revelation 2:1. "The angel of the church."] See Prideaux, Connection, Pt. I, p. 553.Prideaux explains this title by reference to the officer in the Jewish synagogue responsible for offering public prayers on behalf of the congregation, the minister called in Hebrew, "the Angel of the Church" (Old and New Testament Connected, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, p. 553).

"Of Ephesus." "Revelation."Works, 5, 98.

Revelation 2:7. "Paradise of God."] Note on Luke 23:43.

-- 1206 --

Revelation 2:10. "Tribulation ten days."] "Mr. Fleming,Robert Fleming (1660?–1716), a Scottish Presbyterian divine and author of numerous publications dealing with the book of Revelation. with many others, thinks this refers to the persecution under Domitian, which continued about ten years, and was begun when John was banished into Patmos." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 445, n. a.

Revelation 2:14–15.] "Balaam has the same signification in Hebrewבִּלְעָם that Nicolaus has in Greek,Νικόλαος. and both signify conquerors of the people." Doddridge.Family Expositor, 6, 447, n. g.

Revelation 2:17. "A new name written."] See "Scripture," no. 399, the sixth and last paragraph in that number.Works, 15, 398–99.

This "alludes to the custom of princes, who give new names to those whom they have raised to very extraordinary dignity, of which we have many instances in the Old Testament, particularly Genesis 41:45, 2 Samuel 12:25, Daniel 1:7."This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 448, n. h.

"White stone, and new name written," etc. The "white stone" that Christ here promises to give is himself, as the morning star that he promises to give in the Revelation 2:29 is himself. It is himself in his spiritual presence, inhabitation, and divine influence, or himself imparted by his Spirit in the excellent and pleasant benefits of it. Christ is often in Scripture represented as a stone, and that not only as a stone for a foundation, but as a precious stone, a jewel to be laid up and kept in possession. The color white is frequently used in Scripture as the symbol of purity, freedom from guilt and pollution, and especially in this book. In this white pure stone, free of any spot, are the names of believers written or engraven, as their names are written in Christ's heart, are set as a seal on his heart, as the names of the children of Israel of old were graven on the breastplate of the high priest. Christ here promises to give this white stone to those that overcome, and to grant them the sensible possession of it, and to see their new names engraven in it. A new name is written in the stone, alluding to what is common and customary when one sends a present to another, to write their name upon it. And when a prince sends a subject a commission or a present, that is a token of his advancement to a higher station or any new dignity or

-- 1207 --

honor, he is wont to write upon it his new title, or to honor him in the inscription with his new name.

"Which no man knoweth, save he that receiveth it." This implies two things. 1. That no man understands what it implies, how much it carries in it, the excellency of the new state, relation, and dignity, and blessedness which it betokens. None understand this but those that have received that name. 2. None knows it but he that receives it. As to the evidence of it, none knows that he has it but him.This and the preceding paragraph are a separate entry.

"Hidden manna." See "Scripture," no. 262.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 15, 208–209.

"Which no man knoweth." "I have sometimes thought ὁ λαμβάνων might signify, 'one that hath received it,'" i.e. to no other than himself, excepting such as have received the same name that he has. "As it seems, a name given to any person must be known to others, or it would be given in vain.… Otherwise, it must refer to a custom which has sometimes prevailed among princes, of giving particular names, expressing familiarity and delight, to distinguished favorites, whether by discourse or by letter, and which have not been communicated to others, or used by them at other times." Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 448–49, n. i.

Revelation 2:24.] The former part of this verse Dr. Doddridge translates thus. "But I say to you, even to the rest in Thyatira, as many as do not hold this doctrine."Family Expositor, 6, 452. See, concerning "this doctrine," what follows.JE wrote this paragraph sometime after the following two paragraphs.

See notes on Acts 15:28–29. By "this doctrine" in this verse the Apostle evidently means the same with the "doctrine of Balaam," mentioned, Revelation 2:14, wherein he taught "to eat things sacrificed to idols, and to commit fornication," and the teaching of Jezebel, mentioned, Revelation 2:20, who taught the same things. "And which have not known the depths of Satan, as they speak." There were some of their idols that they used to worship with those rites, committing fornication in their temples and at those feasts, wherein they eat their sacrifices. These they called the mysteries, or depths, of the worship of such a god. The Apostle so far uses their language, or speaks as they "spake," that he calls conformity to these things, "knowing the depths." But herein he differs, that whereas they called it "knowing the depths of such a god," he calls it "the depths of Satan." In that expression, "I will put upon you none other burden," he seems to

-- 1208 --

have respect to the expression used at the Council of Jerusalem, when they exhorted to abstain from these two things, eating things sacrificed to idols, and fornication, and two more, things strangled and blood (Acts 15:28–29), it being thought necessary that these should be added, by reason of the then present circumstances of the church in its infant state, great part of the church being lately converted from Judaism, from which the Holy Ghost saw meet gradually to wean them, as a child has some bauble given to quiet it when weaned from the mother's breast, to eat stronger meat, not to put new wine into old bottles, agreeably to the maxims of the Apostle, in Romans 14:15. "But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died." 1 Corinthians 8:13, "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend." And also for the sake of the unbelieving Jews, who were not yet wholly cast off, that they might be the more easily gained by the continuance of these things of the ceremonial law, the contrary to which they had an especial rooted abhorrence and dread of. But now the circumstances of the church being much altered, Christianity being more fully revealed and established, and the Jews utterly rejected, and their city and nation overthrown, and the Jewish dispensation perfectly abolished, Christ reduces the number of these prohibited things. From four to two the burden diminished: and things strangled and blood, that were ceremonial, are left indifferent; and only things sacrificed to idols, and fornication, that were moral, are forbidden. And in the next verse, 'tis signified that these are forbidden not only for present necessity, to be abstained from for a season, but are unlawful forever to the end of the world. "But that which ye have already hold fast till I come" Revelation 2:25]. And that Christ here speaks directly only to the church of Thyatira is no objection against this, for so neither did the Council at Jerusalem, when they forbid those four things, speak directly only to the churches of Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia (Acts 15:22–23).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Dr. Doddridge here has this note: "Lord BarringtonJohn Shute Barrington (1678–1734), a lawyer and Christian apologist, published Miscellanea Sacra; or, a New Method of considering so much of the History of the Apostles as is contained in Scripture: in an Abstract of their History, an Abstract of that Abstract, and four Critical Essays (2 vols. London, 1725). imagines this refers to the gospel decree addressed to the Gentile proselytes, now abolished with the Jewish polity. As if it had been said, Though things strangled

-- 1209 --

and blood were formerly forbidden, as well as idolatry and fornication, yet I will not subject you to this injunction."This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 6, 452, n. d.

Revelation 2:26.] See Luke 12:44.

Revelation 2:27. "And he shall rule them with an iron rod."] See Isaiah 41:15–16 with note.

Revelation 3.] See Psalms 149:5–9.

Revelation 3:4. "In white."] It is well known that white robes were worn on occasions of great joy, and sometimes in triumphant processions, to both which here is probably a reference, as indeed it seems that triumph and feasting would naturally go together. Priests also were clothed in white, and the addition of that dignity may also be implied. (Compare Revelation 1:6.) Some think here is an allusion to the custom of the Sanhedrin. When they examined the candidates for the high priesthood, if they judged him worthy, they gave a white garment. "For they are worthy." See next.

"For they are worthy." I.e. they are fit or meet, in the same sense as it is used, Matthew 10:37 ff., "He that loveth father and mother more than [me] is not worthy of me," etc. They ben't fit for the kingdom of God, as it is said of him that puts "his hand to the plow," and looks back [Luke 9:62], and in the same sense as it is used, Luke 3:8, "Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance." And Luke 20:35, "They which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world." And Colossians 1:12, "Who hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light." See "Miscellanies," nos. 627, and 671, and 688.This paragraph is a separate entry. Works, 18, 155–56, 223–29, 250–51.

"Thou hast a few names in Sardis that have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy." Their keeping their garments pure was thought worthy of a peculiar reward, for their being singular in it, for their keeping themselves pure in a time of general corruption, and withstanding the temptations of general example. We have many instances of peculiar rewards for being singular in piety in times of general corruption, as in Enoch, Noah, Lot, Caleb, Joshua, Elijah, and Daniel.This paragraph is a separate entry.

-- 1210 --

"For they are worthy." The inherent graces and good works of the saints, viewing them in Christ, are acceptable, and amiable, and of great price in the sight of God. But if they are amiable and precious in his eyes, doubtless they are worthy of a reward in his eyes. If they are looked upon by him as worthy of his regard and love, they are therein looked upon as worthy of the testimonies and proper fruits of his regard and love.This paragraph is a separate entry.

See note on 2 Thessalonians 1:11.This sentence is a later addition.

Revelation 3:5. "I will not blot out," etc.] This expression seems to be taken from Psalms 69:28, "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous," which serves to explain the words, and show that by "the book of life" here is meant the roll of those that have been admitted by Christ as head of the visible church amongst his people as righteous men, and not the book of his secret decrees of election.

See "Miscellanies," no. 689, especially §§4 and 9.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 18, 253–54, 257.

Revelation 3:10. "I will also keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth."] "This 'hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world,' seems to relate to the persecution under Trajan, which was greater and more extensive than the preceding persecutions, either under Nero, or Domitian." See Lowman's Paraphrase on the Revelation, p. 23.Paraphrase and Notes on the Revelation, 23, n. e. For a discussion of JE's extensive use of Lowman's commentary, see Works, 5, 55–59.

"Dr. SmithProbably Samuel Smith, D.D., who was the author of The Family Companion: or, Annotations upon the Holy Bible. Being a New and Compleat History of the Old and New Testaments (London, 1735) and The Christian's Guide; on, the Holy Bible: by way of question and answer. Being an exposition of the Old and New Testament… Adorned with maps, cuts, &c. (London, 1738). has observed, in his learned and accurate account of these parts, that the city of Philadelphia was the last of all the seven, here spoken of, which fell into the hands of the Turks; for whereas the rest were subdued by Urchan and Amurath, Philadelphia held out till the time of Bajazet."All three of these figures—Urchan, Amurath, and Bajazet—were sultans in the Ottoman Empire. Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 458–59, n.

Revelation 3:12. "Will I make a pillar."] See note on Ezekiel 40:16.This reference is a later addition. "'And he shall go no more out,' as the priests of the tribe of Levi, in their courses, went out

-- 1211 --

of the temple" at Jerusalem. Boston's Fourfold State.Human Nature in its Fourfold State (4th ed.), 394. Each of the following two sentences are later additions to this reference. See Isaiah 22:23, and note on Ecclesiastes 12:11. See Ezra 9:8.

"Will I make a pillar in the temple of my God;… and I will write upon him the name of my God," etc. This "is an allusion to inscriptions usual on pillars, which sometimes expressed the privileges granted to cities, sometimes the names of benefactors, in memory of privileges granted." Lowman's Paraphrase on Revelation, p. 23.Note f. This paragraph is a separate entry.

"Inscriptions are yet remaining, brought from the Grecian cities of Europe and Asia, and some from islands in the neighborhood of Patmos, in which the victories of eminent persons are commemorated. And as some of these were placed near the temples of their deities, others were in those temples, to signify their being put under the particular protection of those deities, whose names were therefore inscribed upon them, and the names of the conquerors, and of the cities to which they belonged, as also the names of the generals, by whose conduct the victory was gained." Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. Family Expositor, 6, 460, n. d.

Revelation 4:3. "And he that sat was to look upon like unto a jasper and a sardine stone."] See note on Revelation 21:11.

"Like unto an emerald." "Scripture," no. 270.Works, 15, 224–25. See "Revelation."This paragraph is a separate entry. This reference is a later addition. Works, 5, 99.

Revelation 4:4. "And round about the throne were four and twenty seats, and upon the seats I saw four and twenty elders sitting."] Here seems to be an allusion to that, Isaiah 24:23, "when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, before his ancients gloriously." Here John has a vision of appearing in great majesty and glory in heaven, and the elders of Christ's church in heaven in his presence round about his throne. So of old, when God appeared in Mount Sinai, the type of heaven, the elders of the congregation or church of Israel alone were admitted up into the mount to stand before him, and to see the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9–11).

"White raiment… and crowns of gold." "White raiment," to signify that they were priests, and "crowns of gold," to signify that they were

-- 1212 --

kings. "They are called 'elders,' as the presidency of elders was common among the Jews." Doddridge.This paragraph is a later addition. Family Expositor, 6, 467, n. c.

"Four and twenty elders." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 99–100.

Revelation 4:6. "Sea of glass like unto crystal."] The glass or crystal is the matter of the vessel that was the container, and not the matter contained, as the sea in Solomon's temple was called the "brazen sea," or sea of brass [1 Chronicles 18:8]. The laver in the tabernacle was made of the looking glasses of the women, that were of polished brass [Exodus 38:8], wherein those that came to wash themselves might see their dirt and pollution; but this was made of most clear and pure glass, in which men might see themselves much more clearly.

"Sea of glass." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 100.

"Four beasts." "Miscellanies," ww.This reference is a separate entry. Works, 13, 191–95.

Concerning the "four beasts." The divine attributes are sometimes represented by creatures in this book, as the angel, Revelation 14:15, that called to Christ, and bid him thrust in his sickle. This can't mean a created angel thus to speak by way of command to Christ, for they are all his ministering spirits; but it must signify some divine attribute.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Some things that are here represented by animals are in Ezekiel represented by cherubims, which word often signifies angels. But that is no argument that these animals or cherubims are any more than merely visionary persons represented as ministers of such particular divine attributes, each distinct kind of animal a symbolical person that is agent for a certain divine attribute, to whom is committed the care, management, and prosecution of the designs and execution of the effects of such an attribute. Like the angel in the latter part of Revelation 14, that has "power over fire" Revelation 14:18], that is only a visionary allegorical person that is represented as the agent, minister, and executioner of divine wrath and vengeance, such a person perhaps was the destroying angel that appeared to David (2 Samuel 24:16).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 4:7.] That by the "calf" or ox is meant goodness and mercy, is confirmed by Proverbs 14:4. "Where no oxen are, the crib is clean; but much increase is by the labor of the ox."

-- 1213 --

Revelation 4:8. "Holy, holy, holy."] I believe that this threefold repetition, and that in Isaiah 6:3, is because of the three persons in the Trinity,JE deleted "or three holies." and not only as an expression of God's superlative holiness, as the threefold repetition of the word "woe" [Revelation 8:13] signifies not so much exceeding great woe, but three distinct woes, and the threefold repeating of the word "overturn" [Ezekiel 21:27] signifies three distinct overturnings of the crown or supreme authority in Israel, first to the Persian monarchs, secondly to the Grecian, and thirdly to the Roman.

Revelation 4:11. "For thy pleasure they are and were created."] I.e. God created the world not from any necessity, but because it pleased him; and he created it as it pleased him, and created things for his own ends, and to serve such purposes as he saw meet, such as it was his pleasure to propose. The word in the original is διὰ τὸ θέλημά σου εἰσὶν καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν, "by thy will," or "for thy will they are and were created."

Revelation 5:6. "And I beheld, and lo, in the midst of the throne."] "Revelation."Works, 5, 100–101.

Revelation 3:8.] "Harps were a principal part of the temple music. Vials also were of common use in the temple service; they were the same with the censers of gold, in which the priests offered incense in the temple. These censers were a sort of cups, which, because of the heat of the fire burning the incense, were often put upon a plate or saucer. To offer incense to God, or before his presence, in the temple, was an act of honor and religious worship, peculiar to the priests' office; and the prayers of the church are often compared to it. Thus the Psalmist, 'Let my prayer come before thee as incense' (Psalms 141:2). So that these expressions will represent the whole heavenly church of angels and saints, offering a very high act of religious worship and adoration to Christ." Lowman's Paraphrase and Notes on the Revelation, p. 36.Note f. And particularly it may be hence noted that Christ is properly the object of the prayers and supplications as well as the praises of his church.

Revelation 3:11.] "Miscellanies," no. 1246.Works, 23, 181–82. In no. 1246 JE argues that in heaven the saints are higher in privilege than the angels.

-- 1214 --

Revelation 5:12. "Saying with a loud voice," etc.] It appears by this verse that Christ's dying or being slain not only satisfied for sins, but also merited as a righteousness, for he was worthy upon the account of his being "slain to receive power and riches," etc. And if it merited for himself, it merited for the elect, for he merited as a public person.

Revelation 6.] Concerning these seals, see "Extracts from Lowman," "Revelation," no. 94.Works, 5, 219–50.

Revelation 6:9. "I saw under the altar the souls," etc.] That is, they stood by the altar to offer up their prayers, which were offered up upon the altar with much incense by Christ, the high priest, as Revelation 8:3. Here the custom of the children of Israel is alluded to. They that brought the sacrifice, and for whom it was offered, stood by the altar or under the altar (for the altar was a great high thing, and the priest went up to it by an ascent) while their sacrifice was offering upon the altar. So the souls of the martyrs are represented as here offering their prayers at the altar.

Revelation 6:12–17.] As we often find in the Old Testament that the destruction of Jerusalem and the state of Israel is represented as the dissolution of the world, so we find the same concerning the destruction of the state of the chief enemies of Israel, especially Edom and Babylon, Nineveh and Egypt (Isaiah 34:1–10, Isaiah 13:9–11, Ezekiel 32:7–8). And God is represented as coming down from heaven, as here Christ is represented as coming (Isaiah 26:21).

See concerning Nineveh, Nahum 1:4–6.

Revelation 6:14. "And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together."] Here there is at least respect had to what shall be at the end of the world, and that is the event alluded to, though not most immediately intended in this vision. Here we may understand thus much as implied in this representation, viz. that when God made the world, it stood forth as a piece of parchment or paper for him by providence to write what he pleased on. And at the end of the world, God shall have done writing. He shall have finished his tract, and have written all that in providence in the scroll of the heavens by their successive revolutions, by which they have measured out the successive days, and years, and ages of the world, that before was written in the book of his decrees that was to be accomplished

-- 1215 --

in this world. And therefore, having finished the writing, he rolls the scroll together, as a scrivener is wont to do when he has writ out the scroll. In this writing God is Alpha and Omega, the first and last letter in the alphabet.

Revelation 7:3. "Till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads."] "Revelation."Ibid., 101.

Revelation 7:4. "An hundred and forty and four thousand."] "Revelation."Ibid., 102.

Revelation 7:8.] Why the tribe of Joseph is mentioned instead of the tribe of Ephraim, see note on Psalms 80:1.

Revelation 7:9. "A great multitude which no man could number."] "Revelation."Ibid.

Revelation 7:11. "Round about the throne."] "Miscellanies," no. 1246.Ibid., 2, 181–82.

Revelation 7:14. "Washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."] "Revelation."Ibid., 2, 102.

Revelation 7:16. "Neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat."] The work which God has appointed the saints in this world is oftentimes attended with great labor and heaviness. They are forced to labor as it were in the wearisome heat of the sun, and under his scorching beams. But now they shall be perfectly delivered from whatsoever should make their work toilsome and wearisome.JE marked this entry with a large "X."

Revelation 7:16–17.] It alludes to a shepherd that leads and feeds his flock, as in those text[s] in the Old Testament that are here referred to, viz. Isaiah 49:9–10. See Psalms 121:6–7 and Isaiah 4:5.

Revelation 7:17. "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."] As a tender parent, when comforting a child, takes it in his arms, and wipes away its tears from its eyes.

-- 1216 --

Revelation 8:1.] See "Extracts from Lowman," "Revelation," no. 94.Works, 5, 219–50. See the Revelation 8:3 following.

"And when he had opened the seventh seal." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 102.

Revelation 8:5. "And there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake."] "Revelation."Works, 5, 102.

Revelation 8:7.] Concerning the seven TRUMPETS, see "Extracts from Lowman," no. 94, beginning at Revelation 8:7.Ibid., 224–31.

"The first angel sounded." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 102.

Revelation 8:8. "And the third part of the sea became blood."] "Revelation."Works, 5, 102–3.

Revelation 8:10. "The rivers, and upon the fountains of waters."] "Revelation," no. 80.Ibid., 191. See "Revelation."Ibid., 103.

Revelation 8:12. "And the fourth angel sounded."] "Revelation."Ibid.

Revelation 8:13.] See remarks on what Mr. Lowman says of these three woes. See "Revelation," "Remarks on Lowman."Ibid., 251–52.

Revelation 9.] See remarks on Mr. Lowman's exposition of this chapter, "Revelation," "Remarks on Lowman."Ibid.

Revelation 9:1. "A star fall from heaven."] "Revelation."Ibid., 103.

Revelation 9:3. "Locusts upon the earth."] "Revelation."Ibid.

-- 1217 --

Revelation 9:4. "But only those men which have not the seal of God in their foreheads."] "Revelation."Ibid.

Revelation 9:5. "And to them it was given that they should not fill them."] "Revelation."Ibid., 103–4.

"Tormented five months." "Extracts from Lowman," on the "Fifth Trumpet."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 229.

Revelation 9:6. "And in those days shall men seek death, and shall not find it."] "Revelation."Works, 5, 104.

Revelation 9:15. "For an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year."] "Revelation," no. 71.Ibid., 165.

Revelation 10:1.] Most fitly doth Christ here appear with a rainbow about his head, which was given of old as a token and seal of the covenant God made with Noah and all flesh, that the flood should no more pass over the earth. For now Christ appears to promise and swear to his church, Revelation 10:6–7, that there should be that end to the time of her troubles, which is in Scripture compared to the waters of Noah on this very account, because God thus sware that there should be an utter end to them, and that they should return no more. Isaiah 54:9, "For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee."

Revelation 10:1–2.] The angel's being "clothed with a cloud," and setting "his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the earth," signifies his having power to accomplish what he sware (Revelation 10:6–7). It represents his having all power over heaven, and the earth, and sea, that is, the whole universe, and so having power to bring that great event about which he sware at the time appointed. His being "clothed with a cloud" represents his having all power in heaven as his habitation, and as it were the house that he puts on; and his setting his feet on the earth and sea represents his having all

-- 1218 --

power over this lower world, it being his footstool. He had power over heaven, earth, and sea, as he was the heir of his Father who made [them], as he observes in his oath (Revelation 10:6). God's power over heaven and earth, and his creating them, is here made use of to encourage the church that was ready to faint through the length of the time of her troubles, as it is, Isaiah 40:26–28 ff.

Revelation 10:2. "And he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left foot on the earth."] "Revelation."Ibid., 104.

Revelation 10:3–4.] What these "seven thunders" uttered was concerning the precise time when there should be an end to the long-continued time of the church's troubles, concerning which the angel swears in the next verse, for that oath has reference to something that had been uttered before as fixing the period. He swore that the time should be no longer. No longer than what? Why, no longer than that precise time that had before been uttered by the loud voice of the angel and the seven thunders that accompanied it, which seven thunders seems to be the voice of the seventh trumpet, spoken of, Revelation 10:7, as it were explained in seven parts. The angel came down from heaven on this errand to limit the time of the church's troubles, and therefore he came with a rainbow about his head. See note on Revelation 10:1. And therefore what St. John is required to seal up is the same that Daniel was required to shut up and seal (Daniel 12:4, Daniel 12:9). It is that appointed time spoken of, Hebrews 2:3.

Corol. Hence 'tis in vain to expect that the precise time of Antichrist's fall should be known till it be accomplished.

"And cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roareth. And when he had cried, seven thunders uttered their voices.… Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered," etc. A clear full declaration of the marvelous expressions and manifestations of the all-sufficiency and glory of God in his mysterious and wonderful works, especially in his dispensations towards the moral world, is represented by a great thunder. See note on Job 26:14, with the note on the preceding verse.This paragraph is a later separate entry.

"And cried with a loud voice, when a lion roareth." Christ is now come to declare that the time of the church's troubles shall be no longer, and to reveal the time of the church's deliverances from her enemies that she had been oppressed by for so long a time. Now therefore he utters his voice, as "when a lion roareth," agreeable to ancient prophecies concerning

-- 1219 --

God's appearance for his church when that time should come. Isaiah 42:13–15, "The Lord shall go forth like a mighty man; he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war. He shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself. Now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once. I will make waste mountains and hill, and dry up the pools. And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not," etc. Isaiah 31:4, "For thus hath the Lord spoken unto me, Like as a lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them. So shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof." Hosea 11:9–11, "I will not return to destroy Ephraim.… They shall walk after the Lord. He shall roar like a lion; when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble from the west." Joel 3:16–17, "The Lord also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake. But the Lord will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel. So shall ye know that I am the Lord your God dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain. Then shall Jerusalem be holy, and there shall no strangers pass through her any more."This paragraph is a later addition.

Revelation 10:6. "That there should be time no longer."] It is not meant that there shall be the end of time, according to the modern use of that phrase, viz. that the world shall be at an end, for the Scripture is a stranger to such an use of the word "time," in contradistinction to eternity, orThe last five words are a later interlineation. to signify the duration of the present state of things after the resurrection. But the time here meant is the time before the church's deliverance, the continuance of those many troubles and overturnings that are to precede the time of the church's rest and glory here on earth, and the fulfilling of those glorious things so often spoken of in the word of God. And this is what is meant by the "mystery of God," its being "finished, as he hath declared to his servants the prophets" Revelation 10:7]. The accomplishment of these things are the great objects of the church's hope and expectations, and what they continue long wishing and waiting for. And here the angel, for their comfort, swears that it shall no longer be delayed. The words might be rendered, diuturnitaten non fore amplius.I.e. "The length of time is about to be no longer." What the angel swears

-- 1220 --

here is the same thing that the angel swears, Daniel 12:7–8. And if we compare the oath there sworn to this, and the circumstances there mentioned, it will appear evidently to be the same, and that here an eye is had to that. And I believe in what is said here in the Revelation 10:7, "as he hath declared to his servants the prophets," respect is had to the prophet Daniel, and what is said there in the Daniel 12 of his prophecy. Respect is here had to the same thing that the church earnestly inquires about in the Daniel 6:9–11. "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held. And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? And white robes were given to every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellow servants," etc. This season is that which the angel here swears shall be no longer. The word is the same, χρόνος. The angel here in his oath has respect to the same thing, and speaks for the comfort of these souls under the altar. That oath of the angel in Daniel was in answer to the like question, as in the preceding verse. "And one said unto the man clothed in linen, which was upon the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? And I heard the man clothed in linen, which was upon the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven, and sware by him that liveth forever and ever, that it shall be for a time, times, and an half; and when he shall have accomplished to scatter the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished."

The angel's swearing then that the time should be no longer seems to intimate that the time will be long expected as well as earnestly desired before it comes, as seems also to be intimated by the forementioned interrogation in Daniel 6, and Daniel 6:11–12, and as this event proves to be. For how long has the fall of Antichrist already been expected? This is that "appointed time" spoken of, Habakkuk 2:3. See notes on that place.

See remarks on Mr. Lowman's interpretation of this oath, "Revelation," "Remarks on Lowman," second last paragraph.This sentence is a later addition. Works, 5, 252.

"That liveth forever and ever." When the angel swears "that the time should be no longer," he properly swears by him who endures, and lives, and reigns forever through all time, to and beyond the end of time, to order all that comes to pass in time, and to fix the seasons. He whose duration is eternal and unlimited alone fixes the limits of time. The eternity

-- 1221 --

of God, as well as his creating and governing all things, are properly here made use to comfort the church concerning the period of her troubles, here as they are in Isaiah 40:26–28. See the note on Revelation 10:1–2.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"That there should be time no longer." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. Works, 5, 104.

Revelation 10:7. "The mystery of God should be finished."] "Revelation," no. 76.Works, 5, 172–73.

Revelation 11:1. "Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship therein."] This signifies that God [will] preserve and uphold his church, and will not suffer any of his elect people to perish in this time of general overthrow. Particular limits and bounds shall be set which God will maintain. So much shall be measured out for God that he will keep in the time of this great apostasy. The enemies of God and his people, though they so greatly prevail as though they would tread all things under their feet, yet they shall not be able to bring their devastations within these limits, into that part that God hath measured out for himself. At those measured bounds God will say to the overflowing destruction, Hitherto shalt thou come, and no further. Christ will have his church in the exact and determinate number. He'll have the exact portion that God hath given him in the worst of times. It signifies much the same thing as sealing the servants of God "in their foreheads," in Revelation 7:3 and Revelation 9:4.

Revelation 11:3.] Concerning the beginning of the 1260 days, see extracts from Bower's History of the Popes, pp. 9–10.The extracts are in JE's notebook, identified as "Notebook C" relating to the History of the Work of Redemption project, which contains his reading notes derived from Archibald Bower, History of the Popes. Bower (1686–1766) was at times in and out of the Catholic Church and the Society of Jesus. For more on him, see Works, 5, 68–69. On "Notebook C," see Works, 9, 545, 547. On pp. 9–10, JE writes, "Bower's History seems much to confirm that with the pontificate of Boniface the III, which began Feb. 19, 607, began the reign of Antichrist. That this was the true epoch of the 1260 days." According to Bower, Boniface was responsible for advancing the power and authority of the Pope which had been declining for some time. For example, he obtained by decree the title of "Universal Bishop" and was declared "Head of the whole Catholic Church," thus introducing the notion of "papal supremacy," a process JE records from Bower as "antichristian, heretical, blasphemous, diabolical."

"Two witnesses." A small number in this time of general apostasy and persecution, and yet a sufficient number; for in the mouth of two witnesses were things to be established. Therefore were the apostles sent

-- 1222 --

forth two and two, to testify that the kingdom of heaven was at hand [Mark 6:7].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 11:5. "Fire proceedeth out of their mouth."] "Revelation."Works, 5, 104–5.
